#2. How a fashion creator turned audience demand into a 500+ client styling business

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit

This article is part of an ongoing series examining successful creator business strategies. More from the series →

Maddy Gustini built a following by telling men what to wear. Now she’s turning that audience into a styling business — and a stake in a fashion app.

Gustini started creating content in 2023, not long after graduating with a degree in fashion merchandising and joining Neiman Marcus’ buying team. She focused on a gap she saw in the market: practical fashion advice for men. Within a year, she had more than 100,000 Instagram followers. Today she has nearly 300,000.

As followers began asking her for personal fashion advice, Gustini saw an opportunity to turn that demand into a new revenue stream: personal styling. At the time, she was (and still is) making $5,000 to $10,000 a month from brand deals.

“When you think of a stylist, you think of a celebrity stylist. You think red carpet styling. You think something that doesn’t apply or is really feasible for the masses. I wanted to take that and make it into something that would apply to the everyday man,” Gustini said.

Aside from her public styling videos, which she fills with affiliate links, she started Maddy G Style, a personal styling service that charges upwards of $250 an hour for shopping help, $55 an outfit for a style deck or $800 for a full closet redo. “They fill out a form with what they’re looking for, with their budget, all the necessary questions, and I put together outfits for them — whether that’s outfits for a trip or doing a full closet overhaul,” she said.

Gustini wouldn’t provide details on her earnings through her personal styling service, but she has more than 500 style deck and closet redo clients and over 100 regular styling clients. Still, she said around 60% of her revenue comes from brand deals, 20% from Maddy G Style, and 20% from affiliate links.

“You don’t want your income to be completely reliant on if your video gets 100,000 views or not, so you want to direct your audience elsewhere… I can either buy something directly from her or I can work with her directly,” she explained. “Everything comes from my content, and that’s the only way I advertise my styling business.”

Gustini makes content featuring menswear brands she has affiliate deals with and also includes those brands in her personal styling guides, so there are two chances for viewers to snag products for which she gets a cut of sales, on top of the initial revenue she gets from anyone who signs up for her personal styling services.

“People really look to me for advice, and they’re coming to me directly to shop, which I think differentiates my content from a lifestyle influencer that makes videos about their life,” she said.

Her fashion expertise makes brand deals feel like a natural extension of her content: She can recommend products she’d suggest anyway. But that makes choosing partners carefully essential. “If I were to recommend a product, brand, or piece of clothing that doesn’t align with my taste…that is so harmful to my content and my audience,” Gustini said.

Gustini has secured brand deals with J. Crew, Calvin Klein, Todd Snyder, Bespoke Post, Steve Madden, and Aldo.

Still, Gustini wanted to diversify beyond brand deals, the whims of the algorithm and her styling business. So she made an early bet on a startup. That’s where Emily Ward, co-founder of CEO of Shine Management and Love X Money Ventures, came into the picture, vetting creators like Gustini to join Driptail, a social fashion app that helps users find clothes based on their body type, as strategic equity investors.

Gustini was invited by Shine Management, which represents her, into Driptail’s equity investment test pool, where she offered app feedback and advice. Shortly after, she was invited to come on as an equity partner. “Working with a brand in an equity partnership, I think it’s really important that you align with that company and what they represent, and again, Driptail solved those two issues for me, so I was in right away,” Gustini said.

“[She] had such phenomenal insight that the founder [Mark Weinberg] benefited from so much…[the creators] really did shift and shape where Mark was taking the app,” Ward said.

According to Gustini’s representation, she’s driven the most users to the app, alongside creator Alicia McCarvell, who has 1.6 million Instagram followers. When Driptail first launched in March, it had around 100 users. By July, after the equity creators started promoting it, it had nearly 6,000. One post of Gustini’s drove 1,000 new users to Driptail and over 100 purchases in the three days after she posted it.

“You don’t have a paycheck coming every two weeks, you’re really working for everything you make…being able to have income streams long-term with something you’re consistently building is huge,” she said.

#3. Publicis agrees to preserve LiveRamp’s neutrality. Will it matter?

Let Marketing Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

A proposed FTC consent order mandates nondiscriminatory access to the platform and puts firewalls in place, but some Publicis competitors are already pulling back.

Publicis Groupe’s $2.2 billion acquisition of LiveRamp is moving forward after the ad-holding group reached an agreement with the Federal Trade Commission on terms that seek to preserve LiveRamp’s neutrality and accessibility to the broader digital advertising industry, according to a press release. Publicis clearing the regulatory hurdle puts the ad-tech deal on track to close by the end of this year.

Under the FTC’s consent order, Publicis and LiveRamp for five years must provide nondiscriminatory access and support to LiveRamp’s products and services and not deny, degrade or impair customers’ access to those offerings. Firewalls must be put in place to ensure that Publicis cannot access or use LiveRamp customer data and confidential business information. In addition, an independent auditor will review compliance on these measures every six months for the first two years after the LiveRamp transaction closes, and then conduct an audit once a year for the following three years.

Publicis in the release said the order was based on commitments it proactively proposed and underscored that LiveRamp will maintain an “open ecosystem connected to third-party agencies and platforms.” The FTC’s order also requires Publicis to not retaliate against LiveRamp customers who raise compliance concerns with the consumer protection agency. Customers can request an audit of Publicis’ compliance on data protection, privacy and security obligations pertaining to the requesting customer. The proposed consent agreement is open to public comment for 30 days from Oct. 19.

“By requiring LiveRamp to continue operating as it does today as a neutral platform, this order will ensure that Publicis does not gain an unfair advantage over its competitors in the digital advertising marketplace,” said David Shaw, principal deputy director of the FTC’s Bureau of Competition, in a statement.

The FTC and Publicis agreeing on specific guardrails may not matter much to some pockets of the industry, especially Publicis’ direct competitors. WPP has indicated it is winding down its agencies’ use of LiveRamp due to the deal. Omnicom, which was already planning to drop LiveRamp, moved up the timeline for that happening because of the acquisition.

Marketers more broadly have expressed some reservations about the acquisition since it was announced in May, as LiveRamp has long been valued as a sort of Switzerland for a fragmented, opaque digital advertising landscape. The platform is used by scores of publishers, technology providers, agencies and brands, which pour their data sets into LiveRamp’s systems. LiveRamp then acts as a connective tissue between disparate data sets to help marketers better target, activate and measure campaigns while preserving privacy through clean room technology.

Publicis sees the deal as a way to enhance the artificial intelligence agents it develops for clients and to bolster growth. The group expects to raise its 2027 and 2028 outlook to 7% to 8% net revenue growth, up from 6% to 7% net revenue growth, with the addition of LiveRamp, which will be integrated into the technology segment of the network that also includes the Sapient consultancy.

#4. “Convenings” for CEOs will help Semafor reach a second profitable year

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Semafor expects to have its second profitable year, thanks to a growing events, er, convening business, cofounders Justin Smith and Ben Smith announced.

The news company, which launched four years ago, had its first profitable year last year on $40 million in revenue. In a note published Sunday, Smith and Smith said they expect to close the year “substantially bigger” in “revenue and profitability and reach.”

RELATED ARTICLEThe media startup Semafor launches with a “more honest” article format and lots of global ambitionSarah ScireOctober 18, 2022About half of the company’s revenue comes from live events, which Semafor refers to as “convenings.” A two-day convening in November, for example, will cover “Silicon Valley & The World.” The co-chairs include names like OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, and Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella.

In their note, the cofounders wrote that “Semafor is starting to emerge clearly as the thing that we hoped it would become.”

RELATED ARTICLESemafor aims to be the source for “intelligent news consumers” who are “unhappy” and “screaming from the rooftops”Sarah ScireSeptember 7, 2022“We launched with the insight that a leadership audience — CEOs and political leaders alike — was, paradoxically, the most desperate for efficient, fair, and sophisticated news,” they continued.

It’s a stretch to say CEOs and political leaders are “desperate” for news. Existing news consumers tend to be older, wealthier, more white collar, and more politically engaged than those who don’t consume news. The genuinely underserved news audiences are elsewhere. Journalism for “decision makers” is one of the most crowded markets in news. Outlets like Bloomberg, Politico Pro, Financial Times, Punchbowl News, Axios Pro, and The Information operate in a similar space.

But readers aren’t the primary financial supporters of Semafor’s business. That’d be the corporate sponsors paying for access to its audience through ads and events. Although the annual update says the company has 1.2 million subscriptions, those remain free subscriptions for now.

By building a profitable and growing news business, Semafor has done something exceedingly rare. (It now has journalists on the ground in 11 countries and plans to launch in Asia in 2027.) Editor-in-chief Ben Smith explained some of his thinking on an episode of Decoder this summer.

In my memory, we always thought at some point we’d do subscriptions, but in my experience you just cannot be ideological about revenue. It’s hard enough to build a business in news without getting all hung up on the values of the different revenue streams.

Advertising-based publishers will tell you that democracy can only survive in a world where there aren’t paywalls. Subscription publishers will tell you that advertising is corrupting. At some point you realize everyone’s just talking about their book and that sometimes they’re already in a tough business and they’re talking themselves out of incremental opportunities and really successful media companies.

It’s “impossible” for publishers to compete with Google and Meta in the scaled advertising business, Smith told Decoder. He described Semafor as “an anti-scale business.”

If you’re reaching people in a very focused way in various particular environments — in person, in email, in video — that’s a case you can really credibly make to advertisers. We’ve built a big advertising and related convening business that way, and that’s one answer. It’s not the only answer, but it is one.

#5. ChatGPT Search Can Draw On More Pages After A Cloudflare Pilot via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

Cloudflare says its network signals helped OpenAI index hundreds of millions of new pages for ChatGPT search.

Cloudflare and OpenAI say a research pilot has helped OpenAI discover and index hundreds of millions of new web pages. The pilot used a participating cohort of about 1% of Cloudflare’s total network.

The companies shared those early results on Oct. 15 in a post on Cloudflare’s blog coauthored by two OpenAI staff. Cloudflare announced the pilot on July 8.

The post says finding new pages can initially increase crawling, and it doesn’t report how often the new pages were cited in ChatGPT or how many visits they sent.

Cloudflare’s network signals are used by OpenAI to help its search crawler find web pages with value. The blog post gives several examples of these pages, such as the user guide of a particular washing machine, the most recent information regarding passport requirements and fees and a restaurant’s menu and hours. It states that these pages “can be valuable even if few other sites link to them.”

The July 8 announcement stated some of the new signals that will be utilized, including how recently a page has been updated, the quality of traffic to a website and what updates have actually been made to a page. Additionally, the announcement states that this information comes from participating websites. However, neither announcement explains who participated, nor whether the new pages are on their sites.

The Oct. 15 post states that Cloudflare’s signals will also assist in helping OpenAI’s crawlers avoid unnecessary requests. Bots make repeated attempts to obtain files that are not available on the server, some websites redirect nearly any address to their homepages, and other addresses lead to copies of the same content. Change signals indicate to the crawler whether a particular webpage should be visited again versus if there would be no value from doing so.

The companies are also testing signals that flag potentially harmful pages. Their example is a fake login form an attacker planted on one page of a legitimate site, where the goal is to flag that page rather than the whole domain. Early results suggest the signals can help identify pages to keep out of an index, the post says.

The post says the goal is to reduce unnecessary load for Cloudflare customers, though it doesn’t provide figures for crawl volume or server load. It also says, “Finding new pages can initially increase crawling as those pages are evaluated and indexed.”

The October 15th blog post includes the statement “A signal about a page doesn’t grant permission to access it.” The blog also states that the researchers are using metadata from the web to improve search and discovery capabilities of their search engines versus sharing page content for model training.

The document describing how OpenAI’s crawler works divides search and training into two separate robots.txt directives. So if a website blocks OAI-SearchBot (the robot searching for information) then the website will not be included in ChatGPT’s search engine results; however, the blocked websites may still appear as navigational links. If a website allows the crawling by both bots (GPTBot (the bot collecting content that may be used for training), and OAI-SearchBot) then OpenAI may utilize the data collected during one crawl for both purposes.

The Oct. 15 post directs the reader to Cloudflare’s AI Crawl Control which is currently available on every plan. This service shows which AI services are accessing your website and offers you an option to Allow or Block each crawler.

ChatGPT will have another source from which to pull information once a page is in OpenAI’s index. The companies state that OpenAI independently evaluates and ranks the pages it indexes, so there is no guarantee of getting cited when your pages are found through their pilot.

Allowing OAI-SearchBot while blocking GPTBot means that your site remains accessible via the search results for ChatGPT but indicates that your crawled content should not be used for training purposes. OpenAI has provided this same configuration as an example on their crawler page.

Tracking ChatGPT visits depends on a UTM tag or a referrer, and some ChatGPT links lacked both earlier this month, as I reported Oct. 15. One analyst said a fix began rolling out that day.

Cloudflare and OpenAI say that the next stage of development for this project includes improving how a web page is selected by an AI, testing more rapid and reliable indicators for changes to content, and measuring the results when the AI has found new content.

According to Cloudflare, they are currently working with OpenAI to determine how improved content discovery could translate into business outcomes.

Additionally, according to a July 1 blog post from Cloudflare announcing their research on network signals and AI search, Cloudflare intends to provide broad access to that capability at some point during the remainder of 2026 (as I mentioned in my September report). According to the Oct. 15 announcement, there was no specific date announced.

In the meantime, OpenAI’s crawler activity on your own site shows up in your server logs and in AI Crawl Control.

#6. YouTube tests new Shorts incentives

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The platform is experimenting with bonuses for invited creators and expanding its shopping affiliates program, as well as updating shopping analytics.

YouTube is testing a new Shorts bonus program which it hopes will provide more incentives for creators to keep posting content. The app is also testing affiliate bonuses and rolling out updated analytics displays for YouTube Shopping.

First, YouTube is experimenting with a new Shorts bonus program for creators and inviting selected users to participate in an additional monetization program, based around posting consistency and performance.

YouTube hasn’t communicated the specific requirements of the program, which may vary by creator. But the basics stipulate that creators will have to upload a minimum number of public Shorts within a specific period specified in their invitation (16 per month, based on at least one example shared by user Muaaz on X). Meanwhile, creators could also be eligible for additional promotional payments based on what YouTube called “valid, engaged Shorts views.”

YouTube said the test will be open to invited creators in the U.S., U.K., Germany, Brazil, Japan and South Korea, but added that there is no way for non-invited creators to apply at this stage.

YouTube Creator Liaison Rene Ritchie said the platform may invite more creators to the program in the coming months.

Ritchie also said that YouTube is also looking to get more creators involved in its shopping affiliate program by providing exclusive offers for videos that include certain products.

The option will provide another way for brands to incentivize creators to post about their products, by providing additional rewards on top of the regular affiliate revenue share.

As explained by Ritchie: “Creators can head over to YouTube Studio, Shopping Hub, or check Studio notifications and review exclusive offers for your channel. Check eligible products, bonus amounts, commission rates, and active dates right on the campaign detail page.”

From there, creators who post videos that include these items will be eligible for bonus commissions and rewards.

Ritchie said the provided creative briefs and suggestions in these listings are non-binding, and creators are able to use their own approaches when it comes to incorporating affiliate offers into their videos.

“To lock in your bonus, you just need to make sure your video matches the required format,” Ritchie said. “Post a short or a long-form video, tag the participating product directly in the video, check the box disclosing that yes, the video includes paid promotion and keep it public continuously for at least 30 days.”

Finally, YouTube is rolling out an updated analytics display for shopping creators. The revised metrics offer new data on sales driven by content, improved product clicks and impression data and seller breakdowns in advanced analytics.

These insights could provide more tools to help creators hone in on key opportunities and drive better performance with their shopping listings.

#8. Top 50 Most Subscribed YouTube Channels Worldwide • Week Of 10/18/2026

[Editor’s Note: Tubefilter Charts is a weekly rankings column from Tubefilter with data provided by GospelStats. It’s exactly what it sounds like; a top number ranking of YouTube channels based on statistics collected within a given time frame. Check out all of our Tubefilter Charts with new installments every week right here.]

Scroll down for this week’s Tubefilter Chart. 👇

The two channels right behind SASHA SHOW in the Global Sub Top 50 have a lot in common. They both feature sweets in their videos, they’re both preoccupied with large numbers, and, of course, they’re both doing extremely well on YouTube right now.

After perusing this week’s Global Sub Top 50, I’m reminded of a classic Mitch Hedberg joke: “Rice is great if you’re really hungry and want to eat two thousand of something.”

Hedberg would thrive in today’s social media landscape, and not just because he knew how to deliver a short-form punchline. His rice joke is the perfect description of an odd YouTube trend. All over the platform, creators are assembling dishes that contain thousands of food items — and I’m not talking about rice.

Tade Vlogs is at the forefront of that trend. The #3 channel in this week’s Global Sub Top 50 created a novel foodstuff when he debuted the thousand-layer Oreo in a video that has already received more than 64 million views.

The popularity of Tade’s Oreo-tastic dishes unites two prevailing YouTube trends. On one hand, this is MrBeast’s law of large numbers in action. The most successful YouTuber in the world likes to put a round number in his video titles, and Tade is showing why that strategy works. The Spanish creator is mining angry responses at the same time. If you respond indignantly to creations that are frankly unappetizing, then you are giving Tade the ragebait he wants.

Shunkiwii’s signature video is slightly different from the typical Tade upload. Instead of trying to eat thousands of food items, he presents a single snack and hits it with a hammer thousands of times. Whether he’s bashing noodles or Oreos, Shunkiwii keeps his smashing hand strong as his view counter continues to go up. He even gives Bayashi a shoutout, paying homage to the king of culinary ragebait.

Clearly, there’s no portion too big for the YouTube audience, and that brings us back to Mitch Hedberg. If the Shorts audience is going to make “eating thousands of food items” into the next big thing, then chefs who create bite-sized foodstuffs will have an advantage. That’s good news for the panipuri guy we talked about the other week.

Even if the tide turns against this form of ragebait, there will still be opportunities for food creators to reach new fans. Tade, for example, knows that his wasteful excess pisses some people off. That’s why he has a food hack to address that very problem — and haul in millions more views in the process.

This week, 39 channels in the Top 50 are primarily active on YouTube Shorts.

#9. Jay-Z Reportedly Crazy in Love With Performing at Super Bowl 61 Halftime Show

Jay-Z is brushing the dirt off his shoulder, and his set list, with the rapper reportedly set to headline the Super Bowl XLI halftime show.

According to Puck, Jay-Z has chosen himself to perform at the upcoming Super Bowl, which will be broadcast on Disney platforms from SoFi Stadium on Feb. 14, 2027. The rapper’s Roc Nation company has had an agreement with the NFL since 2019 (renewed for 5 years in 2024) to produce the Super Bowl halftime show, which is sponsored by Apple Music.

Puck noted that Miley Cyrus and Justin Bieber were also potential candidates to headline the halftime show. Notably, Jay-Z hasn’t released an album since 2017, but he still has the cachet to fill arenas and has two shows coming up at SoFi Stadium this weekend, where he could reportedly announce the news.

Though Jay-Z’s company has produced and strategized the Super Bowl halftime show since 2019, this will be the first time he’s headlined it. In 2024, he told Entertainment Tonight he thought choosing himself too soon for the Super Bowl would be “selfish” but added, “Maybe one year.”

Last year’s Super Bowl featured Bad Bunny in a Puerto Rico-inspired performance from Levi’s Stadium in San Francisco. According to Apple Music, the NFL, and Roc Nation, Bad Bunny’s Big Game performance had 4.157 billion views in 24 hours across global broadcast, YouTube, and social platforms.

The NFL, Apple, and Roc Nation didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment on Jay-Z headlining the Super Bowl halftime show.

Bill Bradley is Adweek's deputy TV, Media and Sports editor.

#10. Legal experts warn Meta’s new terms still grant broad scraping permissions, despite language changes

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Allowing scraped content to be used for all “advertising and business products” is a substantial expansion of Meta’s permissions.

RELATED ARTICLEMeta’s new commercial terms will allow the scraping of news sites, legal experts sayAndrew DeckOctober 15, 2026Meta has removed the word “train” from its upcoming terms of service for business accounts. The company revised its terms after Nieman Lab’s story on Thursday exposed that the new terms would permit broad scraping of websites “associated with” business accounts, and possibly allow Meta to use that scraped content to train its AI models.

In its revision, published Friday afternoon, Meta removed the word “train” from a list of allowed use cases and limited those uses to “advertising and business products,” rather than all Meta products. But the revised terms will still allow for broad scraping of websites, potentially superseding robots.txt files, according to legal experts.

On Saturday, a Meta spokesperson said the company revised the terms because “it wasn’t clear in the initial consolidation of terms that robots.txt preferences are respected. News sites, like all other content owners, still have the ability to disable the crawler via robots.txt flags. That has been the case, and it has not changed.”

Meta has not included any specific language about respecting robots.txt preferences in its revised terms of service. The new terms are slated to go into effect on October 30. There is no option for business accounts to opt out of the new terms before then.

“I think publishers should remain concerned,” said Matt Topic, a media and intellectual property attorney at Loevy & Loevy. “The revised version of the new terms still allows Meta to use that scraped content to develop any ‘business product.’ That doesn’t seem to be a defined term, and presumably Meta is developing AI business products. I think ‘develop’ is broad enough to include ‘train.'”

Meta currently lists examples of its business products as “ads, Meta Business Tools and Meta Business Suite.”

Virtually every news organization has at least one Meta business account. The accounts let companies manage Facebook pages, Threads accounts, Instagram profiles, and WhatsApp channels from one place.

As of publication time, the section reads (with changes in bold):

#11. Forbes looks to Google AI pilot for insights as publishers seek value beyond the click

Forbes has joined Google’s paid News AI pilot that gives Google expanded rights to its content to test new ways of providing readers with context about stories before they click through.

Speaking at Digiday’s Media Strategies London event last week, Forbes chief innovation officer Nina Gould said the partnership was paid but declined to discuss the terms.

The program pays participating publishers for Google’s use of “enhanced” content as it develops AI features. These include in-depth article overviews on Google News publisher pages, which give readers context before they open a story and offer customizable audio briefings. The features include attribution and direct links to publishers’ original content. Forbes will receive insights into how its content performs across different experiences on Google’s platform, which will help it understand how different categories of content work in different contexts and inform its own products, according to Gould.

As part of the pilot, Google will hold periodic business review meetings to share progress and insights, gather feedback from participating publishers, and discuss opportunities and challenges.

“It really is designed to experiment with experiences within their kind of consumer-facing discovery services to look at ways that publishers’ content can engage audiences ahead of a click,” said Gould.

The partnership comes as publishers look for ways to understand their content’s performance across AI-driven discovery, even as referral traffic declines. Gould said Forbes’ referrals were down about 45% year over year, sharpening the company’s focus on building a more direct, loyal audience rather than relying on page views alone.

Google first launched the program last December with publishers including the Guardian and the Washington Post. It has recently expanded its range of publishers to include titles like Forbes and Reach, taking the total participating publications to more than 400, it stated in a blog post last week.

“It’s a chance for us to learn without having to expend the resources to do the experimentation ourselves,” said Gould. “Testing comes with costs, especially with AI. There’s a human cost in the resources that you’re putting towards it, and there’s also compute costs and token costs that you’re paying to create those AI experiences,” she added. “So, for us to be able to partner with Google, who has a whole team that’s working on designing these experiences and then giving us feedback on how our content is performing and how different categories of content are performing with different types of experiences, is important data for us because we can bring that back to our own site.”

The AI news pilot is one of several variations of licensing agreements Google has going with publishers, which includes its most recent pay-per-value AI contribution pilot, and its ongoing News Showcase deals.

As publishers try to understand how their work is surfaced in AI search, the available measurement tools still provide only a partial view. Forbes uses Profound to track reach and citations, but Gould said publishers lack granular insight into how their content performs across AI platforms. “Those [LLM] platforms are a black box. We really don’t have a ton of insight into how our content is performing there in a granular way,” she said.

Separately, publishers have raised concerns about the difficulty of measuring how Google’s AI Overviews affect referral traffic. Search Console provides broader search-performance reporting, but publishers have sought a clearer way to assess AI Overviews’ impact specifically. The AI News pilot update comes as Google says it is updating AI Mode and AI Overviews with clearer links, more context about sources and timely articles. Meanwhile, the U.K.’s Competition and Markets Authority has been pursuing measures to give publishers greater control and transparency over how Google uses their content in AI search features.

U.K. publisher Reach, owner of titles including Daily Mirror and OK! Magazine, has also recently joined the paid program. Reach CEO Piers North stressed to Digiday that the fact the agreement is time-limited means that both parties can assess whether it has been mutually beneficial ahead of any potential renewal or renegotiation.

For some publishers, particularly smaller and mid-sized ones, the appeal of licensing deals with AI companies like Google depends on more than the payment: the agreements can differ in what they offer for access to content, collaboration and insight into how that content is being used.

Gould said Forbes values the insights it can gain from AI partnerships as well as the revenue. That emphasis on learning alongside payment was echoed by several other publishers involved in the pay-per-value Google AI pilot, who spoke to Digiday on condition of anonymity.

“The AI licensing landscape is weird, and it comes in a lot of shapes and sizes,” said Gould. “I think any publisher who’s doing those deals at any scale knows that they vary a lot…Having an avenue for publishers to be paid for how their content is used within big tech platforms, and having a big player like Google kind of lead that is very appealing to us,” she added.

Forbes’ paid agreement fits into a broader strategy Gould described on stage: preparing for a publishing business less dependent on page views and search referrals. She called the page view a metric of the scale era, one that says little about whether a reader is known, engaged, or likely to return. Forbes is shifting its focus toward loyalty, depth, repeat visits, and building a direct audience.

“We’re seeing discovery being outsourced to AI search, and as we’re seeing our referral traffic go down, we have to really focus on metrics and measurements that represent the future strength for our brand, which for us, and I’m pretty sure everyone in this room, is around kind of loyalty, depth, engagement,” she said.

Although Forbes wasn’t planning for a literal “Google Zero” moment, the sharp fall in referral traffic made the threat more tangible and sharpened the internal focus on building a more sustainable audience business. Gould said Forbes’ 45% referral traffic drop drove an internal urgency around preparing a post-referral-traffic strategy. She said the real pressure came from recognizing the risk of not having enough supply to meet advertiser demand.

“It requires work to shift your thinking around how you’re acquiring an audience; who you’re acquiring,” she said. “You have to shift a bit towards not all page views are created equal. Like not all visitors have the same value to you, whereas in a scale time, they did. Honestly, it was like it blinded you to every other option. If you knew you were optimizing your revenue for that single page view, primarily through ad impressions and ad yield, sacrificing any of that revenue towards trying to build real engagement was difficult.”

Forbes is testing ways to build more sustained relationships with readers, including personalized homepage experiences and newsletter sections. It is also working with brand partners seeking visibility in AI search, using citation data to support affiliate, sponsorship, and native-advertising opportunities.

For Gould, the Google pilot is one piece of that transition: a chance to learn from a platform where audiences are discovering content, while Forbes works to build reader loyalty and revenue streams that don’t rely on page views alone.

A creator with a fashion merchandising degree speaks on her quest to diversify revenue fast, from styling to sweat equity investment.

The Verge has restructured its audience development team to prioritize loyal readers over traffic and page views.

#12. Top 50 Most Viewed YouTube Channels Worldwide • Week Of 10/18/2026

[Editor’s Note: Tubefilter Charts is a weekly rankings column from Tubefilter with data provided by GospelStats. It’s exactly what it sounds like; a top number ranking of YouTube channels based on statistics collected within a given time frame. Check out all of our Tubefilter Charts with new installments every week right here.]

Scroll down for this week’s Tubefilter Chart. 👇

Zack D. Films is leading the Global Top 50 for the second week in a row. The American creator, who explores curious situations and places, was the only person to cross the billion-view mark during the second full week of October. He topped out with 1.1 billion weekly views.

T-Series took second place behind Zack D. Films for the second week in a row. After sitting atop the Global Top 50 throughout September, T-Series is relying on its subsidiary channels to keep the views coming — and at least one of them is delivering in a big way.

In North America, October is spooky season, but in India, the month of Ashvin (which typically coincides with September and October) is filled with Navratri celebrations. The Hindu festival honors the universal feminine power, Shakti, through celebrations of the goddess Durga and her nine forms. In fact, Navratri literally translates to “nine nights.”

There are numerous traditions associated with Navratri, and these days, Hindus turn to YouTube to connect with those traditions. The sacred music associated with Navratri can be found on T-Series Bhakti Sagar, the devotional offshoot of India’s leading record label.

The main T-Series channel is (almost) always found in the Global Top 50, but Bhakti Sagar only makes annual appearances in the ranking. It showed up during Navratri season in 2024 and again in 2025. As Navratri takes over the Hindu world in 2026, T-Series Bhakti Sagar is soaring even higher. It picked up 401.6 million weekly views to reach 32nd place in the Global Top 50. The channel’s classic Devi Bhajan compilations still grab the bulk of the Navratri views, but T-Series Bhakti Sagar continues to add new videos each year as well.

On the surface, Chandni Ji Vlogs appears to be just another family channel aiming for the crowded South Asian market. During Navratri, however, Chandni Ji stands out. Over nine days, it has delivered nine artistic interpretations of Durga’s forms. Some of those sketches have picked up millions of views on their own.

October 19 is the last night of Navratri, and in the following weeks, we’ll see the Global Top 50 course correct. At some point, T-Series Bhakti Sagar will drop out of the ranking, only to return in 2027.

But for channels devoted to Hindu festivals, the fun doesn’t have to end. After all, Diwali begins on November 8, and the festival of lights will give smart channels another chance to break into our rankings.

#13. How to Get Recommended by AI: Being Found Isn’t Enough

Wondering how to get your business recommended by ChatGPT, Claude, and other AI tools? Want to know what to change on your website, Google Business Profile, and customer reviews so AI search matches you with the right buyers?

​In this article, you'll discover a four-step framework to get your business recommended by AI tools like ChatGPT, not just found in search results.

AI platforms like ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Perplexity learn about their users across every conversation, from work projects to recipe conversions. Vivienne Wagner describes the result as more than a personal referral. AI acts as a matchmaker, pairing a user with a business whose products or services fit that user's situation. That match only happens when the business is clear about who it is, what it does, and who it's for.

​Vivienne saw this firsthand after a reaction to several new skincare products. Over three to four months of conversation, ChatGPT helped her identify the problem ingredients and then recommended a $10 cleanser. When she pushed back, ChatGPT reminded her that her goal was to avoid irritants rather than chemicals and recommended the same product again. She bought it.

She never would have searched for that product on Google because she didn't know what to search for, but ChatGPT knew her situation, and the brand was clear enough about its product to be matched with her.

Two conditions make it easy for AI to match a business. First, the business has to treat its marketing as an ecosystem rather than a set of silos. The website, social media channels, email marketing, and Google Business Profile all need to tell the same story. Businesses that have evolved or pivoted often tell two stories at once, one about who they are now and one about who they used to be, and that mismatch confuses both Google and AI.

​Second, the business needs solid SEO. AI doesn't pull answers out of thin air; it relies partly on SEO to find information. New acronyms like AEO, AIO, and GEO don't change that. At its core, SEO answers three questions: who a business is, what it does, and who it's for.

​Vivienne's agency puts these principles into a four-step process called the Clear Choice Framework: define, diagnose, align, and prove it.

The first step is to create a brand positioning statement that clearly states who the business is, what it does, who it's for, and who it doesn't want to work with. Without that clarity, AI has nothing to base its opinion on and can't match the business with the right customer. Businesses evolve, mature, and pivot, so even a company that defined itself years ago should revisit its positioning now. Vivienne's agency went through this process for itself several months ago.

Start With the Best 80%: Identify the customers and offers the business wants more of. For a service-based business, that's the clients behind the 80% of work the team loves doing. For a product-based business, it's the products that make up 80% of sales.

​Draft a First Version: Write down who the business wants to work with, how it wants to make a difference, and who it's there to help. This draft doesn't need to be polished. It gives AI something to react to. Treat it as a thinking-cap conversation for the owner, the leadership team, and anyone else who helps make decisions about what the business wants to be known for.

​Have AI Interview the Business: Give the draft to an AI tool with a prompt like this: “This is what we think we know about ourselves. What are we missing? Please interview us and ask us other things we should be considering as we decide how to position ourselves in the market.” Vivienne notes that some people prefer Claude for this. The interview is necessary because a business owner can't see the label from inside the box, and AI provides a fresh set of eyes.

​Work Through the Hard Questions: During the interview, answer how to get more of the favorite customers, why the business wants to work with them, what its special sauce is, how it differs from competitors, how it will say what it stands for, and how it will quietly signal who it doesn't work with. This is a back-and-forth process, not a single prompt that produces a finished statement. Keep going until the result clearly reflects who the business is now and where it's going rather than where it's been.

​Confirm the Statement Covers Six Components: The finished brand positioning statement should define who the business is for, who it doesn't work with, what it wants to be known for, how it works with its customers, its tone of voice and brand personality, and its value proposition. It doesn't need to be a long mission statement.

Join thousands of small-business marketers at Social Media Marketing World — three days of AI, social media, and marketing strategy taught by world-class experts. April 1–3, 2027 in Anaheim.

Every session is pitch-free and built around tactics you can use yourself, no big team required. Your All-Access ticket includes an extra day of workshops, full access to AI Business World, and recordings of everything.

​Use the Brand Positioning Statement as a Filter: Keep the finished statement as a Bible-like reference document. Every piece of marketing should be checked against it for alignment.

No business serves everyone. Vivienne once worked with a med spa owner who said her ideal client was anyone with skin, a definition AI can't do anything with.

​The fix is describing the person and the problem rather than the service requirement.

​Another of Vivienne's clients provides in-home senior care that helps people age in place. The owner described his ideal client as someone who wants 20 to 30 hours of help per week, but that's a service requirement, not a person. The real ideal client is the adult child of an aging parent who lies awake at night worrying about mom. Mom doesn't want to go into a home, but she's showing signs of dementia.

​That adult child is likely already asking AI about early signs of dementia and what to do about a parent's recent behavior. Vivienne calls these ongoing conversations the new search behavior. A website that clearly speaks to that pain point gives the business the opportunity to be matched with the people who need it.

The second step is to use AI to compare the brand positioning statement with what actually appears about the business online. Vivienne explains misalignment with an analogy: someone who says they're fit, athletic, and always make good nutritional choices, but who is seen on the couch in sweatpants covered in Cheeto dust, has a gap between story and reality. The diagnosis finds the Cheeto dust.

Prompt for the Gaps: Give AI the brand positioning statement and the website, then ask: “Here's my positioning statement. Here's my website. Tell me the gaps.”

​Dig Into Each Gap: Ask follow-up questions about what's missing and why each item counts as a gap.

​Extend the Diagnosis Beyond the Website: Because marketing is an ecosystem, run the same check on social media, email marketing, and every other place the business touches the internet, such as a YouTube channel or Instagram account.

​Fix the Biggest Framing Miss First: The diagnosis will return a long list, so start with the biggest misalignment. Common examples include services the business no longer offers and types of customers it no longer works with. For most businesses, the website is the first place to work.

​Redirect Outdated Pages Instead of Deleting Them: Deleting a page for a discontinued service creates 404 errors. Following good SEO practice, redirect the page or refresh it and explain the change.

​Replace Vague Homepage Messaging: A home page that leads with “Celebrating 25 years in business” doesn't say what the business does or who it's for. Vivienne recommends stating what the business does in a single sentence of 70 characters or fewer. The company's history can still appear deeper in the copy, so AI knows the business isn't a fly-by-night organization.

When rewriting copy, clear concepts matter more than individual words. “It is not important to be the loudest voice in the room,” Vivienne says. “It is important to be the clearest voice in the room.”

​Keywords still help inform that copy. Searches have become more conversational, but people still type keywords phrases into Google, and they often use different words than business owners expect. Vivienne recommends SEMrush or Ahrefs for this research. Here's how to run it in SEMrush:

The AI Business Society filters the noise for you, with expert-led training you can put to work the same day — plus a community of marketers sharing what's actually working.

Google Search Console shows which queries already surface a business's website, but that only reflects what the business is already doing. Keyword research shows what customers are actually looking for. Vivienne compares it to making dinner from whatever's in the fridge versus shopping for the ingredients for the meal she actually wants to make.

​High demand and low supply aren't the deciding factors they once were, but it still reveals opportunities.

One of Vivienne's clients, a psychologist, moved her practice online and described her specialty as depression therapy. Every keyword containing depression, depressed, depressive, or therapy was saturated, with high demand and high supply. But the research uncovered tens of thousands of monthly searches from people seeking help with pornography addiction, because people search for their symptoms and their pain, not clinical labels.

The psychologist treats that issue, so it became a new vertical with a dedicated page on her website. The page isn't keyword-stuffed. It clearly establishes her as a credible authority in that area.

The third step is fixing the gaps the diagnosis uncovered. Diagnosis identifies what's wrong; alignment is the work of correcting it.

Start With Static Services Pages: Update every important services page first so each one tells the story in the brand positioning statement. These pages plant the business's stake in the ground about who it serves.

​Publish Ongoing Blog Content: Blogging isn't dead. A business can only add so many static services pages, but ongoing blog posts keep giving AI more information about who the business is, what it does, and who it serves. Regular posts also signal that the business is recent, engaged, and a subject matter expert.

Attribute Posts to Real People: Publish blog posts under the business owner or other important strategic members of the company, not the business name. Vivienne's agency used to publish client posts as “written by Acme Shop” when ghostwriting, but no longer does. “Authority gets you noticed,” Vivienne says. “Credibility gets you trusted.”

​Add an Author Box: Include an author box with a short bio on every post that presents the author as a subject matter expert. The named author doesn't have to write the post. An agency or in-house writers can do the writing, as long as the author can stand behind the content.

​Link to a Standalone Author Page: Link each author box to a dedicated page that covers the author's years in business, credentials, education, experience, and the organizations they belong to. This is the place to toot their own horn. The page doesn't need to appear in the top navigation bar because AI will still find it.

Write Title Tags of 50 to 60 Characters: A title tag is the text shown on a browser tab and as the blue headline in Google search results. It doesn't appear on the page itself, but Google's crawlers and AI use it to understand what the page is about. The maximum is 70 characters, and the sweet spot is 50 to 60. Use that space to say who the business is and what it does.

​Put Location at the End: Location-based businesses should include their location at the end of the title tag, not the front.

​Give Every Page a Meaningful H1: Treat page headings like an essay outline, a step many business owners skip. An H1 like “Celebrating 25 years in business” conveys credibility but doesn't specify whether the business is a dog groomer or a wedding venue. Instead, the H1 should state what the business does and who it's for. Leading with impact is fine.

​Use Keywords Only Where They Fit: Two years ago, Vivienne would have recommended putting keywords in every H1. Now she recommends a compelling H1 that tells the machines more about the business, with keywords included only if they fit naturally. Never leave an H1 blank or fill it with something unhelpful.

The final step is proving the business is who it says it is. A Google Business Profile is one of the first places AI looks for information about a business because it treats it as a verified source, making it one of the most important assets for getting recommended. Virtual businesses that once couldn't get a profile without a physical address should check again, because that barrier appears to have eased.

Write a Business Description: Describe what the business does.

​Choose the Right Primary Category: Pick the category that makes the most sense and reflects the customers the business is trying to reach. Add secondary categories if the profile allows them.

​Complete the Standard Information: Add business hours if appropriate, an address, a phone number, and a website link.

​List Products and Services With Images: Use the profile's product and service categories and add images for each.

​Post to It Like a Social Media Platform: Treat the profile as a mini social platform. Post small billboards for upcoming sales, behind-the-scenes content, videos, and client testimonials. Many businesses don't take advantage of this.

Reviews are where a business proves its positioning. Make asking every customer or client for a review a regular habit, because if the business doesn't ask, the answer is always no.

​Then respond to every review. A review response isn't written for the reviewer. It's written for every future buyer who reads it before making a decision, and it gives AI platforms more information about the business. A reply like “Thanks for the five-star review. It was a joy to work with you” wastes that opportunity because it could apply to any business anywhere. Vivienne recommends this formula instead:

For example, if a bridal shop customer writes, “I found my dream dress and Kaylee was great,” the response could open with “We're so glad we helped you find the perfect wedding dress for your big day,” and then mention that Kaylee loves working with brides who want long sleeves. That reply celebrates the customer while reinforcing exactly what the shop offers.

​Use the same formula for negative reviews. Many buyers decide whether to work with a business based on how the owner responds to criticism.

Vivienne Wagner, Founder and CEO of Houndstooth Media Group, is a marketing and visibility strategist specializing in AI-driven search visibility who helps business owners be found, trusted, and recommended online. Check out The Clear Choice Framework. Follow Vivienne on Instagram and LinkedIn.

#14. Regain Control Of Google Ads: Better Tracking, Clearer Proof Of ROI via @sejournal, @CallRail

As Google Ads automates more decisions, advertisers must define success beyond platform metrics, tracking leads and sales through to actual business outcomes.

Google Ads has steadily automated more of the decisions advertisers once managed directly.

Bidding is an obvious example, but the shift has gone much further. Google now has more influence over which searches ads can match to, where ads appear, how budgets get allocated, and even which creative combinations users see.

For advertisers, that changes where some of our most important decisions happen.

We may have less control over an individual auction than 10 years ago, but we still decide and guide what Google should optimize toward. Even more importantly, how we define success.

Those inputs become much more important when automated systems use them to make thousands of decisions we simply can’t manage individually.

That’s why measurement deserves more attention as Google Ads becomes more automated.

Conversion tracking shouldn’t just stop at counting leads, purchases, or other actions inside the platform. Marketers need to understand whether those conversions actually produce business outcomes they intended to generate.

That requires PPC expertise to extend well beyond campaign settings.

Having fewer manual controls doesn’t mean PPC teams have fewer decisions to make. Some of the decisions that remain can have a much larger impact on how automated campaigns perform.

Choosing the right conversion goals is one example. If a lead generation campaign optimizes toward form submissions, Google will use that goal to inform bidding. The PPC team still needs to determine whether a form submission is the right signal or whether a qualified lead, booked appointment, or closed sale better represents success.

The same applies to ecommerce. Revenue can tell part of the story, but it may not account for differences in profit margins, new versus returning customers, or which products the business wants to prioritize.

Making those decisions requires more context than Google Ads, or any platform, can provide on its own.

That may also require closer coordination with sales, analytics, e-commerce, or other teams that own parts of that data.

This is where PPC expertise becomes especially important as campaign execution gets more automated. Advertisers still need to give Google clear goals and useful business data, then evaluate whether campaign performance matches what happens after the conversion.

A conversion that looks successful in Google Ads may be far less valuable once you evaluate the actual business outcome.

Conversion volume can tell you how many people completed an action, but it doesn’t always tell you whether those actions produced meaningful results for the business.

A lead generation campaign, for example, may report a strong conversion rate, and an efficient cost per lead. If sales later finds that many of those leads are spam, unqualified, or unlikely to become customers, the Google Ads metrics only show part of the outcome.

That gap becomes more consequential when those same conversions guide automated bidding. If form submissions are the primary goal, Google can optimize toward generating more form submissions without knowing which leads eventually become qualified opportunities or customers. It’s not taking into consideration quality of any sort.

Google recommends using qualified or converted leads as conversion goals when advertisers can send that data back into Google Ads. Enhanced conversions for leads can also connect offline outcomes with the ad interactions that generated them.

Ecommerce advertisers can run into a similar problem when conversion volume or revenue doesn’t reflect the full value of a sale. Product margins, customer type, returns, and other business factors can change how valuable two purchases are, even when both look successful in the platform.

This doesn’t mean every advertiser needs to pass every possible business outcome into Google Ads. The goal is to identify which signals give automated bidding a better representation of the results the business wants to generate.

That requires measurement to do more than report what happened after someone clicked an ad. The data advertisers choose to measure and send back to Google can also influence how campaigns optimize going forward.

As Google takes on more campaign execution, advertisers still have influence over the goals and data that guide those decisions.

That starts with defining what success looks like for the business. A primary conversion action tells Google which outcome to prioritize, while conversion values can provide additional context about which outcomes are worth more.

The measurement setup also determines what advertisers can evaluate on their end.

For example, cost-per-lead (CPL) may be the primary key performance indicator inside a Google Ads account, but qualified lead rate and customer acquisition cost (CAC) provide a better view of whether those leads produced results. Ecommerce advertisers may need to look beyond simple return on ad spend to understand profitability, new customer acquisition, or repeat purchase behavior.

Building that fuller picture often requires coordination outside the PPC team. Sales and CRM data can show which leads become qualified opportunities or customers, while ecommerce and analytics data can add context around profitability, returns, and customer behavior.

PPC teams don’t need to feed every piece of that data back into Google Ads. Some data can improve optimization, while other data helps advertisers evaluate whether the automation is producing the intended results.

Google’s upcoming migration of Local Services Ads into Performance Max provides a timely example of where both become important.

Advertisers who rely on LSAs should understand how those leads perform beyond the initial conversion. That includes whether leads are qualified, turn into booked jobs, and ultimately generate revenue.

Having that context becomes especially useful before the campaign environment changes. If lead volume or cost per lead shifts after the migration, advertisers will need their existing performance data to determine whether lead quality and business outcomes changed along with it.

Building that reference point before a major automation change gives advertisers something meaningful to compare against once the change takes effect.

See also: How To Measure PPC Performance When AI Controls The Auction

A useful baseline needs to capture more than just the metrics available in Google Ads.

Before a major campaign change or account launch, document enough performance data to understand both what the platform reports and what happens after the conversion. The exact metrics will vary by business, but the baseline could include:

For advertisers affected by the upcoming LSA migration, this means capturing those metrics before accounts move into Performance Max. It also means making sure the data covers a long enough period to account for normal fluctuations in lead volume, cost, and quality.

The comparison shouldn’t stop at whether Performance Max generates more leads or lowers cost per lead after the migration. Advertisers should also watch whether lead quality, booked jobs, close rates, and other downstream outcomes move in the same direction.

Give the new campaign enough time and data before drawing conclusions, especially if performance naturally varies from week to week. Comparing the same metrics before and after the migration can help separate normal volatility from changes that may warrant a closer look.

Search Engine Journal’s upcoming webinar, Google Local Services Ads Are Moving To PMax: What To Check First, will go deeper into that process with a before-and-after audit checklist, including what to verify before migration and what to monitor once LSAs move into Performance Max.

A baseline won’t prevent performance from changing, but it gives advertisers a more reliable way to understand what changed and whether those differences are showing up in actual business results.

Google will likely continue automating more of the decisions that go into running campaigns. As that happens, advertisers need to be clear about what they want those campaigns to accomplish.

That means looking beyond whether Google Ads hit a target CPA, ROAS, or another platform goal.

PPC teams need to know whether those results are turning into qualified leads, customers, revenue, or whatever the business ultimately cares about. They also need enough historical context to tell when performance has truly changed, especially when Google changes how a campaign works.

The upcoming LSA migration is yet another good reason for affected advertisers to take a closer look at their measurement now, but this won’t be the last Google Ads change that puts it to the test.

As more campaign decisions become automated, advertisers may have fewer opportunities to adjust every lever themselves. Knowing what a good result looks like, and having the data to measure it, gives them a much better way to judge whether that automation is working for the business.
