If you run Local Services Ads, you’re about to log in one morning and land somewhere different.

If you run Local Services Ads, you’re about to log in one morning and land somewhere different.

Google is moving Local Services Ads out of its own standalone platform and into Google Ads. Your campaigns come along automatically, your ads keep showing in the same places, and you keep paying per lead. But the place you go to manage all of it is changing; your performance history doesn’t come with you.

Here’s what’s actually different, what to do before your move date, and what to check in your CallRail setup afterward.

Google is turning your Local Services Ads (LSA) campaigns into a new campaign type inside Google Ads called Performance Max with pay-per-lead goals.

If you haven’t worked with Performance Max before, here’s the short version. These campaigns are highly automated, and marketers get less control over the individual levers than they do in a standard Google Ads campaign. Google’s AI makes the bidding decisions. They also run across all Google platforms, including YouTube, Gmail, and Display.

However, this LSA pay-per-lead version of Performance Max does not run on all platforms. Your ads keep running only on Google Search and Google Maps, in the same spots they run today.

Google is doing this in waves rather than all at once

Account admins get an email roughly 14 days ahead of their move date, plus a reminder about a week out. Notices go to whoever is listed as the account admin, which isn’t always the person managing the ads day to day.

And through the rest of 2026, you still have to create new Local Services accounts in the old interface, since Google Ads won’t support creating pay-per-lead campaigns directly until 2027.

Your historical Local Services performance reports don’t come with you. Impressions, spend history, weekly lead counts, ad-level performance: none of it transfers, and it’s permanently deleted after your move date.

Download it before your migration day. There’s no recovery path afterward and no second reminder once the dashboard is gone.

For the first few weeks after the move, you’ll have no benchmark to compare your cost per lead against (unless you download those historical reports).

Local Services campaigns route leads to a phone number you specify. That’s the number a lead dials when they tap your ad, and it’s the one field in this change with a direct effect on what you can measure afterward.

If that number is a dedicated tracking number, every call arrives labeled with the campaign that produced it, recorded and transcribed, and you keep that history no matter what Google changes next. If it’s your main business line, you get a mixed stream. A paid Local Services lead, an organic Maps call, a repeat customer, and a supplier all ring the same phone and look identical afterward. That’s workable while a dashboard shows you weekly lead counts and spend. It gets a lot harder once your history resets and your reporting moves inside a more automated campaign type.

Switching does not change the caller experience, since a tracking number forwards to the same place your calls already go. Doing it before your move date gives you a clean read from day one instead of starting the comparison late.

One note for anyone running several trades. Because Google removed per-category target CPA, many businesses will split into separate campaigns per trade to keep control of cost per lead. If you do that, each campaign needs its own number, or you lose the ability to compare lead quality by trade, which is usually the reason you split them in the first place.

If you already use CallRail on your pay-per-lead campaigns, this checklist applies to you.

Nothing in your CallRail account needs to change before your migration date. Your static tracking number set as the Local Services lead routing number carries over automatically. Here are four things to check:

While Google’s reporting starts from scratch, your call history does not. Every call that came through your tracking number is still in CallRail’s Call Tracking with its recording, transcript, and source attached, which gives you the before-and-after comparison Google can no longer provide.

Google is changing where you manage Local Services Ads, not how the ads work. Your Local Services placements, billing model, and routing number all carry over, but the management side really is changing (more so for agencies than for anyone else).

If you don’t export your Local Services performance history before your move date, it’s gone.

Mixing button clicks and purchases in one conversion column trains the algorithm to chase the wrong users. Here's the architectural fix.

Many Google Ads accounts have a conversion tracking problem that is disguised as a strategy problem.

The ad account in this case has every action labeled as a “conversion.” The conversions are form fills, key button clicks, page views, cart adds, and checkouts started, which are all flowing into the same column, and all weighted equally. This less-than-ideal conversion setup is training Google’s Smart Bidding to optimize toward a vague composite of “engagement” instead of what matters for the advertiser.

When accounts are set up like this, the outcome is unfortunately predictable.

The campaigns look healthy inside Google Ads and on reports, the conversions look high, and the return on ad spend appears strong and efficient, yet none of it matches what the advertiser is actually experiencing inside the business. When the business team looks at their financial statements or the money in the bank, the story is different and doesn’t match. The advertiser isn’t growing, and doesn’t feel successful, and the internal reality doesn’t line up with what the Google Ads team claims.

The fix isn’t here isn’t to test another bid strategy.

The solution is to examine the conversion architecture. By using a primary‑versus‑secondary conversion framework, the ads manager can control what Google’s machine learning is allowed to learn from and, more importantly, what data the platform should ignore. When the conversion framework is applied correctly, primary and secondary conversions become an additional lever that actively shapes algorithm behavior and brings the account back into alignment with real business outcomes.

Here’s an example, and while the numbers are fictional, patterns like this show up in real accounts all the time.

A Performance Max campaign generated 4,000 clicks and produced 37 purchases, yet the ads platform reported a 62% conversion rate. That math only works when roughly 90% of the “conversions” are button clicks, form interactions, and abandoned checkouts being treated as equal to revenue. In practice, this looks like:

That is a signal‑to‑noise ratio of roughly 9:1 against the algorithm.

It’s important to reset how we think about Smart Bidding in Google Ads. Smart Bidding is not just a bidding tool; it’s a pattern‑matching engine. Google’s own documentation makes this clear when it explains that Smart Bidding evaluates audiences, the queries a user searched before and after, and a wide range of signals we can’t see. In other words, the bidding system isn’t optimizing for keywords in isolation; the bidding algorithm is optimizing for patterns in user behavior. And the patterns that are learned look at conversion architecture you feed it.

Every primary conversion you record teaches the algorithm what an “ideal customer” looks like. The model uses signals like device, time of day, audience cluster, query intent, landing page behavior, and more to find more users who match that pattern.

When the ad account is set up and mixes high-intent actions with low-intent micro-actions in the same primary pool, the model loses contrast. The bidding algorithm cannot distinguish a buyer’s pattern from a browser’s pattern, because the ad manager told it those two users represent the same outcome.

Many in the industry will say that Google Ads chases the easiest conversion. However, taking a step back, it is more than the system that does what it is designed to do. Yes, Google Ads takes the path of least resistance. This is because button clicks are vastly easier to generate than purchases. Cart adds are vastly easier than completed transactions. So the bidding algorithm aggressively hunts for users who do the easy things unless it is guided differently by the human in charge.

This is not a bug in Google Ads. It is the algorithm executing the instructions perfectly.

The Primary vs. Secondary framework reframes conversion tracking from a reporting concern into an algorithmic training concern.

Two settings, two completely different jobs:

The mistake many ad managers make is ignoring the secondary conversions. These are switches that determine which data the machine learning model is actually allowed to see during training.

Think of primary and secondary conversions as data architecture, not data management. When the account is set up, it’s important to consider what gets fed into the model and what gets stored in the warehouse for human review later. Those are two distinct surfaces with two distinct audiences.

Here is another fictional scenario that can help illustrate how this failure shows up inside Google Ads accounts. Imagine a Performance Max campaign with healthy spend and what appears to be performing well. In this setup, “begin checkout” and “button click” are both designated as primary conversions alongside the actual purchase event. On the surface, the ad platform reports strong results. Underneath, the data tells a very different story:

In this scenario, the Smart Bidding system is not malfunctioning. It is performing exactly as instructed: finding more users who click buttons. The model has been trained on signals that do not correlate with revenue, so it optimizes toward the wrong pattern.

Correcting this issue is not instantaneous. Moving the micro‑conversions back to secondary status forces the system into a relearn phase because the model has been shaped almost entirely by false signals. Performance then becomes volatile and often depressed for several weeks while the algorithm rebuilds its understanding from cleaner data.

The broader lesson is that poor conversion architecture compounds quietly and recovers loudly. The cost of a flat, noisy setup is not paid in the first month; it is paid in the 30‑day relearn that follows the cleanup of the conversions.

Up to this point, the article has shown that the mechanics of a conversion framework matter because misconfiguration compounds over time. The next layer is understanding how Smart Bidding interprets the signals it receives.

Every primary action recorded in the ad platform is treated as a successful outcome. Smart Bidding then works backward to identify the conditions that produced that outcome and increases bids to replicate those conditions. This is why the criteria for primary conversions must be strict. Only true macro goals belong in this category: a completed purchase, a submitted lead form, a booked consultation. These are actions that map directly to revenue rather than actions that merely correlate with revenue.

If a direct line cannot be drawn from the action to a dollar of pipeline, it does not belong in the primary pool.

Secondary conversions operate in observation mode. The bidding system does not optimize toward them, but they still populate the “All conversions” column for reporting. This separation is the core value of the framework. It allows as many secondary actions as needed to map the funnel without contaminating the training data.

Each of these steps provides diagnostic insight into where users fall off. None of them instructs the algorithm to pursue low‑intent traffic. The result is a full picture of funnel behavior without sacrificing data quality.

There is one nuance worth noting. While Google’s documentation states that secondary actions are ignored for bidding, the system likely still uses them as predictive indicators of intent. This means even observation‑only events should represent meaningful steps in the buyer journey. Filling secondary slots with vanity actions risks creating false positives in the prediction layer.

Tracking legitimate funnel steps is the best advice.

Custom goals, on the other hand, override the Primary vs. Secondary tagging entirely.

If you build a custom goal and add a secondary action to it, that action will be used for bidding in any campaign assigned that goal, regardless of how it is tagged at the account level.

This is a powerful feature, and a frequent landmine in Google Ads accounts. Strategists who assume “secondary is always observation” miss that custom goals re-promote those actions back into the bidding signal. A best practice is to audit every custom goal in the account before assuming the framework is intact.

Smart Bidding’s learning phase typically runs 7 to 14 days after a strategy change (though this window extends significantly for campaigns with low conversion volume). During this window, the bidding algorithm is actively building (or rebuilding) its model of what success looks like.

A clean Primary vs. Secondary architecture compresses learning. Fewer, higher-quality signals mean faster convergence. The algorithm has clearer contrast between “buyer” and “non-buyer” patterns and can stabilize bid logic more quickly.

A polluted setup does the opposite for the account. The bidding algorithm grinds against contradictory signals, extending the learning phase and degrading early performance over the long-term. Worse, when the eventual cleanup happens or a restructure, the system enters a forced relearn and that 30-day window where revenue dips while the model unlearns the bad pattern.

There is also a default-state trap that catches even experienced ad managers. When you import conversions from Google Analytics into Google Ads, they are set to secondary by default. If your macro-goal lives in GA4 and you assume the import handled the optimization tag, you have just disconnected your bid strategy from your true revenue signal. A best practice is to verify the status manually after every import.

Phone calls are the most context-dependent action in the framework.

For some businesses, calls are pure informational requests, with questions like “What time do you close?” These belong in secondary. For others, calls are the macro-goal because they result in booked consultations, demos, or sales conversations. These belong in the primary.

The decision is not based on the action label. It is based on the post-call data. If you cannot evaluate call quality, you cannot configure this correctly. Pull a sample of calls and talk to the humans answering the phones. Then categorize the calls and make an informed decision.

GA4 events imported into Google Ads default to secondary. This is intentional because Google does not want imported actions inadvertently changing your bid strategy.

But it means every macro-goal sourced from GA4 must be manually promoted to primary. This step is missed constantly, and the symptom when it is missed is subtle. A campaign that “should be” optimizing toward purchases is actually optimizing toward whatever else was already tagged primary in the account.

For accounts that have not yet reached Smart Bidding’s data threshold (typically 30 to 50 conversions in a 30-day window, although this varies by strategy type), the framework in this post still applies, but the secondary layer becomes more strategically valuable for the account to perform well.

While Google does not officially support using secondary actions as bidding signals, many practitioners infer that the algorithm uses them as predictive indicators of intent, though Google has not confirmed this. For a low-volume account, that prediction layer can offer the algorithm enough texture to begin pattern-matching even before the macro-goal hits volume.

This is why secondary action quality matters more than secondary action quantity. Every meaningful step in the funnel, from a pricing page view to a demo video watch, or configurator interaction, is data that gives the algorithm a directional signal during the cold start.

Of course, garbage actions in this slot, however, create false positives the model may build a flawed early model around. So, it is important to apply discernment when adding secondary conversions.

The framework in this article has limited tolerance for upgrading secondary actions to primary. Cart adds, checkout starts, and page views and chats should not be promoted, regardless of how much volume they generate. Volume does not equal intent. A high-volume “begin checkout” or “chat” action still represents users who did not buy.

The legitimate scenarios for status changes are narrow:

That is the entire list. If a strategist is regularly promoting micro-actions to primary, the framework is not being used, but it is being eroded.

Before any Smart Bidding strategy test, walk the ad account through this audit:

Smart Bidding will continue to absorb tasks that used to be human-controlled. This will happen from bid management to creative and audience targeting. The visible surface of paid search keeps getting smaller but it is important to remember to keep humans in the loop.

What does not absorb is signal architecture and how humans think through problems and outcomes. The algorithm cannot decide what data it should learn from, rather that is a business decision that needs a rational decision and not an optimization decision.

Doing this work requires understanding pipeline math, sales cycles, lead quality, and revenue attribution.

The Primary vs. Secondary framework is where that judgment lives at this point in paid search. If it is configured well, and the algorithm scales in the direction of the right outcomes. If it is configured poorly, and the algorithm scales the wrong outcomes faster and finds more pockets of “wrong.”

The framework is the strategy. The bid is just the output of the setup that has been outlined.

CFOs focus on revenue impact over vanity metrics. Discover the essential PPC measurements that resonate with executives.

You’re finalizing a monthly PPC report, excited to show improvements you’ve seen in the account. You highlight an A/B test that yielded an improvement in CPA, along with a new Meta campaign that is driving marketing qualified leads.

Yet when you present the report to leadership, you still get questions like, “How are these actions helping us grow revenue?”

Knowing your audience is a fundamental principle of marketing, and it applies equally so when creating marketing reports. A report geared to a marketing director who is more in the weeds of individual campaigns will look different from a report geared to a C-level executive.

When creating a report that will be viewed by senior leadership, consider what they are held accountable for. A CFO may answer to shareholders or VC firms, but ultimately, their main concern is increasing revenue. If a report doesn’t clearly answer the question of profitability from an investment in PPC, you’re setting yourself up for failure.

In this article, we’ll consider the metrics your CFO actually cares about when reviewing reporting on paid media campaigns.

Before kicking off any ad campaigns or reporting, make sure that you’ve set up proper conversion tracking on your website to measure key actions in ad and analytics platforms. If you’re not confident in your data measurement approach, you can’t trust the numbers you put in your reports.

Before building your first report, you should talk to key stakeholders about what internal revenue goals are and where PPC fits as part of those. For instance, a business may have set an annual goal to grow revenue by 10% or to increase the customer base by 20%.

When considering the metrics you include and how you talk about them, think about how measurement relates to the shared business goals. For instance, you may be able to show not only that Meta had a 10% increase in conversions but that it was the largest contributing channel to the previous month’s growth goal.

It may also be helpful to include a section in your reporting where you highlight overall goals, such as a graph showing total new accounts or revenue vs. planned.

Cost Per Acquisition (CPA) is a foundational metric for PPC campaigns. However, one common question faced when presenting performance and including this measure is: “What is a conversion?”

Microconversions, such as form fills and asset downloads, can be helpful for optimization in the right instances, but particularly for higher-level executives, you need to be very clear about what you’re reporting on when sharing a cost tied to a conversion action.

Ideally, CPA in this case should be tied as closely as possible to a customer. While, particularly for long lifecycle businesses, it may not be viable to report on actual customers signed in a monthly PPC report, you may be able to report on sales qualified leads.

In turn, if you have proper CRM tracking to monitor leads through the lifecycle of initial contact to customer, you can include CPAs for customer acquisition over a longer period. For instance, if your average time to final sale is 90 days, show a view of the past 90 days, including total cost and CPAs broken down by marketing qualified leads, sales qualified leads, and final sales.

Further reading: Why Do Budgets Overspend Even With A Target ROAS or CPA? – Ask A PPC

This leads to a more comprehensive metric: Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC), which represents total sales/marketing expenses divided by the number of customers obtained in the same period.

CAC can be shown as an overall metric, as well as attributed at the channel level if your CRM has the ability to measure customers by the source they came from. You should report on trends over time, which will show both how particular mixes of campaigns and channels are performing, as well as pointing to seasonal trends.

ROAS may be easier to attribute in some types of accounts than others (for instance, ecommerce vs. B2B products with long sales cycles), but can help point to return on investment from PPC campaigns. If revenue values are being properly measured, ROAS can help to answer the question, “How much did we make from this campaign?”

Of course, be ready to provide context and answer questions about how ROAS is being calculated for your brand. For instance, ad platform numbers may or may not include added costs such as shipping and taxes.

As with CPA and CAC, you should report on ROAS at a blended (cross-account and cross-campaign) level, as well as more granularly, where it makes sense to call out specific efforts.

Gaining new customers is great, but what if a customer buys one cheap product and never purchases from your brand again? Or if they pay for a one-month subscription but then cancel?

Incorporating LTV into reporting allows you to see not only which channels and campaigns are driving the most customers but which are contributing to the most valuable ones.

For an ecommerce business, you may look at data for how much revenue is generated from items any one person has purchased over time. For a SaaS business, you may look at the total subscription cost over time. For an industrial equipment supplier, you may look at both how much revenue has come from product purchases and if a customer uses your business for ongoing servicing.

When testing a new channel, campaign type, or offer, a key justification for funding is proof that it can drive new revenue that would not otherwise have come from existing efforts. Showing new customer counts and revenue amounts that are incremental to your testing efforts will help in maintaining funding for the future.

Relying solely on in-platform tracking can be tricky here, as a new Google campaign may readily take credit for conversions that are also being tracked in and influenced by Meta. While ad platforms are adding their own methodologies for tracking incremental attribution, these are ultimately still siloed at the platform level.

Using a Media Mix Modeling (MMM) tool here can provide a broader view of how adding to or subtracting from your paid media portfolio is impacting revenue. You can also run incrementality tests either by isolating campaigns to specific geographies and comparing against similar regions, or by comparing two periods of time. Looking at the results at the end of the test can show if a new initiative helped to lift customer and revenue growth.

When presenting on incremental performance, be transparent about the testing methodology, but explain concepts in a way that keeps in mind your leadership team’s level of technical knowledge. Lead with results, and include more technical documentation in an appendix.

When including the above measures that are relevant to your client or stakeholder, think proactively about what questions will come from the data. If conversions are down, you’ll likely be asked why that is the case.

You’ll build rapport with executives reviewing the report if you can be transparent about negative performance, but also be able to provide a reasonable explanation why that is the case. For instance, you might compare seasonal performance to last year at the same time and note that business generally dips. Or a technical issue with a form on the website may have interfered with the ability of prospects to contact you.

Ideally, include brief bullet points in the report addressing these potential concerns up front, and be prepared to talk through deeper explanations if asked.

Think through the metrics surfaced in this article, along with tactics for presenting them to your CFO and other executives. Now think through how you’ve previously been reporting and any pain points you might have had in reaching shared understanding of performance.

Build on a foundation of solid tracking to highlight the numbers that will resonate the most with the individuals accountable for the purse strings. Be open to hearing out questions you’re asked and additional data that stakeholders might request, and continue to tweak your reports to meet your stakeholders where they are.

#17. Dollar Shave Club markets ‘perfectly good’ razors as AI push continues

Let Marketing Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The brand looks to tie together its advertising efforts under an omnichannel campaign, explains Chief Brand and Innovation Officer Laura Higgins.

Dollar Shave Club has spent the last few years returning to its marketing roots and reasserting its irreverent brand voice. Those efforts continue with the Oct. 20 launch of “Perfectly Good Is Perfect,” a new omnichannel campaign that finds another target in its anti-B.S. advertising: the quest for perfection, in both grooming and the search for a razor.

A 30-second hero video begins with a spokesperson in an ice bath, using a Shake Weight, holding a green smoothie and wearing an infrared mask: all icons of a culture of self-optimization and the looksmaxxing trend. The spokesperson then walks through a bathroom set to show off a lineup of razors that are meant to meet individual consumer needs around shaving.

Dollar Shave Club this year has launched artificial intelligence-powered campaigns around America's 250th anniversary and in support of the company's viral Ball Spray product. The brand, which private equity firm Nexus Capital Management acquired in 2023, is looking to make “Perfectly Good Is Perfect” the platform for future creative.

“For the last six months, we've had a spattering of campaigns that haven't necessarily been connected; they've been more focused on the product themselves,” said Chief Brand and Innovation Officer Laura Higgins. “This concept… will be what ties us together across all the new product launches, and it will be omnichannel.”

The campaign was informed by insights around the rise of perfectionism, including psychological research showing how college students feel more pressure to be perfect than ever before. Dollar Shave Club connected that social phenomenon with concerns about how personal care has become exhausting and expensive — especially as economic concerns have caused some to trade down to lower-quality disposable razors.

“I don't know the last time you used a disposable razor, but man, they hurt,” Higgins said. “It's perfectly good to use a two-blade if you're looking for a comfortable, cost-effective shave; a four-blade for someone that shaves every couple days; or a six-blade for that everyday shaver. It's more about using the right number of blades for you.”

“Perfectly Good Is Perfect” will span connected TV, YouTube, Meta and TikTok, with social activations rolling out throughout the month. Stunts include a “Red-ish Carpet” effort that saw the brand give regular people celebrity-style interviews in a handful of “perfectly good” cities including Cincinnati and Knoxville, Tennessee.

The campaign was created in-house and used real people behind and in front of the camera, but is another example of how Dollar Shave Club is using artificial intelligence to supercharge its marketing. AI was used for quick visual gags, like the spokesperson holding six fingers when showing off the six-blade razor.

Higgins wrote the brief and worked through the concepts with a cast of comic talent, but the use of AI helped the brand and agency partner Humanaut shorten production time to about two and a half months.

“We didn't need [AI] for the concept, but it helped us push on different areas to start figuring out what those images could look like and how to bring it to life,” Higgins said. “We've had to become more choiceful around where we're using [AI].”

As AI continues to evolve, so does Dollar Shave Club’s principles around using the technology, even in the short time since it released an AI-powered “Danglers” campaign video in July. For example, the company is hesitant to use AI to show shaving in action as the technology still can’t get it right, visually. But the company continues to use AI to automate other tasks, and is working to step up AI use at Truly Beauty, the body care brand it acquired last month.

“We have very strict standards on templates. We have a brand book that is really solid. Every campaign we create has a tool kit with it, for every channel,” Higgins said.

Dollar Shave Club is shooting the second phase of “Perfectly Good Is Perfect” as it incorporates the women’s line into the effort and extends a “Hairbernation” social campaign that has encouraged women to shave only what shows when it's cold outside. Overall, the campaign allows the brand to advertise around value amid a downtick in consumer perception surrounding the brand’s quality.

“There's been a ton of work done over time to enhance the quality of our razors,” Higgins said. “I don't want people thinking of us as just the value brands. In this age of perfectionism, spend money where you want to, but we are perfectly good and we can do it at a good cost.”

#19. Meta’s new commercial terms will allow the scraping of news sites, legal experts say

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Starting October 30, business accounts will consent to Meta scraping their websites if they continue using Facebook, Instagram, or WhatsApp.

The update, set to go into effect on October 30, will include news publishers with business accounts. These accounts allow companies or public figures to manage Facebook pages, Messenger accounts, Instagram profiles, or WhatsApp channels from one place. While journalism isn’t the only industry that will be affected by this update, virtually every news organization has at least one Meta business account, including Nieman Lab.

The new terms broadly cover business accounts that manage pages and groups, run advertisements, push marketing messages, and use the platform’s business account dashboard. As written, the new terms could be used to argue that Meta can scrape content from news sites and use that content to train the company’s AI products, according to three legal experts who reviewed the terms at Nieman Lab’s request.

RELATED ARTICLE“An astonishing theft of unprecedented proportions”: Court records show what Microsoft and OpenAI actually thought about AI trainingSarah ScireSeptember 18, 2026“This is a remarkable provision to bury in [the] terms of service, given that this would give Meta access to material that would likely cost many millions of dollars in a licensing market,” said Matt Topic, a media and intellectual property attorney at Loevy & Loevy. “It’s not clear whether a court would enforce this, but publishers should assume that it would be enforceable.”

In early October, Meta alerted users to the update in a blog post and on the Meta Business Suite. The updated terms explicitly state that Meta can use the content it collects from associated websites to “train” Meta products. Elsewhere in its terms of service, the company defines “AI at Meta” as one of those products.

Here’s the new language about scraping in full:

You authorize us (or any entity acting on our behalf) to use automated software (such as web scrapers, bots, robots, spiders, crawlers, and user agents) and create test credentials to access, index, cache, analyze, collect, retrieve, or crawl the domains, web pages, or URLs (and any content available through them) that are associated with your products or services, or that are made available through your or users’ use of Meta Company Products and services, and to periodically pull updates from such domains, web pages, or URLs. Meta may use any content from such domains, web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of, the Meta Company Products, services, and features provided under these Commercial Terms and any other applicable supplemental terms.

“For news publishers, this clearly represents permission to Meta to train AI on any content from their sites and possibly to deploy some of that content, even in competition with the publishers themselves,” said James Grimmelmann, a professor of digital and information law at Cornell Law School. “On the broadest possible interpretation, this would be used to develop a comprehensive archive of all content that Meta would then serve as it wanted to directly or through AI.”

Currently, there is no option for business accounts to opt out of these new terms ahead of October 30. The update reads, “If you do not agree to the updated terms, please stop all access or use of our Products for business or commercial purposes.”

In short, “publishers either have to trust that Meta doesn’t mean the full extent of what these terms say, or they have to stop [using business accounts],” said Grimmelmann.

On its developer page, Meta currently has instructions for how to block its crawlers using robots.txt, a file that tells bots which parts of a website they can and cannot access.

However, legal experts said the new language creates an opening for Meta to argue its commercial terms supersede other blocking instructions. The update also states that Meta can create “test credentials” in order to scrape websites associated with business accounts. Grimmelmann said this would technically allow Meta to “sign up as a fake user” to bypass registration walls on a publisher’s site to access content. Meta declined to answer Nieman Lab’s questions about whether the “test credentials” would bypass paywalls or other paid content.

RELATED ARTICLEFederal appeals court upholds Thomson Reuters’ landmark AI copyright winAndrew DeckSeptember 30, 2026Any attempt to train Meta’s AI products with content collected under these new terms would still hinge on unsettled legal questions about AI training and fair use, legal experts said. Several lawsuits between publishers and AI developers are currently winding their way through federal courts. That includes a class-action suit filed in May by five large book publishers, alleging Meta pirated millions of books in order to train its Llama large language models (LLMs).

Meta’s decision to tether access to its business products to broad scraping permissions echoes a concept in antitrust law called “tying,” according to Benjamin Sobel, a law professor at the University of Wisconsin. “If you want to use the Meta products that require acceptance of the commercial terms, you have to also acquiesce to the scraping and crawling permissions exacted in those terms.”

Sobel compared the move to Google’s recent policies around its AI search products. In order to appear in Google’s traditional search results, publishers previously had to consent to their content appearing in AI Overviews and AI Mode. As of August 2026, all websites now have the option to opt out.

Meta’s new commercial terms come on the heels of the company’s rollout of its paid subscription service, Meta One. The cash-for-links program restricts the number of external links that some accounts on Facebook and Instagram can post without subscribing. Put another way, Meta has begun charging users to post links to the same content that it will be permitted to crawl for free. Earlier this month, Press Gazette reported that some news publishers are currently exempt from the link limit. Meta declined to answer Nieman Lab’s question about the service.

RELATED ARTICLEMeet the journalists training AI models for Meta and OpenAIAndrew DeckFebruary 20, 2025Nieman Lab first learned about Meta’s new commercial terms through a reader tip. Stephen Beale, the founder and editor of The Steampunk Explorer, got in touch when he saw a notice of the upcoming change in his Meta Business Suite dashboard.

“Traditionally, you have this idea that Meta might be using content [posted] on Facebook or Instagram for training,” Beale told Nieman Lab. “But this was different because they’re saying that [since you are] a business user of Facebook, they have the right to go out and grab information from basically wherever you have a presence.”

Beale has long depended on Facebook as a way to connect with his audience and refer traffic to his site. Fans of steampunk — a retrofuturistic subgenre of science fiction — skew older, he said, and the community is “totally entrenched on Facebook.” For many, their only interactions with the community happen on Facebook or at in-person events that they learned about on Facebook.

Beale said he’s seriously considering shutting down his accounts before October 30.

“I know my site has been scraped to death,” he said. “But it just seems like such an arrogant, in-your-face move on [Meta’s] part… It just makes me angry and I don’t want them to get away with it.”

#20. Apple finally explains its Safari block, and identity companies are in its sights

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit

A month after Apple started cutting off companies that follow people around the web in its Safari browser to target them with ads, the company has finally explained itself.

All of them were among the first companies Safari cut off when Apple rolled out its latest software update in September, along with Permutive and Audigent. Apple’s blog post confirms the block reaches beyond iPhones and iPads to Macs and its Vision Pro headset. Once someone updates, Safari stops talking to those companies altogether and the tracking stops with it.

Logging out of a site or unsubscribing from a newsletter doesn’t help either, Apple wrote in the blog, since the third party keeps the tracking code and the email address regardless. Over time, the  third-party builds on what it’s kept. Every login and form adds another detail, until it has a profile of each person, which the industry calls an identity graph. Nobody signing up for a newsletter, Apple argued, expects their details to be handed to a third party for something else entirely.

Hence the bluntness of the block. Safari shuts out the whole web address of any company it targets, so fiddling with how a request is built won’t sneak it through.

Apple is clear about why it’s going after this kind of tracking. What it means for publishers is murkier. The company said a business personalizing things for its own customers isn;t tracking and isn’t what the block is for. For a publisher, that would cover using what it knows about its own readers to recommend articles or tailor its pages. Where Apple draws the line is the outside firms publishers often pay to match the data up. Even when every detail comes from a single company’s own customers. Apple wrote, those firms can still link the same person across different sites, which no single site could do alone.

That describes a fair few of the companies publishers rely on to make their readers more valuable to advertisers. Which of those vendors Apple has in mind is one of several things the post doesn’t say. It doesn’t name a single company, explain how one ends up on Apple’s list or say how it could get off it. The answers matter because Apple’s list has already caught at least one company by mistake. The Trade Desk’s ad server, the tech that puts its winning ads on a reader’s screen, was blocked alongside its UID 2.0 identifier in the first days of the update. It has since been switched back on after being caught up by accident, according to a person with knowledge of the matter.

For now, the block has caught only a handful of companies. Digiday’s own testing found most of the ad tech web addresses it checked were still loading. Apple’s post makes it clear it doesn’t plan to stop there, however. “We’ll continue to prevent covert and cross-site tracking by default,” it wrote.

However clearly Apple spells out why its going third far to stop its customers being tracked, some in the ad industry will still suspect it has another motive in mind. They’ll point to its track record.

This time, Safari’s block has landed as Apple’s own ads business is pushing into Maps and hiring on a scale it rarely has before.

Apple has 86 open roles tagged Apple Ads, though plenty of those listings predate the block by months, which suggest a buildout planned well in advance. Asked about the hiring push, Apple pointed to its blog post and declined to comment further,Whatever the reason for it, an ads team hiring on that scale is one with growth in mind. Ad execs will be watching closely for what those plans turn out to be.

In Cupertino it’s hiring a director of algorithms for ads engineering and, as of October 19, a product manager for AI and machine learning in the Apple Ads marketplace, along with a senior ML engineer for ad campaign optimization, among its vacancies. Meanwhile in New York, home to 17 of the 86 roles, Apple wants three client partners to look after advertisers and someone to run campaign management for brand advertising. Most of the other jobs there are engineering.

Then there’s a team called Signals Intelligence. According to its listing, engineers there fine-tune language models to label and summarise ads and search queries, and those labels help decide which ads get pulled up and ranked. A product manager on the Apple Ads marketplace team in Cupertino is wanted to run the next generation of ad matching and search intent, with a job spec that reads like a glossary of semantic search. Apple never says what all of it adds up to. Instead, the postings promise to respect or protect user privacy.

With Apple saying nothing, ad execs have filled the gap with theories of their own, most of them shaped by the last time Apple changed the rules.

As one ad tech exec lead at a publisher explained: “The bigger question for publishers is not whether Apple should protect privacy. Of course they should. The question is who gets to decide what privacy-preserving advertising looks like. Apple controls the operating system, the browser engine and increasingly the technical infrastructure through which advertising reaches the user. If Apple can decide which ad-tech companies are technically allowed to communicate with Safari, it is effectively making market-access decisions.”

However this shakes out, it’s a reminder of how long a shadow Apple casts over the ad industry, whether it means to or not. Expect that shadow to stretch further. Before taking over from Tim Cook last month, John Ternus told Apple staff that services would keep growing under his leadership. That’s the part of Apple its ads business sits in.

#21. Reddit Tactics, Instagram Tools, and Industry News

Here’s a recap of the most important insights, trends, and updates you need to know about today! Catch up in minutes and go into the rest of the week prepared.

🗞️ Industry news from Instagram, LinkedIn, and more

Not sure which subreddits are worth your time, or what you could possibly add to the conversation? This research process will help:

Start with your customers' problems, not your product. Ask your own customer support team what people complain about most and what makes those problems go away. Then read your competitors' support forums and look for the gaps.

Copy every review you can find on sites like Capterra and G2, paste them into ChatGPT, and ask, “What are the biggest challenges this customer base is dealing with in my niche?”

Search Google and ChatGPT the way your customer would. Note what the ads and bolded words say, which Reddit threads appear, and where the pros and cons cluster. You'll start to see the same two or three subreddits come up again and again.

In each of those subreddits, sort by Top and set the range to the last 12 months. Open those posts and read the top comments to learn which kinds of answers this community values most.

Read the subreddit rules before you do anything else. Ask yourself whether you're allowed to participate and whether you genuinely have something of value to add.

Pro Tip: Accept that you are not the solution for every person. Focus on the few problems you solve really well, because the overlap between your customers' real problem and what you're truly good at is where Reddit comes through for marketers.

This matters because Reddit now shows up almost everywhere your buyers look. Brent points out that Reddit results appear in 97.5% of comparison searches and that Reddit is the top cited source across large language models (LLMs). Buyers skim an AI summary, then turn to Reddit to hear from real people. Showing up in the right communities with useful answers puts you in that validation moment.

1. Go where your prospects already are. At another conference, Mike spotted big brands he’d never landed as sponsors. So he flew his sales director out on a few hours’ notice. In two days, she talked to about 25 companies.

2. Know when to kill an experiment. The team emailed 1,500 customers asking for video testimonials and got just two. So they stopped asking and turned to the 40+ professionally shot testimonials they’d already recorded at the conference in April.

3. Show AI great examples before asking it to create. Before having AI turn those testimonials into video ads, Mike had it study some great samples. The result was a reusable ad-making skill and a set of high-quality videos the team can use on the website and in paid ads.

4. If you do all the work, you’re also the ceiling. That’s what Mike’s coach told him. Now Mike is exploring how AI can help raise that ceiling.

#23. I Tested DeepSeek’s New Search Api, Here’s How It Ranks And Scores Websites via @sejournal, @suganthan

In this webinar, learn to rewrite spec-sheet product copy into the words shoppers use, and make product pages readable to AI.

Invalid traffic on AI Max search doubled to 5.28%. Get the channel-by-channel retail benchmarks before Black Friday.

In this webinar, learn to rewrite spec-sheet product copy into the words shoppers use, and make product pages readable to AI.

Join this webinar to choose a channel to test, set a starting budget, and identify results to track before investing more.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

DeepSeek opened its search API with authority scores and a promise to filter SEO and GEO spam. I spent $0.08 testing what it actually returns.

DeepSeek has opened access to its own search engine through a public Search and Fetch API. It returns an authority score for every result and says it filters out SEO spam, GEO manipulation, and low-quality AI content.

The announcement on Oct. 17, 2026 came alongside an update to its Flash model. DeepSeek says the search engine already powers search on its website and through its API, indexes hundreds of billions of pages and handles hundreds of millions of searches a day.

We can now query that system directly, inspect the sources it returns, and see some of the scores attached to them. That gives us something concrete to investigate before an AI model turns those sources into an answer.

Naturally, I wanted to see what it thought of my site. And whether the spam filtering held up.

My site came back with an authority score of 1. Spam PDFs on government and university hosts came back with authority 4. The Fetch API also presented itself as Firefox from Hong Kong and returned content from URLs disallowed by robots.txt.

I ran 110 calls on Oct. 17, 2026 from Dubai: 93 Search calls and 17 Fetch calls. Around 103 were billable under the documentation’s billing rule, costing approximately $0.08.

The tests covered score distributions, authority across different hosts, six queries related to my own tools and research, localization, date filters, and fetch behavior.

I used the Search and Fetch documentation as the reference. Where the responses differed from the documentation, I’ve kept the observed results clear.

Each search result includes two fields worth paying attention to:

These definitions come from the Search API reference. The authority tier is DeepSeek’s own assessment, and the documentation describes it as a property of the page.

Across 20 SEO and GEO queries at count=50, I collected 1,000 results. Their rerank scores ranged from 0.75 to 2.70, with a median of 1.63. Results were consistently sorted by that score, and 68% scored 1.5 or above.

Only 196 distinct scores appeared across those 1,000 results. The returned values looked bucketed, although that alone doesn’t tell us whether the underlying scores are rounded or calculated in fixed steps.

Across all 4,322 results in the run, authority tiers -1 and 0 never appeared. The distribution looked like this:

Higher authority tiers came with higher median rerank scores in this sample. That doesn’t isolate the effect of authority from the other ranking signals, but it makes the field worth investigating.

I then ran 16 site: probes across 16 hosts. On every host, every returned URL had the same authority score. Here are some examples:

So although the documentation calls this a page authority tier, it behaved like a host score in my tests.

The Reddit subdomains were especially useful here: qh.reddit.com scored 1, while www.reddit.com scored 2. That points towards the host being the relevant unit, rather than the entire registrable domain sharing one score.

A search for site:suganthan.com filled the 50 result cap. It returned my homepage, /resources/, notes and blog posts. DeepSeek was finding content across my site. Those pages all carried authority 1.

Being indexed was clearly only part of the story.

I ran six target queries with count=50 from the UAE.

Package registries, app stores, and marketplace listings did well on these tool queries. PyPI, npm, Apify, the Chrome Web Store, WordPress.org, and GitHub were the kinds of hosts surfacing.

My Gemini article and FanoutFox both had authority 1. Their rerank scores of 1.14 and 1.37 also fell below DeepSeek’s documented 1.5 high-quality threshold.

For my site, having content directly about the thing being searched for wasn’t enough to beat those hosts. The low authority tier is a plausible part of the explanation, although these tests don’t tell us its exact weighting.

DeepSeek explicitly says its engine filters SEO spam, GEO manipulation, and low quality AI content. I wanted to see how that claim lined up with the results.

I also saw self-published “frameworks” on zenodo.org receive authority four and rank #one and #three for “generative engine optimization.” That is another observation about how authority behaved. Self-publication alone doesn’t make a page spam.

The government and university examples are hard to square with the promise of filtering this stuff out. Those uploads still received the highest authority tier.

This is why the apparent use of a host score matters. A system that carries a host’s authority across its pages can end up giving parasite content the same treatment as legitimate material on that host.

The results don’t tell us how much spam DeepSeek removed. They do show that these examples got through, and that a high authority tier wasn’t a reliable judgement of the individual page’s quality.

Here is a request using an API key stored in an environment variable:

Search and Fetch each cost $0.75 per 1,000 successful requests. Under the billing rules, failed requests, empty search results, and timeouts are not billed. Returning 50 results costs the same as returning fewer.

There is a separate temporary exemption for the server-side Search and Fetch calls already made when using the DeepSeek API through Claude Code or Codex. Those remain free until one November 2026 at 00:00 Beijing time, which is 31 October at 8:00 PM GST. Per request, billing starts then. My direct API tests were billable.

Leaving out localization produced the same results as specifying a UAE IP across all six target queries. I was calling from Dubai, which is consistent with DeepSeek using the caller’s IP as the default.

Set this field explicitly to an IP address in the market you want to test. Otherwise, your audit may reflect wherever the script happens to run.

Using a UK or U.S. IP changed the rerank scores of 26 to 41 of the 50 results and swapped 4 to 15 URLs. The mean score delta was small, around ±0.05. It mostly reshuffled the results, without substantially changing the score scale.

A Chinese IP, 114.114.114.114, behaved similarly to the UK and US settings. I didn’t see a clearly separate Chinese result set in these tests, although this doesn’t establish how DeepSeek organizes its indexes.

The ori_question field lets you supply the user’s original question alongside the search query. DeepSeek says this can improve query understanding.

Across my six queries, it changed the rerank score for only zero to two of the 50 results and swapped at most one URL.

The after: and before: operators produced zero date violations across four queries.

They also removed every undated page. 11% of the unfiltered results had date: null, and those URLs disappeared when a date filter was applied.

That matters if your content needs to appear in searches for recent information. Put an appropriate machine-readable date on the page, then check that DeepSeek actually recognizes it. A page it treats as undated can disappear from a date-filtered search.

Every returned date that was present ended in T16:00:00Z, which corresponds to midnight Beijing time. The filtering behavior pointed to Beijing calendar days in these tests.

I also found two differences between the documented and observed text lengths:

That is worth knowing if you are building a tool around these responses. The summaries I received were considerably longer than the documentation suggested.

The Fetch requests I inspected did not identify themselves as DeepSeek. They used this user agent:

There was no From header, bot token, Signature or Signature-Input. The requests presented themselves as Firefox, with no DeepSeek identifier to match in the user agent.

Five fetches came from five different IPs, all identified as AS136907, Huawei Cloud, Hong Kong:

In the rendering test, it loaded CSS. It did not run JavaScript, load images, or fire the XHR beacon. Content that required JavaScript did not appear in those fetches.

These observations concern the Fetch API. They don’t establish how the crawler that builds DeepSeek’s search index behaves.

The Fetch API returned full content from three URLs disallowed for User-agent: *:

I could not confirm whether it ever requested /robots.txt. What I could confirm was that the disallowed URLs still returned content through the API. Those rules did not prevent the fetches I tested.

If your access logs record Accept-Language, this will help surface requests matching the observed headers:

A more specific filter combines the Firefox version, language header, and ASN. A Cloudflare custom rule in that shape would be:

Treat that combination as a fingerprint to investigate. It is based on what I observed in these requests and could change.

There is no DeepSeek-specific user agent here, and blocking the Firefox string alone can catch legitimate browsers. AS136907 is also a general Huawei Cloud network. Blocking the whole ASN can affect other tenants, so don’t assume every request from it belongs to DeepSeek.

The useful part of this release is that we can inspect the search results and scoring directly.

For me, the most interesting finding is the combination of visible authority tiers, weak rankings for some original tool content, and obvious spam receiving the highest authority tier. It gives us specific questions we can now test.

This was one day, 110 calls, six target queries, and one calling region, with additional probes for scores, hosts, filters, and fetching. I still couldn’t confirm whether the fetcher requested robots.txt. Treat the numbers as directional, please.

#28. Amy’s Kitchen tackles ultra-processed food myths in national campaign

Let Marketing Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The brand’s newest creative looks to inform shoppers on its new Non-UPF Verified certification.

After becoming one of the first nationally distributed packaged food brands to receive a Non-UPF Verified certification from the Non-GMO Project, the organization responsible for the non-GMO label often seen in grocery stories, Amy’s Kitchen, a privately owned company established in 1988, is looking to educate consumers on what the term “ultra-processed foods” means and to position itself as a healthy, but still convenient, alternative. The company has ramped up its marketing efforts in recent years, launching its first campaign in over a decade last year.

The multifaceted campaign kicked off at the Third Street Promenade in Santa Monica, California, in early October with a 40-foot installation. “End the Era of Ultra-Processed Food” was projected onto the Clock Tower Building. The five-week campaign will run through Nov. 15 and is intended to reach health-conscious consumers between the ages of 24 and 44. Retargeting by MikMak will connect consumers with retailers via an add-to-cart function. The Whole Foods Market campaign, which began Oct. 15, consists of in-store digital ads in select markets and targeted digital ads through Amazon DSP.

To enhance its in-store presence, the brand developed a series of in-store assets, including freezer and floor clings, shelf talkers and strings as well as print and digital ads. The material is intended to help educate shoppers on the new designation.

An analysis commissioned by the brand and conducted by Lindsay Allen, Ph.D., a health economist at Northwestern University’s Feinberg School of Medicine, challenges the notion that ultra-processed foods cost less. The cost of food continues to be a major concern for many Americans as the rate of annual grocery inflation fluctuates and could hit 2.7% due to rising fuel costs. The campaign is intended to position minimally-processed foods as the better bargain in the long run.

A Talker Research survey of 2,000 Americans, also commissioned by the brand, reported nine in 10 respondents are eating ultra-processed food without knowing it. Additionally, half are not confident they know the difference between processed and ultra-processed foods, per press materials.

#29. A new report argues newsrooms need to do more experiments — like, the kind with randomization and results

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Mississippi Today had a question. Did the stories around its Pulitzer Prize-winning investigative reporting affect the way those investigations were received?

It’s the kind of question local newsrooms can’t easily test on their own. But researchers from Local NExT Lab at Syracuse University could.

In a national survey, 1,768 adults were shown the same investigation surrounded by a different mix of stories. In one, the investigation was shown alongside positive community stories. (Think: “How a local fossil park changed science history.”) In another, the investigation was featured alongside other investigative stories.

The investigation was rated more accurate, important, and relevant when it was surrounded by community-focused stories, not other investigative stories. (Audience reaction to a third story mix, where the investigation was surrounded by stories about legislation, was not consistent.)

The result was described in the first report from the Local NExT Lab. Joshua Darr, director of the lab and associate professor at Syracuse University, believes that although dashboards and engagement analytics are “very important tools” for newsrooms, they aren’t enough.

“Engagement data can’t tell you what caused audiences to engage, settle a hunch, or isolate your contribution,” the report reads. “Randomization can.”

“The key word there is ’caused,'” Darr added in an email. “Without randomization, you can tell when engagement is up or down or if a particular story is doing well, but it’s hard to know exactly why that is happening.”

RELATED ARTICLESearching for gold: Making sense of academic research about journalismAngie Drobnic HolanApril 27, 2023At Nieman Lab, we often hear from both sides of academic-practitioner partnerships. Researchers wonder why newsrooms don’t pay attention to their findings or fail to respond to their overtures about experiments. Publishers, editors, and journalists, meanwhile, tell me they don’t have time to read dense and jargon-filled academic papers. They can be annoyed by requests to spend time or resources they don’t have. And it’s not always fun to be someone else’s test subject.

When partnering with Local NExT Lab, Darr emphasized, the local newsrooms don’t have to commit money or manpower. They agree to two or three conversations. The researchers listen and then design, field, and analyze the experiments. In return, the newsrooms get their ideas tested and causal evidence.

In another experiment, the Local NExt Lab found that Instagram Reels including reporters’ faces drove the most interest and engagement, but when it came to clicking “follow,” profiles that looked like traditional news brands won out. Respondents chose to follow newsrooms (in this case New Orleans Public Radio) more often than reporter-named accounts.

The first batch of tests was funded by the W.K. Kellogg Foundation. Additional support from the American Journalism Project will allow for further tests on a larger cohort next year. The full report is here.

#30. Inside the post-Google playbook: Subscriptions, AI and team reorgs

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit

Publishers’ hemming and hawing over the Google Zero post-search era has reached a fever pitch. Now, they’re finally doing something about it.

Companies like Axios, The Verge and Time have started rewriting their playbooks to prepare for a future in which Google isn’t providing meaningful traffic.

They’re revamping subscription offerings, selling AI visibility products and restructuring their internal teams to survive in what could best be described as a search-pocalypse.

Senior media reporter at Digiday Sara Guaglione and senior media editor Jessica Davies joined a recent episode of the Digiday Podcast to discuss the publisher investments that seem the most promising — as they were discussed at this year’s Digiday Publishing Summit and the Digiday Media Strategies in London.

Here are three ways publishers are trying to survive a post-Google world:

Subscription publishers have been scrambling to figure out how to monetize agentic audiences, said Davies. She added, “Axios is the best example in terms of the detail that publishers have been willing to give on that so far.”

Also at DPS, Esther Cohen, director of audience and subscriptions at The Verge told Digiday that audience teams are being reorganized around specialists. Specialist areas include newsletters, platform engagement and audience analytics. The Verge has managed to expand the team over the past two years and avoided layoffs through the changes.

The Verge isn’t alone in its team restructuring. Politico’s Francesca Barber stepped into a new role that combines product, audience and AI under one person. Meanwhile, The Wall Street Journal’s head of digital Taneth Evans detailed new roles in the newsroom, including a new head of multimedia and head of shows.

“Publishers, when they do these kind of things, it’s like ‘OK, this is a new era. This is real disruption. We can’t just wish it away. It’s here to stay and we need to figure out what the heck we’re going to do about it. That requires new titles, new job responsibilities to really reflect on the moment that we’re in,” Guaglione said.

Time is seemingly taking the approach of “if you can’t beat them, join them.” The publisher has begun serving ads to AI agents to squeeze revenue out of its growing bot traffic. (AI-powered search engine Perplexity blocked those ads from influencing its own search index last than two weeks after Digiday’s initial report.) In the same vein, Future is offering GEO service while Ziff Davis is offering AI visibility services.

“There was a real divide, really, between publishers who’ve chosen to block everything [regarding AI web crawlers], and the publishers who haven’t been quite as hard on blocking,” said Davies, “but as a result have said that they’ve had really strong AI visibility as a result. Now, they’re benefiting from that when it comes to now selling that with clients because they’ve got so much data on that.”

There’s a growing bifurcation in the creator economy. While the Alix Earle’s and Mr Beast’s of the world take on the role of agencies, nano and micro creators have become media buys.

On the Digiday Podcast, Digiday staffers break down the state of play among major agencies using sports analogies and The Golden Girls.

OpenAI has billion-dollar goals for its ChatGPT ads by the end of this year. But can it woo advertisers enough to make good on those goals?

#31. Making Instagram Reels Easier, Faster & Scalable

Wondering how to create Instagram Reels faster without losing quality or reach? Want to know which new Instagram and Edits features help you edit, analyze, and scale Reels?

​In this article, you'll discover how to use First Draft, the Edits app, Reels analytics, pinned posts, and translations to make Instagram Reels easier to create, faster to edit, and more scalable.

Instagram's newest editing tools shorten the time it takes to produce an Instagram Reel, but Elizabeth Marberry says they don't yet replace human editing judgment. The time they save pays off only when it goes toward publishing enough Reels to learn from while keeping each one good-enough to hold its reach.

First Draft is a one-tap auto-editing tool built into the native Instagram app, so there's no need to switch to the Edits app to use it. Once the clips for a Reel are selected, a single tap removes pauses and trims the clips, generating an initial video in about 10 seconds. There's no prompt box for instructions. The single tap is the entire interaction.

​Elizabeth says Instagram named the feature accurately because it produces a first draft, not a finished Reel.

When she tested it on a scripted yapping video, a direct-to-camera video of the creator talking, it missed how she records. She often repeats a line to deliver it in a more enthusiastic or more grounded tone, and First Draft didn't recognize the repeated line, so it left both takes in. It also kept moments where she coughed and rubbed her nose, treating them as part of the video. First Draft works best for creators who leave long, clean pauses and never clear their throat on camera.

​The Cut Silences feature in the Edits app handles one sequence at a time, while First Draft works across a batch of clips. First Draft also works on B-roll, not just direct-to-camera footage. Elizabeth tested it on B-roll her husband filmed of her walking through an open house. It picked a few good shots, but the result was lackluster because the cuts ran too long. A B-roll video like that needs an edit every 2 seconds.

​She hasn't tested First Draft on voiceovers. Because the tool lives in the Instagram app, the way to test it is to record a voiceover in Edits, upload it to Instagram Reels, and run First Draft to see whether it tightens the audio.

​A busy business owner can't yet record a talking-head video, tap First Draft, add captions, and publish. Even the Cut Silences feature in Edits leaves clips that still need a little more trimming by hand.

Elizabeth's answer to whether faster editing should go toward more Reels or better Reels is both. Quantity builds skill as a content creator and marketer, since no one hits it out of the park on the first attempt. It also produces enough data to show what's working, as long as the marketer commits to paying attention to what's working along the way.

​Volume on its own backfires. High-volume, mediocre content is a race to the middle. In the words of Elizabeth's 13-year-old, it's “mid.” Over time, the algorithm reads that content as something no one is interested in, which hurts reach. The goal is consistent reps paired with constant refinement, so quality improves as the reps add up. Elizabeth recommends posting often enough to stay consistent as a brand and collect meaningful data.

​The data set also has to be large enough before judging the results. Elizabeth sees many businesses commit to 3 high-quality Reels per week, stick with it for about 20 days, and decide it isn't working. That's too little data to draw a conclusion.

Quality encompasses messaging, fit with the target audience, and entertainment value, as well as the technical quality of the footage. Earlier this year, Elizabeth stopped using filters in her videos because low video quality was hurting her reach, and she realized she needed to start filming in 4K.

​Every social platform has its own culture, and it keeps changing. In 2021 and 2022, it was standard on Instagram to use a light beauty filter to feel more confident on camera. Today, those filters look outdated. Elizabeth hasn't noticed a large difference between 1080p and 4K, but she recommends filming at the highest video quality the phone allows. Instagram has long said that grainy or unclear video negatively impacts reach.
