Every session is pitch-free and built around tactics you can use yourself, no big team required. Your All-Access ticket includes an extra day of workshops, full access to AI Business World, and recordings of everything.

The Edits app is Instagram's creative workspace for producing Reels at volume, while the Instagram app is where content gets published and offers simple editing tools. Edits adds folders to organize drafts, projects, and templates, and offers more in-depth analytics than the Instagram app. Other recent additions to Edits include an AI feature that turns still photos into moving clips based on a description of the motion, and one-tap color correction.

​Elizabeth recommends marketers start using Edits while it's still free. She expects Instagram may eventually charge for it with a model similar to CapCut, which offers a free version and a paid version with added features, though she doesn't know that for certain. She sees Edits as Instagram's move to compete with CapCut for market share, following uncertainty around TikTok that sent many creators looking for alternatives to TikTok and CapCut.

Edits templates are Reels that other creators have made reusable, with every clip already timed to the music. Creators make them available by turning on a setting that allows their Reels to be used as templates.

​After choosing a template, the creator taps to add their own videos. Some editing is still required. If the template is 10 one-second clips back-to-back, the creator has to find the one-second segment in each uploaded video worth showcasing and then edit the on-screen text.

Labs is the opt-in area where the Edits app tests new features before a wider release. Other accounts may see a beta program instead, and the features available may differ from account to account.

​Labs is found by opening the Edits app, tapping the profile photo in the top-right corner, and scrolling to Labs at the bottom of the menu.

Toggling on the Carousel Editor lets you build Instagram carousels in Edits and export them to Instagram. Labs works like a secret menu, and Elizabeth calls the feature new and secret. She recently used it to create a carousel about living in New York City during 9/11 and found the process seamless. The advantage is creative control, including far more font variations than the Instagram app offers.

​At the time of recording, Labs also included Auto Adjust, which color-corrects and adjusts lighting with a single tap, and Improve Audio, which reduces background noise.

​Pro Tip: Elizabeth recommends turning on every feature in Labs to test them all. She calls it a marketing life hack.

Insights is the analytics section of the Edits app, and Elizabeth uses it to find patterns in her top-performing Reels. It's marked by a small graph icon in the lower-right corner. In the upper-right corner of Insights, the view can be changed to the past 90 days. Elizabeth always reviews the last 90 days because the largest possible data set gives her the most information.

​Insights can sort content by most shares, most likes, most follows, and most saves, quickly surfacing top-performing Reels. Reports can also be exported as PDFs, which helps marketing teams that need to show data to stakeholders or partners. A PDF report can also be uploaded to an AI tool for help with analysis.

Edits can compare three Reels side by side. Elizabeth warns that the button to do this is buried, so searching online for a screenshot of its location saves time.

​Before comparing anything, Elizabeth starts by defining the content's goal. Attraction-style Reels are designed to act like a magnet for the ideal customer and then invite them to taking a next step. If three attraction-style Reels all share one call to action, such as commenting GUIDE to receive a free Instagram monetization guide by DM, views aren't the main measure. The number that matters is how many people commented with the keyword and received the lead magnet.

​Many marketers get distracted by views and followers. Elizabeth doesn't dismiss those numbers, but without a clear goal for each piece of content, there's no way to measure whether it's working.

​When comparing top performers, Elizabeth studies four variables:

She looks for patterns across these variables and analyzes them like a scientist, always in line with the account's goals. If the top three performers are all 60-second yapping videos, that's the account's sweet spot. If all three are B-roll of the creator talking about how they're using Claude in their business that month, the next step is more of that content, such as more videos about Claude filmed in the kitchen.

The AI Business Society filters the noise for you, with expert-led training you can put to work the same day — plus a community of marketers sharing what's actually working.

Failing forward means treating Reels that flop as part of the process and staying consistent long enough to produce winners. Elizabeth posted a Reel every day for a year with little to no growth. Over the next 12 months, her two brands gained a combined following of more than 120,000, resulting in an 84% increase in revenue that year and more than 5,000 people on her email list.

​She still posts Reels every week that flop. Her approach is to keep posting until a winner comes, stay out of the mental drama, focus on what's within her control and what energizes her as a creator, and learn from every attempt that doesn't perform.

Cross-posting Reels from Instagram to Facebook takes only a toggle, and the analytics in the Instagram app show how views are split between the two platforms. Elizabeth cross-posts wedding dance content, including first dances and father-daughter and mother-son dances. She has seen videos reach 150,000 views that she assumed came from Instagram, only to find in the analytics that much of the audience was on Facebook, where the comments came largely from mothers and grandmothers.

​Elizabeth finds the Facebook audience skews older than the Instagram audience. If most of a Reel's engagement is on Facebook, the hottest prospects may be there, and the content strategy can shift to focus on them.

The three pinned posts at the top of an Instagram profile matter more than how the rest of the grid looks. Elizabeth says the perfectly curated, color-coded grid that mirrors a brand's website belongs to 2018. It's still a valid choice for brands that love the aesthetic, but it's no longer required.

​A new visitor typically sees a Reel or carousel, clicks through to the profile, and reads the bio to learn who the account is for, how it can help, and its overall vibe. Then they scan the grid. That first impression forms within about 5 seconds, and the pinned posts shape most of it.

Elizabeth's three-part pinned post strategy fills the top of the grid with a founder or team story, a top-of-funnel next step, and signature content. The three posts can appear in any order.

​Pin a Founder or Team Brand Story: This post shares the heart and mission behind the business, because people buy from people, not products or services. The story can be simple, and an unexpected career change makes it more interesting. Elizabeth's version is a video under 30 seconds long of her dancing in her kitchen, while on-screen text introduces her by name and lists a few quick facts: her current role, her family, and her surprising past career. Brands without a founder on camera can share how the team works or the mission. The post can be a Reel or a carousel.

​Pin a Top-of-Funnel Next Step: This post moves viewers to the next step in the customer journey. Choosing it starts with mapping that journey and answering one question: what's the next step in the business, and how does someone move from Instagram into an ecosystem the business owns? The post shouldn't be an ad or a Canva graphic telling people to grab a free guide, because that doesn't work. Instead, Elizabeth pins an attraction-style Reel that performed well and connects to her offer. Viewers comment a keyword, and DM automation sends them her free Instagram Visibility Jumpstart Kit to grow her email list. She has three possible next steps for her business, and the one she pins depends on what she's marketing that month.

​One of Elizabeth's clients owns a wedding venue in the Hudson Valley and is much more likely to close couples who tour the property. Her pinned attraction-style content invites engaged couples to a private tour: comment TOUR, and she'll send a link to her calendar. Because couples request tours by commenting TOUR, she can track how effective the funnel is. The next step could also be a lead magnet, a discovery call, or an audio download.

​Pin Signature Content: The third post is a piece of content that performed well, that the creator loves, and that quickly shows what to expect from the feed.

Instagram now lets brands add posts they're tagged in to their main profile grid instead of leaving them on the separate tagged tab on the far right of the profile. The grid can still be rearranged, and a tagged post can be removed from the profile without removing the tag from the original post.

​Elizabeth sees this as a significant opportunity for brands that are frequently tagged in customer and client posts or Reels. Tagged posts on the grid serve as social proof and spare the marketer from creating another piece of content that day. The update also helps credit go where it's due, a common frustration when tags land on the wrong company.

​Tagged posts also fit the pinned post strategy. A guest tagged in a post about a high-profile podcast appearance could feature that post on their grid.

Elizabeth's main method for earning more tags is to build tagging into the business's onboarding and offboarding systems rather than relying only on social media. Asking followers in Stories to tag the brand also works.

​In one of Elizabeth's businesses, which teaches couples their wedding dances, couples automatically receive a follow-up form 1 month after their wedding. It asks for their social handles, their Instagram handle, and the handles of their vendors, such as their photographer and videographer. The form automates collecting content from customers and gives the business the handles it needs to tag people and set up strategic collaborations.

​The second approach is to gamify it. A coffee brand, for example, could invite customers to take a selfie with its coffee, post it to their Instagram Story, and tag the brand for a chance to win a prize.

​Elizabeth considers Instagram collaborations an under-leveraged tool. When one brand invites another to collab, the post appears on both grids. Whether the goal is more tags or more collabs, she recommends starting with what's in it for the other person. Her wedding couples want to give credit to the vendor team that made their day happen, and they're excited to share it.

Automatic Reels translations use AI to dub a Reel's spoken words into other languages, and Instagram has expanded the feature to include Japanese, Korean, French, German, and Italian. Elizabeth supports anything that makes content accessible to more people, but setting up translations takes several steps.

​Translations can't be added after a Reel is published. They're set while uploading and editing the Reel by tapping More Options, then Accessibility and Translation, and selecting the languages.

​When Elizabeth tested the feature on a direct-to-camera video in Hindi and Portuguese, the AI altered her mouth movements, so she appeared to be speaking those languages. The feature translated her spoken words, but not the caption or the closed captions she had embedded in the video.

​Elizabeth typically doesn't use Instagram Reels translations due to the extra time and steps involved. Whether it's worth it depends on the target audience. For businesses that sell products that can ship anywhere in the world, translations may be worth the extra steps.

​Pro Tip: Elizabeth adds her own closed captions to every direct-to-camera video, including her Instagram Stories. Captions make content accessible to people who can't hear the audio, and many people still watch Instagram with the sound off.

Elizabeth Marberry, an Instagram marketing strategist, helps small businesses drive more organic leads and sales. Explore her Strut It podcast. Follow her on Instagram.

#34. What Personal AI Agents Like Meta Muse And OpenAI Dots Mean For SEO via @sejournal, @slobodanmanic

In this webinar, learn to rewrite spec-sheet product copy into the words shoppers use, and make product pages readable to AI.

Invalid traffic on AI Max search doubled to 5.28%. Get the channel-by-channel retail benchmarks before Black Friday.

In this webinar, learn to rewrite spec-sheet product copy into the words shoppers use, and make product pages readable to AI.

Join this webinar to choose a channel to test, set a starting budget, and identify results to track before investing more.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Webinar: The Link Building Graveyard: What to Bury & What Still Wins

Meta's Muse and OpenAI's dots reach websites through a connector or a browser. What that means for robots.txt, on-page SEO, and analytics, and what to do now.

Personal AI agents like Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s Dots are splitting the web into two kinds of websites: the ones the agent has a deal with, and the ones it walks into pretending to be your customer.

Muse and Dots both take a request from a person and carry it out on the web. They research a product, fill in a form, and can even add the product to cart and check out. Meta has documented how Muse does this, in detail. OpenAI has published much less about Dots, so most of this article is about Muse, with Dots wherever OpenAI has said something.

I think agents like these will increasingly be how people use the internet. Before the iPhone made mobile browsing a real thing, computers were the only way most people ever interacted with websites. Computers’ share of traffic fell from 98% of worldwide web traffic in January 2010 to under half in 2026, by StatCounter’s count. We are about to see that same thing happen to browsers used by humans, as agent-driven browsers take a share.

The comparing, booking, and reordering a person used to do across 10 tabs can now become one request. Muse is already available to anyone 18 or over in the U.S. and Canada, free for most uses. That is why this matters now, even before anyone knows how many people shop this way.

For SEO teams, the part where the AI agent searches is familiar ground, and so is most of what it reads once it arrives: headings, link text, alt text, and the facts in visible text. The part where it completes the purchase, the named buttons, labeled fields, and checkout, has always belonged to front-end teams.

An agent in a browser finds websites the way a person does, by name or by searching, so the ranking work still applies, even if neither Meta nor OpenAI says which search engine its agent uses. After the agent arrives, page structure decides whether it can read the page, interact with it, and complete the task, whether that is a booking, a form, or a purchase.

For marketers, attribution and audience data assume the visitor is the person. When an agent browses, your analytics will most likely count it as your customer. When it buys through a connector, your website analytics sees nothing, and the order appears only in your platform’s order records.

This article covers which SEO controls still apply to these agents, which ones no longer work, where agent activity shows up in reporting, and what to check on your or your clients’ pages.

Muse’s first tier is the connector. Meta says Muse “launched with dozens of partners along with access to the entire Shopify catalogue,” and is adding Walmart, Best Buy, Sephora, Wayfair, and others. For the connectors it launched with, Meta says it “worked closely with the service provider to integrate their API.” Dots have their own version. OpenAI says: “Through our ecosystem of plugins, they can readily connect to over 4,000 apps.” Any business can build one and submit it for OpenAI’s review.

The browser tier is everyone else. Muse runs, in Meta’s words, “a real up-to-date Chromium-based browser” on “a dedicated secure computer.” OpenAI says dots “can do nearly anything using their own cloud computer, their own browser, and the apps you’ve connected.” Meta’s documentation for businesses building connectors says: “Muse can already browse websites. Your connector should improve on what’s possible in the browser experience through better information, account access, more reliable actions, or fewer steps.” Without a connector, the agent comes to your website in its browser because a person gave it a task, such as buying a shirt from a named designer, and it works with whatever the page shows it.

If you’re on Shopify, the platform can choose your tier for you. Its default setting, “Allow Shopify to manage for me,” is found under Sales channels, then Agentic, enrolls stores in its AI shopping channels. Shopify says products are “shared with Meta by default through Shopify Catalog.” A store on a custom platform is in the browser tier unless it builds a connector.

I first described these two tiers in Meta’s Muse documents in September.

See also: Getting Your Product Into ChatGPT Isn’t The Hard Part, Getting It Through Checkout Is

Most of the controls SEO teams use, from robots.txt rules to crawler allowlists, were built for crawlers that announce who they are. Neither Meta nor OpenAI has published a user agent, request header or signature for the Muse or Dots’ browsers, so there’s no name to put in robots.txt. Meta’s page for website owners lists five crawlers, and Muse is not one of them. OpenAI’s page lists four, and dots are not on that list either.

Meta describes what a website sees when Muse visits it: “When Muse browses the internet, it will appear as your activity, so if you ask Muse to buy a shirt from a clothing designer’s website, that designer might use your visit to show you an ad on Instagram.”

Think of Frank Abagnale in Catch Me If You Can. He walked through airports in a pilot’s uniform, and nobody checked whether he could fly, because the uniform was right. Muse walks into your website wearing your customer’s uniform and, in Meta’s words, “your activity.” Robots.txt only ever worked with names, and this visitor doesn’t give one.

Robots.txt has always been an honor system. The standard says its rules “are not a form of access authorization,” and a crawler follows them only if its operator chooses to.

A name lets a website recognize the visitor and decide what to do with it. For example, Amazon’s robots.txt names 99 agents, and Muse and Dots are absent because there is no name to write. When Amazon blocked Muse in September, it did it through its Conditions of Use, the terms its customers agree to, as I wrote in Amazon’s block of Muse. GeekWire reported Amazon’s three reasons: Meta didn’t tell Amazon that Muse would access its store, the agent doesn’t identify itself when it browses, and it appears to capture and store customer credentials.

Dots have a second route. OpenAI’s documentation tells users: “If a website blocks the cloud browser, ask your dot to try your connected computer.” For ChatGPT’s computer use more broadly, OpenAI says websites “may treat approved clicks, form submissions, and signed-in actions as coming from your account.”

For SEO teams, the decision moves from robots.txt to bot protection, and that is usually someone else’s system. A firewall or your platform’s bot filter sees a Chromium browser on a cloud machine, and it either blocks it or lets it through as a person.

HUMAN Security, as reported by PPC Land, says its bot-detection product can identify Muse, which is a reason to ask your bot vendor whether it can tell if a Chromium browser is operated by a human or an AI agent.

See also: Everyone Is Negotiating With Google While Meta Reads The Web For Free

Meta says Muse’s browsing sub-agent reads a page through the accessibility tree: “The sub-agent, which drives the Browser, sees an accessibility tree snapshot of the page, not the raw DOM.” The sub-agent also “has no ability to run JavaScript in the page context.” Your page’s own scripts still run, because it is a real browser. Muse can’t add any of its own. OpenAI has not published how the dots browser reads a page. Google’s guidance for website owners says browser agents may gather what they need by “analyzing visual renderings (like screenshots), inspecting the DOM structure, and interpreting the accessibility tree.”

The accessibility tree is what screen readers use. The browser builds it from the DOM and keeps, in Chrome’s description, “only elements from the DOM tree that are relevant and useful for displaying the page’s contents in a screen reader.” Each item has a type (button, link, heading), a name, and a state. Design does not appear in it.

Most of what the agent reads is on-page SEO you already do, but the part that completes the transaction is front-end work.

To see what Muse sees, open a page in Chrome DevTools, go to the Elements panel, then the Accessibility tab, and toggle “Show accessibility tree.”

I checked the structured-data row on a real product page from a large store on Shopify, reading the accessibility tree Chrome 154 built for it. Chrome is built on Chromium, and Meta says Muse runs “a real up-to-date Chromium-based browser.” The page’s structured data listed six of the seven sizes in one color as out of stock. A person sees those six buttons grayed out and crossed out, through styling alone. In the accessibility tree there are seven identical buttons, “Select size eight” to “Select size 14,” with nothing marked unavailable. The stock information existed for Google and for human eyes, and Chrome’s accessibility tree, the version Meta says the agent reads, had neither. The tree did catch up after a click: select size nine and an “Out of stock” note and a “Notify me” button appear. An agent learns what a person sees at a glance only by trying each size, one by one.

What a shopper sees: size 8 available, sizes 9 to 14 crossed out. (Image from author, October 2026)

What the agent reads: seven buttons, “Select size 8” to “Select size 14,” with nothing marking six of them sold out. (Image from author, October 2026)

On the same page, the shipping eligibility and the free-shipping threshold appeared only after the page’s scripts ran, so a crawler reading the raw HTML would have missed them.

Meta has not said whether Muse reads structured data by another route, and businesses in the connector tier hand their data over by API without depending on the page at all.

Google Analytics 4 added an AI Assistant channel on May 13 that sorts visits from AI assistants such as ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude without setup. It works from the referrer, so it counts only the second row, and only when the app sends one.

Shopify says its classification of bot sessions in analytics is “designed to be conservative because it’s better to miss some bots than incorrectly label real customers as bots,” so an agent session is more likely to land in the human count. Nobody has published logs showing how GA4 or any bot filter labels these sessions.

Search engines read your website. AI answers cite it. Agents use it. SEO gets a page found, and GEO gets it cited in an AI answer. An agent like Muse finds the page, reads it, then keeps going: It picks the size, fills in the form, and pays. GEO stops at the answer, and SEO’s job used to end at the door. Now the page SEO got found is also the page the agent has to use.

That is also why the shortcuts sold for AI visibility miss this visitor. A markdown version of a page and an llms.txt file are text prepared for a machine to read. They are the AMP page all over again, served to a visitor who came ready to check out. Both leave out the buttons, the forms, and the checkout, which is exactly what an agent came to use. I wrote about this in The Text-Only Version Of Your Website Strips Out The Wrong Layer. Muse reads the page through its accessibility tree, and neither Meta nor OpenAI says its agent reads either file. For an agent that came to buy, markdown is pointless.

I called the full picture Machine-First Architecture when I wrote about it for Search Engine Journal in May. It rests on four parts: identity, structure, content, and interaction. SEO and GEO mostly work on content, and agents need the other three as well.

For leadership, that means four decisions.

Getting cited is what pays today; I can’t argue that. But OpenAI, Google, and Meta, the companies whose AI answers cite you, are each building agents that can also use your website and even buy from you. Stop at the citation, and that agent can quote your website but can’t buy from it.

#37. The Real Value of an Ad Starts With Attention

This post was created in partnership with Viant

An ad can generate millions of impressions, spark controversy, or rack up views. But none of those measures alone reveals whether people watched the ad.

That question drove the conversation at ADWEEK Exchange in New York, part of a national roadshow from Viant and ADWEEK exploring how attention data can help marketers evaluate creative, media investments, and business outcomes.

Yan Liu, CEO of TVision, opened the event by examining the gap between ad exposure and human attention. Americans spend nearly four hours watching television daily, he explained, but only about nine minutes represent actual attention to commercials.

Conventional measurements such as reach, viewability, and completion rates don’t necessarily reveal whether someone was watching.

Liu illustrated the distinction with new data on Coca-Cola’s AI-generated “Holidays Are Coming” commercial, which drew criticism following its 2025 release.

Despite the negative social reaction, the AI-generated ad earned as much real human attention as Coca-Cola’s typical holiday ad, garnering a Creative Attention Score of 101, slightly above Coca-Cola’s average of 100. TVision’s second-by-second measurement also showed attention increasing when the lights turned on and the brand’s logo appeared.

“We’ve been measuring a lot of AI creative these days, and in general, the performance is on par, and sometimes it’s actually better than average creative,” Liu said. “I think that gives us the confidence that the AI creative definitely can help our industry to move forward to capture more attention.”

The findings suggest that negative commentary about AI-generated creative doesn’t necessarily translate into lower audience attention.

For PJ Pereira, co-founder and creative chairman of SILVERSIDE and Pereira O’Dell, the studio involved in producing the campaign, AI presents opportunities to develop and refine creative faster.

“Being able to bring your ideas to life in real time is an incredible gift our generation has been given. But just because you can create something doesn’t mean you know how to make it resonate,” Pereira shared. “Capturing an audience’s attention, making them dream, and creating something that delivers real value for brands takes more than imagination and technology. It takes experience, creative judgment, and a deep understanding of how storytelling and marketing work together. What this data shows us is that when all those disciplines come together, something powerful happens.”

In the brand panel that followed, marketing leaders discussed how attention data could inform media, creative, and business decisions. Moderated by Will Lee, CEO of ADWEEK, the panel featured Danielle Sporkin, SVP of media and marketing services at Ferrero; Dai Kageyama, SVP of marketing at The Hartz Mountain Corporation; Holly Dunn, head of North America investment at Havas Media Network; and Chris Vanderhook, COO and co-founder of Viant.

At Ferrero, brands such as Nutella, Kinder, and Tic Tac have different marketing needs. Sporkin said CTV can build awareness, drive engagement, and support purchases, with retailer data helping connect advertising to conversion.

Hartz, a pet care and supplies manufacturer, faces a related challenge in understanding CTV’s impact. Kageyama said the company uses retail media to reach younger pet owners but has struggled to isolate CTV’s contribution when multiple campaigns run simultaneously.

“It’s very difficult to really understand, OK, what did CTV do for you?” Kageyama explained. To address that challenge, Hartz brought retail media planning, execution, and reporting in-house to make faster decisions.

For Dunn, the growing supply of streaming inventory makes attention data increasingly valuable. “Not every impression is equal,” she noted. She emphasized that the context of an ad and the environment in which it appears matter when making media investment decisions.

Vanderhook emphasized that marketers need attention data they can act on. “They want two things: one, tie it out to outcomes,” he said. “And then two, don’t make me fight internally within the brand to activate on attention.”

He pointed out that automating those decisions would make it easier for marketers to act on attention data and improve campaign performance.

The discussion also turned to how brands are adapting their creative strategies to connect with different audiences as media options multiply.

“We no longer just think about creating a TV commercial. We think about creating a creative umbrella, and then all the different assets that fit underneath that umbrella,” Sporkin said.

She described Ferrero’s approach as precision at scale, developing major campaigns alongside creative tailored to different audiences. For Kinder Joy, that means targeting grandparents with one message and Harry Potter fans with another, for example.

Kageyama also emphasized the importance of emotional authenticity in creative, particularly the moments that resonate with pet owners, such as a dog wagging its tail or a cat eagerly enjoying a treat. He said those moments reflect the content pet owners naturally share on social media.

Tim Vanderhook, CEO and co-founder of Viant, closed the event by outlining how brands can incorporate attention into campaign planning, activation, measurement, and optimization.

“Attention is not the outcome; it is the gate that opens up and allows the downstream outcomes to happen,” he explained.

Vanderhook recommended starting with one campaign, one business KPI, and one quarter, then comparing the results after making changes.

Ashley R. Cummings is a professional freelance writer, specializing in SaaS, marketing, and advertising. She also runs Content Connect, the newsletter and community to help you grow your content marketing muscles.

#38. Google’s News AI pilot expands to over 400 publications, including U.S. local news outlets

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

In December, Google launched its News AI pilot program, which licenses content from select publishers and uses it to test new AI features in Google News. On Thursday, the company announced that the program has added new partnerships, bringing the total number of publications in the pilot to more than 400 worldwide.

At launch, the program partnered with international publishers like The Guardian, El País, The Times of India, and The Washington Post. More publications are now coming on board, including CNN, The Financial Times, Axios, and Forbes.

RELATED ARTICLEDiscover isn’t the only place Google is experimenting with AI-generated snippetsAndrew DeckJanuary 26, 2026As part of the expansion, the program has also added local news publishers across the U.S., including The Post and Courier in Charleston, South Carolina; Oil City News in Casper, Wyoming; the Illinois- and Iowa-based newspaper chain Shaw Media; and the nonprofit newsroom The Texas Tribune.

“People’s information consumption habits are changing, and we want to make sure publishers of all sizes, local newsrooms included, can navigate these shifts,” Brianna Puccini Duff, a spokesperson for Google, said in a statement to Nieman Lab.

Google declined to comment on the exact terms of the deals. However, Duff clarified that the News AI pilot does not operate on a “pay-per-value” model, meaning publishers are not compensated based on how much their content contributes to an AI-generated output. (The pay-per-value model is part of a parallel program that pays publishers for content surfaced in AI Overviews, AI Mode, and Gemini, according to a recent report by Digiday.)

With the News AI pilot, publishers are instead paid to provide content that appears in experimental AI-powered features. That includes “story previews” — in-depth, AI-generated article summaries of recent stories that may show up on a publisher’s Google News page. Here’s a Washington Post example, with a disclaimer noting the copy is AI-generated and “may include mistakes.”

An AI-generated “story preview” on the Google News page for The Washington Post

Another test feature is “audio briefing,” a customizable, AI-generated podcast in the Google News app that stitches together daily headlines. Users can select the topics they’re most interested in hearing about, including “World,” “Gaming,” or “Sports” news. The feature includes citations that link to articles mentioned in the briefing.

#39. Ad Tech Briefing: Can flipping the ad auction wrest control of ad tech from Google?

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit

This Ad Tech Briefing covers the latest in ad tech and platforms for Digiday+ members and is distributed over email every Tuesday at 10 a.m. ET. More from the series →

Last week, one of the industry’s premier fall ad tech gatherings took place, where host Prebid offered a sneak peek of a bold vision: an open internet without Google’s dominance.

Prebid, a non-profit organization that helps publishers monetize with open-source tools, wants to spearhead industry efforts, read: independent ad tech and publishers, to break its reliance on Google, at least in sell-side ad tech.

Of course, that was the main point of debate at the most recent U.S. antitrust trial involving Google, where the presiding judge stopped short of ordering a divestiture of Google Ad Manager assets and instead insisted that it integrate with Prebid’s tech.

Digiday sources claim the proposals are not concrete yet, but the early buds of its proposals were previewed at the New York City event; AdExchanger first reported the pre-brief, and, if realized, it would essentially turn a key piece of programmatic advertising on its head.

Currently, Prebid runs its auction and passes the winning bid to an ad server (usually Google’s GAM), where it competes against demand from Google’s AdX. However, the new proposal reverses that order: ad servers would bid into Prebid, with sources telling Digiday the proposals previewed at the Oct. 13 event are awaiting final sign-off after a period of public consultation.

To many, this may sound like dry details, or “plumbing,” to quote industry parlance, but much of the power in programmatic advertising lies in those details.

Under the model, publishers could potentially access demand from AdX without making Google’s ad server the place where the final competition occurs. Instead of Prebid sending a winning bid into GAM, GAM — and potentially other ad servers — would send bids into Prebid, changing both the sequence of the auction and the information available to the companies participating in it.

For those that need a refresher, Google’s ownership of both GAM and Google’s ad exchange, a.k.a. AdX, has long been at the center of complaints about how the programmatic auction operates.

Under the current arrangement, the winning Prebid price enters GAM before AdX competes against it; reversing the flow would put AdX into an auction controlled outside Google’s ad server, essentially separating AdX and GAM without requiring Google to divest either one.

Prebid is targeting early 2027 for formalization rather than promising an immediate rollout, and Google has not committed to implementing Prebid’s preferred architecture, with sources at the conference claiming Google has already attempted to “claw back” some of the provisions ordered by the courts.

But the proposal illustrates a broader shift underway in ad tech, i.e., companies outside the largest platforms are increasingly trying to move the point at which decisions get made in a bid to insulate themselves from the policy whims of players such as Apple and Google — the recent uproar over Apple’s iOS 27 changes, and the implementations for ad targeting within Safari are a painful reminder of this need, for many.

However, as others have already asked, is this too little, too late, especially as we move to agentic systems?

Elsewhere last week, and away from the mechanics of programmatic advertising, Google offered an olive branch to Madison Avenue’s buy-side, telling advertisers who want more say over automated systems that they can “say goodbye to all-or-nothing channel targeting.”

On Oct. 14, Google rolled out optional channel prioritization and budget allocation controls across Search, Shopping, Performance Max, and Demand Gen. Advertisers can designate higher-priority channels to receive budget first and cap what goes to secondary channels, rather than handing the entire allocation decision to Google’s automation.

Of course, Google is pitching such developments as giving advertisers more levers around the automation of its systems, but those experienced industry observers will have a long list of horror stories as to why continued vigilance is essential.

In summary, these developments point to three parallel trends: Prebid wants to change who runs the auction, Google is giving advertisers more control — or appears to — over how its automated machinery allocates money. Meanwhile, the iPhone-maker can disrupt the whole Apple cart (pun intended) and alter the economics of the whole exercise with a software update.

So, while the mechanics of programmatic advertising may be getting rewritten, the real levers of control remain concentrated at a handful of critical points; Prebid’s latest proposal attempts to chip away at one of them, but whether Google agrees to move with it is another question.

#40. Billion Dollar Boy Group bets B2B is creator marketing’s next big wave

Let Marketing Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The company has acquired three-year-old Creator Authority, a LinkedIn specialist agency, to deepen its B2B services and grow its U.S. footprint.

While the creator economy is maturing in the business-to-consumer realm, BDB Group and Creator Authority see B2B as the next big opportunity. Fifty-nine percent of B2B buyers pay attention to creator content on LinkedIn, besting other social media platforms, per LinkedIn findings cited in the acquisition announcement.

BDB Group will integrate Creator Authority clients including Amazon, Adobe, AT&T, IBM, Dropbox, Gamma, HubSpot, Lovable, Mastercard and Notion. Buying Creator Authority will also expand BDB Group’s U.S. presence beyond an established office in New York. The firms see the West Coast as having a wealth of enterprise, technology and B2B marketers.

BDB Group, which is headquartered in London, more broadly is doubling down on the U.S., East said. The company is looking to top $100 million in global revenue next year following the Creator Authority deal’s close.

Three-year-old Creator Authority will work alongside existing BDB Group offerings, including its namesake social agency, the creator entrepreneur and community platform FiveTwoNine and intelligence solution Companion. Creator Authority co-founder and CEO Brendan Gahan, who previously founded Epic Signal before it was acquired by Mekanism, is taking on the title of senior vice president of B2B, leading market development and new business growth under BDB Group. Creator Authority’s other co-founder, Cassie Jackson, will serve as group account director for B2B, working out of Austin, Texas.

B2B marketing tends to be less flashy than B2C marketing, but creators could give the fustier category a fresh edge. B2B influencers provide brands with access to credible voices in different industries and a way to build trust in professional communities, the announcement said. Creators are also seen as a way to help brands stand out in answers from artificial intelligence chatbots, a channel customers are increasingly turning to for product reviews and recommendations.

B2B creator marketing ranks as the second most popular creator economy investment so far this year, per BDB Group’s survey of 1,000 marketing decision-makers across the U.S. and U.K. BDB Group also indicated that B2B creator marketing delivers better return-on-investment compared to other tactics it assessed.

Search engines made up a smaller share of publisher pageviews in most regions than a year earlier. A lower share alone doesn't show search sent fewer pageviews.

Search engines accounted for 12% of all page views at North American publishers in Chartbeat’s network, based on the data found within the analytics firm’s Q3’26 Audience Report, which was released October 15th, 2026, whereas they represented 21% of page views as reported in the firm’s Q3’25 report.

The two reports contain search engine page view share by region. There are ten total regions included in each report. Nine of these regions have experienced a decrease in the proportion of their total page views generated through a search engine versus last year. Only one of the ten has seen an increase in this number, that being Africa.

Central Asia’s search share decreased by the most, as it dropped from 53 percent down to 33 percent. North America’s share dropped by nine percentage points, as did that of the Middle East. Meanwhile, Africa’s search share increased from 41 percent to 46 percent.

Of those nine points lost for North America, five were lost between the third and fourth quarters of 2025. In fact, North American search share was 16% in Chartbeat’s Q4 2025 report, then 13% for Q2 2026 and 12% for Q3 on the latest chart.

Search’s share of total page views for each region is shown as a bar in the reports’ charts. Search share (or search’s percentage) may go down because search sent fewer page views during that time frame than it had before, because another source or sources sent more page views, or both.

No specific number of page view traffic was given by the takeaway from the Q3 2026 Report on overall traffic. The same exact sentence (“overall traffic to publishers in the Chartbeat network remains steady”) was also written in the Q4 2025 Report. Neither Q3 report gave an indication of how many websites were included in these statistics or whether the same website(s) were analyzed each year. The company, which sells analytics tools to publishers, concluded the Q3 2026 Report with an advertisement inviting users to request a demonstration.

The Q3 2026 Report’s takeaway does not say why search’s share declined, but two older reports have pointed to AI. The Q4 2025 report stated that the decline is “likely a result of AI’s growing impact on search.” The Q1 2026 report indicated that this is likely partly due to how AI affects content discovery.

Chartbeat reports all search engines (such as Google and Bing) as one category within its chart data. Therefore, we cannot tell if the decline came specifically from a drop off in Google Search page views. However, the 2026 Publisher Playbook by Chartbeat, which I covered in September, reports Google Search separately for the entire network.

A search-share benchmark from Chartbeat’s Q3 2025 figure for North America is nine points higher than the same for Q3 2026 in that market area.

Using this comparison for yourself will help you determine if your search share (your ratio of page views that came from search) fits within the traffic mix of other publishers on the same network as you.

The quarterly search shares shown here are a way to get an idea of the percentage of page views that come from search in each region. By tracking your own successive quarterly search-referred page view counts against each quarterly search share, you can see if there have been changes over time, either fewer page views from search, or a shrinking portion of a changing total.

#45. Instagram Chief says stronger AI slop prevention is needed

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The company is actively trying to combat artificial intelligence content replication, Adam Mosseri said in both a weekly Q&A and a separate Threads post.

As Meta continues to promote the use of its evolving artificial intelligence tools, the company is also reckoning with an influx of AI-generated slop and the impact that this low-quality digitally created content is having on creators and users.

Last week, an artist complained that Instagram was allowing users to post AI-generated content that replicates his work. In response, Instagram Chief Adam Mosseri said it’s not practical for the platform to ban AI content, but that the app wants to stop people from using AI to rip off creators’ work.

Mosseri reiterated this sentiment in his weekly Q&A session, posted in a temporary Instagram Story: “We do not throttle the reach of AI content just for being AI content. Our idea with ranking is to connect you with content that you like and not with content that you’re not interested in, whether or not it’s AI. Now, there’s some great AI content and there’s a lot of slop out there, and so, ideally, ranking is doing its thing, but obviously we make some mistakes sometimes. We do want you to know that something was AI if it was generated with AI, and so we’re trying to figure out how to best do that.”

Mosseri said the platform plans to add more labels to AI content and it wants to incentivize creators to voluntarily tag their AI-generated content in order to improve overall transparency.

“To be clear, I am very worried about this trend,” Mosseri said in a recent Threads post about AI content replicating artists work. “We are actively working out what to do, it's just a tricky problem. We already let people make copyright claims against content, and take stolen copyrighted material. That's not enough though, as assume many comedians and dancers haven't gone through the trouble to copyright their material. We need a way to help those creatives without letting bad actors make more fake claims (happens all the time unfortunately).”

The issue highlights the delicate balance Meta is trying to maintain as it promotes its AI tools. The company has invested hundreds of billions of dollars into AI projects, and it continues to prompt users to use those tools to generate images and videos in-stream.

Yet that also leads to these latest concerns. As more users share derivative, copyright-infringing AI slop, it could push creators away from Meta’s apps.

As Mosseri said, this is a difficult problem to solve, but it’s also a problem that Meta itself created.

The end result, then, could be that more creators avoid Meta’s apps, which could have a significant impact on the company’s viability moving forward.

The data is in: News creators and influencers are a major source of news for Americans, especially people under 30. This is the latest edition of Creators of Record, an occasional series of interviews with popular creators about how they do their jobs.

On a September afternoon in Manhattan’s Union Square neighborhood, Shreyas Sinha is sitting on a toilet, wearing a blue suit. Looking into the camera, he asks, “Why is it that everything I’ve been eating this year is giving me diarrhea?”

Sinha is about to link the 2026 cyclospora outbreaks to decades of problems at the Food and Drug Administration. “I’m only allowed to make three diarrhea jokes in this video,” Sinha says. “I live in tyranny.”

The toilet video is one of the tamer stunts that Sinha and his co-creator, Gaurav Srivatchan, have pulled for their YouTube channel, A Show About The News, a weekly deep dive into major business and politics stories (tagline: “Critics are calling it the worst alternative to mainstream media, and those are just the critics I’m related to.”)

In a video about why young people can’t afford to buy homes, Sinha pops out of a cardboard box on the street and takes former New York City mayor Eric Adams to a studio apartment filled with men. Other recent videos include a 45-minute interview on the street with former White House communications director Anthony Scaramucci, an explainer on prediction market ads, and a rap music video on why retirement investments are safer than get-rich-quick schemes.

Sinha, 25, and Srivatchan, 22, met in 2023 when they were students at New York University’s Stern School of Business. They teamed up to make short vertical explainer videos, but those didn’t take off as much as they’d hoped. In 2024, Sinha quit his finance job to pursue A Show About The News full-time, and they transitioned to creating long-form deep dives with a dash of their own humor.

I chatted with Sinha and Srivatchan about how they launched their media careers, how they use humor to explain the news, and what they think business opportunities are for creators today. Our conversation has been edited for length and clarity.

It seemed like everything was [pointing to], “Hey, you should start making short-form videos.” And then Gaurav was like, “Hey, I’m actually really good at editing videos.” We were not really thinking of it as a YouTube channel, but as making short-form stories. At the time, we were called Fifty50 Media. We were all about trying to distill the world into bipartisan perspectives. We eventually started focusing more on deeper-dive stories. We renamed ourselves to A Show About the News. It’s very easy to put out a political opinion that goes viral, but we really wanted to focus on good stories. YouTube and social media are like a theater where you can leave and go watch another movie at any time. That’s the challenge of making videos on the internet.

Sinha: After our first video that got a million views, we were like, “Oh shit, this is it.” And it wasn’t. We added followers, but it wasn’t like we were going to get 100,000 people to come back in the next short. We were competing against the new Frozen movie and The Office and Mr. Beast exploding dynamite in his backyard. Tameez: Tell me more about how the Morning Brew deal happened. Srivatchan: I was in London, studying abroad. I slapped a bunch of logos as watermarks on our old videos [and sent them as] demo reels to news outlets. Sinha: We literally got zero responses…then an opportunity came to make a video for [Morning Brew] and it was a great experience. We made another and another, and then they were like, “You guys should just do this for us.” Srivatchan: Morning Brew provided us access to this office. It’s great to not meet under a lofted bed in Shreyas’ apartment. Sinha: They’re an excellent partner [because] they believe in allowing editorial control to be with the person who makes the video. We’re not going into meetings asking, can we do this topic next week? It’s a very high-trust environment, which, from talking to other people who work at other media companies, is extremely rare. Tameez: You guys both left careers in finance to do this full-time. Sinha: It was an economically stupid decision, but I knew that if I failed now, I would be young enough to start again. It’s easy to have the golden handcuffs of waiting until the right time, but there is never a right time. It was taking a bet on myself and someone who I really trusted. Still, our videos were getting 12 views at that time; it wasn’t as if something took off and it was like, “Okay, this can pay our bills.”

Srivatchan: I had the advantage of being younger. [Shreyas left] a full-time job. I did my summer internship in consulting and got my return offer, but it was a lot less of a risk for me, personally. It obviously helped that we had some backing from Morning Brew. Tameez: Why is making A Show About the News important now? How does it fit into the larger information ecosystem? Sinha: What we do, in the context of where we went to school, is the equivalent of becoming ballerinas. All of my friends are investment bankers in private equity or in consulting. That is the tried and true method [for NYU Stern graduates]. If you tell people, “Hey, I’m not recruiting for banking, I’m thinking of doing consulting,” they look at you like you just said you want to be an art major. When we said we were going to build a media company, it was truly mind-boggling for people. I loved what Fareed Zakaria did, what Ezra Klein did, but my favorite people when I was a kid were Jon Stewart and John Oliver, Hasan Minhaj and Seth Meyers and Conan O’Brien and Nathan Fielder. I knew I wasn’t going to be a great stand-up comedian, I wasn’t going to be a great writer, but maybe I could combine those to make a job out of it. It’s easy to pat ourselves on the back and say there’s a lot of garbage out there. But also, it has never been a better time to be an independent creator. If we both wanted to go into media today, we would be grabbing water for hosts who get paid $60 million a year. Instead, we actually get to put our own ideas out there.

If we both wanted to go into media today, we would be grabbing water for hosts who get paid $60 million a year. Instead, we actually get to put our own ideas out there.

Tameez: Tell me about your workflow, from video ideation to posting. Sinha: We don’t do short-form clips [from longer videos]. We script our shorts. That takes a ton of time. [But] long-form is the priority. It takes much more time, but you really get to have a relationship with the audience. Srivatchan: When it comes to shorts, either Shreyas or I will have something that really interests us for the week. We start scripting it, then we switch the scripts and each of us does a pass on the other’s. Then we revise them and film them. That takes roughly two out of five workdays. We spend the rest of the time on long-form. We’re also doing a weekly livestream to discuss the headlines with the audience and build that audience connection. So our output is two native short-form, one long-form, and one live stream per week.

We’re also doing a weekly livestream to discuss the headlines with the audience and build that audience connection. So our output is two native short-form, one long-form, and one live stream per week.

Sinha: Do we actually have something new to say about it? There’s no point in making a video that someone else has already made.

A lot of people have made videos about how people aren’t having kids anymore. That doesn’t mean we wouldn’t [cover that topic], but we need to have something new to say. In our video, we talked about how governments have spent tens of billions of dollars but it hasn’t resulted in any more babies. We talked about demographic trends and got into studies. We brought in a bunch of 19- and 20-year-olds and asked them why they’re not having more sex. Then we went to a bunch of older people and were like, “So, you guys were doing it hella in the 90s. What’s the secret? Let’s give it to these kids.”

Sinha: We try to be funny, maybe to a deficit. In one of our worst-performing videos, we had a guy come in on an inflatable horse. Gaurav was wearing a Will Smith mask and slapped me. But sometimes it really works. We filmed this thing where we were having a shootout with Abraham Lincoln as he smoked a vape. That did great for us.

I listen to a lot of podcasts of serious, smart people. The way they talk, I’m like, how are you not ripping your hair off right now? How are you not just slamming your head against your desk?

Srivatchan: We have all these sources that we regularly read. For a lot of politics and inside scoops on Capitol Hill, Politico is great. For more niche stories, ProPublica is great. Each source has its own strength. We send stuff to each other all the time.

Once we’re in the research phase of a video, we do everything possible to learn about what the scope of the video is and what sources and articles can fall into that.

Sinha: We do a lot of our own fact-checking. Corrections often occur in the way of Gaurav coming to me and being like, “Shreyas, you moron, you said this and it’s actually this.” Then we record a voiceover, or we change it in the captions, or we just put it up as text.

Sinha: If you go on YouTube right now, high production quality is the expectation. It’s not like when I was young and my favorite YouTubers were clearly filming in their bedrooms. There’s so much money that is being invested into it, which is awesome, but if you want to have authentic relationships with your audiences, you need to do more.

Srivatchan: Earlier this year, TBPN [Technology Business Programming Network] was sold to OpenAI for $100 million. Their whole thing was live-streaming. They didn’t get that many viewers concurrently on their livestreams — everything was clips, targeting a very specific niche — but we saw how they grew through clips.

Sinha: When we started making these videos, I was writing articles on the side and freelancing so that I could pay rent. Eventually, this was able to pay rent.

By no means are we rich. But we really believe in the business model of digital media. It’s important to incentivize people to invest in media that is fact-checked, that is telling stories that are new and not just polarizing or viral for virality’s sake. You can’t ask people to only think of [media] as a charity expenditure or as a nonprofit, because those are the first things that go away when the market goes down, and the first thing people are going to stop cutting checks to if they don’t see the ROI.

We spend most of our time thinking about content, but it’s important to be creative about our business models. We always tell ourselves not to think about ourselves as employees or YouTubers, but to keep reminding ourselves that we’re founders of a startup that is trying to do something for the world.

The prevailing narrative that news media is doing poorly is because news media for generations was run by journalists, and that was fine because they could get cable carrier fees. But the reason they were able to do that was because they had a monopoly. You could only watch CNN, CBS, and ABC News because that’s all you had.

[I asked Sinha and Srivatchan to answer a few final questions via email. Their answers are below.]

Sinha: It’s hard to say what’s legacy and what’s new these days. Morning Brew has never had a TV broadcast or print media arm, but it’s owned by a media conglomerate, Axel Springer. Other news companies, from CNN to The Wall Street Journal, have pretty successful social media presences and journalists who’ve made a name for themselves.

The crisis for news companies that dominated in the 20th century is that they relied on fixed distribution: cable, broadband, local stations, and papers. A random Joe couldn’t get their ideas placed in those, so the competition for viewership was highly limited.

Today, competition is high. Legacy journalists who struggle often blame the changing tides of information consumption, when in reality they’re just struggling to compete for attention. Many have been successful in making the transition, so we don’t think it’s fair to paint all of legacy journalism as having something to learn from news creators. But our message overall would be that traditional news shouldn’t blame consumers for not maintaining their expensive newspaper and cable subscriptions, but instead [should] figure out how to compete and win in this new age.

Srivatchan: For journalists who have been successful in their careers but want to transition to social media, we think they severely underestimate how well-prepared they are to make the jump. They’ve already been writing strong articles and hooks to get people to click. We think journalists underestimate how that skill can translate on a platform like YouTube, where everything is dependent on the packaging that gets someone to click on your video.

Often, when someone from traditional media starts a new Instagram or YouTube page, they make very lo-fi content, talking to their phone with their headphones mic. I think they see influencers doing that and think viewers want authenticity. That works for some people, but our view is that investing in strong production is the baseline expectation on social media.

Instead of seizing the social media opportunity, often, legacy journalism is falling into the trap of liquidating its reputation for more attention and to better monetize its declining assets. It’s partnering with gambling apps — CNN’s partnership with Kalshi, or [Dow Jones’] with Polymarket — and inviting inflammatory internet voices rather than the trusted ones that educate.

#47. Liquid I.V. Swaps Singing Toilets for F1 Precision in Its McLaren Debut

Liquid I.V. is using its partnership with McLaren Racing to position hydration as a performance essential, launching a new campaign featuring Formula 1 drivers Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri.

The “Thirst for More” ad uses a split screen to draw parallels between the testing, measuring, and precision behind McLaren Racing and Liquid I.V.’s approach to hydration science.

Extreme heat during a race can cause dehydration, affecting drivers’ reaction times, focus, and endurance. The ad opens with the line: “It’s another hot one today, stay hydrated out there.” Sports and entertainment agency UEG Worldwide is behind the spot.

It is the first campaign to come out of the electrolyte brand’s multi-year sponsorship deal with the McLaren Mastercard F1 Team, under which it became the team’s official functional hydration partner.

Brittany Shaw, vice president of integrated marketing at Liquid I.V., said the two partners are a natural fit, as both advocate that performance can be continually improved through science and innovation.

“It allows us to take ideas like testing, precision, preparation and endurance out of a lab and put them into a world where those things have very visible consequences,” Shaw said.

The hydration and electrolytes category is increasingly crowded and marketing-heavy. To cut through, Liquid I.V. is banking on “product efficacy and credible science,” Shaw said.

The 30-second spot marks a shift from Liquid I.V.’s Super Bowl commercial, which featured a collection of singing toilets encouraging people to check the color of their urine.

Liquid I.V.’s creative approach has long been to find unexpected ways to challenge category norms, said Shaw.

“Sometimes that means humor and absurdity, like you saw at the Super Bowl,” she said, adding that the McLaren campaign had to be different.

“We’re entering a world built around precision, preparation and relentless optimization, so the creative expression should reflect that,” Shaw continued.

The F1 campaign and broader partnership will be measured on both brand equity and commercial performance. One of the most important things Shaw will be tracking is whether it “strengthens” what Liquid I.V. means to consumers, she said: “As a brand, we’re focused on building stronger associations with product efficacy, credibility and relevance in people’s everyday lives.”

Threaded throughout all of Liquid I.V.’s work is an “attitude” rather than a set aesthetic, Shaw explained.

“Liquid I.V. wants to challenge the expected way hydration is portrayed and make something people actually want to engage with,” she said.

Hannah Bowler is a journalist covering the global advertising and media industry, with a focus on agency networks, brand strategy and the evolving role of creativity in business.

#51. How marketers can optimize their media mix as confidence takes a turn

Let Marketing Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

Only 57% of advertisers are confident their organization has the right media mix, according to Kantar’s 2026 Media Reactions report.

Today’s advertising landscape has put more data in marketers’ hands than ever before, but that doesn’t mean it’s any easier for marketers to determine the most effective media mix.

Fifty-seven percent of advertisers are confident their organization has the right media mix, down from 64% a year prior, according to Kantar’s 2026 Media Reactions report. Further, 51% of advertisers feel they are getting actionable intelligence to support their marketing goals.

Only half of advertisers this year are confident that they have the right balance between brand building and performance marketing. Comparatively, 60% of advertisers felt confident in that balance in 2025. Despite the uncertainty around their media strategies, marketers are still placing fresh bets on areas including artificial intelligence and creators.

“I don't think marketers have lost their faith in media,” said Jeff Greenspoon, CEO of Americas at Kantar. “I think it’s that the media ecosystem is fragmenting, changing and probably outgrowing the way decisions have been made for the last 25 years.”

Kantar’s annual Media Reactions report is based on surveys of 806 senior marketers globally and 23,452 consumers in 33 markets. The surveys were fielded from May 25 to July 21 and July 3 to Sept. 10, respectively.

Many advertisers struggle to understand how to build long-term brand affinity without sacrificing short-term sales, but multichannel marketing offers the opportunity to achieve both, Greenspoon explained. Between 2020 and 2025, 43% of campaign performance was attributed to channels working together, up from 18% pre-2014, per Kantar.

Still, cross-channel measurement remains a challenge, with various platforms and measurement tools making it harder to clearly determine what works and what doesn’t.

“Media, creative, brand, performance, and commerce all have different dashboards. They have different partners, and those partners are incentivized differently,” Greenspoon said. “[They] are measuring the instruments and not the orchestra.”

Advertisers need to ensure their media partners provide evidence of why and how their inventory will help the brand reach the agreed-upon business outcomes, while also providing data that can be easily combined and analyzed, Greenspoon said.

Many advertisers are actively experimenting with new strategies and platforms. Greenspoon pointed to the impact AI is having on brands: Nearly two-thirds of marketers anticipate generative AI will play a major role in brand recommendations and 75% plan to increase their investment in AI assistants next year. However, consumers remain skeptical, with only 23% trusting AI’s recommendations.

“If you look at the number of people that are using it across the journey, that is continuing to increase,” Greenspoon said. “The more it gets used, the more consumers get comfortable with it, and the more they begin to trust it.”

Brands are also refining their creator strategies with a focus on smaller creators. Marketers next year plan to boost their spending on micro- and nano-creators by 66% and 61%, respectively, compared with increases of 42% and 48% for mega- and macro-creators, per Kantar.

“The creator with the largest audience is not going to be the creator who makes your brand the most meaningful,” Greenspoon said. “The shift we’re seeing is from borrowing fame through some of the bigger influencers to trying to earn relevance amongst a smaller audience, but in a way that will actually move the needle for either brand-building or sales.”

Despite an increasingly fragmented media landscape, none of these diverse channels work in isolation — from creators to AI to retail media, each channel can reinforce the other. Once marketers can align their goals and measurement tools to reflect that, they will likely be more confident in their media mix.

“We have to look at portfolio-level measurement, where we look at what each channel does independently, and then determine the value that is created across channels and how that value changes and compounds over time,” Greenspoon said.

#52. AI Landing Pages: From Project Plan to Published Page

Wondering how to use AI to build landing pages that convert without hiring a developer or designer? Want a step-by-step workflow for creating landing pages with ChatGPT and Codex, from the first project plan to a live, published page?

​In this article, you'll discover how to plan, design, write, host, and connect AI-built landing pages using ChatGPT, Codex, GitHub, and Vercel.

The biggest misconception Dan Sanchez sees among marketers using AI is that productivity means progress. Most marketers now use AI, and many use several AI tools, so output has gone through the roof. But more output doesn't always produce more revenue or move the right projects forward. Dan says it's easy to chase shiny ideas. He can spend a long walk dictating new concepts to ChatGPT, yet none of them touch the work that's actually slowing down growth.

​Every company is in one of three places: growing and struggling to keep up with that growth, plateauing and trying to break through, or declining and trying to reverse the slide. In all three cases, the job is to find the idea that fixes the problem. That might be new packaging, a new offer, a new message, a new front-end and back-end offer combination, or restructured pricing.

​No one knows the answers to those questions in advance. The only option is to test them, and nearly all of that testing now happens digitally on a landing page. A poll on social media can hint at interest, but people really vote by subscribing with their email address or making a small purchase, and both require a landing page.

​Dan found that he could only test new offers as fast as he could set up landing pages. Writing the promotional email with Claude was quick. But even with a background in graphic design, HTML, CSS, drag-and-drop builders, and WordPress, a single landing page and everything that goes with it took him four to eight hours and sometimes two days. With AI, he now builds landing pages faster, and he says the results are better than anything he could design before. That speed shortens the feedback loop on every idea.

An AI-built landing page is rarely just one page. Before building anything, Dan recommends roughly mapping the entire campaign around it.

​Define the Offer and the Goal: The starting point is what's being tested and what visitors should do on the page. The idea might be a new package, a different price, or a new lead magnet that feeds the sales team or nurtures leads before they see an offer. The plan needs the main problem the page solves and the offer that solves it.

​Choose the Copy Approach: The next decision is which copywriting frameworks will shape the page. Marketers who don't know the common frameworks can ask ChatGPT to recommend them. Some copy can be drafted ahead of time.

​Plan the Form: The form's requirements come next. It could be a multi-stage form, a single form, an email-only field, or a purchase.

​Plan the Thank-You Page: Dan says this is where many marketers leave money on the table. Visitors are at their most excited right after they complete the action, so the thank-you page is the place for another offer, such as an upsell or a downsell, or a survey that captures more information as they enter the email list. If the funnel asks for more, there may be additional pages.

​Plan the Follow-Up: The plan should also cover whether an automated email sequence follows the signup. Even a simple three-part email sequence needs planning, along with what happens when someone doesn't take the next step. A multi-stage funnel may need several email sequences, each triggered by where a person drops off.

​Mapped this way, a landing page becomes a full campaign. Dan points out that assigning a three-page funnel with two automated follow-up sequences to a team used to take a long time. That's the scope AI can now handle.

Before moving into a coding tool such as Codex or Claude Code, Dan brainstorms and plans the entire project on the chat side of ChatGPT or Claude.
