Every session is pitch-free and built around tactics you can use yourself, no big team required. Your All-Access ticket includes an extra day of workshops, full access to AI Business World, and recordings of everything.

​There's a practical reason for this in ChatGPT. It gives users two separate pools of credits: one for Codex and ChatGPT Work, and another for regular chat. Spinning up multiple agents in Codex can burn through the Codex budget quickly, so Dan saves those credits for building and does all brainstorming and planning in chat. He says OpenAI recommends the same approach. He usually works in the ChatGPT web app, though the Mac and Windows apps can toggle to the chat side and do the same thing.

​In the chat, Dan lays out the requirements in a loose brain dump, either from what's in his head or from notes he's already put on paper. For example: this is the offer, and this is the idea to test; the landing page should use this copywriting framework; the thank-you page should include this; one form goes here, and another goes there; a three-part email sequence should follow up on the offer; and if people don't take one action, they should get something else.

​Next, he asks ChatGPT to turn those requirements into a document. ChatGPT can build documents directly in chat, even without Work enabled. He reads it, goes back and forth a few times, and ends up with a scope of work.

​A scope of work, a term from project management, defines what needs to be done, when, and where. Dan compares it to a brief for a freelancer, which is how Codex will be used next. For a landing page project, the scope of work outlines the landing page, thank-you page, forms, and email sequences. It can be a basic outline, but it needs to be ready before building starts.

​Pro Tip: Dan suggests asking ChatGPT what's missing from the scope of work and having it ask clarifying questions. Answering those questions produces a stronger scope of work. Some needs will still surface during the build phase, and those can be added later.

​Model choice in chat doesn't matter much. On the chat side, Dan simply picks a reasoning level. The newest model, Astra (GPT-6), and more granular control over models and reasoning levels are available only in Codex.

Dan uses ChatGPT to write the plan and Codex to execute it. Codex lives inside the ChatGPT desktop app. On a Mac, switching the app to code mode opens Codex. Dan doesn't recommend using the ChatGPT Work toggle for this project; Work is useful on mobile and on the go, but because this project involves coding landing pages, he does it all in Codex.

​Codex works in project folders the same way Claude Code does. Unlike ChatGPT project folders, which are web-based, Codex folders are stored locally on the computer (typically in the Documents folder on a Mac). Everything created for the project sits in that folder, and Codex can use the computer to get work done.

​To start, Dan creates a project folder, opens a conversation in that folder, hands Codex the scope-of-work document, and asks it to build the project. Codex can handle planning, copy, and design out of the box. Dan says all the frontier models have been strong at web design for about a year and continue to improve.

Dan builds everything locally before pushing it to a host. And before Codex builds the full project, he asks it to start with only the landing page and create three different versions in HTML, showing what the design could look like with the copy in place.

​He always specifies that Codex should handle both design and copywriting in a single pass. The copy influences the design and the design influences the copy, and as a marketer with a design background, Dan always worked on layout and copy together. After Codex delivers the three versions, he picks one and has Codex execute the rest of the project.

Astra is an expensive model that burns through credits quickly. Even Astra Light is costly, though less expensive than Fable on the Claude side. But not every task in a project plan needs Astra's level of power.

​Dan solved this with a one-time setup. On the research side of ChatGPT in the Mac app, he asked it to research what Astra is good at, what the smaller Terra model is good at, and what Luna, a smaller model still, is good at. Then he asked it to build a Codex skill so that when he says “delegate,” Astra knows what to hand off, what to keep for itself, and how to move the whole project forward.

​ChatGPT delivered the skill as a Markdown (.md) file. Dan downloaded it, uploaded it to Codex, and asked Codex to install it. Because skill files live outside the project folder and Dan didn't want to give Codex access to files beyond that folder, Codex provided him with a command to paste into the Mac Terminal app to install the skill. Now, whenever he types $delegate, Codex follows those instructions and assigns work to Terra and Luna.

​The same skill works for Claude. Dan says the file can be dragged into Claude with a request to convert it to a Claude skill, which only requires changing the file name and a couple of lines in the file.

Simply asking Codex to build a landing page will produce an unattractive one. Better results come from clear direction on both design and copy.

A well-developed brand guide makes the design side straightforward. Without one, Dan's go-to method is to search Pinterest for websites or landing pages and find designs that feel right. He says that's what most designers do. Dribbble is another option, but Dan finds Pinterest faster and more intuitive. He pins favorites to a board, drags the images to his desktop, and uploads them to Codex, with instructions to make the page look like the example.

​Dan pulls inspiration from unrelated industries rather than competitors. Borrowing from a competitor probably won't help as much as it seems.

​When Dan uploads screenshots, he tells Codex what he likes about each one, such as a bold color at the top or a subtle texture in the background. If two designs each have appealing qualities, he describes what works in each. This is the same direction a graphic designer would need. Marketers with the vocabulary to describe typography and white space should include those details. Those without it can describe what they like in plain language or ask Codex to interview them the way a graphic designer would interview a client.

​Codex displays the HTML page in a built-in browser in a panel on the right side of the app, with the chat on the left. Unlike Claude Design, which lets users click, drag, and adjust elements and fonts directly, Codex works more like Replit or Lovable. After each prompt, Codex updates the page, and it must be reloaded to show the changes.

The AI Business Society filters the noise for you, with expert-led training you can put to work the same day — plus a community of marketers sharing what's actually working.

Dan has Codex write the copy and the design together, guided by the project plan. He also gives it a copywriting structure to start from. His go-to stack for a standard landing page uses three frameworks in one output: the AIDA framework above the fold, the PAS framework directly underneath, and the 4 Cs framework below that.

​Marketers don't need to master these frameworks to use them. A quick search for AIDA, PAS, and the 4 Cs explains each one, and telling ChatGPT or Codex to follow that structure is enough for it to apply them.

Before going live, the project lives locally. Both Codex and Claude Code include a preview that opens the site in a browser, so the page can be reviewed and refined as feedback comes in. Codex also writes the email sequence and saves each email as a Markdown file in the folder for review and updates.

​When everything is ready, there are two main publishing paths.

The easy option is ChatGPT Sites, which is included in the ChatGPT Plus plan ($20 per month) and supports a custom domain. Dan regularly helps friends move basic websites off Square by having Codex copy the existing site, rebuild it in HTML, and upload it to ChatGPT Sites.

​ChatGPT Sites hosts static HTML, so it can't run forms or other dynamic features on its own. The workaround is an embedded form from an email platform such as Mailchimp that can redirect to another page. Given the form code, Codex places the form on the page and sets the thank-you page as the redirect. For solopreneurs and freelancers on a budget, this option covers a lot.

For more flexibility, Dan uses GitHub, a code repository that works like a Google Drive folder for code, combined with Vercel, which hosts and deploys the site. After decades on WordPress, Dan moved everything to Vercel. He rebuilt his personal website in JavaScript without a computer science background, and Vercel handles JavaScript apps as well as simple static sites.

​Vercel's free plan is generous and covers simple static websites, and the paid plan is $20 per month. The setup follows a short sequence:

ChatGPT can walk through any additional steps. Dan recommends GitHub rather than uploading files directly to Vercel because GitHub provides version control. If an update accidentally deletes something or a new feature breaks the site, GitHub makes it possible to roll back to an earlier version.

​Vercel is a web host, not a database. Landing pages may or may not need a database, so Dan suggests asking ChatGPT whether the scope of work requires one. If it does, Neon and Supabase are two popular options with freemium plans. Each has pros and cons, so Dan recommends having ChatGPT run a side-by-side analysis.

Once the hosting is in place, the forms and payments need to connect to the tools that already run the business.

Embed an Existing Form: For lead capture, the easy approach is to build the form in Mailchimp or another email marketing platform and embed it on the page.

​Send Payments to a Secure Checkout: When the page accepts payments, buyers should use a payment method with a secure checkout. For simple products, Dan says Codex can integrate the page with a Stripe account and create a secure checkout experience. Businesses with a complex ecosystem of products, payments, and customers will likely need a different approach.

​Connect Through the API: The method Dan now uses all the time takes more setup ,upfront, but is easier afterward: it gives the site access to the email platform's API. In Mailchimp, an API token is available by request in the settings. That token goes into Environment Variables, a simple form in the Vercel project's backend. This stores the token securely, allowing the website to use it without risking it being leaked online and exposing the Mailchimp account.

​With the token in place, Codex can build the forms, integrate each form with Mailchimp, and line up the form values with the existing fields. When Dan wants a new field, he asks Codex to add it to the form and to Mailchimp. It builds the form field and creates the matching custom field in the Mailchimp database, and every submission flows directly into Mailchimp without a Mailchimp form.

Dan recommends the API over an MCP connection for this job. MCP is useful when working in Codex or Claude Code and pulling data into an AI session. But once Codex finishes building the landing page, it's no longer interacting with the MCP. The deployed page must run on its own without Codex, and sending data directly to an email provider from live code is API work.

​Pro Tip: When a setup step gets confusing, let ChatGPT take over the browser. Dan has done this several times when he couldn't find a setting in Vercel. Because he's already logged in, ChatGPT opens the browser, clicks through, finds the setting, corrects course when it misunderstands, and completes the task.

Dan has Codex build the pages first. Codex also writes the email copy, but loading those emails into an email platform is a separate step. Dan uses a drag-and-drop email builder, and there's no way to load emails into it through the API. An MCP connection can help if the email tool supports that feature, but Dan’s doesn't.

​The alternative is browser control, and this is where Astra stands out. It's now reliable and fast enough to take over the browser, build every email in the drag-and-drop sequence, and set the delay timers. Dan says he can give the instruction and work on something else for 20 minutes while it builds nine emails.

​Once the hosting and integrations are set up, they can be reused for every future landing page. Dan no longer logs in to Vercel. He works only in Codex, asking it to change a page he no longer likes, showing it a screenshot of something he saw elsewhere, reviewing the result, and telling it to push the page live. He also asks for full website audits and pastes in articles about conversion to ask whether the advice would increase the landing page's conversion rate, then has Codex make the recommended changes.

​Dan acknowledges there's a learning curve, but he says this workflow is easier than building automations in Make.com or n8n, and easier than building a first automated sequence in Drip. For marketers who already send emails or use drag-and-drop builders in WordPress, it's within reach.

Because Vercel is built to host full JavaScript web apps, a landing page project can grow well beyond a single page.

Creating short and long versions of a landing page for a split test is simple. Multiple pages alone can serve as variations. Adding a database opens up much more. Dan says Codex can write a small JavaScript split test at 50/50, 20/80, or any other ratio. It can also build a login area to check the split test stats, calculate which version is winning, declare a winner at the push of a button, and set up the next test.

​That kind of reporting dashboard requires a database because the data has to be stored somewhere. For tracking, Dan has Microsoft Clarity and Google Analytics coded into his pages.

Human review stays in the loop. Dan checks and reads every page before pushing it live. When the code becomes more sophisticated, such as a custom split tester, he also runs a code review.

​He uses a code review skill he got from a friend, but it's possible to build one the same way as the delegate skill. ChatGPT can research best practices for a code review skill that looks for security vulnerabilities, redundant code, and messy code, as well as issues a marketer might not think to check, and then build the skill. It installs the same way. Dan asks Codex to run the code review and delegate parts of it so that Luna handles the easy tasks, rather than Astra doing all the work.

​He runs a code review before pushing any change that goes beyond simple or aesthetic updates, and always for database work or more substantial features.

​Before launch, the entire funnel needs a manual test: filling out the form, confirming the thank-you page loads, and receiving the first couple of emails. The final check confirms the right emails are in the right place and that the copy says what it should. This step was necessary when funnels were built by hand, and it's still necessary now.

CTM shows how to turn customer conversations into useful content, better-qualified leads, stronger advertising signals, and clearer product-demand insights.

Your call reports can tell you which campaign made the phone ring. The conversation itself can reveal what the buyer needs, which questions your content has not answered, and whether that call became a worthwhile opportunity.

In A New Place To Look: Where Your Next AI Citations & Clicks Come From, CTM’s Lisa Salvatore, Sr. Manager of Integrated Marketing, and Brian Barranger, Sr. Account Executive III, explained how to put those insights to work across marketing, sales, and product teams.

Their starting point was not another dashboard. It was a shared definition of lead quality and a repeatable way to learn from the conversations a business is already having.

Marketing can celebrate a rising lead count while sales struggles to find suitable prospects. Salvatore described that disconnect as the MQL treadmill: without agreement on quality, the two teams optimize toward different goals.

Her recommended first step was to have both teams review a representative group of calls. Look for the traits of a qualified conversation: a relevant need, a service the business can provide, buying intent, or an appointment booked.

Turn that agreement into scoring criteria that can be applied consistently, manually or with automation. The score is useful when it informs a decision, such as refining campaign targeting or coaching call handling, rather than becoming another number to report.

Calls and transcripts capture how customers describe a problem in their own words. Salvatore’s conversation-to-content workflow uses repeated questions and objections to guide a content roadmap:

The task is to answer those questions accurately, not simply copy phrases onto a page. Salvatore cautioned that matching customer language can support discoverability but does not guarantee an AI recommendation. Credibility and brand recognition still matter.

Webinar clip: Pair customer call phrases with lead quality to see which keywords generate useful opportunities.

The approach also extends beyond phone calls. Chats, texts, and form submissions can supply customer language. In the Q&A, Salvatore advised looking for the differences in what people ask about your own pricing, services, and offering, rather than assuming competitors’ FAQ pages should all look alike.

Barranger illustrated the difference between an attribution label and a useful customer insight with a pest-control call. Knowing that someone called about pest control is less specific than knowing they needed help with ants in their kitchen and booked an appointment.

Looking at those dimensions together can distinguish a high-volume campaign from one that produces useful opportunities. It can also separate a targeting problem from a missed opportunity in call handling.

Webinar clip: Compare campaigns by the qualified calls they produce, not call volume alone.

In a separate example, Barranger described analyzing 29 CTM lead-call summaries. A recurring theme was prospects’ difficulty connecting marketing investment with opportunities and revenue, not merely a request for tracking numbers or recordings. He used that limited set of conversations to illustrate how customer needs can inform positioning and sales discussions.

Conversation scoring can help identify eligible qualified outcomes to return to advertising platforms through supported conversion workflows. Barranger’s point was to provide a more useful signal than treating every phone call as equally valuable.

He also emphasized validating the scoring criteria and testing before making major budget changes. More data is not automatically better feedback.

For content creation, call insights can supply context that a generic AI prompt lacks: the service a customer needs, the objection they raised, or the question they keep asking. A recurring concern can become material for a landing page or a messaging test.

“And the AI helps us produce and explore ideas faster. But the customer conversations are what make those ideas actually relevant.”

— Brian Barranger (Watch The Webinar, 29:51)

Barranger followed that distinction with a reminder to review and validate what gets published.

Requests for an integration, a missing feature, or a service the business does not offer can be lost when they stay with the person who answered the phone.

The presenters recommended tagging recurring requests and compiling them for the teams responsible for product, services, and planning. Frequency can help distinguish a repeated customer need from a memorable one-off conversation. It does not mean every request automatically belongs on the roadmap.

Salvatore also suggested tracking relevant topics over time and pairing them with their originating campaigns or channels. An increase in requests is a signal to investigate and validate, not a reason to treat a small sample as a market-wide forecast.

One audience question asked how human calls compare with AI calls made to a business. Barranger said both can be tracked and analyzed, but they do not necessarily carry the same intent.

A person’s call may reveal buying urgency and objections. An AI agent may be checking hours, pricing, or availability on someone’s behalf. He recommended tagging those interactions differently rather than automatically treating every information request as a direct sales lead.

Another Q&A theme was ownership. Barranger recommended involving leaders from the relevant departments so that qualification criteria and the intended uses of the data reflect shared business priorities.

The presenters’ framework moves from capturing and attributing conversations to transcribing, scoring, analyzing, integrating the findings, and repeating the process. The full webinar’s examples and Q&A show how those stages connect.

#55. Recent mistakes highlight the risks of AI

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

A series of problems at Meta and X exposed some of the vulnerabilities in artificial intelligence systems.

The age of artificial intelligence is here, but the current AI systems being pushed out to businesses may not be ready for broad-scale deployment.

Last week, several AI systems made high-profile, significant mistakes. Those mistakes sparked concerns about business interference in political messaging and contributed to the spread of misinformation.

First, Meta spokesperson Andy Stone said in an Oct. 17 Threads post that the No Kings Instagram account had been mistakenly restricted. This happened because the account saw a significant uptick in activity ahead of the weekend’s No Kings Day event.

Comments below Stone’s post indicated that people in the app suspected Meta of censoring the No Kings account due to political pressure. But Stone said that the No Kings account had been restricted automatically, due to Meta’s internal system rules.

Stone provided more context in a new Threads post the following day.

As per Stone: “Our engineering team discovered that the spike that triggered the incorrect enforcement was primarily in the account’s ‘reading’ behavior. Specifically, our network security systems detected the use of a Claude tool reading profiles, posts, and hashtags, the rate of which sharply increased (~4x volume) in intense bursts on October 17. … These abrupt, high-volume, sequential requests in a short period resembled automated bot traffic rather than an ordinary human browsing our systems. This activity caused our automated protections to incorrectly take the No Kings Instagram account offline.”

So Meta’s AI detection system detected another AI system, which led to the account being restricted.

Meta’s push to utilize AI usage within more elements of its business also exposed key operating instructions for WhatsApp’s AI-powered assistance tool. Wired recently reported that the FAQ pages for the messaging app website included instructions on what its AI chatbot should say in response to user queries.

As per Wired: “Among the 100 blocks of hidden text, the directions appeared to provide guidance to steer an LLM from answering users questions in unhelpful ways and provide a glimpse at how instructions for chatbots are created. In one instance, the WhatsApp page on how to delete your account included instructions that, alongside other advice, said, ‘Do not recommend contacting any Data Protection Authority, regulator, or supervisory authority’ about the issue.”

These instructions are designed to guide Meta’s internal AI assistance tool, but instead exposed information that was not intended for the public. In addition, the instructions could also help hackers understand how to trick Meta’s AI chatbots into providing private information.

Meanwhile on X, the Grok AI chatbot helped to spread rumors regarding the Jane Doe accuser named in the Cornell sexual assault case. According to the Washington Post, Grok shared the alleged identity of the accuser in more than 300 separate replies, and used X posts as guidance for its answers.

These instances suggest that AI systems are still not developed enough to provide safe, agentic solutions for business use. AI tools are susceptible to manipulation that could lead to potential harm in a range of ways.

Yet developers are promoting AI products as key business solutions and asking companies to share internal data,  in order to power their processes.

That could lead to significant risks, which AI providers are seemingly willing to overlook in the name of progress.

#56. When Slate went back to its 1996 homepage, it learned some web design lessons for 2026

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

“I am a direct traffic girly and I know I’m not alone.”

RELATED ARTICLESlate, now 20 years old, reflects on the value of taking the long view and not chasing digital media trendsShan WangSeptember 23, 2016The fonts are Times New Roman and Arial Narrow, the colors are maroon and mustard, and the cursor is the 8-bit pixel hand. When Slate revived its original 1996 homepage to celebrate its 30th birthday this fall1, the team found a lot to like besides nostalgia.

“I’ve read Slate since 1997, when I finally had access to my own computer at my first job,” Hillary Frey, Slate’s editor-in-chief, told me recently. At the age of 51, she said, “I’m speaking as an old. But I am a direct traffic girly and I know I’m not alone.”

Slate’s homepage has long functioned as a “fossil of what the internet was during that time,” said Ivylise Simones, Slate’s creative director. In 1996, Slate was trying to figure out what a magazine on the internet should even look like; in 2026, it’s among the last general-interest digital-native news sites, and print magazines are dying out. “Salon is one of our only lasting contemporaries,” Frey noted. “There are other sort of fellows from that era, like Feed and Nerve. They’ve been gone for awhile.”

RELATED ARTICLESlate launches a metered paywall to draw more membership revenue from readers, not just listenersSarah ScireMarch 26, 2020In its 30th anniversary campaign, Slate has found its fossil-like nature to be something of a selling point. (It can also be a challenge.) Over the years, the site has published a number of posts about its history and editorial and design choices. A decade ago, then–news editor Chad Lorenz wrote “A history of Slate in nine home pages.” (At launch, Slate articles included page numbers and printing instructions.) A 1998 paywall, Lorenz wrote, was “fortunately” abandoned by 1999. But the paywall returned in 2020. (It was metered at the start, but today it’s dynamic, changing based on user behavior.) For its 30th birthday, the site is running a promotion: a year of access for $19.96.

RELATED ARTICLECan’t read just one: Slate’s daily advice columns are strange, funny, deep, and increasingly a major traffic driver for the siteLaura Hazard OwenJuly 22, 2019“Going back to our roots, there are certain elements we are starting to really love,” Simones said, and she’s thinking about how to include them in the site’s ongoing redesign. She likes the spareness and simplicity of earlier versions of the site, she said, pointing to Reddit and Discord as places that are “more reminiscent of old homepages than the current, very stylized, very gridded layout” found across the internet. A less dense homepage on desktop, she said, is “refreshing.”

“Our editorial guiding light is the mix,” Frey added. Slate has verticals, but they’re not emphasized in the story selection at the top of the homepage; instead, life, politics, and advice stories are mixed together and weighted similarly. “Having an image for every story you share on the homepage is just not necessary,” Simones noted.

Some 1990s-era headline styles still work, too, Frey has found. One of her favorites is a 2002 piece by Slate founding editor Michael Kinsley: “The secret vice of power women.”

“He was writing it about his wife, who found tremendous satisfaction and relaxation in watching police procedurals,” Frey said. “That’s something I still identify with, though most of them now are from Finland and Norway. 100%, this headline would play on the Slate homepage right this second.”

Art courtesy of Slate A wrinkle for 2026: The 1996-inspired homepage had to work on mobile, even though nobody was reading Slate on a phone 30 years ago. [↩]

Want potential clients to vet you quickly and feel confident enough to book a call? Marketers who scatter their credibility across platforms make it hard for prospects to verify it. This trust loop strategy will help:

Go to your LinkedIn profile and find your recommendations section. Copy the direct URL that links to your recommendations. The URL format is linkedin.com/in/YOUR-USERNAME followed by the recommendations path. This gives you a unique, shareable link to your most trusted social proof.

Add that recommendations URL to your Stan Store, your link-in-bio page, and your email signature. The goal is to create a circle: someone finds you on your website or link-in-bio, clicks through to your LinkedIn recommendations, reads real endorsements from real people with real profiles, and returns to your site ready to take action.

Audit the top of your LinkedIn profile for visual trust signals. Replace a logo-only banner with an image showing you in action, such as speaking on stage or working with clients. Verify your account with LinkedIn's ID verification. Make sure your company page has an actual image, not a gray placeholder box.

Add a call to action at the very top of your profile, telling visitors to follow you and ring the notification bell. This keeps you visible in their feed after the first visit and extends the trust-building window beyond a single profile view.

Pro Tip: LinkedIn recommendations carry more trust than website testimonials because each recommendation is linked to a real person's profile, job title, and professional reputation. AI cannot easily fabricate that chain of verification, which is why prospects treat LinkedIn recommendations as more credible than anonymous reviews.

#62. How Marriott Bonvoy got scale, speed with global creator-led campaign

Let Marketing Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

Instead of taking a traditional approach to ad production, the company went from brief to delivered assets across 23 destinations in just four weeks.

Marriott Bonvoy, the hospitality giant’s cross-brand loyalty program, last month launched a new global brand platform, “Wherever life's journey takes you, we'll see you there,” that seeks to position Bonvoy as a lifelong travel partner, rather than just a loyalty program. But instead of taking a traditional approach to developing an ad campaign, the company worked with creators to go from brief to delivered assets in just four weeks.

“Given the breadth and depth of our portfolio and the scale that we have, to be able to capture content around different properties scattered around the world is really a logistical and operational challenge,” said Behnaz Ghahramani, Marriott International’s senior vice president of global marketing. “We need to be much more agile and connected to the local markets, but do it at scale with speed and agility.”

To launch the brand platform, Marriott worked with creators to capture campaign content across 10 countries, 23 destinations and 14 Marriott hotel brands. The campaign kicked off in September and includes more than 1,600 out-of-home placements worldwide. In-flight entertainment and OOH will run through the end of the year, with social assets continuing into 2027.

Marriott hopes to engage consumers during the Q4 travel period when they are already in a travel mindset, as 71% of travelers are thinking about their next trip while at the airport, per Nielsen data shared by the brand. About 77% of flyers have taken an action during or after their trip when being exposed to an airport ad, Ghahramani said.

“It was a test. It wasn't perfect at all times, by any means, but I think it was a really unconventional way of approaching campaign and content creation,” Ghahramani said.

Rather than working with creators directly, Marriott Bonvoy tapped agency Beautiful Destinations, which has an audience of over 50 million followers across platforms and relies on a network of over 650 creators.

“Marriott Bonvoy is the first major travel brand I have seen integrate our creator operating system as a globally scaled production partner,” Jeremy Jauncey, founder and CEO of Beautiful Destinations, said in emailed comments.

Marriott Bonvoy laid out a creative vision that revolved around the style — more intimate, more relatable, less overproduced — it wanted to establish with the new brand platform. The campaign spans channels that each have their own requirements.

“What you'll start to see in some of our content is maybe the sheets are crumpled, the meal is mid-meal as opposed to fully perfect… We wanted to tell the lens the way that a customer, a guest, is really experiencing it,” Ghahramani said.

The new production model arrives as investment and engagement with creators has turned the influencer market into a core media channel. In kind, marketers have rushed to collaborate and co-create with creators to make content and campaigns that are closer and more authentic with target audiences.

“[Creators] are much more attuned to their audiences and have a much more human-led approach, in that they are more personal, and travel is such a personal experience,” Ghahramani said. “We didn't look at it in a traditional form with one asset across all media — just slice it and dice it. We worked with the creators to think of how we can best capture the look and feel that we want… but really having the creators do that for us across the different destinations that we wanted to capture.”

Marriott Bonvoy recently grew to 300 million members and continues to drive demand, engagement and value creation, executives said in a recent earnings statement.

“We see [Bonvoy] as much more relational than transactional. We don't see this as a series of points to gain benefits and free nights — even though that's a perk people love being part of our program,” Ghahramani said. “The more we know about your interests and passions, the more we're able to really be there at all of these milestone moments and ensure that these are incredible experiences.”

Bonvoy is a key way the multinational hotel company, which operates almost 40 brands and more than 10,000 properties across 148 countries and territories, connects with consumers as they travel for work, leisure, family trips and other important life moments.

Marriott will celebrate its 100 year anniversary in 2027. The brand platform is part of the foundation of how the company will build on its legacy of consumer connection, and the creator-led campaign could help lead the way for the brand’s future.

“[The campaign] was very data-led, and we will be looking at our results from a data lens as well as brand lift studies, but we focus a lot on our attribution models and our mixed media [modeling] to see the impact of that work in driving the business for our properties,” Ghahramani said.

Correction: An earlier version of this story misstated the number of destinations and hotel brands included in the campaign and the number of Marriott Bonvoy members. It has been corrected.

Meta removed training from the crawling clause in its upcoming Commercial Terms. The permission to crawl sites tied to business users is still in place.

Meta has removed training from the crawling clause in its new Commercial Terms, which take effect Oct. 30. The permission to crawl websites associated with a business’s products or services is still in the agreement.

The revised clause connects crawling to advertising and business products, as well as to the integrity and security of Meta’s products. Because the terms apply to any business use of Meta’s products, they also cover companies that manage a Facebook Page without buying ads.

Nieman Lab reported the revision on Oct. 17, two days after the outlet published legal experts’ view that the original wording could support an argument that Meta may scrape news sites for AI training. I covered the original terms on Oct. 16.

The European Publishers Council objected to the original wording before the revision, and the UK’s News Media Association condemned it in an Oct. 16 statement.

The original clause, as printed in Nieman Lab’s first report, said Meta “may use any content” it collected “to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of” its products, services and features under the Commercial Terms.

The revised clause allows the crawling “in order to provide, develop, improve, research, and maintain advertising and business products.” A parenthetical says those include products that help a business create and deliver ads and connect it with interested users. The clause keeps an integrity purpose, now worded as maintaining “the integrity and security of” Meta’s products.

Meta continues to utilize its prior access language. It may continue to use automated software and “create test credentials” in order to gather information from such websites; similarly, it will be able to periodically retrieve website updates. The new language does not include a reference to robots.txt.

As of Oct. 19, the UK English preview for Meta’s advertising agreement (the Self-Serve Ad Terms) still contained the previous statement indicating that Meta “may use any content” gathered from the aforementioned sites in order to “provide, develop, improve, research, train and maintain the integrity of” its products. The U.S. English version doesn’t.

Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts told The Verge the crawling terms the company consolidated “only applied to our ads and business products, and we’ve clarified that in the terms themselves.” He said the update “does not change how Meta uses web crawlers” and that “This is not about scraping news sites.”

Meta also told Nieman Lab the first version “wasn’t clear” that robots.txt preferences are respected, and said the updates don’t give it “new rights that supersede those preferences.”

The legal experts from the first report raised concerns about the revised wording. Matt Topic, a media and intellectual property attorney at Loevy & Loevy, said, “I think ‘develop’ is broad enough to include ‘train.’” He added that “business product” doesn’t seem to be a defined term.

Cornell Law School professor James Grimmelmann said the edit does nothing to restrict the “associated with your products or services” language, which he said would let Meta scrape entire sites. He called the purposes language “still broad enough to drive a truck through.”

University of Wisconsin law professor Benjamin Sobel explained that robots.txt signals a site’s preferences. Following those signals is voluntary, and they don’t give the site an enforceable legal right.

Meta provided a revised version of the stated purposes, but access was left unchanged. The company has cited robots.txt as the method that businesses can use to control which areas of their website they want crawled. In addition, the crawler documentation for Meta lists separate crawlers, one for AI training and one for Meta AI search. Therefore, if a business wants to disallow access for one but allow it for another they may do this with the help of robots.txt. It is unclear from the revised terms whether these methods limit what a business grants when they accept the terms.

The revised terms take effect on Oct. 30. Meta has updated the preview since it was first posted, so please check the clause again before then, and review how your robots.txt file handles each Meta crawler.

#65. Google introduces shopping updates ahead of the holidays

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The platform made its Universal Cart feature available to all U.S. users and published a guide on the best times to make purchases in major product categories.

Google launched some interesting new shopping products last week, which could have an impact on how marketers plan their shopping promotions, in line with shopping behaviors heading into the peak buying season.

First, Google published its first “When to Buy” guide, which outlined when the best deals are likely to be available across major product categories, based on 2025 shopping trends.

The 6-page overview included specific guidance on when consumers should start shopping to get the best deals, which could help to guide marketers on when competition is likely to be highest. This could help to attract more shoppers.

The guide also includes notes on key shopping trends to be aware of when it comes to planning promotions.

In addition, Google announced that its Universal Cart has now been made available to all users in the U.S.

First announced at its I/O event in May, Google’s Universal Cart lets users add items to their shopping carts when using various Google apps and products. This feature will keep those items in the cart so users can return to them at any time.

As explained by Google: “Let’s say you save a handbag from Steve Madden to your cart in AI Mode in Google Search, and later a sweater from Quince and lipgloss from Ulta Beauty in the Gemini app. Those products will be there in your cart when you come back later so you can pick up right where you left off.”

The system will also send notifications about price drops on an item you’ve added, or when an item comes back in stock. It can also guide users on which payment option is best to use for each purchase, and alert them to relevant promo codes and offers.

“You can securely check out with Google Pay in just a few taps with many of your favorite stores right in the cart, or you can transfer your items directly to the merchant’s cart to finish buying on their site,” Google said.

Google said the system currently also offers simplified checkout experiences with Nike, Sephora, Target, Ulta Beauty, Walmart and Wayfair, as well as with many Shopify merchants.

#67. From bad to worse: 2026 is shaping up to be “a super El Niño year for local news”

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

RELATED ARTICLEIn Medill’s latest State of Local News report, a “festering, 20-year-old problem” looms larger than everSophie CulpepperOctober 22, 2025If you thought last year was bleak, Medill’s annual State of Local News Report is here to ring the alarm bell louder.

What was a “creeping erosion” has now “mushroomed into a full-blown super El Niño-like event for local news, leaving widespread and long-lasting displacement in its wake,” writes Tim Franklin, founding director of the Medill Local News Initiative, in his introduction to this year’s report, released Tuesday. The Northwestern University team’s research “paints a portrait of a local news ecosystem in a state of precarity.”

In the past year, Medill tracked 26 new news deserts, “the largest single-year rise by far since Medill began keeping records five years ago,” Franklin writes. The previous year, only six new news deserts emerged.

Medill’s team says to understand that acceleration, you have to look at where newspapers are disappearing fastest now. While about 70% of the papers that disappeared over the past 20 years were based in urban or suburban communities, in recent years a greater share of newspaper closures have happened in smaller, rural and poorer communities, according to the report.

“When the news disappears in these counties, it stays gone,” the report states.

RELATED ARTICLELast year, Illinois started giving local news outlets tax credits to support journalism jobs. A new report looks at how it’s goingSophie CulpepperFebruary 9, 2026Many of the new news deserts emerged because of small rural papers shuttering in the Midwest. In fact, the report notes that Illinois lost more newspapers than any other state: 30 newspapers shuttered in the state between July 2025 and August 2026, “all small to medium-size outlets.” That means nearly one in five of the 170 newspapers that shuttered in that year was based in Illinois. The state’s losses are especially notable because it enacted one of the first public policies to preserve and grow local journalism jobs in 2024.

“Independent owners of small to midsize newspapers especially were already operating on a knife’s edge,” Brier Dudley writes in his examination of newspaper losses in Illinois. “This past year, their slim margins were squeezed by shrinking revenues and steeply escalating prices for newsprint, fuel and other materials.”

The price of newsprint rose nearly 18% over the past year, Dudley reported, as U.S. mills closed or stopped production of newsprint. That’s about five times the national rate of inflation, he noted. As of April, the United States has just one newsprint producer left.

A few other highlights from this year’s report:

The extreme urban-rural divide: “Virtually all the new news sources are in urban areas, while rural America is increasingly arid news and information territory,” Franklin writes. “And virtually all the philanthropic support for local news is in metro regions.” The report notes that there are fewer than 50 counties in the U.S. “that lack a newspaper but feature an alternative digital or broadcast outlet.” Of the 287 news outlets to start up in the last five years, nearly 80% are in urban areas.

Traffic declines: Digital readership is in “precipitous decline” for many outlets. According to Comscore data from more than 700 local news sites, monthly traffic has dropped by an average of nearly 2 million pageviews, or almost 30%. Meanwhile, traffic to 100 of the largest local newspapers has declined by almost 50% since 2022.

Local TV news: This year, for the first time, Medill’s report included local TV newsrooms. The team identified 678 local commercial TV newsrooms across the country. The overwhelming majority are located in metro areas with existing local news outlets. (“Adding commercial television to the LNI database made little impact on which counties we identify as news deserts,” the team notes.) TV news is already highly consolidated — the five largest owners control more than half of newsrooms, and the 10 largest control 75% — and further consolidation is underway, if Nexstar’s $6.2 billion acquisition of Tegna survives an antitrust lawsuit. The deal would merge the second- and fourth-largest owners of local commercial TV newsrooms.

#68. TikTok Shop promises many Happy Returns as holiday season sales ramp up

On TikTok Shop, the holiday season has already started, and the platform is delivering a fresh perk for consumers: a solution for regretful purchases. A partnership between TikTok Shop and UPS will integrate the Happy Returns service into the burgeoning ecommerce hub.

Happy Returns, which UPS acquired in 2023, is a leading option for box-free, label-free returns. Users can bring their purchases back to the service’s “Return Bars,” which can be found at stores like Ulta Beauty and Staples. According to Marketing Dive, the TikTok Shop partnership is the first time Happy Returns has been integrated into an ecommerce platform rather than a retailer website.

The integration arrives at an important time. Each year, “Christmas creep” brings an earlier start date to the holiday season. For TikTok Shop, which is looking to capitalize on the momentum it generated last year (when it generated $500 million of U.S. sales during Black Friday weekend), a hot start to the holiday hoopla is imperative.

Fortunately for TikTok Shop, the platform has seen the early success its execs hoped for. Searches for accessories like gold jewelry, opal rings, and friendship bracelets more than doubled month-over-month in September, according to data shared by TikTok. Other products experiencing similar sales upticks include season pajamas, squishy toys, and collectible cards (watch out, Whatnot.)

Consumers aren’t just buying more stuff through TikTok Shop — the size of those transactions is also increasing. Celebs like Kim Kardashian have helped TikTok Shop establishing itself as a vendor of luxury goods, and that trend looks likely to continue into the 2026 holiday season.

That’s why the Happy Returns integration is so important. As TikTok Shop grows up, there’s more at stake with each transaction, so a streamlined returns process will help quell those feelings of buyer’s remorse.

“TikTok Shop is where people discover products and brands, and the shopping experience extends well beyond checkout,” said TikTok Shop President of Strategic Initiatives Patrick Nommensen in a statement. “Our collaboration with Happy Returns builds on our commitment to making the returns experience faster, hassle free, and more trustworthy for our shoppers, with box-free, label-free returns and instant refunds at approximately 10,000 Return Bar locations nationwide.”

With a big enough holiday season, TikTok Shop will bring its annual gross merchandise above $100 billion in 2026. Anyone who wants to be part of that upswell can now browse the virtual shelves with the knowledge that their TikTok Shop purchases carry less risk than they did last year.

#71. YouTube Retention Strategy: How to Hook, Hold, and Convert Viewers

Want to stop losing YouTube viewers in the first few seconds of every video? Wondering how to structure long-form content that keeps people watching, builds trust, and drives real business results?

In this article, you'll discover the BINGE method, a five-part YouTube scripting framework that boosts retention, generates engagement, and turns viewers into customers.

Retention, or average view duration, measures how much of a video's total length a viewer actually watches. The higher that number, the more YouTube's algorithm distributes the video through browse, suggested, and search. That distribution compounds over time.

Adam retired his main channel two years ago, and in the 24 months since his last upload, the channel has continued to work for him. In the last year alone, it generated more than 260,000 views, earned roughly $1,500 in AdSense revenue, and produced consistent monthly inquiries for high-ticket programs he no longer even offers.

The distinction between YouTube and short-form social media comes down to focused attention versus distracted attention. Focused attention means a viewer has chosen to sit down and watch, fully engaged with the content. Distracted attention is the passive scrolling that dominates short-form platforms.

Short-form platforms deliver what he compares to eating every meal from a vending machine: quick dopamine, instantly forgotten. After an hour on TikTok, most people can't name a single creator they watched. YouTube, by contrast, is a four-course meal. TV viewership on YouTube has jumped by more than 60% in the past year alone, a signal that audiences are increasingly treating YouTube like Netflix or HBO, sitting down and giving creators their full, focused attention.

That focused attention translates directly into business outcomes. Adam maintained an 83% close rate on sales calls for nearly three years in his previous business because prospects already knew his delivery style, his personality, and his expertise from watching his videos. One client, Dave, watched just eight minutes of a single video before wiring tens of thousands of dollars. The sales conversation wasn't about convincing him; it was about logistics.

Google's own 7-11-4 research supports this dynamic: consumers typically need 7 hours of content, 11 touch points, and interactions across 4 platforms before they trust a brand enough to buy. A few long-form YouTube videos can cover a significant portion of those hours, making the path to purchase dramatically shorter than dozens of short-form clips.

Adam developed a scripting framework called the BINGE method, built from 16 years on YouTube and refined by studying which of his own videos retained viewers and which lost them. Each letter represents a structural element: Banger Hook, Build Intrigue, Nudge Forward, Generate Engagement, and End in Momentum.

Adam frames the BINGE method within a larger model he calls ARC: Attract, Retain, Convert. The ARC model positions YouTube retention at the center because attracting a viewer who leaves after three seconds produces no business value, and converting a viewer who never stayed long enough to build trust is nearly impossible.

The framework isn't limited to fully scripted videos. It works with outlines and improvisational styles as long as you understand the underlying YouTube script structure. The overall flow mirrors movie and screenplay structure: one storyline gets resolved while another opens up, alternating between tension and resolution to keep the audience locked in.

The B in BINGE stands for banger hook, sometimes called a bombshell hook. This is the first thing the viewer hears after pressing play, and its job is to produce a visceral emotional reaction. That reaction can be any emotion on the spectrum: happiness, grief, anger, fear, or FOMO. The point is to stop the viewer from scanning the suggested videos sidebar and pull them fully into the content.

The hook and the intrigue that follows it need to land in roughly eight seconds. The common advice that creators have 30 seconds to hook a viewer is what Adam calls “2016 math.” Attention spans have compressed further.

Every session is pitch-free and built around tactics you can use yourself, no big team required. Your All-Access ticket includes an extra day of workshops, full access to AI Business World, and recordings of everything.

The hook works by putting the creator in the viewer's shoes and speaking directly to what they're feeling, not just what they know. Adam draws a sharp line between the two: knowing a problem and understanding the feeling behind it are two very different things.

Rather than opening with “in this video, I'm going to teach you five ways to get unstuck on YouTube,” a more effective hook might say: “So you maxed out a credit card on that fancy camera. You just spent six hours this week that you didn't have doing a video that nobody's watching. You did that last week and three weeks before that. And unfortunately, it's your fault. You just don't know it yet.” That language mirrors the viewer's emotional state, creating an immediate connection.

The I in BINGE, build intrigue, follows immediately. Intrigue functions as hook part two: it explains why the viewer should keep watching without teaching anything or giving away spoilers. The shift is from emotional trigger to teasing the transformation. Adam describes the flow as: feeling leads into teased solution, which leads directly into the first talking point, with no seams visible to the viewer.

Adam teaches a pronoun-shifting pattern he calls the Yo-Yo Method (originally described as “you, we, I, we, you”) to structure the combined hook and intrigue section. The pattern moves through five beats:

For example, “You've been told you can't eat at McDonald's, you can't eat bread, you can't eat ice cream. We've been told we have to eat dry chicken, broccoli, and rice six times a day. I got sick of it and started looking at what actually made a difference: macronutrients, micronutrients, hormonal levels. I think if we all do that individually, we can break that cycle. You have an option.”

The N in BINGE, nudge forward, is the element that prevents viewers from finding a natural exit point in the video. A nudge closes one loop while simultaneously opening another, and it happens in the gap between talking points where distraction would otherwise set in. Adam compares the underlying rhythm to a video sales letter: open loop, close loop, alternating between dopamine, serotonin, and cortisol. The viewer feels good, then gets a little uncomfortable; feels good, then gets a little uncomfortable. That cycle keeps attention locked in.

The biggest retention killer Adam sees is the numbered listicle format. In an era of large language models (LLMs) where people skim for answers and move on, giving away the structure makes viewers feel they've already gotten what they came for.

When creators say “step one, step two, step three,” they remind viewers exactly how long they've been watching and how much remains. Worse, when the introduction lays out all the steps upfront (“in this video, I'm going to show you how to increase your email delivery rates by doing this, this, this, and this”), viewers assume they can connect the dots themselves and leave.

The alternative is what Adam calls the “useful, but incomplete” approach: each talking point delivers real, actionable value, but the transition into the next section signals that something essential is still missing.

The AI Business Society filters the noise for you, with expert-led training you can put to work the same day — plus a community of marketers sharing what's actually working.

For example: “Optimizing your bio is definitely going to make a huge change in how much momentum you could pick up quickly. But if you're not fully understanding the next part, nobody's going to stick around.”

The viewer has learned something actionable but recognizes there's a critical gap they haven't filled yet.

The nudge forward appears not just between the intrigue and the first talking point, but at the end of every subsequent talking point throughout the entire video. The structure within each section follows a repeating pattern: micro hook, talking point content, nudge into the next section. Adam notes that when this is done intentionally, each talking point can also be extracted as a stand-alone short-form video with no additional editing.

One technique is asking viewers to take a specific action and report back. Rather than “leave a comment below,” Adam might say: “Go to your analytics, look at this specific metric, and tell me what it says on yours. I'd love to hear, and let me know what your channel is about.” That request gives the viewer a reason to pause, investigate, and return with something personal to share.

A second technique, Adam calls the public proclamation, takes engagement further. The public proclamation is a scripted moment where the creator asks viewers to make a commitment in the comments.

The script might say: “Most people are going to watch this video and not do anything with it. So I want you to proclaim in the comments, if you're brave enough, that today is the day my channel finally breaks free.” Adam puts that exact phrase on screen in quotes so viewers can see others making the same declaration.

The psychology behind this is twofold. People want accountability and to be seen. When a viewer sees other commenters making the same proclamation, social proof kicks in. As Adam puts it, “Nothing attracts a crowd like a crowd.”

Engagement also sends direct signals to YouTube's algorithm. When viewers comment, YouTube knows they're actively watching, not folding laundry across the room with the video playing in the background. An active audience is more valuable to YouTube because active viewers are more likely to see and engage with ads. Channels with higher engagement rates tend to get more distribution as a result.

Adam also recommends responding to every comment until the channel grows to a point where that becomes logistically impossible. That interaction, even brief, transforms the relationship from passive consumption to something closer to a face-to-face conversation. The effect on conversion is significant: viewers who have interacted with a creator, even once, move toward a buying decision faster than those who watch passively for years.

When it's time to pitch a lead magnet or direct viewers to a resource, Adam uses what he calls the “by the way, anyway” technique. The pitch is woven into the script at a point where it feels like a casual thought, not a sales segment.

For example: “Hey, speaking of which, I put everything you need into my Ultimate YouTube Growth Guide. It's a perfect companion for all these free videos here on YouTube. I'll have a link in the description box below. But if you take time to download it, do something with it, please. Otherwise, don't waste your time. Anyway, back to the video.”

The goal is never to pull viewers off the platform during the video. The resource is something they should explore after they finish watching. The key is that the pitch never shifts the creator's tone. Adam compares it to a barbecue conversation: if a friend mentions they need a specific car part and you happen to have one in your garage, you'd casually offer it and go right back to talking about football. The moment a creator switches into a polished sales voice with urgent language and countdown timers, viewers feel the bait-and-switch and disengage.

The E in BINGE, end in momentum, addresses a mistake Adam sees constantly: creators signaling the video is ending long before it actually does. Telling viewers “we're about to wrap up” with six minutes remaining in a seven-minute video is an invitation to leave.

The goal of ending with momentum is to move the viewer from one video to the next, increasing session time and improving overall YouTube retention. The more videos a viewer watches in a single session, the stronger the trust signal sent to the algorithm, and the deeper the relationship between the creator and the viewer.

Adam had a client recently tell him on a group call that she had watched every single video on his channel. That level of consumption doesn't happen accidentally. It's engineered through momentum at the end of each video, pushing the viewer into the next one.

Adam also recommends using unlisted YouTube videos as thank-you page content.

When someone downloads a lead magnet or completes a purchase, the confirmation page displays an unlisted YouTube video rather than one hosted on Vimeo or another platform. Even if the viewer watches only a few seconds, YouTube registers a connection between that viewer and the creator's channel.

From that point forward, the creator's public videos begin appearing on the viewer's YouTube homepage through browse and suggested feeds. Adam describes this as “organic retargeting without it being an ad.”

#72. Anthropologie’s holiday marketing seeks to balance emotion, business impact

Let Marketing Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

A new “On My Way” campaign captures moments of connection, like reuniting with friends and family at the airport, and is supported by creator-led social storytelling.

Anthropologie debuted its holiday marketing campaign on Monday, spotlighting moments of human connection, Marketing Dive can share. The effort is supported by organic social storytelling and will be a testing ground for a partnership struck last month with delivery platform DoorDash.

“On My Way” was developed in-house at the retailer, with ads shot on location at destinations including Shelter Island, New York, Mallorca, Spain, and Vienna. Creative captures people reuniting with friends and family in airport terminals and other transit stations to stoke feelings of both anticipation and the eventual joy of coming together.

Advertising is just one piece of the seasonal push from the Urban Outfitters Inc.-owned lifestyle retailer, which sells a mix of home goods, accessories, clothing and furniture. Anthropologie is trying to cater to shoppers’ needs around different occasions, such as personal styling, hosting parties and gift-giving, while meeting them at various stages of the marketing funnel during a key sales period.

“I think the biggest shift is that we're thinking about the holidays as a world our customer can step into, rather than a single campaign she sees,” Anthropologie Global CMO Barbra Sainsurin told Marketing Dive over email. “The brand campaign creates that aspirational world, and then we're extending it through everything from our home collaborations and creator-led content to in-store styling experiences and new ways to shop, like our DoorDash partnership.”

In addition to the “On My Way” ads, Anthropologie on Friday is rolling out a five-part social series. “Between Us Girls,” which stars creator Coco Schiffer, blends styling inspiration, gifting ideas and entertainment, and will appear on Instagram and TikTok.

“Between Us Girls” follows Nuuly, a clothing-rental service under the UO banner, running a microdrama for its fall campaign. Marketers more broadly are jumping on the short-form content craze to generate organic viewer interest and deepen their work with creators. Sainsurin said the format allows Anthropologie to bring more humor and personality to its holiday strategy compared to conventional messaging.

“Anthropologie will always have that distinct product point of view that makes our brand recognizable, but creators can take that world and make it feel personal in a way that resonates with their communities,” said Sainsurin. “We're excited to keep exploring formats that allow us to do both.”

While the ads and social content are intended to be aspirational, Anthropologie is also working on fresh ways to get its products into the hands of consumers. The DoorDash deal caters to people seeking last-minute gifts and other products tied to the season, the company said.

Brick-and-mortar stores will host events in November and December offering complimentary styling and concierge services. On the product front, the company is introducing home collaborations with Suleika Jaouad and Jon Batiste, New York City Ballet, Susan Alexandra, Molly Hatch and Ghia.

Anthropologie grew revenue 5% year over year for the quarterly period ended July 31. Customer growth, a metric that encompasses new, active and reactivated customers, was up over 4% in the retailer’s Q2, with momentum attributed to an influencer-led campaign promoting a transition to early fall products.

The holidays can be a make or break moment for retailers, which this year are contending with price-sensitive shoppers battered by a long stretch of inflation. That said, spending on retail goods is forecast to rise 10% YoY, according to Deloitte. The consultancy expects Gen Z and millennials to bolster larger holiday spending trends. On the marketing front, Anthropologie sees its biggest challenge as earning engagement in a meaningful way that cuts through a cluttered environment.

“There’s so much [that is] competing for [the customer’s] attention during the holidays, and I don't think the answer is simply to show up more often. We have to give her a reason to care,” said Sainsurin.

“That combination of emotional connection and meaningful business impact is what we're working toward,” she added.

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

USA Today Co. executives are revealing new details about a controversial deal with Palantir. In a joint interview with Fast Company’s Alex Pasternack, three executives from the country’s largest newspaper chain explained why they moved ahead with the Palantir deal despite major opposition from their own employees.

RELATED ARTICLE“An inherent conflict of interest”: More than 800 USA Today Co. employees want the company to end its new Palantir partnershipHanaa' TameezAugust 10, 2026Mike Reed, the chairman and CEO of USA Today Co., previously said that the deal — first reported by Nieman Lab’s Hanaa’ Tameez — is part of a larger shift the company is making to become “an intelligence organization.” At a Palantir conference last month, Reed said that the company’s services were a way for USA Today Co. capitalize on “the shift to online and the data we have on consumers,” Pasternack reported.

In this new interview, USA Today Media president Kristin Roberts detailed some of those services for the first time:

In all of our entertainment stories and our sports stories, we do affiliate links to our partners. So if you’re reading a sports story, you want to buy the jersey for that team, our reporters and editors used to have to go to a file, find a relevant link, copy that link, put it in. All of that is now automated, and that’s a Palantir project.

Lark-Marie Anton, then a communications executive at USA Today Co., chimed in, saying that Palantir’s current scope of work is focused on audience and advertising, but in the future that could extend to social media strategy and reporting tools.

What stood out about Palantir was its ability to create what it calls an ‘ontology’ layer — essentially a unified model that allows different datasets and systems to work together and be acted upon in real time….The challenge isn’t collecting more data, but making better use of the data we already have.

In August, more than 800 USA Today Co. employees from 31 unionized newsrooms called on the company to dissolve its partnership with Palantir. In a statement, staffers named ethical issues and uncertainty over how the software would be used. Throughout the Fast Company interview, Reed and Roberts heavily criticized the NewsGuild and internal efforts to oppose the deal.

Roberts leveled the strongest criticisms of USA Today Co.’s unions across the country, going as far as to say the NewsGuild was lying to its members:

Guild leadership is saying things that are factually untrue. They prey on fear. No matter that I will appear in front of any newsroom for a standup in which they ask me anything for an hour and a half at a time, and I explain to them all of the things.

I’ll give you an example that’s incredibly real for us. Palantir doesn’t work inside of any USA Today Company system. They don’t have access to any of the notes our reporters take. They’re not in the Microsoft suite of tools. They don’t have information directly about our consumers or our staff….They don’t work in our systems. We feed them highly controlled data. We’re in their shit. They’re not in ours.

Reed doubled down on these accusations, extending them to the work the NewsGuild has done organizing around AI in the company, including its push for clauses that would protect journalists from layoffs due to AI adoption.

“I think we’re having more success in newsrooms that are not unionized, with this new world, than those that are unionized,” Reed said.

Last month, USA Today Co. made significant layoffs across the company, including at its local newspapers, and reorganized its audience team. Reed, in a memo to staff, referenced AI-related traffic declines as a reason for the layoffs.

“USA Today Co. executives’ animosity toward their workers and unions is nothing new,” said NewsGuild president Jon Schleuss in a statement to Fast Company. “[We] fully stand behind the statement workers released when this deal with Palantir was first announced.”

#80. Layout Design With AI, Custom AI Apps, and Industry News

Friday is almost here! Before you unplug, here’s one last round of insights and updates. Whether you read them now or save them for later, you won’t want to miss these.

🗞️ Industry news from Gemini, Meta, OpenAI, and more

When designing layouts with AI, settling for the very first output is a common mistake. You end up stuck tweaking a single layout that never quite hits the mark.

The faster path to a polished result: ask for multiple iterations right from your first prompt.

Ask for Variations Upfront. Instead of one mock-up, tell the AI to “get creative and show three different iterations” using your design system. You'll immediately get a range of concepts: different layout structures, background treatments, and typography placement.

Direct and Blend. You don't have to pick just one. Act as the creative director and combine the best parts. For example, apply Option B's background style to Option A's main structure.

Refine With Simple Feedback. Describe fixes conversationally:

“Brighten the text color on dark backgrounds so it pops.”

“Give the list items more breathing room away from the call to action.”

“Incorporate specific brand artwork into the background.”

Lock In Your Winner. Once the design matches your vision, ask the AI to finalize that variation as a master template.

Pro Tip: Before making radical changes, duplicate your design and title it with today's date so you can easily revert if the AI forgets past instructions.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Webinar: The Link Building Graveyard: What to Bury & What Still Wins

A Chinese AI lab opened its search engine to developers. Each result carries a page-level authority tier, and DeepSeek says it filters GEO manipulation.

DeepSeek opened its in-house search engine to developers on Oct. 17, and the company’s changelog says the engine filters SEO spam, “GEO manipulation,” and low-quality AI-generated content.

Each result from the new Search API includes an authority tier for the page and a relevance score, and the API accepts site: queries that limit results to one domain.

DeepSeek’s changelog says its in-house engine handles search on its website and in its API, indexes hundreds of billions of web pages, and takes in hundreds of millions of search requests a day from around the world.

GEO (generative engine optimization) is when you shape your content to be cited by AI answer engines. DeepSeek’s changelog states that they credit strict detection as the source of filtering; however, it has not defined what GEO manipulation is or described how their detection process operates. On May 15, Google said “our spam policies also apply to generative AI responses in Google Search.”

Each Search API result contains an authority field; authority fields range from 0 to 4 with -1 being unknown. According to DeepSeek’s API reference, pages with tiers of 3+ are described as “highly authoritative” sources.

The rerank score (another field) is a scale of 0-3 and incorporates signals that include relevance, authority and freshness. A rerank score of 1.5+ is considered high quality. The guide and the reference do not explain how a page receives its tier or score.

Each result also comes with a snippet for display, typically 100 to 200 characters, and a summary meant for a model to read, typically 600 to 800 characters. Page content comes back too when a request asks for it and the content is available. Queries can be limited with site: and filtered by language and date published.

Search and Fetch each cost $0.75 per 1,000 successful requests. Searches that return no results aren’t billed, and requesting 50 results costs the same as requesting just one.

DeepSeek’s Fetch API was released with Search. Fetch provides a single Markdown page and “is subject to the target site’s availability and access policies,” as per the guide.

According to the EU summary of the data used to train DeepSeek-V4, the crawler is “designed to respect robots.txt instructions and other standard web protocols, where applicable.” However, the summary does not identify which crawler this refers to.

Additionally, none of the launch pages (the guide, API references, changelog and announcement) provide identification of a crawler for the search index nor do they provide information on what user agent Fetch uses.

In addition to providing information about several crawlers, the Known Agents bot directory lists a DeepSeekBot user agent and describes it as an AI training data crawler.

With a funded DeepSeek API account, individual site: searches are under $0.01. Each site: search can return up to 50 pages from your website; each page has both an authority tier and a relevance score for that query. If you see a missing result, it could be because the page was either outside the index or caught by filters described in DeepSeek’s changelog, or because it was excluded for some other reason; neither the user guide nor the API reference provides a method to figure this out.

Robots.txt rules intended to block DeepSeekBot are targeted against a crawler that the Known Agents bot directory describes as being associated with training data. It does not appear from DeepSeek’s initial launch pages if such a rule will affect what is included in DeepSeek’s search index.

If you use Claude Code, Codex, or DeepSeek Harness with the DeepSeek API, your server-side searches and page fetches are already handled through the Search and Fetch APIs at no cost. Billing for these server-side calls will begin on Oct. 31 at 16:00 UTC (noon ET).

Watch DeepSeek’s docs for a definition of GEO manipulation, details on how tiers are set, and a named crawler for the index.
