#86. Fox News attacks the media roughly every 15 minutes, our study finds. (CNN? Every 140 minutes.)

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

“Disparaging journalism is a far more central part of Fox News programming than it is of either MSNBC or CNN programming.”

In 2025, trust in journalism reached a record low. According to Gallup, only 8% of Republicans expressed trust in the news media, compared with 51% of Democrats. New data show an uptick among Republicans, but overall trust remains near this record low, and the gap between Republicans and Democrats remains substantial.

One of the key drivers of this lopsided decline in trust in journalism may be the extent to which news outlets spend time bashing other news outlets, or bashing the news media in general — a phenomenon we call inter-journalism disparagement. Our research team at Duke University’s DeWitt Wallace Center for Media & Democracy recently completed a study of the prominence of this phenomenon on each of the “big three” cable news networks (CNN, Fox News, MSNBC/MS NOW); whether it has increased or decreased over time; and whether there are significant differences in the rate of disparagement across networks.

The results were stark. Fox News far exceeds the other networks, with inter-journalism disparagement taking place once every 14.5 minutes. In contrast, CNN engages in inter-journalism disparagement roughly every 140 minutes, and MSNBC every 61 minutes.

To conduct this analysis, we gathered 15 years of cable news transcripts (2011-2025) for each network. We gathered a random sample of one week’s worth of programming for each year.1 With this approach, we ended up with 3,543 transcripts and almost 19 million words across the three networks, which equates to roughly 62,000 pages of text.

Given the volume of text to be analyzed, we trained OpenAI’s GPT-5.5 to identify attacks against the news media. We developed a 20-page instruction document to help the model code instances of disparagement. GPT-5.5 consistently achieved 99.5% accuracy at identifying inter-journalism disparagement and 100% accuracy for avoiding false negatives, compared to human-coded samples. (You can read more details about the entire training and analytical process here.)

We defined inter-journalism disparagement as negative statements about the conduct or content of an explicitly identified journalism target (such as a specific news organization, or the news media in general). Our definition, which is described in greater depth in the full paper, needed to be quite detailed in order for ChatGPT to produce accurate results. Examples of inter-journalism disparagement include:

What we found when comparing the three networks tells us a lot about the dynamics of contemporary cable news and partisan journalism.

First, Figure 1 shows the rate of journalism disparagement across each of the big three networks. Because the volume of text that we analyzed varies across each network, our primary metric was the rate of disparagement per 1,000 words of transcript text. In this figure, we show not only the rate per 1,000 words, but we also convert that rate into a time-based frequency, using the industry standard of 1,000 words equaling approximately six minutes of air time.

In Figure 2, we graph the frequency of inter-journalism disparagement over time. Here, we see that the massive difference between Fox News and CNN/MSNBC persists over the 15-year time period. Still, we do see some dips in the volume of disparagement on Fox News in the two-year periods leading up to the 2016 and 2024 elections, with journalism disparagement levels on Fox News rebounding to near-peak levels in 2025. We haven’t figured out yet what to make of this pattern.

CNN and MSNBC seem to converge in their disparagement activity starting around 2017, with MSNBC’s disparagement rate decreasing somewhat, and CNN’s disparagement rate increasing somewhat. This pattern aligns with recent research that has shown, in other contexts, that CNN and MSNBC programming are converging in ways that suggest diminished differences between the more “centrist” CNN and the more left-leaning MSNBC.

A key takeaway here is that we should not think about Fox News and MSNBC as flip sides of the same partisan journalism coin. At least in relation to inter-journalism disparagement, these left- and right-leaning cable networks behave very differently. Disparaging journalism is a far more central part of Fox News programming than it is of either MSNBC or CNN programming.

In order to get a deeper understanding of these differences, we also identified the targets of the disparagement. These results are presented in Figures 3 through 5.

Figure 3 presents a breakdown of the most common targets of disparagement on Fox News. By far the most frequent target of disparagement on Fox News is “the media.” Following in a distant second is CNN, with the “mainstream media” rounding out the top three targets. Other relatively frequent targets include The New York Times, MSNBC, and The Washington Post.

As should be clear, Fox News devotes far more attention to disparaging journalism as an institution than it does to attacking individual news sources. This stands in stark contrast to what we see when we look at the results for CNN and MSNBC. Looking first at CNN, Figure 4 shows that the network’s most frequent target is Fox News (though with a frequency that wouldn’t crack the top three of the Fox News list).

Similarly, as Figure 5 shows, Fox News is also the number one target on MSNBC. Both CNN and MSNBC have the same top three, with Fox News followed by “the media” and the “right-wing media.” These instances of institutional disparagement happen far less frequently on CNN or MSNBC than they do on Fox News.

Finally, we were also able to identify which hosts or anchors were the most frequent disparagers of their fellow journalists. Those results can be seen in Figure 6. Given the lopsided amount of inter-journalism disparagement on Fox News, it is not surprising that this graph is dominated by Fox News personalities, with Sean Hannity taking the top spot, followed by Greg Gutfeld and Tucker Carlson (note: our graph for Howard Kurtz reflects his move from CNN to Fox in 2013).

This study didn’t distinguish further in terms of the nature of the disparagement across the three networks (for example, in terms of severity or legitimacy). This is something we are exploring in the next stage of this work. Nor did we examine whether viewer exposure to inter-journalism disparagement reduces trust in specific outlets or the institution of journalism. That certainly seems like a reasonable assumption, given the dramatically lower levels of trust in journalism among Republicans that we noted at the outset. We plan to investigate this relationship directly in future research.

But what we do see in this research is that disparagement of the institution of journalism, and of particular news outlets, is a much more prominent component of Fox News programming than it is of either CNN or MSNBC. Some researchers have proposed that this kind of high-volume disparagement of news sources that don’t tow the same partisan line takes us beyond traditional notions of partisan journalism and into the realm of “anti-media media.” The goal of anti-media media is to “weaponize the facade of journalism against the roles assigned to journalism” in a democracy. Based on our findings, Fox News fits this characterization.

Philip M. Napoli is the James R. Shepley Professor of Public Policy, director of the DeWitt Wallace Center for Media & Democracy, and director of undergraduate studies for the journalism and media minor in the Sanford School of Public Policy at Duke University. Adam Meskouri is a politics researcher at Harvard and Duke. Anjini Mani is an undergraduate at Duke. Grant Socol is a graduate research assistant at Duke. Harrison Walley is an undergraduate at Duke. Rather than analyze the entirety of the networks’ output over this time, we created a “constructed week” for each year, which is a common practice in this kind of content analysis. This involves selecting a random Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, etc. within each year, so that the sample of programming was reasonably representative of the year as a whole. We included all programming across all dayparts in our constructed weeks. Note: MSNBC was only available through 2023; the network became MS NOW in late 2025. [↩]

#87. YouTube tests AI replies in searches

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

U.S.-based users in the experiment group may be given artificial intelligence-generated responses to their search queries in the app.

YouTube is experimenting with an expansion of its Ask YouTube responses which will see users given artificial intelligence-generated replies for all in-app search queries, not just those posed to Ask YouTube direct.

Ask YouTube is the platform’s in-stream chatbot, which enables users to pose conversational queries and get expanded overviews, as well as recommendations for related videos.

Ask YouTube was made available to all U.S. users last week, and now, YouTube has begun showing some users AI-generated replies in every search query, as opposed to only displaying traditional keyword-matched video listings.

As explained by YouTube: “If you are part of this experiment, you may see an Ask YouTube response at the top of your search results when a structured overview can add extra context beyond a standard list of videos, such as open-ended, how-to, or skill-based questions without a single right answer (like "how do I get marks off painted walls?").”

YouTube said that Ask YouTube will provide more comprehensive answers to queries, which could add value to more searches.

“When Ask YouTube responses appear in your search results, you can select ‘Show more’ to view the full response and ask follow-up questions, or simply scroll down to browse standard video results,” YouTube said.

Essentially, YouTube wants to bring its AI-generated responses to every query as a means to drive discovery beyond the regular list of videos that match search terms.

That could provide more value, though the change could potentially be less welcomed by some users.

YouTube said that its expanded AI answers are currently live “for select signed-in desktop users in the U.S. searching in English.”

#89. Claude Design: How to Create On-Brand Visuals With AI

Want to create professional-looking slides, websites, and animations without hiring a designer or learning complex software? Wondering how to keep every piece of visual content on-brand across platforms?

In this article, you'll discover how to use Claude Design to build a design system, create on-brand visuals, and automate content workflows that used to take hours.

When most people hear “AI” and “design” in the same sentence, they immediately think of generative AI tools like Midjourney or ChatGPT that create images from a prompt. Claude Design does not do that. It does not generate images at all.

Instead, Claude Design is a layout and front-end design tool built by Anthropic. Think of it more like Adobe InDesign than an image generator. It handles the arrangement of fonts, colors, spacing, and visual elements that make a page or a slide look polished and professional.

The layout side of design is what most creators actually struggle with. Anyone can generate an image with a prompt, but composing that image alongside text, white space, and branding elements in a way that looks intentional is a different skill entirely. Claude Design handles that composition.

For solopreneurs and small teams without access to a professional designer, Claude Design serves as an on-demand front-end designer. A front-end designer's job is to design the look and the feel of something, whether that's a website, a slide deck, a PDF, or a landing page. The careful selection of colors, fonts, images, and white space that makes a website look beautiful rather than cluttered is exactly what Claude Design produces.

The platform is accessible through claude.ai by clicking the design button at the bottom left of the screen. The desktop app has the same entry point. The tool is still in Anthropic's labs, so the interface continues to evolve. When Claude Design first launched, it had its own separate usage limits, and users would frequently time out. Now it ties into the general Claude credits, so there is no separate usage meter to monitor.

The single most important step before creating anything in Claude Design is building a design system. A design system is essentially a standard operating guide for how a brand or product should look. It includes fonts, colors, swatches, logos, spacing rules, animation styles, and any other visual element that defines a brand's identity.

Many creators are familiar with Canva's brand kit, which stores a logo and fonts that get pulled into new designs. Claude Design takes that concept further. Rather than just storing assets, the design system considers how those assets should be used across different contexts. It adjusts usage depending on whether the output is a website, a slide deck, or a client-facing PDF.

Because the design system is stored as code, specifically as a Markdown file called design.md, the system is portable. That design.md file can be plugged into any AI model or platform. If the AI landscape shifts and a new tool becomes dominant, the design system can be transferred without starting from scratch.

What’s more, Claude Design supports multiple design systems within a single account. A creator who runs two shows or works with multiple clients can maintain a separate design system for each one, switching between them depending on the project.

Jeff creates design systems for his clients based on their logos and podcast artwork. When he sends a report or even an email template using the client's own design system, the result looks so professional that clients ask how he did it. Building design systems for clients is also a service that can be offered as a paid deliverable.

Building a design system takes about 10 minutes or more. The process begins with providing materials. Logos, color swatches from Pinterest, screenshots from websites, podcast artwork, or any visual reference that represents the desired look can be dragged directly into the interface.

Claude Design will ask clarifying questions during setup. This is by design, as visual preferences are personal and the tool needs specific input to get the system right. The setup process in Claude Design asks design-specific questions that go beyond what Claude Code or Claude Cowork would ask when prompted to build something visual.

Join thousands of small-business marketers at Social Media Marketing World — three days of AI, social media, and marketing strategy taught by world-class experts. April 1–3, 2027 in Anaheim.

Every session is pitch-free and built around tactics you can use yourself, no big team required. Your All-Access ticket includes an extra day of workshops, full access to AI Business World, and recordings of everything.

Jeff Sieh recommends skipping the one-click answer buttons during setup and instead using the open text fields to provide more context. Voice input through a tool like Wispr Flow works especially well here because speaking naturally provides far more detail than clicking preset options.

Providing a website URL during setup is also valuable. Claude Design will scrape the site and pull in not just visual style but also written tone, giving the system a fuller picture of the brand.

The design system doesn't just store colors and fonts. It stores understanding. The more context provided during setup, the more intelligently the system applies that understanding across every output.

When Jeff was building his own design system, he wanted to capture a 1950s and '60s retro-futurism aesthetic, something like The Jetsons meets Fantastic Four. Through workshopping the concept back and forth with Claude Design, he discovered the style was called Googie architecture.

Once he added that term to his design system, Claude Design understood the entire architectural style and began applying it throughout his work, from background elements in layouts to the image prompts it generated for ChatGPT.

The most effective way to interact with Claude Design is to speak to it. Using a voice-to-text tool like Wispr Flow, designers can dictate instructions naturally rather than typing requests or clicking through menus.

Claude Design is essentially a chatbot that also happens to be a designer, so instructions like “I want more white space between the headline and the body text” or “Show me this in a darker color palette” work exactly the way they would if spoken to a human designer.

One of the strongest techniques for achieving good results is to ask for multiple options at once. Rather than requesting a single landing page design and iterating from there, asking for five different versions at once works far better. Claude Design will generate all five, and then the refinement conversation becomes more productive.

Once a design is generated, elements can be edited directly by clicking and dragging. Text can be retyped, headlines can be repositioned, and spacing can be adjusted manually. These direct edits do not consume any credits, which makes them the most efficient way to handle small tweaks.

Claude Design supports skills, which are reusable instruction sets that modify how the tool operates.

Jeff uses an anti-AI slop skill that ensures all generated text avoids common AI tells, such as excessive hyphens, generic phrasing, and emojis. This skill runs directly inside Claude Design, so the text in every layout is cleaned up during creation rather than in a separate editing pass.

He also uses a voice-matching .md file that has analyzed his emails and writing style, so Claude Design produces text that sounds like him.

Claude Design includes built-in templates for mobile app design, slides, documents, wireframes, animation, user interface, mockups, resumes, 3D objects, research, HTML emails, color and type pairing, diagrams, and filler. These templates serve as starting points, but the real flexibility comes from combining them with a custom design system. Any template can be generated using any design system, so the output always matches the brand.

The built-in templates shouldn't be treated as boundaries. Anything that can be imagined can likely be built, even if no template exists for it. When a specific capability, such as a camera push-in effect, isn't available, Claude Design can build the tool to create it.

Claude Design stores projects, design systems, and templates in separate tabs. Templates can be created for any repeating format.

Jeff has built templates for landing pages and even for Ecamm Live scenes, the live-streaming software he uses for Creator News Live. When he needs a new scene layout, the template gives the design system a starting point that already matches his show's visual style.

Claude Design can produce complete web pages, landing pages, and website mockups. The output is functional HTML that can be deployed directly or handed to a developer for integration.

The AI Business Society filters the noise for you, with expert-led training you can put to work the same day — plus a community of marketers sharing what's actually working.

Jeff uses Claude Design to build web pages for clients and for his own projects. When his link-in-bio service shut down, he pointed Claude Code at the broken tool, referenced his design system, and it built a custom WordPress plugin that automatically pulls in his latest YouTube videos and blog posts, all styled to match his brand.

For software teams, Claude Design opens up a mockup workflow. For the NoteGo app, Mike’s team created a design system specifically focused on software user interfaces. New features and functions can now be mocked up in Claude Design and reviewed before any code is written. Previously, the developer would build the full feature in Claude Code, only to learn the design needed changes. The mockup step catches those changes before development time is spent.

Claude Design includes animation capabilities that go beyond simple transitions. The tool can produce After Effects-style motion graphics, the kind of high-end animations that traditionally take days to create manually.

The animations Claude Design creates are vector-based and rendered in code rather than as video files. This means they take up almost no storage space and can be embedded directly into websites or other digital content without the file size concerns that come with video.

For a practical example, a five-step instruction process can be animated within the design system. Claude Design figures out how to draw each step using vector animations that render on screen, creating a polished walkthrough without ever generating a video file.

The animation tools can also be used to build custom effects. When a standard slow push-in or pull-back camera move wasn't available, Claude Design offered to build the tool to create that specific effect. It's limited primarily by imagination rather than by a fixed set of capabilities.

Because Claude Design handles layout and composition but not image creation, pairing it with ChatGPT fills that gap.

Claude Design can write image generation prompts that include the exact hex codes from the design system. Those prompts are copied to ChatGPT, which generates images that match the brand's color palette. The images are then dragged back into Claude Design and placed into the layout.

This same approach works with Midjourney. The design system's carousel skill produces two sets of prompts, one formatted for each image generator, so creators can choose whichever platform produces the best results for a given project.

The real power of a design system emerges when it's connected to automated workflows. Three examples from Jeff's production process demonstrate how far this can go.

Jeff wanted to create a downloadable cheat sheet for every episode of Creator News Live, something inspired by Amy Porterfield's approach of offering a downloadable resource with each podcast episode. Before AI, this would have required a team and most of a day's work per episode. Now the entire show production takes 30 to 45 minutes, and the cheat sheet is part of that.

The automated system reads the episode transcript, pulls the relevant information, applies the design system to format the cheat sheet, generates a thumbnail, uploads it to Jeff's website, and publishes it as a draft kit ready to distribute. The entire process runs automatically after the show ends. The results can be seen at jeffsieh.com/cheatsheet.

The carousel workflow is a multi-step automated process built in Claude Code that turns an hour-long show transcript into finished carousel posts for Instagram and LinkedIn.

The system follows this sequence: it takes the transcript, identifies sections that would make strong carousel content using a specific formula (hook, two builds, payoff, and call to action), and then generates dual image prompts, one optimized for Midjourney and one for ChatGPT. Both prompts include the exact hex codes from the design system, so the generated images match the brand colors.

The only manual step is rendering the images in ChatGPT (or Midjourney) and placing them in a designated folder. Once the images are in the folder, the system detects them automatically. A Python script analyzes each image to determine optimal text placement, and then the system builds the complete carousel with alternating dark and light backgrounds.

The output includes the carousel images formatted as a PDF for LinkedIn since LinkedIn uses PDF format for carousel-style posts), individual images formatted for Instagram, captions written specifically for each platform based on the transcript, and the entire package delivered to Slack for the team to review and post.

A newer application pairs Claude Design with ChatCut, an AI video-editing tool (not to be confused with CapCut). ChatCut connects to either OpenAI or Claude Code and allows video editing through voice commands.

Because ChatCut can reference a Claude Design system, all motion graphics, lower thirds, and visual elements generated during the edit automatically match the brand. Jeff edited an entire episode of Creator News Live without touching a keyboard. Every visual element was spoken into existence and matched his design system.

When a design system is loaded into a Claude Code project, Claude automatically references it whenever visual assets are needed. Jeff's thumbnail workflow inside Claude Code writes the image prompts with the correct hex codes for ChatGPT without being asked, because the design system is already part of the project. The thumbnails come back matching the brand colors, fonts, and overall aesthetic every time.

The design system can be exported from Claude Design to work across multiple platforms. Although Claude Design lives in its own environment, separate from Claude Code and Claude Cowork, several export options bridge that gap.

The export options available directly within Claude Design include PDF, project HTML (which packages all assets into HTML for developers), PowerPoint, and direct connections to Claude Code, Adobe, Canva, Gamma, and Google Slides. More integrations continue to be added.

For creators who want to use their design system in Claude Cowork or Claude Code, the process is straightforward. Inside Claude Design, ask it to create a design.md file, a Markdown file that contains everything the design system needs. Download that file, then drag it into any project folder in Cowork. From that point forward, any design work within the project automatically references the design system.

The design.md file can also be shared with other AI systems. Because Markdown is a simple, widely understood format, the file works across different AI platforms without conversion or compatibility issues.

Gamma is an AI slide-generation tool that integrates directly with Claude. After building a design system in Claude Design, the system can be tied into Gamma. Slides built through Gamma then automatically use the correct colors, fonts, logos, and other brand elements.

The workflow for a presentation looks like this: outline the talk, have Claude help refine the hooks and structure, then send it to Gamma. Because the design system is already in place, the slides come back fully branded without any manual formatting.

Jeff Sieh is a visual marketing consultant and strategist who helps marketers and creators grow their audience and business with AI-powered visuals and live video. Check out the free CNL Cheat Sheet Club. Follow Jeff on Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn, X, and YouTube.

#93. Optimizing ad spend ahead of Black Friday: What the numbers say

Let Marketing Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

Data from AppLovin indicate that promotion-based digital advertising outperforms evergreen product messaging when it comes to seven-day attributed revenue.

The marketing lead-up to Black Friday seems to get earlier and earlier every year. Between the widening shopping window and the increased importance of Cyber Monday and Small Business Saturday, marketers may struggle with how to best cut through the noise. Last November, 63% of advertisers refreshed their creative during at least three weeks of the month, according to recent AppLovin data.

“Black Friday is no longer a single-day shopping event, and our data reinforces just how important the lead-up has become,” said Sam Appelbaum, senior director of consumer at AppLovin, in an email to Marketing Dive.

“BFCM 2026 Part 3: Four creative decisions that drive results,” draws on checkout and revenue data from e-commerce advertisers and AppLovin campaign data for the 2025 holiday marketing window around Black Friday and Cyber Monday. Creative was defined as a set of assets delivered in an ad. AppLovin previously released research on when to start creative and determine success and customer acquisition tied to Black Friday.

Advertisers that released new creative almost every week in November of 2025 reaped the rewards. Return on advertising spend seven days after the first interaction with the ad was 23% higher compared to those who refreshed creative once or twice, per the report. The ROAS when consumers interacted with the creative for the first time increased 20% for assets uploaded in November compared to those over 60 days old. After seven days, the ROAS was 15% higher than for the older creative.

Newer creative was also more efficient, with the cost per purchase 19% lower than baseline at the first interaction and 13% lower at day seven.

“Waiting until Black Friday to ramp up campaigns risks missing valuable demand. Launching campaigns earlier provides more time to learn, optimize and scale efforts ahead of peak purchase intent,” said Appelbaum.

However, getting an early start doesn’t mean keeping messaging the same throughout, according to Appelbaum. Instead, marketers should think about how to build early interest then release promotions as Black Friday nears.

“The goal isn't to be the first brand to announce a sale. It's to create a connected shopping journey that builds interest and converts that demand when shoppers are ready to buy,” he said.

Over half, 58.2%, of creative content comprised evergreen product messaging. However, this content made up just 37.8% of delivered spend, according to the report. Promotional messaging surrounding Black Friday or Cyber Monday accounted for 64.2% of day seven attributed revenue. The day seven ROAS for deal-centric marketing was slightly higher than for product messaging. The numbers suggest that finding a balance between promotional and product advertising may be beneficial for advertisers, per the report.

Shorter ads performed the best in terms of first interaction ROAS, with Black Friday or Cyber Monday ads delivering an 83% lift compared to the June through September nonpromotion baseline. For videos between 16 and 29 seconds long, the lift fell to 39% and to 24% for ads 30 seconds or longer.

Brands should test different video lengths in order to figure out what works best, according to Appelbaum. Shorter videos can help break through the crowded holiday marketing environment by creating urgency or pushing a promotion. Longer-form videos can help with product education.

What comes after the video can be just as important, per the report. Interactive HTML endcards delivered a first-interaction ROAS lift of 35% compared to the June-September nonpromotional baseline when looking at a mix of new and returning customers. When looking at the same group and timeframe, the ROAS of static-image endcards fell 11%.

The day seven ROAS lift for interactive endcards was 40%, while for static-image, ROAS fell 5%.

When looking at new customers alone, the first interaction and day seven lift in ROAS for interactive endcards were both 48%. Static images also delivered positive lifts in ROAS at both first contact and day seven. At initial connection, it was 6% and for day seven it was 14%

“The biggest takeaway for marketers is that Black Friday/Cyber Monday success isn't just about offering the deepest discounts or spending more during the holiday weekend,” said Appelbaum. “Our data underscores the importance of preparing early, adapting creative and messaging as shopping behavior evolves, and testing different approaches throughout the season,” Appelbaum said.

#94. Week of Oct. 5 Cable News Ratings: CNN Up in Both Measurements

This is TVNewser’s basic cable network ranker and cable news report for the week of October 5, 2026.

CNN, which in recent weeks has been in the news because of the White House press ban and its new ownership situation, stood tall among its competitors, finishing the week as the only one with gains in total viewers and the Adults 25-54 demo during primetime and total day.

The now-Skydance network closed the demo between it and MS NOW during total day, leaving a difference of only 1,000 viewers between the two networks.

MS NOW was the only network with across-the-board declines, but it also had some positive news. In the 9 p.m. ET hour, The Rachel Maddow Show was the most-watched show in total viewers on Monday, October 5. It was also the most-watched network in both measured categories during the 6 a.m. ET hour, when Morning Joe airs on Monday, Tuesday, and Friday.

As for Fox News, its bright spot was its primetime demo growth during the just-concluded week. It’s still the most-watched network by a large margin.

According to Nielsen big data + panel for the week of Oct. 5, Fox News averaged 1.6 million total viewers and 145,000 A25-54 viewers during primetime. The network was down -2% in total viewers but grew by +4% in the demo compared to the prior week (the week beginning Sept. 28).

During total day viewing, Fox News averaged 1.07 million total viewers and 94,000 A25-54 viewers. Based on its average from the previous week’s measurements, the network was flat in total viewers and the demo.

Fox News dropped from second to third place in total primetime viewership and was sixth in demo viewership among all basic cable networks. During total day, it remained first in total viewers and finished in fifth place in the total day demo.

MS NOW averaged 902,000 total viewers and 88,000 viewers in the A25-54 demo for the week that just concluded. The network was down -2% in total viewers and -1% in the demo compared with its primetime average the prior week.

During total day, MS NOW averaged 570,000 total viewers and 57,000 demo viewers. It was down -1% in total viewers and -8% in the demo compared with the network’s average the prior week—the only network with declines in this comparison.

Among all basic cable networks, MS NOW slipped from third to fifth place in total primetime viewers and was 15th in the demo, tied with Comedy Central. It also ranked third in total viewers and finished in eighth place in the total day demo.

CNN averaged 577,000 total primetime viewers and 100,000 demo viewers. It grew by +4% in total viewers and +3% in the demo compared to the previous week.

During total day, the network had 393,000 total viewers and 56,000 viewers in the demo. For CNN, this represented gains of +7% in total viewers and +8% in the demo during this daypart.

Among all cable networks, CNN moved from seventh to sixth place in total viewers and was 11th in the demo during primetime. It slipped to No. 5 in total day among total viewers and was ninth in the demo.

When looking at these networks’ performance during the same period a year ago:

Fox News held 12 of the 15 spots among the week’s most-watched cable news shows, with The Five in first place with 2.649 million total viewers at 5 p.m. ET. MS NOW was represented in the chart by Monday’s 9 p.m. ET airing of The Rachel Maddow Show, with 1.779 million total viewers at No. 6. The Last Word with Lawrence O’Donnell, airing weeknights at 10 p.m. ET, had 1.122 million total viewers at No. 14, and The Briefing with Jen Psaki, airing Tuesday to Friday at 9 p.m., was in the No. 15 position, with 1.078 million total viewers.

The Rachel Maddow Show dethroned The Five to take the top spot in the Adults 25-54 demo, with 252,000 viewers. Despite this, Fox News held 12 of the 15 top spots in the demo, with The Five averaging 239,000 viewers to take second place. CNN was represented by CNN NewsNight with Abby Phillip, which airs five nights a week at 10 p.m. ET and finished in eighth place with 144,000 viewers, and The Source with Kaitlan Collins, which airs weeknights at 9 p.m. ET, and finished in 14th place with 116,000 demo viewers.

What a model learned from fictional biographies complicates the promise to make it remember your brand.

In It Was There a Minute Ago, I mentioned that reading research papers had become something of a hobby … It’s borderline masochism. I’ve kept going, working through papers and white papers and trying to connect the dots between experiments. What interests me is how a finding in one study changes the way I read another.

Last time, I looked at what a missing answer lets us diagnose. This time, I want to look at the apparent success: The model seems to have learned the material, and we are ready to congratulate ourselves.

A model can become extremely good at predicting the facts in a biography and still struggle when you ask where the person works. Researchers documented that gap. The reading had gone very well. The questions were a bit of a problem.

Think of a pupil who can recite a passage from the textbook, right up to the punctuation. Ask a question that requires taking a fact out of that passage and the performance changes. We would probably want to see the exam results before declaring the revision a success.

That is the distinction I keep pointing to when people talk about getting a brand into model memory. The phrase makes the difficult part sound finished. Once the model has encountered your name during training, it is supposed to know you well enough for the recommendations to follow. Very efficient, if that is all it takes.

Physics of Language Models: Part 3.1 uses fictional biographies to separate memorizing text from extracting its facts. The researchers pre-trained small models on the biographies, then fine-tuned them on questions about some people and tested questions about the others.

Here, pre-training means learning from the biographies from scratch; fine-tuning is the subsequent training on the question-answer task. Both change the model’s learned parameters, or weights. Information it can use from those weights, without fetching a source, is what we mean here by parametric memory.

The model had seen each test person’s biography, but had never been trained on questions about that person. Failure cannot be waved away as never having received the material.

The pupil comparison helps with the difference between recitation and answering. It tells us nothing about whether a model understands something in the human sense. The question is whether it can use facts learned in one form to answer questions asked in another.

A model that completes your product description, when given the beginning, has passed a particular test. A buyer asking which product suits their needs has set it another. I would be cautious about a memory claim that slides between them without saying so.

The obvious response is more repetition. Give it the lesson again, until it sticks.

In Quantifying Memorization Across Neural Language Models, duplication in the training corpus increases verbatim extraction: supply the beginning of a training passage and the model becomes more likely to reproduce the continuation.

So, the comfortable counterclaim, that copies teach a model nothing, is too broad. Repetition can improve a measured result. The question is: Which result?

A newer paper, Don’t Forget! Decomposing the Training Dynamics of Memorization in Language Models, asks what happens to a memorized passage as training continues. The researchers used saved versions of Pythia models to simulate training updates, changes to their learned weights.

In those simulations, learning from other data worked more strongly against predicting frequently repeated memorized passages than rare ones, especially in the model with one billion parameters. The researchers suggest that repetition may help keep those passages reproducible despite that interference.

They did not vary repetition and the competing training data separately to prove that explanation. And they tested word-for-word continuation, not answers about the facts.

Coming back to our analogy, the pupil also has the rest of the syllabus to contend with. A mention count cannot tell you how learning from other material affects the result you want.

Being able to finish the passage still leaves open whether the model can use its facts to answer a different kind of question. More successful recitation cannot settle that on its own. Nor is a repeated publication automatically a repeated training exposure. The model provider still has to collect the copy, keep it after filtering and actually use it in training.

I can see why counting mentions appeals. You can count them before you know what they will teach.

In the biography experiment, the researchers varied the wording, shuffled sentence order, and repeated each person’s full name throughout their biography. Accuracy on factual questions about the test group rose from 9.7% to 96.2% in a 124-million-parameter GPT-2 model. Those were synthetic facts in a small-model training experiment, not commercial brand recommendations.

The result gives me a better way to think about a brand fact than simply asking how often the sentence appears. Consider an invented payments company. One description explains how its payout feature helps marketplace sellers; another explains how the same feature handles a customer’s payment problem. The descriptions concern the same product, but could help answer different questions.

That gives me a reason to test clear descriptions of a product in different situations. It does not tell me that publishing those descriptions will make a commercial model remember the product better.

The researchers chose their training material and trained the model on it themselves. A publisher can put pages online, but the model provider decides whether those pages enter training, which copies to keep, and how to use them.

If you use that result to sell a package of webpages, you are promising an improvement the researchers never tested. Putting the paper in the proposal does not fill that gap.

Better descriptions could still help. I would want evidence that the publishing work improved recall before promising it to a client. And the large gain in this small biography model does not tell us what improvement to expect from a much larger commercial model.

The researchers also kept one group’s biographies unchanged while adding varied biographies for another group. Accuracy on questions about the unchanged group rose from 4.4% to 86.8%.

For the later question-answer training, they used examples about only the added group. The test group’s biographies had not gained extra versions, and its question-answer pairs were never used in training. Training on material about other people had helped the model answer questions about this group. The transfer depended on sufficiently similar material.

Back in the classroom, the pupil gets better at using a lesson because the teaching has improved elsewhere. Their own passage has not acquired another paragraph.

This is the finding that makes a neat brand-content explanation feel incomplete to me. The quality of everything written about a brand may matter. So may the model’s ability to use information of that kind, developed through training on other examples.

If similar transfer matters for commercial facts, your brand could become easier to recall after a model change without anyone having rewritten your brand material. That is a hypothesis about production systems, not a result these researchers measured.

Better answers about your company, given without retrieval, would not necessarily mean your latest content program taught the model something new about you. The provider may have changed how the model learns to use what it encounters.

I have been tempted to explain better recall through more varied descriptions of each brand. That may help, but it cannot be the only explanation here: the tested biographies did not gain any extra versions. If my explanation needs extra pages about the company, it cannot account for this result.

I like the content-diversity hypothesis. I would rather keep it as a hypothesis than make the paper say it is the whole mechanism.

A separate study, Fine-Tuning or Retrieval?, also finds benefits from paraphrased training material. On its new-fact multiple-choice test, Mistral-7B scored 50.4% after training on the original documents and 58.8% with paraphrased material.

Giving it relevant passages with the question did better: 87.5%. That is retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG, supplying evidence at answer time.

The questions were generated from the same chunks of text that the retrieval system could supply. This favors retrieval: The questions concern facts in the material available to it. The test also provided answer options, so it measured recognition rather than producing an answer without options or recommending a product.

For me, that is another reason to say what the work is supposed to improve. A gain in recognition, a gain in factual answering, and a change in product recommendations need different evidence.

The name on a search result can affect the choice too. In Source Preference in the Wild, the researchers kept the titles and snippets fixed, changed the source shown alongside them, and saw the models’ choices change. The models chose from snippets without opening the pages.

The researchers also trained models on pairs of better and worse selections, a form of preference training. They made one source accompany the better item more often during training. Later, the models favored that source even when the test items met the same measured requirements.

This shows one way training can create a source preference. It does not explain how the search agents acquired their existing preferences. Your product can pass a recall test while a competing result gets picked for a reason the test never examined.

My interest here is commercial too. I work at geoSurge, where model memory is central to the approach. Better recall is an outcome worth pursuing. A publishing recipe that promises it still has to establish the connection between the work performed and the result claimed.

The training experiments give me reasons to take model memory seriously. Changing the material and the training tasks can improve factual answering. That is a useful starting point for further work.

The awkward part is who controls the training. Publishers can make information available and describe it clearly. Providers decide what enters training and how it is used. The biography experiment shows why the material about somebody else can matter too.

If a model starts answering questions about a company better, I would want to understand what changed in the model as well as what changed on the company’s website.

The provider gets to change the curriculum while your content calendar changes the reading material on offer. Confuse those powers, and you can keep assigning homework long after the pupil can recite the lesson.

#96. Sinclair’s new Substack repackages its local TV reporting into a video podcast

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

“How young is too young for a life in prison?”

“SpaceX debris is washing ashore. Who’s responsible?”

“Why schools get paid even when students fail.”

Those are the top headlines so far on Sinclair Broadcasting Group’s new Substack publication, The National Press, launched this week.

The National Press repackages some of the top stories from Sinclair’s 178 local news stations — which employ around 1,200 journalists — into a daily, 30-minute broadcast-style show. The program is hosted by former Newsmax and Christian Cable Network anchor Lyndsay Keith, who summarizes the stories and interviews the local journalists who first reported them. In the videos, Keith sits at a desk with a microphone; the dimly lit background is illuminated just enough to make out two American flags in a mug. (It gives off a true-crime YouTube podcast vibe.)

As Axios’s Sara Fischer noted on Tuesday, Sinclair has long been accused of conservative bias in its local news operation. The National Press is launching in partnership with New Media, the company behind Bari Weiss’s The Free Press, and the two publications look somewhat alike (in part because they both run on Substack). New Media staffers will help create the content and maintain the site and the company will take a portion of Sinclair’s revenue from Substack, Fischer reported.

The National Press is currently free to access, but has paid tiers that include ad-free viewing, community chat access, and merch. Subscriptions start at $5 per month or $50 per year. The five posts on the site so far have between seven and 14 likes each.

Wednesday’s episode focuses on a story about how Michigan is reconsidering lifetime sentences for people sentenced between the ages of 18 and 20. It also tackles AI regulation debates in Congress, drawing on reporting by Capitol Hill reporter Ahtra Elnashar. The show doesn’t appear to be filmed in one take like a true TV news broadcast (Keith is first seen in a black blazer, then a brown one, before switching back to black by the end of the video).

Another video, “Worth Noticing: School Bus Incidents,” is just two minutes long and compiles stories of school bus crashes from around the country. From the text accompanying the video:

We trust school buses to get our kids from the safety of our homes to school every day. So why are we seeing so many serious injuries and incidents? Is this simply a string of unrelated tragedies? Are staffing shortages the problem here? Training gaps? Weak safety protocols?

We’re going to be following these stories. Have you seen incidents like this in your community? Is this something that is keeping you awake at night?

Because these stories are horrific; we’re talking about every parent’s nightmare.

The National Press isn’t Sinclair’s first effort to reach a younger, video-first audience. In 2015, it launched millennial-focused news site Circa, which shuttered four years later.

As explained by LinkedIn: “You can now design and personalize your LinkedIn business card to express who you are professionally, add it to your digital wallet, and easily stay connected with people you meet in person. Rolling out globally over the coming months.”

As shown in this image, posted by Entrepreneur Magazine Editor-in-Chief Jason Fiefer, who at LinkedIn’s “Connection by Design” showcase event last week, the new LinkedIn digital business cards will include a headshot and job role description from a users’ LinkedIn profile, plus a QR code.

Users will also be able to customize the card display with a range of design options for the feature, as shown in these screenshots posted by Ishan Sharma on X:

This simplified, customizable digital card should provide another way to streamline LinkedIn connection at events.

Though it’s not the first time LinkedIn has tried out this option.

In 2018, LinkedIn added profile QR codes for offline connection.

The idea then was conceptually the same as this latest digital business card option, though without the custom design and creation options.

So it’s not entirely new, and the previous iteration never appeared to catch on as a significant connection tool.

But maybe this new version will provide another means to drive more IRL connection opportunities.

Running out of new angles for your Facebook ads? This customer survey process will help:

Build a short survey in a tool like Typeform and send it only to customers who have owned your product for at least 30 days. Recent buyers haven't used the product long enough to tell you what they like about it.

Ask why they bought, what pain point or struggle led them to purchase, what they like about the product, what they wish you would launch next, and what other pain points they're dealing with in their business or personal life.

Offer an entry into a $100 gift card giveaway for completing the survey. Frame it as a giveaway entry, not a guaranteed reward for every respondent.

Announce the winner roughly 48 to 72 hours after you send the survey email.

Mine the survey responses for the exact pain points, motivations, and phrases your customers use, then turn them into new hooks, avatars, and desires to test in your ads.

Pro Tip: When you've exhausted your survey insights, search Google for site: reddit.com followed by a pain point, benefit, or customer avatar. The threads that come up reveal before-and-after states, frustrations, and relatable scenarios in your customers' own words, which you can turn directly into ad scripts.

#100. Social commerce edges past SEO at The Independent for the first time

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit

The Independent’s social-commerce revenue edged past its SEO-based commerce revenue for the first time in September, CEO Christian Broughton said at Digiday’s Media Strategies event in London this week.

He described the gap as narrow, but said the trend was shifting toward social.

The company doesn’t publicly break out the figures, so the milestone offers a directional signal rather than a measure of how far social commerce has pulled ahead. But it illustrates the broader shift Broughton argued publishers need to make: build revenue around trusted brands and audiences across platforms, rather than depend on search to bring readers to their websites.

The search-and-social model that powered digital publishing for years is over, and AI referrals or purchased traffic won’t fill the gap. “The business model of the 20-teens, early 2020s” – built on abundant traffic, social referrals and programmatic advertising – is “dead,” Broughton said. The response, he argued, has to be more than a series of experiments layered onto the existing business. Publishers need to change how the business works.

Broughton identified four areas the company is building for: AI, creator-led studio work, e-commerce and membership. Together, he said, they are expected to account for nearly half of Independent Media’s revenue in 2026, with those areas growing at close to 30% year over year.

The Independent generated £55.1 million ($73 million) in revenue in 2025, up 4% from 2024. Profit before tax rose 9% to £3.5 million (£2.5 million post-tax), marking the company’s ninth consecutive year of growth and profit, per its most recent earnings. The U.K. generated £36.4 million ($48.3 million), while the U.S. and Canada were at £13.3 million. The company said that the results came despite a difficult year for digital publishers, with global trade disruption affecting advertising budgets and changes to Google search creating pressure. It currently has 368 staff, up from 332 in 2024.

For Broughton, AI productivity is valuable partly because it could create capacity to invest in that broader business: more podcasts, newsletters, video and documentaries, alongside membership. He pointed to the Independent’s eight-part podcast series SAS: The Shadow, developed over roughly a year, as an example of original, relationship-based journalism he says the company wants to invest in.

The argument is not that AI alone can repair publishing’s economics. It is that AI, paired with a willingness to reorganize the business, can help create room for work audiences value, and for new ways to earn revenue from it.

At the Independent, that change starts with putting AI against measurable economic goals. Broughton described the company’s AI-powered news app, Bulletin, as an early step, and pointed to a broader overhaul of editorial workflows. He said the app, has accrued 12 million monthly users since its launch last April.

Under U.K. editor Barney Henderson, who joined in April, the company is restructuring the editorial team around AI-enabled workflows. Broughton said the company didn’t want to simply plug AI tools into existing work practices; it needed to rethink how the team operated.

“He’s creating a new live news team, which is based around tools… And before anyone asks, yes, the live news team is run by humans. It’s not just AI. Real human editors,” he told delegates. “We’ve created about 15 roles, more than that actually now in that department. They’re using the tools and the workflows built and thought through by Barney and his team, and the outcomes have been really dramatic.”

Editors using its AI tools are now “six times” as economically productive as colleagues in comparable roles who aren’t using them, he claimed.

“I think we’ve all seen too many nice-to-have little experiments that people have done with AI,” he told delegates. “Some of them don’t always kind of really build up audiences. They don’t really drive business success. They’re not rocking the CFO’s world. So my advice is to put really hard economic targets behind what you do with AI.”

The tools he described take on work such as applying the Independent’s style guidance, surfacing relevant reporting from its archive and monitoring organizations for potential news. The aim, Broughton said, is to give journalists time back for reporting and original work – not to automate journalism itself.

He stressed that AI has been deployed beyond solely an efficiency tool internally. He cited its conversational AI feature Eva, which answers questions users ask on the site, by drawing on the publisher’s previously reported stories, using its tone of voice. He said Eva has reduced bounce rate by 10%, lifted user journeys by 20%, though he didn’t reveal what baselines.

“The purpose of AI at the Independent,” Broughton said, “is not to replace journalists. It is to make the economics of investing in exceptional journalism work again, and to make it work better than ever.”

Let Marketing Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

Arby's has appointed Jenna Bromberg as chief marketing officer, effective Nov. 2, per a company blog post. The executive will lead all marketing efforts at the Inspire Brands chain, with a focus on accelerating profitability, engaging consumers and marketing the brand through personalized digital experiences and “culinary storytelling,” per the post.

“Jenna brings a powerful blend of creative brand-building and commercial leadership,” David Graves, Arby’s brand president, said in a statement. “She has a strong track record of driving growth, building meaningful consumer connections, and developing culturally relevant marketing that delivers results.”

Previously, she served in senior marketing roles at Yum Brands, Carter’s and Hilton.

“Arby’s has a rich heritage and an exceptionally dedicated fanbase. The brand’s willingness to disrupt category norms and stand apart from competitors is what makes this opportunity so compelling; it’s a marketer’s dream,” Bromberg wrote on LinkedIn.

Inspire Brands, which also owns Dunkin’, Baskin-Robbins, Buffalo Wild Wings, Arby’s, Jimmy John’s and Sonic, in May indicated that it was considering an initial public offering. The franchise holding company formed in 2018 when Arby's merged with Buffalo Wild Wings.

#103. “Uber agents,” undercover AI personas, and other ways newsrooms are using AI in investigations

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Hacks/Hackers and The New York Times hosted more than 100 journalists at the AI x Investigative Journalism Forum.

Late last month, about 150 journalists, researchers, and technologists gathered on the 15th floor of The New York Times Building for a forum on how AI is changing investigative journalism.

Just outside the event space was a hallway commemorating the paper’s more than 140 Pulitzer Prize winners, dating back to 1918. One photograph had yet to be hung: a portrait of this year’s winners of the Pulitzer Prize for Investigative Reporting. For one of their winning stories, a team of Times reporters conducted an audit of the SEC’s crypto lawsuits to show weakening enforcement under the second Trump administration. The reporting was assisted by large language models (LLMs).

The Times isn’t the only major newsroom using AI tools in major investigations. A record-breaking eight Pulitzer awardees this year disclosed AI use to the judges. They used LLMs to organize, summarize, analyze, and translate large document dumps.

“At the Times we’re not doing ‘robots tell the news,’ but a number of different [kinds of AI adoption] that can make the work we do more efficient, more effective, and able to do things that otherwise would be very, very hard to do,” said Juliana Castro Varón, the Times’ senior design editor of AI initiatives, in a keynote. Often, “the most useful part [of AI] is the fact that it understands images and understands text, more than creating [them].”

RELATED ARTICLEA record-breaking eight Pulitzer awardees disclosed AI use this yearAndrew DeckAugust 3, 2026The Times’ AI Initiatives team, a group of nine journalists and technologists leading AI strategy and deployment in the newsroom, co-hosted the event with Hacks/Hackers, a nonprofit that brings journalists and technologists together to discuss media innovation. (Hacks/Hackers hosted a summit on AI and journalism in Baltimore for the past two years.)

The day was packed with workshops, panels, and presentations about the promise of AI for investigative journalism, led by the technology’s most vocal advocates in newsrooms. But the limitations of these tools — including persistent hallucination problems in LLMs, concerns about vibe-coding errors, and budget constraints as AI token costs pile up — were also a common theme.

“AI is very good at generating leads, but much less capable of establishing publishable evidence,” said Afrooz Mosallaei, a research associate at the Center for News, Technology & Innovation, during a talk about the nonprofit’s recent report on the topic. “A lot of tasks in an investigation — including verification, source development, textual understanding, and editorial judgment — remain fundamentally human responsibilities.”

The release of the Epstein Files was a huge moment for AI in investigative journalism. Journalists across the U.S. woke up on January 30, 2026 to a Department of Justice drop of over 3.5 million pages of documents and tens of thousands of images and videos.

Duy Nguyen, who leads AI science research at the Times, noted that the PDFs in the Epstein Files would stack as high as the Empire State Building if they were printed out, and would take 11 years for one reporter to read. (Epstein sent an average of 65 emails every day for a decade.) It would take a reporter a month to listen to and watch all the audio and video clips.

RELATED ARTICLEAI-powered search is fueling a wave of Epstein Files transparency projectsAndrew DeckMarch 4, 2026Many newsrooms decided that the early organization and research into these documents was a task primed for AI technologies. Engineers from the Associated Press, NPR, and the Times led a session on how they built tools to help reporters sift through the documents.

NPR built an internal search tool that let reporters across the newsroom find the documents relevant to their beats, said Kriti Singh, a design technologist at NPR’s AI Labs. Her team classified documents by type (email, legal filing, flight log, witness list), grouped them by location (city, county, hotel, university), and extracted entities (making sure, for instance, that a search for “Prince Andrew” also surfaced files that mentioned “the Duke of York”).

The Times AI Initiatives team built the Epstein Files Engine, an internal chatbot to help reporters comb through the files. “There are so many sorts of threads that you can pull from such a big corpus, and the chat interface really allows [reporters] to dive deep,” said Nguyen. The engine’s interface was built with LibreChat, a free, open-source, self-hosted AI chat platform.

“Look at our Epstein coverage over the past three months and cross-reference with names of people most mentioned in the documents. Give me a subset of names we haven’t covered as often.”

“Find me Kathryn Ruemmler’s email where she said she is missing her ring in Epstein’s apartment.”

“Construct a timeline of Epstein’s death, give me a table that I can copy into a spreadsheet. Be very detailed. Surface witnesses, links and quotes where available.”

Ultimately, more than 100 Times journalists posed more than 5,000 questions to the engine, and it contributed to at least 20 published stories. “This was a signifier of just how powerful an agentic chat interface could be in a newsroom,” said Nguyen. (His team recently published an academic article detailing the tool’s development.)

Since then, the team has created other agentic search tools. Ahead of the Times’ 175th anniversary series, they built “Morgue Bot,” which made it easier for reporters to dive into the Times’ archive.

Now, the team is taking chatbots to the newsroom at large. In July, they launched News Agent, which they’re calling the “front door to AI at The New York Times.” The general-purpose internal chatbot plugs into not just the Times’ archives and the Epstein Files, but other databases, internal documents like the Times’ style guide, and the web. News Agent also allows any Times reporter to build their own custom agentic search tool, tailored to a specific project.

“It’s an omnibus agent or an uber agent that basically acts as a drop-in replacement for chatbots like Gemini or ChatGPT,” said Nguyen, “but specifically geared to help reporters and editors within the Times newsroom.”

The team’s copy for the tool reads, “Ask anything.”

Any beat reporter will tell you they have a love-hate relationship with their source spreadsheet — that Google Sheet or Excel file that lists the name, title, email address, and phone number of every source they’ve spoken to over the years. Such documents are perfect for remembering the name of a researcher you spoke to five years ago without having to dig through your inbox. But they’re tedious to update.

“It can become a dead document that never gets checked,” said J.D. Capelouto, a technology reporter and the newly named AI lead at Semafor.

RELATED ARTICLEHow The New York Times uses a custom AI tool to track the “manosphere”Andrew DeckFebruary 11, 2026To try to keep his own source spreadsheet alive and up-to-date, Capelouto made a tool in Google Apps Script, a platform that lets users build small “assistants” within Google Workspace. When he emails someone for the first time, he adds an inbox tag called “New Source.” At the end of each day, the script scans his inbox for any tagged emails, then populates a Google Sheet with all the relevant information about them, including adding a category tag and generating a logline summarizing what they discussed. (There are obvious risks in handling anonymous or sensitive sourcing, but Capelouto said the tool creates minimal new security vulnerabilities since it stays within Google’s ecosystem.)

From there, Capelouto started building on top of the spreadsheet. A pop-up sidebar lets him ask who might be a good person to speak with for a story; the tool combs through the spreadsheet and suggests names.

Every morning, a script also scans the web for the news of the day on Capelouto’s beat, cross-references those headlines with the source spreadsheet, and sends him an email suggesting a topic to cover and a source to contact. Some of the suggestions aren’t useful, Capelouto admitted, but others have actually prompted him to reach out to someone he’d forgotten about.

“A lot of times in journalism, some of the source management work is just saying, ‘Hey, how’s it going?” he said. “This can begin a conversation, then you get a scoop from that.”

Philip Bump of Hearst Connecticut Media Group presents at the AI x Investigative Journalism Forum in The New York Times Building on September 25, 2026. (Photo courtesy of Hacks/Hackers)

Most conversations about AI-generated imagery in investigative journalism revolve around verification. As AI-altered images and deepfakes flood the internet, how do reporters verify the images they come across online, or those sent to them by whistleblowers?

The forum didn’t tackle these questions head on, but one presentation highlighted the ways that AI image generators can be harnessed to protect the identity of journalists.

Last year, The Markup co-published an investigation into Match Group, the dating app giant that owns Tinder, Hinge, and OkCupid. The nonprofit tech publication owned by CalMatters found that despite an official policy of banning users who are reported for assault, the company failed to keep them off their platforms and hid the scale of the problem from the public.

In one case, a Denver cardiologist who was repeatedly accused of drugging and sexually assaulting women he met on Hinge remained active on the platform for three years, even after two different women reported his abuse. (In 2024, he was convicted of crimes against 11 women and sentenced to 158 years to life in prison.)

RELATED ARTICLECan we gamify that? The innovators turning investigations on spying scandals and vote rigging into video gamesBhavya DoreAugust 17, 2026The Markup’s reporters decided to go undercover. They posed as users on Match-owned apps, then reported themselves from other accounts to see how easy it was to stay on the platform.

There was only one problem. “We came across this ethical dilemma: Am I gonna ask my staff or myself to take a photo and put it on the Tinder account?” recalled Sisi Wei, the chief impact officer at The Markup and CalMatters.

Even stock photos would subject real people, who had not consented to their likeness being used in the investigation, to reputational harm. Instead, The Markup turned to AI image generators. They found a company that generates visual test imagery and had developed a way to train models without relying too heavily on images of real people.

“They look like real human beings, but if you turn on a light switch, you can tell that AI is here,” said Wei. But they were still “real” enough to bypass the dating apps’ content moderation filters. With these new AI headshots and personas in hand, the reporters went back on the apps and created 50 different accounts.

Ultimately, their investigation found that even after one of these personas was reported and kicked off a Match-owned dating app, they could get back onto the platforms without changing identifying information. Earlier this year, the 18-month long investigation won a SABEW Award for best technology business reporting.

“AI became a way for us to protect our own staff from needing to be a part of the experiment,” said Wei.

Researchers posted about a made-up concept on sites AI search tools cite. Four English-web tools cited it within a week. Other topics mostly didn't land.

ChatGPT, Perplexity, Grok, and Google AI each cited posts about a made-up concept within seven days of the posts going up, according to a paper from researchers at Fudan University.

The researchers published the posts from ordinary accounts on nine sites the tested tools already cited often. On two other topics, an opinion question with existing discussion and a made-up product, the same four tools picked up little in the same seven days.

The paper uses the label “Google AI” and links to Google’s general AI site, but it doesn’t specify which Google product was tested. The tests were conducted in March and April, and the paper was posted on arXiv on Oct. 8.

In March, the Fudan team ran 120 questions through 10 AI search tools and recorded the sites each tool cited. The researchers classify ChatGPT, Perplexity, Grok, and Google AI as English-web tools; the other six, including Doubao and DeepSeek, are Chinese-web tools.

Across those questions, Reddit was the most-cited site for Google AI and Grok, YouTube for Perplexity, and Wikipedia for ChatGPT. Six to 10 of each tool’s 10 most-cited sites accepted posts from ordinary users.

In April tests of 22 posting platforms, the researchers rated Medium, GitHub, LinkedIn, and Facebook easy to join and post on, while Reddit’s karma requirements and strict deletions made posting harder.

For each tool, the team then picked its most-cited site that a new account could post on, which gave them nine sites, including Medium, YouTube, and Sohu.

The research team posted articles about the fictional “Cactus Gravity Protocol,” whether AI would supplant junior programmers inside of five years, and a fictional keyboard. The first drafts of each article were created using ChatGPT, then each was manually revised and carried planted details (e.g., fabricated names and numbers) to allow the authors to identify if the AI tools repeated that information.

The researchers ran checks before posting to verify that none of the tools provided an informative response to either of the fictional topics or repeated the planted information. Following posting, the researchers ran the same five questions for each of the three topics on all tools daily for one week.

In June I covered a Cornell Tech paper on planted text that tested open-source research agents in a simulation. This team posted on the live web and queried the tools through their public interfaces.

Eight of the 10 tools cited the made-up concept, the Cactus Gravity Protocol, within a week, including all four English-web tools. Counting answers from the first day each tool cited the posts through the seventh day after posting, Grok linked to a post in 30 of 32 answers, Google AI in 15 of 33, Perplexity in 13 of 35, and ChatGPT in 7 of 20.

Fewer responses to questions included a planted detail from the source posts. Of Grok’s responses (n = 32), 53% did; for ChatGPT (n = 20), 10%; for Google AI (n = 33), 6%, and Perplexity (n = 35) none. In total, among all 10 tools and all three topics, there were links from 176 of the 1,004 answers to the posts during the week.

The only English-web tool that cited an “opinion” post was Perplexity, in 11.4% of its responses (n = 35), and none of the four cited keyboard posts within the week. The authors do not isolate which of the topic, competition, and type of question caused the differences across the three topics, since all three changed together.

In a follow-up, the team put one post each on Sohu, YouTube, and CSDN for 10 more made-up topics. Nine drew at least one citation or planted detail across the 10 tools, and Perplexity was one of the three tools that cited the most of them. The paper doesn’t break out the other English-web tools there.

To assess location, the researchers created paired postings about 5 relatively unknown vacation destinations. One post was located on a source frequently referenced by the tools; the second post was placed on a site that was very rarely, if ever, referenced. In all cases, the post on the frequently referenced source produced the first reference/citation or planted detail.

The best case on the lesser-referenced side required 20 postings and 40 postings on a self-hosted WordPress site received zero references within seven days. These are presented by the authors as results for specific topics, not as general rules.

A separate experiment tested six fictional subjects using varying numbers of Sohu postings (between 1-20). The total number of citations across all ten tools increased from 24 to 128. However, ChatGPT never generated references to those posts and Google AI only did so when citing the three lowest-volume subject topics. Since each of the volumes utilized a unique subject, the researchers referred to this increase as an association rather than an effect of increasing the number of posts.

Lastly, the research team purchased a Chinese web posting package via a GEO vendor for $14. All 13 postings were delivered to the web within approximately 28 minutes after purchase. A Doubao reference to one of the postings including a planted detail occurred within one hour of delivery and is presented by the authors as one confirmed instance of success, not a success rate.

The topic every English-web tool cited within a week existed only in the researchers’ posts. Posts on the other two topics, an opinion question and a made-up product, mostly didn’t get through to the same tools.

None of the topics the researchers posted about was a real brand or product, so the tests don’t show whether the same pattern holds for brand or product searches, including ones with little coverage elsewhere.

Google’s guide to its AI features says seeking inauthentic “mentions” “isn’t as helpful as it might seem,” pointing to core ranking systems that focus on high-quality content and other systems that block spam. The paper doesn’t say which Google product it checked.

The researchers’ tests ran in March and April, before Google clarified on May 15 that its spam policies cover attempts to manipulate generative AI responses in Google Search. The authors say exact rates may drift as the tools change.

The researchers say they disclosed what they found to all 10 platforms, and that ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Google AI were among those that acknowledged receipt. I’ll update this story if a revised version of the paper changes the findings.
