#106. AI Slop Sites Are On The Rise. Is Ad Tech Ready For Its New MFA Challenge?

Ad industry insiders have consistently warned that generative AI would ignite an explosion in made-for-advertising (MFA) sites that cynically monetize via programmatic ad tech.

Well, research is starting to prove the case.

A study released Tuesday by advertising supply chain intelligence company DecryptAds uncovered more than 2,100 AI-generated recipe sites that take a page straight out of the MFA playbook, with multiple overlapping ad placements crammed onto pages filled by low-effort content. DecryptAds found ads from major blue chip and Fortune 500 brands appearing on these recipe sites.

The report examines sites populated by AI-generated recipes, although the same publishers operate all sorts of other ad-supported sites, such as political news aggregators and car, anime and video game forums.

By examining ads.txt and sellers.json files, DecryptAds determined that the recipe sites appear to be monetized by SSPs that work with ad tech partners located in what DecryptAds refers to as “risky geos.” These “risky geos” are associated with high degrees of cybercrime or often have adversarial relationships with the US, according to Zach Edwards, co-founder and chief of product and research at DecryptAds.

The idea that US citizens – including, potentially, government officials – can access these sites, have their data harvested by ad tech vendors and possibly be targeted with malvertising schemes presents major cybersecurity concerns, Edwards told AdExchanger. However, he noted that DecryptAds has not uncovered evidence of any crimes committed by these sites or their ad tech partners.

Regardless, the ad inventory on the sites is of dubious value, Edwards said. Just like with MFA, the sites are packed to the gills with ad placements designed to game viewability.

They duplicate viral recipe trends or copy popular pages from other cooking sites to produce close-enough versions that were clearly not reviewed by a person. The sites sometimes feature crazy foods that only make sense as a bucket of search keywords (“Hot Cocoa Buffalo Chicken Gingerbread Dip with Marshmallow Topping, anyone?”).

But to anyone with eyes, it should be clear that these sites have no place in a healthy programmatic supply chain, Edwards said, especially in light of recent Google Search changes that deprioritize sites featuring AI-generated authors and creators.

But whether to serve ads on such sites is a choice that many SSPs are still grappling with.

Part of what makes these sites hard to police is that they’re built to look like the work of real people.

The networks of sites uncovered by DecryptAds feature fabricated authors on their “about” pages. These author profiles often include AI-generated human avatars or, in some cases, stock images, stolen pictures of real chefs and even slightly altered images of celebrities, such as actress Emily Blunt.

A screenshot of the DecryptAds report showing a recipe website with an edited image of Emily Blunt on its author’s “about” page.

These sites rarely disclose that their authors are not real people, which means they run afoul of a Google helpful content update rolled out just this month.

The new Google Search policy states that “fabricating creator profiles (such as by using AI-generated headshots, made-up names or false credentials to make content appear as if it was written by human experts) is a form of deception. Any form of deception makes a page untrustworthy to both users and our automated quality systems, and is a signal of a low-quality page.”

According to Edwards, the advertising industry should take Google’s new policy as a sign that if websites don’t disclose their use of AI-generated authors, then the publishers and their vendors risk being officially classified as “low-quality” and therefore unfit for monetization.

A screenshot of a suspicious recipe site that AdExchanger randomly tested from a list of hundreds of sites provided by DecryptAds. The author’s “about” page features a clearly AI-generated image covered in targeted ads.

But according to a source at an SSP who spoke with AdExchanger on background in exchange for candor, the Google guidance only applies to Google’s search business and should therefore be treated separately from best practices suggested by Google Ads.

This source also disputed the premise that sites featuring AI-generated authors have no inherent value for advertisers or audiences. After all, real people click those links and engage with AI-generated content all the time, they said.

But quibbling over philosophical questions about AI avatars and bylines is arguably beside the point.

After all, the issue appeared on the DecryptAds team’s radar, Edwards said, because of concerns about potential cybercrimes and state-backed bad actors exploiting the ad supply chain.

It’s worth reiterating that the report does not contain evidence of any crimes committed by the sites or their ad tech partners, Edwards said. The operators appear less like sophisticated threat actors than opportunists running a low-effort content-farm playbook.

But cybersecurity concerns did inform the methodology used by DecryptAds. The team first discovered the more than 2,100 recipe sites covered in the report during its regular monitoring of ad tech companies registered in what they consider “risky geos,” Edwards said.

Think Russia, China, Cyprus, Turkey and the United Arab Emirates. These nations, Edwards said, are either under direct US sanctions, have an adversarial relationship with the US, maintain little to no privacy firewall between the government and tech companies or have associations with high degrees of cybercrime and ad fraud. DecryptAds groups these nations into threat tiers, with US-sanctioned nations like Russia in the top tier.

DecryptAds started by examining the supply chains of about 300 ad tech companies based in these risky geos, Edwards said, eventually deriving a list of publishers working with those 300 companies. It got this data by looking at ads.txt files. DecryptAds also determined which SSPs work with those 300 ad tech companies by examining the sellers.json files maintained by the SSPs, as well as by looking at domain name system (DNS) data, SSL certificates and Google Analytics data.

Using a list of food-related keywords, Edwards narrowed the list of sites monetized by the 300 ad tech companies to an initial list of “400 suspicious recipe websites,” he said. He manually confirmed that each of these websites use AI-generated avatars while obscuring their true authorship. (AdExchanger tested several still-active URLs provided by DecryptAds, and most either immediately failed the AI sniff test or featured stock author images easily uncovered by a reverse image search.)

Then, DecryptAds analyzed the sites to create more than 190 “technical footprints” to find other sites operated by the same owners, Edwards said.

DecryptAds eventually found 2,116 such sites that had slipped into the programmatic ad supply chain via the convoluted reseller relationships between global ad tech partners. The technical footprints DecryptAds created also helped it track the ownership of some of these sites to additional risky geos, with many of the sites having social media profiles tied to Morocco and Algeria, Edwards said.

With so many intermediaries in the programmatic supply chain, Edwards said, it’s easy for shady site operators to blend in.

In some cases, he suggested, the monetization of these sites demonstrates that some SSPs and ad tech platforms aren’t effectively vetting publishers before onboarding. But he also acknowledged that even when SSPs try to strictly and proactively weed out MFA inventory or AI slop, junk can still slip through the cracks.

The DecryptAds research is a testament to how important ads.txt and sellers.json have been for spotting weak links in the programmatic chain. They’re all we have to publicly verify the relationships between publishers and ad tech vendors.

But ads.txt and sellers.json files are an imperfect transparency tool. The files are rarely updated by most publishers and can include errors.

For instance, one entry in the DecryptAds report concerns a site called dailytastekitchen.com. It flags HBAgency as the site’s SSP and highlights HBAgency’s connections to “eight ad tech companies on our risky geo list,” based on account IDs stored in the site’s ads.txt file. These eight companies include Between Digital (an ad tech company based in Russia), Mintegral (based in China), AdMatic (based in Turkey), Monetix Ads (based in the UAE) and four other ad tech partners based in Cyprus or Turkey.

But of those partners named in the report, HBAgency only works directly with Monetix Ads, an HBAgency spokesperson told AdExchanger.

“As far as we understand, Monetix Ads uses technology provided by AdMatic, but HBAgency has no direct commercial relationship with AdMatic,” the spokesperson said. “Monetix Ads and AdMatic are based in Turkey, a NATO member and EU candidate country that is not subject to sanctions. Monetix Ads went through our vetting process and operates under contractual data protection obligations consistent with GDPR.”

Furthermore, HBAgency tells AdExchanger that every publisher onboarded to its SSP is screened by an independent third-party fraud provider. It also screens publishers for invalid traffic and runs “enterprise-grade malvertising protection across our supply,” the spokesperson said.

They added, “We review publishers on an ongoing basis and disable accounts that breach our terms and conditions. We do not serve ads in countries, including Russia, Belarus, Iran and North Korea, and we do not accept publishers or work with partners based in sanctioned jurisdictions.”

But, according to the DecryptAds report, HBAgency is allegedly a monetization partner for 1,631 of the 2,116 AI slop websites it uncovered.

Whether the error lies in the methodology used by DecryptAds or in HBAgency’s vetting process is unclear – and illustrates the headaches advertisers and SSPs face when trying to avoid monetizing such websites, Edwards said.

“We purposefully tried to only mention the SSPs briefly [in the report],” he said, “because these things are so complex that it’s hard to attribute things back to any one specific entity with complete accuracy and confidence.”

Rather than pointing fingers at SSPs and ad tech providers, Edwards said, DecryptAds is trying to raise the alarm that more of this AI-fueled MFA inventory is going live every day, and the industry will soon be swamped by low-quality sites if no measures are proactively taken to force-shift budgets elsewhere.

Given the moving target nature of auditing the open web for AI content, AdExchanger asked the other SSPs and ad tech vendors mentioned in the DecryptAds report to comment on their quality controls for their publisher networks and ad tech partners. In addition to HBAgency, whose comments are reflected above, AdExchanger contacted Ezoic, Culture G, MonetizeMore, Between Digital and Mintegral.

Ad revenue optimization company MonetizeMore was flagged by DecryptAds as monetizing just 11 of the 2,116 AI slop sites. After AdExchanger provided a list of those 11 sites to MonetizeMore, its CEO and founder Kean Graham said, “We are not actively running any MonetizeMore demand or our demand partners on any of the 11 sites listed.”

The company also initiated a wider review of its publisher inventory in light of the report, he said, and is committed to demonetizing any sites that don’t meet its standards.

Graham added, “One site [flagged by DecryptAds], Bakerias.com, still has a legacy connection to our reporting platform but runs its own AdSense account. We do not monetize that publisher because the domain did not pass MonetizeMore’s high site traffic requirement and ad inventory quality standards.”

Graham also confirmed that MonetizeMore is aware of the recent Google helpful content update that says sites with AI authors are untrustworthy. He said Google’s guidance aligns with MonetizeMore’s existing publisher standards.

“Inventory that relies on deceptive authorship violates Google’s guidance,” he said. “We do not think advertisers should be buying it and we do not monetize it.”

Ezoic, which DecryptAds says monetizes 407 of the AI recipe sites in its sample, took issue with the idea that AI authorship makes content inherently low-value.

“The internet is filled with low-quality content, both human-written and AI-generated. We believe the industry should judge content by its quality and usefulness, rather than treating how it was produced as a substitute for that assessment,” the company said in a statement.

On how it screens publishers, Ezoic said it “has an extensive review process and rejects more than 98% of sites that apply. We evaluate the quality of a site’s content or tools, the audience it attracts and how meaningfully that audience engages. We use our in-house identity graph to evaluate visitors, combine automated checks with human review to assess sites and analyze brand safety and contextual relevance in real time.”

The company also argued that AI-generated recipes can serve real people and real advertisers.

“Consider someone who discovers a pot roast recipe on social media, visits the site and uses its instructions to prepare dinner. That is useful content serving an interested consumer and a meaningful opportunity for an advertiser to reach that consumer. Whether AI helped produce the recipe does not, by itself, determine its value. What matters is whether the recipe is accurate, works and delivers what it promises.”

Both Culture G (which DecryptAds says monetizes 34 of the AI recipe slop sites in its sample) and Between Digital (which is mentioned in the report as an ad tech provider registered to a risky geo) did not reply to requests for comment.

Mintegral, the last company AdExchanger contacted, did respond, though its comments focused more on the report’s data security concerns.

Although Mintegral was listed among HBAgency’s ad tech partners for monetizing the site dailytastekitchen.com, a Mintegral spokesperson told AdExchanger that the company “reviewed our records and found no record of having served ads directly on the specific site referenced in the report.”

They added, “We do not support the use of fabricated author identities or credentials intended to mislead audiences or advertisers.”

Regarding the vetting of publisher inventory for AI-generated content, the Mintegral spokesperson said that its “core business focuses on mobile in-app advertising. While limited mobile web inventory may be accessed through third-party advertising exchanges, this is distinct from directly onboarding traditional content websites.”

“Regarding third-party web traffic,” the spokesperson continued, “we receive standardized bid data from our exchange partners, subject to applicable data protection and privacy safeguards. These partners operate under legal and privacy vetting designed to limit the data to what is necessary for advertising purposes and to comply with US privacy law.”

And, regarding concerns raised in the report about Mintegral being based in a “risky geo” (China), the company spokesperson said, “Mintegral has no history of security incidents or regulatory actions concerning user data, and has not been subject to any government requests to access user data. It’s important to distinguish between legitimate questions about data security and generalized assumptions based on a company’s geographic associations.”

Correction 10/20/26: This story was updated to clarify that DecryptAds based its summary of which ad tech partners worked with HBAgency to monetize the site dailytastekitchen.com on account IDs stored in the publisher’s ads.txt file, not HBAgency’s sellers.json file.

Most brands and businesses are trying to figure out how to improve their metrics when it comes to AI – and also what those metrics even are.

Minerva wants to turn fragmented customer data into something marketers can use, with AI agents doing the work behind the scenes.

VideoAmp is competing in the measurement space by sharpening its focus on TV audience data, ad performance and, of course, AI. The company is also making strategic hires and promoting from within.

The Prebid Summit in New York City on Tuesday exceeded the event’s reputation for liveliness.

The ad industry has become a community of people who say things like “This is going to sound relatable” and follow it up with a sentence that may as well be Martian to 99% of America.

LG home screen inventory is now available through agentic buying, opening up a premium TV placement to faster, more automated campaign setup.

#107. How to Use AI on LinkedIn While Sounding Human

Want to use AI to create LinkedIn content without getting flagged or losing credibility? Wondering how to integrate AI tools into a LinkedIn workflow that still sounds like a real person wrote it?

In this article, you'll discover how to use AI strategically at each stage of content creation on LinkedIn, plus updated tactics for comments, video, live streams, and ads that reflect how the platform works right now.

LinkedIn has been quietly waging war on AI-generated content. The platform has blocked hundreds of thousands of automated comment attempts daily and billions of posting attempts over recent months. Members can now report content they suspect is AI slop, and LinkedIn's analytics dashboard shows creators whether their audience perceived a post as heavily AI-generated.

The crackdown isn't just about bots. LinkedIn is replacing its “enhance your post” AI feature, which rewrote content in a generic AI voice, with a proofreading-only tool designed to preserve the author's original voice. The signal is clear: LinkedIn wants AI to assist creators, not replace them.

AJ Wilcox points out that the platform's detection isn't just algorithmic.

Real people are flagging content that reads as inauthentic, and LinkedIn is listening. In fact, AJ believes the AI slop reporting feature is currently functioning as a training mechanism for LinkedIn's detection models, not as a direct penalty on flagged posts. The reports aren't yet suppressing content, but AJ expects that to change as LinkedIn refines its systems. In the meantime, AI-generated comments that get flagged tend to receive very few likes and responses, so natural engagement pushes them to the bottom on its own.

The shift puts creators in a position where understanding how to use AI correctly isn't optional; it's the difference between content that builds authority and content that gets buried.

The most effective way to use AI on LinkedIn, according to AJ, is to break the content creation process into three stages, with AI handling the bookends and human expertise filling the middle.

Ideation: AI excels at brainstorming. Before writing a post, a creator can use AI to generate a list of angles, supporting points, or frameworks around a topic. This stage is about volume and possibility, not finished prose.

Human Expertise: The middle stage is where the creator's actual knowledge lives. This is the part that shares original experience, industry-specific insight, and the kind of nuance that only comes from doing the work. AI can't replicate this, and skipping it is what makes content feel like slop.

Polish: After the post is written in the creator's own voice, AI can help make it more readable and easier to scan. Tightening sentences, fixing grammar, and improving formatting. AI is editing the creator's words, not generating new ones.

AJ recommends thinking of it as a sandwich: AI on the outside, human expertise in the middle. When the middle layer disappears, the audience notices, and so does LinkedIn.

AI detection is a constant cat-and-mouse race, with platforms and audiences continually adapting to new tells. Certain patterns immediately signal AI-generated content to readers. AJ identifies several specific tells to watch for.

Em dashes are one of the most recognizable. AI models use them far more frequently than most human writers, and their presence in LinkedIn posts has become a red flag. Similarly, emojis dropped into comments, particularly when they don't match the commenter's usual style, trigger skepticism.

Join thousands of small-business marketers at Social Media Marketing World — three days of AI, social media, and marketing strategy taught by world-class experts. April 1–3, 2027 in Anaheim.

Every session is pitch-free and built around tactics you can use yourself, no big team required. Your All-Access ticket includes an extra day of workshops, full access to AI Business World, and recordings of everything.

Specific phrases also give it away. Language like “guard your mental faculties” or “this is silently killing you” reads as AI-generated because it follows patterns these models default to when generating dramatic or attention-grabbing copy.

Some creators have considered intentionally leaving typos in their content to appear more human, but AJ cautions that this isn't a reliable strategy. AI can just as easily be told to insert a typo or two, making intentional imperfections an unreliable signal.

Pro Tip: If a post genuinely shares something of value, it's unlikely to be called out as AI slop, regardless of how polished it is. The audience reacts to emptiness, not polish. A well-edited post with real substance behind it reads differently than AI-generated filler, even if both are technically well-written.

AJ's recommended posting schedule is straightforward. For two posts per week, publish on Tuesday and Thursday. For one post per week, Wednesday is the strongest single day.

Monday should be avoided because competition for attention is highest as everyone returns to work. Friday is equally weak because professionals are mentally checking out for the weekend.

One critical rule: never post twice in one day. AJ explains that the second post steals engagement from the first, cannibalizing the creator's own reach. Even spacing posts too closely together can hurt. A new post shouldn't go live while the previous one is still gaining traction, because LinkedIn's algorithm shifts attention to the newer content.

LinkedIn announced approximately 6 months ago that it would let posts live longer in the feed. AJ has seen some evidence of this, with likes and comments occasionally coming in on older posts, but notes that it hasn't changed the fundamentals all that much. The most recent post still receives the majority of daily engagement, reinforcing the importance of giving each post room to breathe before publishing the next one.

LinkedIn has made significant changes to how comments work, turning commenting into a stand-alone growth strategy.

Comment impressions are now visible to the commenter. This feature, released approximately a year ago, allows creators to measure the reach of their comments in the same way they measure posts. For accounts that don't yet have a large following, commenting on posts from larger accounts is a way to get impressions without needing their own audience.

LinkedIn is also surfacing comments more prominently in the feed. Previously, comments were hidden behind a click. Now, LinkedIn shows them directly, and “top comment for you,” a personalized comment recommendation, is replacing the generic “top comment” label. Time spent in comments across the platform is up 18% year over year.

Marketers and creators can leverage this shift for a viable growth strategy built entirely around commenting: rather than posting original content, spend your time leaving thoughtful comments on relevant posts from established accounts. The impressions data shows it works, and it requires less creative energy than producing original posts.

Executing this strategy requires curating the LinkedIn feed to surface the right posts. AJ notes that curating a feed is a long process, but the investment pays off over time as the right content surfaces naturally.

The AI Business Society filters the noise for you, with expert-led training you can put to work the same day — plus a community of marketers sharing what's actually working.

He recommends searching for relevant hashtags to find people posting about a specific topic. For example, searching #LinkedInAds surfaces everyone posting in that niche. To reach potential clients rather than competitors, broaden the search to adjacent topics.

To train LinkedIn's algorithm to show more of these posts, follow and connect with industry people, engage with their content, and have DM conversations behind the scenes.

Not all comments carry equal weight. AJ references a conversation with the head of LinkedIn's company pages team, who shared that the metric they care most about is “comment density,” which measures the depth and substance of comment threads rather than their length alone.

Shallow comments like “great post” or “thanks for sharing” don't register as meaningful engagement. LinkedIn's algorithm looks for real conversational depth, where commenters engage with the ideas in the post and add their own perspectives.

The most effective follow-on lines to invite deeper discussion are “Am I wrong?” and “What am I missing?” Both prompt diverse replies from different people rather than a single back-and-forth thread. AJ notes that a conversation between two people spanning 16 exchanges doesn't help the algorithm as much as a thread with many different contributors.

Timing matters too. The highest-impact window for commenting is the first 1 to 2 hours after a post goes live. Most posts lose momentum by evening if they were published in the morning, though viral posts can continue attracting valuable comments for 2 to 3 days.

Controversial or negative posts tend to generate the deepest comment threads, but AJ argues that positive, substantive discussion is more valuable for building professional relationships and reputation.

The conversation produced a three-step framework for respectful disagreement: open with a genuine compliment about the original post, follow with “I have a slightly different take,” and close by asking for the other person's thoughts. The approach keeps the conversation productive rather than adversarial.

AJ endorses what he calls the Ted Lasso principle: “Be curious, not judgmental.” The goal is to contribute to the discussion rather than win an argument.

LinkedIn has introduced AI-powered tools for live streams that solve one of the format's biggest problems: discoverability after the live event ends.

The AI automatically identifies standout moments from a live-stream and generates short-form clips. It also creates chapters for the replay, allowing viewers to jump directly to specific topics rather than scrubbing through hours of footage. Previously, live-stream replays on LinkedIn were unwatchable after the fact because viewers couldn't skip ahead and had to watch in real time.

These tools are available globally, though AJ notes they currently appear to be limited to LinkedIn Pages rather than personal profiles. LinkedIn also keeps live-stream replays available for approximately 6 months, significantly longer than Facebook's 30- to 60-day window.

AJ sees a particularly strong use case for executive content. Many CEOs and company leaders resist creating video content because of the production overhead. Live streaming lowers that barrier because it doesn't require editing or scripting. Once the live-stream is finished, LinkedIn's AI handles the clip creation, pulling out the strongest 30 to 60-second moments automatically.

The workflow AJ recommends for this is to set up an interview format in which someone asks the executive a series of questions. Record in a high-quality environment using tools like Descript, Squadcast, Riverside, or StreamYard. Capture in 4K on a phone with a good external microphone. The AI then finds the best clips from the conversation.

LinkedIn now offers AI-powered creative tools within its ad platform, though AJ notes they're currently limited to text generation for headlines and introductory copy.

The tools aren't doing anything a creator couldn't do with ChatGPT, but the convenience of having them inside the ad platform saves time.

The more important tactical point involves LinkedIn's recommendation to run five or more ad variations per campaign. LinkedIn claims this produces a 20% higher click-through rate, but AJ strongly disagrees with this advice.

The problem is mechanical. Running five or more creatives breaks LinkedIn's frequency cap, which normally limits how often the same user sees an ad to twice per day. With more than five variations, the system treats each as a distinct ad and enters more auctions, showing ads to the same users more frequently and driving up costs.

AJ recommends 2 to 4 creatives per ad set. A common setup is one image paired with two different intro texts, or one intro text paired with two different visuals, or a combination totaling four variations. This stays within the frequency cap while still providing enough variation for testing.

Pro Tip: Don't bring Meta advertising best practices to LinkedIn. Meta's algorithm rewards high volumes of creative and broad placement targeting. LinkedIn's system doesn't work the same way. The one crossover that does work: bring the highest-performing creative from Meta campaigns to test on LinkedIn, but don't flood a LinkedIn campaign with dozens of variations the way a Meta campaign might.

AJ Wilcox, founder and CEO of B2Linked, helps B2B companies spend less to generate more qualified leads and drive business with LinkedIn Ads. Listen to the LinkedIn Ads Show podcast. Follow him on LinkedIn.

#108. Ownership, control, margins: the brand playbook for microseries is still taking shape

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit

Brands are testing two routes into creator-led microseries: partnering with an established hit to tap its audience, or building a series around their own brand. The first can offer built-in distribution; the second can cost less but give brands more control. But with ROI hard to pin down, and questions about who owns the IP, neither path is a sure bet.

That tension surfaced at Advertising Week New York last week, where several panels examined the growing appeal, and uncertain business case, of microseries. These short-form videos, often made for vertical viewing, span genres from comedy and horror to drama and appear on platforms including TikTok, YouTube and subscriptions services dedicated to vertical storytelling.

Brands are increasingly creating their own or incorporating into existing ones, from jewelry brand Alexis Bittar’s Bittarverse mockumentary featuring fashion icons like Law Roach and Michasel Kors, to SharkNinja products sitting inside the hit comedy microseries Brooklyn Coffee Shop.

The buy-in is there, but with inconsistent ROI and a variety of ways to activate in the space, the future of the microseries is unclear. To get some clarity, Digiday spoke with a brand building their own microseries, a creative agency pitching them to brands, a comedy creator, and three creator economy executives about the future of the microseries, the questions they’re raising, and who’s winning when the deals are signed.

First, brands have to decide exactly how they want to enter this world – do they latch onto an existing, successful microseries (either on free platforms like TikTok and YouTube or paywalled ones like ReelShort and Drama Box), or do they look to hire smaller creators to make their own branded series to build awareness on popular social channels?

“The cost to get involved with the microdramas that we’re making with TikTok are probably higher than they’re spending on making their own,” said Ian Schafer, co-founder and president of branded entertainment studio Ensemble, which sits under actor Issa Rae’s Hoorae media company. “But what they’re hoping for is what we’re guaranteeing, which is distribution.”

But for smaller creators and studios, brand integration is a lower-risk investment. Harley Block, CEO and co-founder at creator-focused media company IF7, pointed to comedy microseries, Secondhand Exchange, and how the entry point is much more accessible cost-wise as it’s still growing its audience.

“You can’t buy credibility or content integrity,” he said. “I think doing it from the ground up as a brand, the deck is stacked against you. It doesn’t mean it can’t be done. I guarantee you, there are brands that can do it, but do you want the built-in credibility or not?”

For creative agency Dayna’s House, however, they’ve pitched building microseries from the ground up in nearly every recent meeting with brands, according to founder Dayna Carney. Nuuly, the fashion rental company, was the first one to bite. The agency helped build a microseries about dating in New York City, starring actor Wally Baram and featuring creator Milky Tran as director. The videos have racked up millions of views on TikTok and tens of thousands on YouTube in just two months, and Carney said the cost was low.

Photographer and creative director Cris Molina, who recently worked with Floridian resort SkyBeach on a microseries set on the property said that microseries “can cost a master brand a quarter of what they spend with us on traditional advertising.”

Adam Wescott, CEO and co-founder of Home Game Studios said that the budget on average is around $200,000 per series’ season, and with the number of episodes decreasing on average (from around 70-90 one-minute episodes to 40-50), so there’s more money to work with on a per-minute average per episode. Despite this, Wescott said there’s not a “huge margin” for producers and creators, but it does often give them, crucially, ownership.

As brands and creators are navigating the microseries waters, a few questions repeatedly rise to the top about ROI, which is still uncertain; ownership, which varies; and where the genre goes from here.

For Schafer, Ensemble guarantees a certain floor for each brand it works with, and thanks to their partnership with TikTok (which just announced a second co-production partnership with Tanya Cohen’s Made By Us studio), can hand-wave away production costs when they ask. “We’re delivering them the media value for every dollar that they spend,” he said. “We’ve already greenlit microdramas for a season two that haven’t launched yet because our testing says that they’re going to do so well.”

But that kind of guarantee isn’t common across the microseries space. Nuuly’s series is all about brand storytelling and building a world in which the fashion rental company is “a character,” according to Carney.

So ROI is wiggly, but what about ownership?

In the case of microseries built explicitly for a brand (like Nuuly) creators don’t own the IP and can’t capitalize off of its success doing spin-offs or utilizing the character created for the series in other work. But the playbook for when the series ends is still unwritten.

“Is there an expiry date? Is there a license to use it? Does it return back to, you know, the director or the hero talent? How will that work?” Carney asked.

The goal in many cases is for IP ownership to stay with studios and creators, but if it doesn’t, Wescott says there are higher budgets and creator fees for branded entertainment to make up the difference. In the case of IP created and produced entirely by a creator or a studio like Home Game, ownership is a case-by-case basis, but ideally, creators can do whatever they want with them. Gray Fagan, a scripted creator with 5 million followers on TikTok, said he always ensures he retains ownership of his characters.

As for the future of the microseries, it’s unclear. Wescott has seen the format begin to incorporate more genres like true crime and horror, hence the shift towards the “microseries” verbiage and away from “microdramas.”

Schafer worries that, as more brands try to wrangle the microseries (which he says is surprisingly difficult since each episode has to have a beginning, middle, and cliffhanger, done several dozen times), they’ll increasingly rely on rehashing old tropes or generative AI to better guarantee success.

“Any time there’s an exciting new format, tech, celebrity that audiences flock to, brands have 100 meetings about it,” said Schafer. “I love the experimentation that’s happening, but I do sometimes question the strategy of saying ‘This is something that’s hot. We should make our own.’ One of the reasons why it’s hot is because the brands aren’t making their own.”

#109. Nieman Lab has a new look

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

More layout diversity, new typefaces, and restructured archives.

You may have noticed that things look a little different around here. We’ve just launched the third major redesign in Nieman Lab history. Hope you like it!

My No. 1 goal for this design (internal codename: Roscoe) was increasing design diversity on article pages — to enable a greater degree of art direction. In our previous design, we’ve had three basic layout choices for an article — which basically came down to how large we wanted to play its art. Now we have vastly more room to tie the design to the article — multiple layouts, multiple arrangements of headlines/decks/art, multiple background colors, multiple optical sizes, and more. Here’s a sampling:

For about a decade, we’ve divided our stories into “hubs”: Business Models, Mobile & Apps, Audience & Social, Aggregation & Discovery, and Reporting & Production. Those had started to feel a little outmoded; it’s been a while since “mobile” was anything other than the middle of the mainstream, for instance. So we’ve replaced them with six “beats” more attuned to the times: AI & Journalism, Search & Platforms, Audience & Creators, Local News, Reporting & Production, and Business & Revenue. With a little AI assistance, we’ve populated those collections with all 12,000-plus articles we’ve published since 2008.

Those 12,000-plus articles were one of the biggest challenges — making sure they all made the transition cleanly. More than 100 of those articles used custom CSS; each one had to be checked (and most of them updated) to match new layout structures and typefaces. In all, there are more than 100,000 unique URLs on niemanlab.org that now have a new look. And we now have enough history to finish off the homepage with stories we’ve published on this day over the decades.

Our new primary typefaces are TypeTogether’s Literata as the serif and Bakken & Bæck’s Schibsted Grotesk as the sans. (Schibsted Grotesk is, of course, the custom typeface designed for the European media house.) My thanks to the Freight collection (Text, Display, and Sans) for its decade-plus of typographic service.

I’ve designed and coded every iteration of niemanlab.org since founding the Lab in 2008, and it’s been a point of perverse pride for me to be a journalist with some technical ability. But it also means that, over the past 18 years, our backend has accumulated the handcoded cruft of a zillion PHP bugfixes and CSS hacks. So this time I was happy to do the vast majority of the work in Claude Code, which made some of the more ambitious ideas I had far easier to implement. The code is clean and organized in a way that should make it easier to build further.

#110. What Frogs And Socks Can Teach Us About AI Implementation

Conventional wisdom says that you need clean data before you can use AI. But Rebecca Sykes isn’t so sure the data needs to be pristine.

Sykes, a partner at The Brandtech Group who leads its emerging technology practice, says generative AI can work with the kind of fuzzy, siloed and sometimes badly labeled data that used to stop projects cold.

“We’re less worried about messy data or bad data than no data,” she says on this week’s episode of AdExchanger Talks. Brand-specific data, even when it’s disorganized, is critical, because it’s what keeps AI outputs from turning into a generic sea of sameness.

“For brands, the biggest risk here is that AI takes you toward convergence rather than divergence,” Sykes says. “And divergence is the lifeblood of brands.”

But even with the right data, plenty of AI pilots stall at scale. To explain why, Sykes has a fable she likes to cite from a new business book about AI transformation, and it involves a frog and a sock.

Think of AI as a frog, which was born to leap. Now picture the frog stuck inside a sock, which represents a company’s existing operating model. The frog can try to leap all it wants, but if it’s trapped in a sock, it’s not going anywhere.

“In general, no one’s sock is wrong or broken,” Sykes says. “It was just built for a different time.”

For example, a client might use AI to reduce the amount of time it takes to do one part of a task by, say, 70%, but then be disappointed, because the entire task still takes four days to complete. Where’s the efficiency?

But the reason why it still takes so long is because the overall work still moves through multiple different systems and rounds of cutting and pasting, and the data in one system doesn’t always match the data in another.

In other words, AI sped up one step, but the process around it never changed. “You have to look at the entire end-to-end efficiency of a work process,” Sykes says, “not just the piece you can automate today inside a single system.”

But shedding the sock isn’t something companies can do thread by thread, she says. They have to start over and build new ways of working around what technology can do. The majority of effort in any AI transformation should go toward people and processes, she says, and that means creating new roles, including jobs related to AI governance, systems ownership and workflow maintenance on both the client and agency sides.

As the cost of making content falls, Sykes says, the value shifts to owning the system. But that also requires treating transformation as an ongoing capability rather than a one-time initiative.

“Transformation is not a project; this is a capability,” she says. “It’s a muscle you have to exercise.”

Also in this episode: The thinking behind Brandtech’s new global data and AI practice, how Jellyfish’s “share of model” tool tracks what AI models say about a brand, the role video plays in AI brand recommendations and why Sykes has never seen “The Goonies.”

Webinar: The Link Building Graveyard: What to Bury & What Still Wins

Get journalist outreach pitches seen and understood by improving targeting, email authentication, subject lines, and the details AI inbox summaries pick up.

Everyone is clamoring for news coverage (linked and unlinked), and AI has made it easier to find and spam journalists.

In this post, I’ll show you why the landscape is very different from what it used to be, based on four major studies I published, including 14.3 million emails by domain age, 39 million emails by subject line, 628 AI summaries, and data on the journalist workforce.

I’ll focus on four areas: journalist attention, domain optimization, subject lines, and AI summaries.

In the AI era, there are a LOT more PR professionals in the space than ever before and they outnumber journalists.

In the U.S., I estimated about two or three PR pros for every one journalist (though our research showed a big discrepancy based on where you look: the U.S. Census says 1.8; the Bureau of Labor Statistics says 7.2). In the U.K., it’s roughly 1.5 pros per journalist.

Now, take all those PRs and add the fact that many link builders are also migrating to PR as an inroad to AI exposure.

AI-generated pitches, even fake experts, now flood the market, and journalists are underwater with irrelevant AI slop pitches.

We are seeing this playing out in the data as well. Muck Rack’s State of Journalism 2026 found that 47% of journalists say they seldom or never receive pitches that match what they cover!

You are going to hear this a lot from me, but it all comes down to quality over quantity.

Finding the right journalist for a campaign means going beyond a bio or job title and looking at what they actually cover.

Look at an author page and gauge relevance by the last 10-20 articles they’ve written.

I thought things like domain age or email authentication were throwaway factors until I looked at the data.

But they can drastically change whether or not an email even lands in a journalist’s inbox.

Like Google’s search algorithm, we don’t know what goes into email deliverability or how email platforms gauge sender reputation, but we do have data that can provide directional guidance.

Based on our study, older domains (5-6 years old) got better open rates (34.9%) on average than domains 1-2 years old (21.6%).

I thought at first that the older domains just had more experienced senders, but both seasoned digital PR practitioners and brand-new accounts had equally low opens with a new domain, around 25%.

Young domains with full SPF/DKIM/DMARC still averaged 17.9% open rates.

While you’re building domain age, you still need to maintain proper emailing practices throughout, which again comes back to quality vs. quantity.

SPF/DKIM/DMARC authentication is essentially a set of rules that tells email providers how to handle emails and senders.

In a study we conducted on 1,588 sending domains, we found that fully authenticated domains got almost 4x better open rates (30.1% avg. open rate) than unauthenticated domains (7.8% avg. open rate).

Proper SPF, DKIM, and DMARC authentication has become much more important as providers fight against spam.

Google and Yahoo rolled out new sender requirements in 2024, followed by Microsoft a year later. Missing them can get you blocked (which we’ve actually seen happen to BuzzStream customers).

SPF, DMARC, and DKIM records are located in your domain’s DNS settings.

Typically, a developer can tackle these in under an hour.

AI tools can also easily walk you through it (they helped me do it in just a few minutes).

If you’re curious where yours stand, I built a free checker for this.

The subject line is the true differentiator these days for standing out in a journalist’s crowded inbox.

Here’s a screenshot of an inbox from U.K.-based freelance journalist Rosie Taylor:

Image courtesy of Rosie Taylor, October 2026

Imagine trying to find a relevant piece of coverage while swimming through a sea of irrelevant emails, marketing emails, and AI-written emails.

That said, I recently published two big subject line studies that I think show you how to stand out.

Lines that stated a finding (e.g., Raleigh Among Best for New Homeowners) got 43.1% opens and 1.37% replies.

Subject lines that teased a finding (e.g., Which City is Best for New Homeowners?) got 39.8% opens and 0.88% replies.

Similarly, we found that concrete subject lines (e.g., Raleigh Ranked #1 City for New Homeowners) got 43% open rates and performed better than vague ones (34.6%) (e.g., New Study on the Housing Market).

You can start to see a pattern here: it’s all about specifics.

Write the main takeaway out as a sentence first, then start rearranging.

When you’re done, put yourself in the shoes of a journalist and ask yourself:

Hone it in. Ask your friends, colleagues, even AI for some feedback.

In the same study, subject lines that put the key stat or information in the first 1-3 words got 46% open rates, compared to those in words 4-6 (38.9%).

Word placement matters because of email subject-line character limits.

Every email platform has its own limits, and they differ.

Roughly ~60 characters on desktop and ~42 on mobile is the sweet spot, but it varies greatly.

Think about delivering the key stat as succinctly and quickly as possible.

This might mean flip-flopping your subject lines.

Instead of “Best City for Homeowners is Raleigh,” you start with what will be most eye-catching and applicable to your target journalist: “Raleigh Named Best City for Homeowners.”

Test it out in your own email provider to see how it gets cut off.

Gmail, Apple, and Microsoft all now have AI summaries that appear at the top of email messages, changing how journalists may perceive your message.

In a study we did with digital PR agency Aira, we uncovered some tendencies in how these platforms summarized, and more importantly, where they pulled information from.

In general, content from the first half of emails appeared more frequently in AI summaries across Apple, Google, and Microsoft email platforms.

87.1% of Google’s AI-generated summary content came from the first half of the email. Apple: 82.5%, and Microsoft: 65.4%.

AI-Generated Email Summary Keyword Matches By Position*

*Data from Buzzstream and Aira AI-Generated Email Study

(In general, Microsoft was a little more spread out because their AI summaries tended to be around 150 words long, compared to Google’s 30 and Apple’s 50.)

This aligns with other studies showing that AI tools are more likely to pull information from the beginning of a page.

Personalize who you pitch, not the opening line.

If your story and email are relevant enough for your target journalist, the personalization isn’t necessary.

Lines like “I read your previous article on X, and found Y” don’t seem to have the impact that they used to, which makes sense given how time-crunched everyone is.

In fact, in our study, personalized intros were mostly not included in Google’s (11% of the time) or Apple’s (0%) AI summaries.

(Microsoft had the highest chance of inclusion at 61%, but again Microsoft has longer summaries, so it makes sense they would include more.)

Another big takeaway for me was that, across all platforms, bulleted text influenced AI summaries at least 64% of the time.

AI-Generated Email Summary Bulleted Text Inclusion Rate*

*Data from Buzzstream and Aira AI-Generated Email Study

Microsoft included information from the bullets 92% of the time, followed by Google (65%) and Apple (64%).

I’ve always been told that bullets should support the main takeaway.

So if your takeaway that “Raleigh was named the best city for homeowners” appeared in the opening section of your email body, you don’t need to repeat it in the bullets.

Instead, the bullets should help explain more of the why and how.

Digital PR expert Hannah Smith of Worderist once suggested on our podcast that I try to write an article from a PR pitch I wrote.

When writing your bullets, put most of the key info that helps fill out the article there.

If you’re following that, the AI summaries should pick up the most important information anyway.

Although this won’t help you get coverage, it’s important to know that Apple and Microsoft AI summaries misrepresented information from the original email in about one in three summaries.

They mainly misrepresented data and expert quotes. So, when you do get coverage, double-check that it’s properly represented.

This is good practice in general, but even more so in the AI age.

In many ways, these are the same challenges we’ve always faced when getting a pitch read, but AI has supercharged everything and added a new one: AI summaries.

But if you can take one thing from this data, it’s that a good story isn’t enough anymore.

The good news is that focusing on relevance will help at every step.

Pitching the right journalist can protect your sender reputation.

Knowing what they cover makes it easier to write a subject line.

Writing a clear, direct pitch is far less likely to get slopped up by AI in a summary.

You can optimize all you want, but if you aren’t reaching the right journalists, you are doing yourself a disservice.

Not only do you risk spam complaints, but you add to the noise that’s making all of this harder in the first place.

#113. Future of Marketing Briefing: The holdcos long, awkward courtship of the C-suite

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit

Publicis Groupe CEO Arthur Sadoun said this week that he’s pitching directly to CEOs, and the industry hasn’t stopped chewing it on since.

Some of the messages landing in Digiday’s inbox have him down as a leader in the fullest sense. Plenty of others aren’t buying it. How many chief executives, the doubters ask, decide their business needs transforming and make the first call to an ad holding company? A few go further and read the whole thing as bravado papering over a trail of pitches that went nowhere. Strip out the cheerleading and the snark, and what’s left is an identity crisis holdcos have been struck in for the best part of two decades.

It started around 2008. Clients cut ad budgets the moment the economy wobbled, and the holdcos, badly exposed, went looking for a way into the boardroom. Some managed it. Sir Martin Sorreil made his name at WPP partly on his access to chief executives, and Mark Read kept a smaller version of that going after him. Sorrell’s great rival, Maurice Levy, worked edge same circuit for Publicis long before handing the job to Sadoun. Over at Omnicom, John Wren pulled the same trick, which goes some way to explaining how the group has held on to the likes of Apple and McDonald’s for so long. Still, those relationships tended to grow out of the CMO-holdco tie rather than any standing the holdcos had earned with the rest of the C-suite.

Publicis, according to Sadoun, has found its way in. CEOs, he said, are “increasingly” involved in what the business does, mostly because they’re passionate about AI and need to understand it well enough to make the right calls. It doesn’t take much to work out who he has in mind for the tutoring.

And why not? Few CMOs carry much weight with the rest of the C-suite, and most don’t last in the job long enough for an agency relationship to outlive the retainer. So the holdcos hedged. They spent years buying data companies and consulting shops to prove marketing could move the numbers a finance chief watches, and occasionally to catch the CEOs eye along the way. It only ever half worked. When a chief executive goes looking for outside counsel, the shortlist still tends to start with Accenture and Deloitte, whose boardroom relationships go back decades.

That’s a completely different way of working for agencies. Consultancies are built to play the long game and their staff learn early that helping a client’s people get ahead, even with no fee attached, is how the bigger work eventually lands. Agencies grew up selling to a single buyer in the CMO, one brief at a time. For most of them, the reward for winning a pitch has been the chance to defend it at the next one. Unpicking the kind of loyalty a consultancy has spent decades building with a CEO will take holdcos a lot longer than a good AI pitch.

“Agencies don’t typically have meaningful access to that level of the clients they work with. In packaged goods, they do, luxury is the same – because they are a pretty material part of the business,” said Brian Wieser, media analyst and author of the Madison and Wall newsletter. “What has struck me when I’ve seen it in the wild, is that it’s like a big deal for a an agency CEO to get to meet the CEO of a financial services company or an auto company where advertising and marketing is like a low single digit percentage of total activities.”

Get that meeting, though, and it can pay off handsomely. Sadoun said this week that Publicis Sapient helped land two of the year’s biggest accounts without a pitch. If CEOs can make reviews disappear, they’re the closest thing to a cheat code the agency business has seen in years. The theory is that a holdco gets through the technology door and the media and creative work follows. Getting that to compound is another matter. Sapient is the part of Publicis that’s shrinking — outside of the U.S. at least — down mid-single digits in the second quarter and still slipping slightly in the third. Transformation work is lumpy and can stall the moment clients get nervous, as delayed programs in the Gulf showed this year. The holdcos have also bled the senior people needed to hold the boardroom relationships together, sometimes by design and sometimes by accident.

Then there’s the risk of getting exactly what they asked for. CEOs ask awkward questions for a living, and the holdco model has plenty worth asking about: data charges, tech fees folded into bundled deals and principal media, where the holdco buys inventory itself and sells it on at a margin clients don’t always see.

“All of that stuff doesn’t hold enough water for the rest of the C-suite,” said Steve Boehler, who runs consultancy Mercer Island Group. Pull those executives into the relationship and the holdocs will have “really smart people trying to look under the hood,” he said, who may be unable to see what they’re really buying.”

None of this means holdco bosses are wrong to covet CEOs. Boehler sees the push as part of a wider shift in what marketing covers, closer to the old four Ps of product, price, pace and promotion than to the advertising the agencies were built around. The holdco now has “at least on paper,” the capability to address the needs that “touch multiple people in that C-suite,” he said. That spreads the buying decision across more desks. The silos inside most big companies “have considerable power and influence,” said Boehler, so the CEO and CFO end up with a say in the pitches that used to sit with CMO, whether they show up in the room or not. He expects considerably more to happen before any of it sticks. The ambition itself, he said, is “a real intention” of the holdcos.

When it does stick, the marketers who used to own the relationship can find themselves on the outside of it. A senior marketer at one advertiser described a holdco deal that has run for several years with an agency the team likes. The trouble is that the holdco’s chief client officer has grown closer to the company’s C-suite. When the internal media buying team raises a complaint now, it struggles to get a hearing, because it’s no longer the agency’s main sponsor inside the business.

Two decades spent trying to get past the CMO and the holdcos may find the CMO was the one relationship they couldn’t afford to lose.

Billion Dollar Boy has bought something. The social marketing agency spent a decade building its business organically, so its acquisition of Creator Authority, a B2B creator marketing specialist with LinkedIn accreditation, marks a charge in habit. The deal also gives BDB more presence in LA and Austin. Thomas Walters, the agency’s chief innovation officer, said the firm spotted B2B marketing heating up 18 months ago and hinted that more deals are coming. The conversation that follows has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

Walters: We identified about 18 months ago that B2B marketing was heating up. Its shown promise for a ling time but hasn;t had the same rigor or professionalization, apart from specialists like Creator Authority. Spend is increasing and marketers are seeing very high ROI for B2B brands, even more markedly than B2C because it’s newer. Creator Authority was growing very quickly and dealing with some of the growing pains we went through as a younger business. We can support them through that. We’re very confident that with the combination of our global platform and Creator Authority’s special relationships, and LinkedIn accreditation,-that we can make a really serious mark in professionalizing and advancing the B2B creator marketing industry as a whole.

How much do the two client bases overlap?

Walters: The client mix is different but there’s crossover. Microsoft, for example, is a client we share. Some businesses sell to other businesses, some sell directly to consumers and some do both. CMOs already work with a proliferation of agencies. Where a client has a B2B and B2C audience we can now offer a combined solution, which saves them managing different partners.

Walters: Historically we’ve built things organically, whether that’s investing in creative tech or building direct access to creators. This is our first acquisition. Our long-term plan has strategic moves on it that we’re planning to make and the two approaches compound. As scopes get bigger and capability needs get wider we want to have solutions in market.

Walters: We’re seeing a creator way of thinking applied to more channels and more parts of the funnel than ever before. Creator content is supporting SEO and now AEO. Creators are being integrated intro branded entertainment and brand films. CMOs want partners that can work across that mix and we’ve been building against those changes for some time, from evolving Billion Dollar Boy into a social agency to creating our production arm about five years ago.

Does calling a BDB a creator agency pigeonhole it?

Walters: Our mission is to transform how brands grow in a creator world. Billion Dollar Boy is a social agency with a creator instinct. We’ve delivered broad social copes for many years and creator fluency has always been in our DNA. In 2026 we;re in what we call social 3.0 where creators are the lifeblood of social media. If brands don;t understand that their advertising won;t engage audiences or drive impact. Many others in the social space are still operating with a social 2.0 mindset.

“So more and more we have a region manager and we will ask them to focus on cross-fertilization, on the integration of creative and media. And I would say the ambition in terms of new biz is really attracting this new integrated client that gives to Havas all the assignments from media to production including creativity, data, PR or event.”

— François Laroze, cfo and chief operating officer at Havas on the holdco’s Q3 earnings call earlier this week

#115. Subscribers are up, but growth is down. Here’s what worker-owned Hell Gate is trying next.

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

One tactic: “Turning off the free stuff every once in awhile.”

With around $1.5 million in revenue, 2026 is on track to be a break-even year for the worker-owned local news site Hell Gate.

“We’ve spent a lot of money growing this year,” Hell Gate co-founder Nick Pinto told me, “so the fact we’re ending the year in the same place with regards to our bank account, it’s basically good. But it would be better if we were ending with more money than we started with.”

Hell Gate expects a revenue boost thanks to a new tax credit from New York State. To collect the $157,000, its worker-owners have to jump through a series of hoops, including refiling their personal taxes for 2025.

Hell Gate, founded by five journalists in 2022, now has 10 employees, including a couple of part-timers. Currently, only full-time editorial employees can become worker-owners, and only after a vesting period. Shares can only be owned by workers so when co-founder Esther Wang departed this summer, the rest of the owners got the shares back under a buyback policy.

“When we organized Hell Gate, in our fevered idealism, we wrote it into our operating agreement that there’s no way for anybody to make any money selling Hell Gate,” Pinto said.

“To the extent that we contemplated the possibility that we’d even still exist [four years later], I don’t think any of us thought we’d ever want to leave,” Pinto added. “The arrangement makes ownership stakes about control of the direction of the company rather than about, you know, accruing value on an investment. That means our ownership is a thing that keeps us pulling together rather than having us fight over money.”

RELATED ARTICLEJournalism coops seem utopian. What’s it like working in one?Neel DhaneshaFebruary 3, 2026But, even in worker-owned news organizations, money can be a source of tension. “Compensation and how to structure it has reliably been the single most difficult conversation for Hell Gate owners,” the report notes.

Hell Gate once paid journalists the same salary. Last year, it paid reporters $75,000/year and its two editors $85,000/year. Now, in 2026, Hell Gate salaries range between $83,000 and $100,000, “according to a slightly complicated formula intended to reflect both longevity with the company and the extra work and responsibility carried by editors.” The news org expects to keep tinkering with the pay structure.

“The wise words of one of Hell Gate’s advisory board members continue to be borne out: In setting compensation, the best you can hope for is to minimize the inevitable dissatisfaction,” the report reads.

#116. How to Build Your Own AI Apps (No Coding Required)

Are you spending too much every month on software subscriptions that don’t actually fit the way your business works? Wondering how to build custom AI-powered apps and tools, even without any coding or technical experience?

In this article, you'll discover how to brainstorm, build, and launch custom AI apps that replace expensive software, even with zero technical background.

Business owners no longer need to accept the tradeoff of paying for software that partially solves their problems. AI-powered tools now make it possible to build custom apps from scratch, without writing code or hiring a developer.

Erika Stanley describes this as building for a “market of one,” where the software serves one specific business instead of thousands of generic users.

Traditional software is designed for mass markets, which means individual business owners adapt their workflows to someone else's product. The features they need most are often missing, while features they'll never touch inflate the cost.

Erika points to her own client management system as an example: it costs more than $300 a year and handles leads, contracts, client communications, and invoicing, but it has never quite worked the way she needs it to. There are features she'll never use and capabilities she wishes it had.

That dynamic is shifting. With AI-powered vibe coding platforms and tools like Claude, business owners can now build custom AI apps that solve their specific problems, no coding required. Erika is not a software engineer, yet she has replaced more than $1,200 worth of annual software subscriptions in just a couple of months using this approach, all while paying just $100 per month for a Claude Max plan.

To justify upgrading from Claude's $20-per-month plan to the $ 100-per-month Max plan, she set a simple goal: cut at least $100 per month in software costs to make the upgrade pay for itself.

The benefits extend beyond cost. Custom-built tools do exactly what the builder needs, nothing more and nothing less. When requirements change, the builder can go in and add features rather than emailing customer service and waiting for a response. And once the skill set is in place, the same approach can be applied to new problems.

The app doesn't have to be business-related at all; once the skill set is in place, any problem in daily life becomes a potential build. Apps built this way can become products for memberships, communities, or direct sales.

Erika's first MVP project was replacing a $29/month subscription tool she'd used for more than two years. Fixer did two specific things for her business. First, it used AI to sort, tag, and color-code her email inbox while generating draft responses that matched the tone of each thread. Second, it provided an AI meeting note-taker that joined every client Zoom call and auto-generated follow-up emails, placing them in drafts ready to send.

Rather than building a full replacement, Erika identified that she already had access to the same capabilities through existing tools. Claude's connectors could handle email sorting and tagging. Fathom's free tier could provide meeting transcripts. And Claude itself could generate the follow-up emails from those transcripts.

The prompt she used to start the project was simple: “Here's the problem I'm having. Here's the software I'm using now. Is there a better way?” She described the problem and the desired outcome, not how to solve it. She let the AI determine the best approach.

The solution wasn't a fancy dashboard or a separate app. It was a scheduled task within Claude that runs every morning at 5:30 AM, a time chosen specifically to conserve tokens. The task processes the inbox, generates an email digest, and sends it via Slack, with each follow-up email delivered as a separate message that can be copied, reviewed, and sent.

Every session is pitch-free and built around tactics you can use yourself, no big team required. Your All-Access ticket includes an extra day of workshops, full access to AI Business World, and recordings of everything.

The entire build took less than half a day, and Erika was working on other tasks simultaneously. Claude Code handled the building independently, only pausing when it needed her input to answer a question or approve a step.

The biggest mistake new app builders make is trying to build everything at once. Erika recommends starting with the concept of a minimum viable product, or MVP. The starting point is a friction point: something where, if that one thing were just a little bit easier, the whole day would run smoother.

The analogy is a skateboard. Instead of trying to build a car on day one, Erika suggests starting with the simplest version that solves the core problem. A skateboard has four wheels and two axles. It does the job. It gets from point A to point B faster than walking.

From there, the product can evolve. Add steering, and the skateboard becomes a scooter. Add pedals, and it becomes a bicycle. Each iteration adds functionality while keeping the product usable at every stage. “A working skateboard beats a non-working car sitting in your garage,” Erika says.

Once a friction point is identified, the next step is brainstorming a solution with AI.

Erika recommends opening Claude then to describe the problem and the desired outcome, not to prescribe the solution. The AI's internal knowledge of available tools, integrations, and workflows often produces a more elegant solution than what a non-technical user would design independently.

Pro Tip: Erika notes that Fable Five, Claude's highest-level model, is particularly strong at problem-solving. It excels at connecting the dots between a person's problem and the solution they need.

The next step is creating a product requirements document, or PRD.

In traditional software development, a PRD is the first thing an engineer requests. It's a comprehensive list of everything the product needs: what it should look like, how it should operate, and what should happen when a user takes a specific action. Branding can be included if the app needs a particular visual identity.

Any LLM can generate a PRD from a conversation. Erika recommends describing the product concept and then asking the AI to “create a PRD for me.” The AI will produce a detailed requirements list that should be reviewed line by line. Because the model has to make some inference jumps when creating the document, it's important to check that every requirement is accurate, that nothing critical is missing, and that the AI hasn't misunderstood the intent.

The AI Business Society filters the noise for you, with expert-led training you can put to work the same day — plus a community of marketers sharing what's actually working.

For business owners who aren't sure what to include in a PRD, the AI can conduct an interview that walks users through PRD creation.. It asks questions back and forth, covering what the product should do, what problem it solves, and how users will interact with it. Each answer fills in the gaps, and the result is a polished requirements document ready to feed into a building platform.

Pro Tip: Erika recommends completing all brainstorming and PRD work in Claude or ChatGPT before entering the vibe coding step. Vibe coding platforms charge tokens for every exchange, and credits run out quickly during active building, so arriving with a finished PRD saves credits. She also recommends paying monthly rather than annually, bumping up to a higher tier during active building, and dropping back to the lowest tier once the app is finished and only needs hosting.

With a PRD in hand, the next decision is where to build the app with vibe coding.

Vibe coding is the practice of describing what an app should do in plain language and letting AI generate the code, no programming knowledge needed. Several vibe coding platforms exist, including Lovable, Base44, Replit, and Bolt.

Erika has used multiple platforms and currently prefers Lovable at $25 per month. Lovable functions as an end-to-end solution, taking a project from brainstorming through development to deployment, ending with a live URL that can be shared with anyone. The platform includes hosting and a database, so there's no need to set up external infrastructure.

She finds Lovable more intuitive than alternatives for two reasons: the brainstorming and chat experience feels more natural, and the deployment settings are easier to navigate.

Once the PRD is loaded into Lovable, the platform builds the app. Making changes is handled through a chat box in the left sidebar. Requesting a change, such as adding light mode and dark mode, generates a prototype that can be tested within the platform before publishing. Once the update is ready, clicking publish automatically replaces the live version that all users see.

Claude Code offers another path. It can accept the same PRD and build a functional app, but it builds locally on the builder's computer. This makes it ideal for personal-use apps where only one person needs access. Regular Claude can also publish apps as artifacts, but Erika notes that those are meant to be prototypes, not production-ready applications.

Publishing for multi-user access takes extra steps, covered in the hosting section below.

Pro Tip: To design the app interface with a polished look, Erika recommends using regular Claude to mock up what the login page, homepage, and interior pages should look like based on the PRD. Claude Design can take those mockups further, adding branding, colors, logos, and generating multiple variations to choose from. Pinterest mood boards can serve as visual references for the desired style.

Two hosting platforms work well for vibe-coded apps: Vercel, which is free and suits simple apps with low traffic, and Railway, which costs approximately $5 per month and handles apps that need a database, like the book club app. Both connect to GitHub, a code storage platform that tracks every version of the app, similar to how Google Drive works for documents.

Lovable and Base44 handle hosting automatically, so there's nothing extra to set up. They also support custom URLs within the platform. To avoid the cost of purchasing an additional domain name, Erika sets up a redirect from her website so that users visit a clean, branded link like AIQueens.com/appname rather than a Lovable domain.

Apps built in Claude Code need a separate hosting service to make them accessible online. Claude can walk through the setup process step by step.

Security is essential for any app that handles user logins, email addresses, or passwords. Erika notes that hackers are specifically targeting vibe-coded apps, making security checks a necessary step before publishing.

Lovable and Base44 include built-in security checks. Before publishing, the platform flags major security issues with a red indicator and can fix those vulnerabilities automatically.

Claude Code can also address security issues, but it won't flag them on its own. Builders using Claude Code should specifically ask what security vulnerabilities might exist and request fixes before deploying.

For version control, connecting each app to the same GitHub repository used for hosting makes it possible to recover previous versions if an update causes problems. Lovable also allows rolling back several steps without a GitHub connection.

For Claude Code builds, Erika recommends telling the AI to back up to GitHub. With smarter models, instructing the AI at the beginning of a build session to make periodic backups can work, though she notes that reminders are sometimes needed throughout the process.
