#117. Political Campaigns Are Bringing Broadcast Habits To CTV. That Could Cost Them Billions

Political campaigns are set to spend more than $11 billion on advertising in the midterms, and a growing share will land on connected television (CTV). But shifting the budget to streaming without shifting the thinking behind it can lead to a tremendous amount of waste.

For years, the industry has debated linear versus streaming and broadcast versus CTV, and how quickly budgets should migrate from one to the other. As viewers have moved to streaming, advertisers have followed them. The problem is that many campaigns are bringing old broadcast habits along for the transition.

Campaigns already spend enormous amounts of time and money determining which voters matter. They build voter files and modeled audiences. They identify likely supporters, likely opponents, potential donors, infrequent voters and persuadable voters whose decisions could change an election’s outcome. That same audience-first thinking should carry through to how they use CTV.

Traditional television buying has always required campaigns to work in broad strokes. They choose media markets, programs, dayparts and demographic groups likely to include the voters they want to reach. Inevitably, their ads also reach plenty of people who are irrelevant to the campaign’s objective. CTV gives campaigns tools to be much more precise.

Yet too many campaigns revert to broadcast-era targeting strategies when approaching CTV. They use streaming as another way to reach a large television audience, buying impressions against wide geographies or audience groups when they could be much more deliberate about who sees their ads.

Campaigns should begin with the voters they need to reach and use CTV’s targeting capabilities to find them. They should also identify people who have already taken the desired action or are extremely unlikely to move, rather than continuing to spend money reaching them. The objective should be to make every impression work more effectively, especially in an election with a fixed deadline and a finite universe of voters who can affect the outcome.

Viewing behavior can make that strategy even smarter. How people consume media signals where and how to reach them. A household that spends hours watching free, ad-supported streaming services presents a very different advertising opportunity from one that pays to avoid commercials whenever possible.

Imagine that both households contain voters a campaign needs to persuade. The first may be readily reachable through a CTV campaign. The second may rarely see the campaign’s 30-second streaming spot, no matter how good it is. That knowledge lets the campaign put more emphasis on reaching those voters through online video, social, pre-roll, audio, other digital channels and, yes, even broadcast.

Those insights are most valuable when they are available early enough to affect the strategy. Audience intelligence should help campaigns determine who belongs in the CTV buy, who needs to be reached elsewhere, how to divide resources among channels and how often individual voters should encounter a message. It can also inform creative decisions when different audiences consume media in different ways.

That requires campaigns to share audience information more broadly across the people making strategic, creative and media decisions. Media teams often have useful information about how audiences consume content that never reaches the people developing messages or producing creative. When teams consider those insights earlier, campaigns can build communications programs around actual audience behavior rather than assembling separate media plans after major strategic decisions have already been made.

As billions of dollars pour into advertising during the final weeks of the midterms, the campaigns that get the most from CTV will use the data and targeting capabilities available to reach the voters who matter, learn from how those audiences consume media and adjust the rest of their communications accordingly.

Otherwise, the consequences could be measured in close races lost and opportunities squandered. CTV can give campaigns the edge in those races, but only if they use it as the precision tool it is, not as broadcast by another name.

#118. Brands turn to content series and Jimi Hendrix to improve AI search performance

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit

Brands can’t tell ChatGPT how to talk about their products. One of the things they can do, however, is invest in more branded content, on their website or elsewhere, in an effort to give the models beneath chatbots used by consumers more to work with.

It’s leading companies like guitar manufacturer Fender and amp-maker Marshall to invest in website experiences and editorial content.

Fender’s interim CMO Kelly Magrath told Digiday the company had undertaken an overhaul of its website, aiming to turn it into a “front door that we can use as a storytelling platform” for the storied brand.

The new destination site includes short videos explaining Fender’s heritage, highlighting the artists who’ve played its guitars, such as Jimi Hendrix, as well as the skilled craftspeople behind its instruments. The company typically funnels paid media spending toward search, YouTube and social platforms; Magrath didn’t disclose its annual budget.

Much of that editorial is also distributed through owned social channels like YouTube, where guitar enthusiasts can find video series marking 75 years of the Telecaster (favored by George Harrison, Chrissie Hynde and James Hetfield) or pedal demos.

The effort is partially intended to improve Fender’s visibility during the product discovery or research phase of the consumer journey. Seven out of 10 U.S. consumers use ChatGPT or AI summaries when researching products or companies, according to a survey published by content marketing agency Skyword.

Hendrix might have played a Fender Stratocaster upside down (he was a lefty), but he plugged it into a Marshall amp. Marshall Group, the firm behind Marshall amps and headphones, has been pushing a YouTube series of its own, staging gigs by new bands in long-extinct venues like the London Fog or New York’s China Chalet. ‘Dead Venues’ is part of a wider brand campaign the company has been running since May; it’s also making use of digital paid inventory like YouTube, as well as partnerships with indie music publishers, out-of-home and experiential activity.

The work promotes a connection between support for today’s live music scene — Marshall maintains its own record label and sponsors tours and venues — and the company’s kit. In particular, it’s focusing on distinguishing itself in the competitive headphones market, according to Christine Kennedy Grant, vp of brand marketing.

“We’re a challenger,” Kennedy Grant said. “We are known as an iconic guitar amp brand, and as we differentiate into these new categories, we’ve really needed to reconsider who we want the consumer to know us as.”

Such efforts should also improve its visibility in AI search tools. “It’s such an important place for us to show up,” said Kennedy Grant of AI Overviews and LLM tools.

“AI is making it easier for consumers to find answers, but it’s also making it harder for brands to be remembered,” explained Andrew Wheeler, CEO of Skyword. “That puts a premium on the content brands create themselves based on their unique expertise; strong editorial that is distinctive gives AI and consumers specific ideas, resources, and points of view to trust, cite and recommend.”

In each case, search performance is far from the only consideration. Kennedy Grant is keen to ensure gig-goers and record collectors think of Marshall as “a brand that stands for something,” she said. “These headphones keeps live music alive.”

Magrath, meanwhile, said that Fender’s e-commerce presence required an overhaul that replaced its “transactional” shopfront with a platform that emphasizes consistent brand messaging and Fender’s custom guitar-building service.

It’s a path being taken by marketers worried about their SEO, or GEO, performance. “One of the best places to start is content where you have a right to win,” said Jim Yu, founder and CEO at SEO company BrightEdge.

Such activity doesn’t necessarily have to drive direct web traffic, as long as it improves citation or visibility scores, noted Urvashi Manral, associate director of discoverability at Attention Arc.

She said clients were increasing the budgets available to SEO teams in the hope of improving LLM recommendations. “ChatGPT is the new word of mouth,” said Manral. “If you really want to be the dominant result in those AI engines, the biggest and the quickest way to move the needle is through content.”

Paid search practitioners are keeping a close eye on how content can affect search performance. Stephani Estes, chief media officer at agency The Shipyard, said her agency was experimenting with owned content, creator activity and whether ‘boosting’ videos made by brands on platforms like YouTube might aid their intake by LLMs. Whether a brand can juice its profile with paid media, she said, was an open question.

“I don’t know that there is a silver bullet yet,” she said.

Brand marketers aren’t hanging around to find out the definitive answer, though. Three-fourths (75%) of marketers plan to increase spending on visibility in AI assistants next year, according to a Kantar survey published at the beginning of October.

Longer-form owned content can aid brand visibility, in part, because users have begun entering longer queries into search engines — moving on from the keyword-studded search strings deployed by web users prior to the advent of AI. “Originality is the key differentiator,” said Emma Sibbles, head of content at IDHL.

In some cases, that looks like the glossy documentary-style video content Marshall and Fender are putting out; in others, it’s a blog post.  “A brand with a real point of view, expertise, examples, experiences and useful context gives an AI platform a much richer source to retrieve from than a blog post engineered to breadcrumb 20-30 keywords,” said Emily Stutzman, CEO at creative agency Happylucky.

The agency has been creating style editorials for client Adidas, she said: “We’re also seeing more owned content scopes from brands like Stanley 1913, and Salt & Straw.”

Again, these efforts aren’t solely directed at robot readers. They can, of course, also fulfill a brand-building function with human customers. “The brand that consistently publishes original thinking, useful expertise, distinctive opinions and firsthand experience is building a body of knowledge that can become a brand advantage when consumers are in a moment of search,” said Happylucky chief creative officer Ben Hennes.

A brand’s own content may be only one of several sources LLMs typically draw from when composing answers. But it’s one a marketer can control.

As Apple spells out its case for blocking identity companies in Safari, its job board shows an ads business with big plans.

Prebid wants to change one of the key fundamentals of ad tech.

This fall, there’s been a steady drumbeat of new brands launching in the big-box retailer’s home category.

#119. OpenAI’s API Only Partly Matched ChatGPT’s Citations, Paper Finds via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

In this webinar, learn to rewrite spec-sheet product copy into the words shoppers use, and make product pages readable to AI.

Invalid traffic on AI Max search doubled to 5.28%. Get the channel-by-channel retail benchmarks before Black Friday.

In this webinar, learn to rewrite spec-sheet product copy into the words shoppers use, and make product pages readable to AI.

Join this webinar to choose a channel to test, set a starting budget, and identify results to track before investing more.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Webinar: The Link Building Graveyard: What to Bury & What Still Wins

A paper tested whether Google results and OpenAI's API can stand in for ChatGPT's citations. They matched cited sites more often than the exact pages.

Google search results and OpenAI’s Responses API together found 26.2% of the pages ChatGPT cited in a preprint’s tests of the GPT-5.5 Instant setting. They found 48.7% of the sites behind those citations.

Figures in this paper were posted on Oct. 11 by researchers at the National University of Singapore and Xi’an Jiaotong University. It included four versions of ChatGPT, from GPT-5.2 Instant to GPT-5.5 Instant, along with the majority of data collection from March 29 through July 29, 2026. The two stand-ins were able to be queried without having to open ChatGPT; the researchers compared both stand-ins’ results for similarity to the pages cited by ChatGPT’s web app.

Researchers recorded the flow of data ChatGPT’s web application received during its writing process, by recording what was happening in their own signed-in sessions. In this data flow you can see the searches ChatGPT performed, which pages resulted from the searches and the pages ChatGPT chose to be sources. A page was counted as cited if ChatGPT selected it as a source; i.e., both pages that are individually listed as their own link and pages in groupings included as a single selection as a source.

There were 80 questions. These 80 questions originated from Search Arena. This is a public database of actual user interactions with search-enabled chatbots/AI models. There were two languages used in these 80 questions: 40 English and 40 Chinese. Four types of requests were made: recommendation, fact lookup, information synthesis and analysis. Each of the 80 questions was run 20 times on GPT-5.3 Instant and GPT-5.5 Instant. GPT-5.2 Instant and GPT-5.4 Thinking had fewer questions run due to being decommissioned prior to completion of data collection.

To create the substitutes, researchers retrieved up to five pages of Google’s organic results per question through SerpAPI for each of the 80 questions. On average they got about 43 results per question. For each question, researchers also sent 20 queries to gpt-5.3-chat-latest and gpt-5.5 via OpenAI’s Responses API, with web search enabled. All of this was done within three days of running ChatGPT for the exact same query. The paper is an arXiv preprint. arXiv does not do peer review of papers.

Combined, Google’s results and the API found 28.3% of the pages GPT-5.3 Instant cited and 26.2% of the pages GPT-5.5 Instant cited. In terms of sites, the same combination found 50.3% and 48.7% of all cited sites (with subdomains being treated as different sites). The paper calls a page cited if it has been cited on ChatGPT in at least one run of the 20. The percentages are then the averages across the 80 questions.

The Google search results alone accounted for 9.4% and 6.4% of cited pages, and 26.1% and 22.8% of cited sites. The API’s entire source list accounted for more than that, showing 22.9% and 22.5% of all cited pages. The pages the API cited in its own answers covered less; however, when comparing them to ChatGPT’s citations, we can see that they were a closer match. When looking at averages over the 80 questions, GPT-5.5 Instant also cited 23.3% of the pages the API cited. This is higher than the percentage of API-cited pages that were cited by GPT-5.3 Instant (at 16.4%).

OpenAI’s help page explains that when ChatGPT search utilizes an external provider, it usually transforms a query into one or more specific search terms. In both GPT-5.3 Instant and GPT-5.5 Instant runs in which searches could be seen, ChatGPT never queried using the exact wording of the original question. However, in GPT-5.2 Instant, it did so in 5.5% of all runs.

Among the runs that included visible searches for questions written in Chinese, GPT-5.3 Instant (67.0%) and GPT-5.5 Instant (69.6%) utilized only the English language. Additionally, in February, I discussed results from Peec AI that found that in its tests, 43% of fan-out queries for non-English prompts ran in English.

Additionally, there was variation in results between individual runs. For example, 44.5% of the distinct pages returned for a given question were shown in only one of the 20 GPT-5.5 Instant runs. Similarly, 40.8% of the distinct pages returned for a given question were shown in only one of the 20 GPT-5.3 Instant runs. The degree of overlap between runs was greater at the level of site than at the level of page. Also, as noted by the authors, while pages that appeared in more of the other runs associated with a particular question had higher likelihoods of being referenced, they noted that this does not indicate that citing is influenced by the frequency of appearance of a given page.

I previously covered the CiteChoice preprint about how rerunning identical inputs flipped 15% of cite-or-not decisions. Here, two collection sessions transitioned to another model after running for 14 and 16 runs respectively, and the authors therefore suggest checking which model generated each response.

In the tests described here, neither of OpenAI’s API results nor of Google’s search results showed ChatGPT’s cited pages exactly as they were cited. This would mean that an OpenAI API or Google ranking-based test would find a larger share of the same site(s) than of the same page(s).

The authors’ suggestions for how to monitor are to monitor at both the level of individual webpages and of sites, run the same prompt multiple times, and take into account the fact that ChatGPT rewrites your prompts into its own searches. Check if any comparison of webpage-level results from a tracking tool versus what ChatGPT reports uses data collected through the API or directly through the ChatGPT application. The paper didn’t test any commercial tracking tool.

Every setting in the paper predates GPT-5.6 and GPT-6. OpenAI’s model help page notes that GPT-6 is rolling out in Chat to eligible Plus, Pro, Business, and Enterprise users, while GPT-5.6 Luna is becoming the default for Free and Go users.

Around the GPT-5.5 change in May, Sistrix data showed day-to-day variation in German-language ChatGPT citations jump to 47%, against a normal 1% to 2%. The paper’s authors say monitoring strategies should be re-evaluated when the model behind ChatGPT changes. Until the comparison is repeated on GPT-6, the paper’s figures describe the models that were current from March to July.

#120. A study of nonprofit newsrooms reveals some cracks in the model’s foundation

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Plus: Audiences aren’t too keen on AI news anchors, journalists say government funding doesn’t compromise their independence, and disillusionment in the profession is prevalent.

Editor’s note: Mark Coddington, Seth Lewis, Tamar Wilner, and Nick Mathews write a regular newsletter on recent academic research around journalism. We’re happy to bring each issue to you here at Nieman Lab. Over the past decade, nonprofit news has been seen as one of the bright spots in U.S. journalism — an emblem of hope for the future amid a landscape littered with failures and financial struggles. RELATED ARTICLENonprofit news is growing strong — especially local nonprofit news, a new report showsHanaa' TameezOctober 8, 2025With an average of 10 local newspapers closing each month, joining the thousands that have met that fate already, conditions out there are grim. Largely in response, more than 6,000 nonprofit foundations have made major investments in local news initiatives, totaling some half a billion dollars or more in direct funding for journalism. As a result, the number of U.S. nonprofit news organizations has been growing by double-digit percentages year-over-year. It’s fair to question whether this is sustainable. But in the meantime, at least, what’s not to like about this arrangement — this major push to subsidize local journalism at a time when the for-profit model for it is rapidly vanishing? Behind the scenes, it seems, there are cracks in the foundation, ones that appear to call for greater scrutiny to understand how sustainable and effective this model truly is moving forward. As described in an ethnographic study published recently in Journalism & Mass Communication Quarterly, Jocelyn McKinnon-Crowley of the University of Memphis spent four months in late 2023 and early 2024 embedded in a four-person nonprofit newsroom in a midsized Rust Belt city, and also interviewed news workers at seven other nonprofit outlets. She focused on the question of labor: What is the impact of this type of journalism on the work and the workers involved? Her main finding is blunt: “The emphasis on funding, on money, and on organizational concerns has become the top priority for individuals working for nonprofit news entities.” And, as journalists “busy themselves” with these administrative chores and organizational imperatives — to keep grant money coming in, to keep funders happy, etc. — it not only comes at the expense of the journalism product but also extracts a heavy toll of unpaid labor from the news workers involved. The situation, McKinnon-Crowley writes, “leads to a double worker exploitation where journalists feel morally obligated to do good work as journalists and to do good work for a morally just (nonprofit) organization.” This exploitation, she says, is perpetuated by the nature of nonprofit reliance, as foundations often “take decision-making power away from journalists and the institution of journalism.” A clear example of this, she says, is the grant-making process, which can require an undue level of administrative burden and can force journalists to put the priorities and interests of funders ahead of those of the community. The result, she contends, is a pernicious cycle: Rather than allowing space for journalists to center the needs of their community, the voices and opinions of the funders are prioritized into perpetuity as nonprofits continually need external funding. This reproduces social inequality, as journalists are incentivized to favor those who can distribute wealth, mirroring similar global trends where the news contributes to making the “information rich get information richer.” Part of the challenge is that, unlike the wall that typically exists between editorial and advertising at for-profit news organizations, there are few clear lines of separation. Funders tend to sit on boards overseeing the news outlets. They shape application forms and set renewal cycles. Journalists interviewed described the “mental formulas they are constantly calculating to keep producing the news.” While such concerns have always been present to some degree — and for-profit news managers, no doubt, are often plenty stressed about their own funding arrangements — McKinnon-Crowley suggests these problems are particularly tough for nonprofit newsrooms given how small and precarious they tend to be, and given how quickly funding provided through one grant cycle can disappear entirely in the next. Even more, the researcher found a distressing level of unpaid work that seemed to be the rule, not the exception, in small-outlet nonprofit journalism. In one example, there was a journalist who officially held titles as executive director and managing editor, though he was not necessarily compensated for such higher-level work. Moreover, that was only the start of his duties required to keep the organization humming. McKinnon-Crowley writes: From what I observed, here is a list of some of his unofficial job duties: fundraiser, party planner, grant writer, mentor, teacher, board member, publisher, figurehead, reporter, editor, tech support, building maintainer, sounding board, community-liaison, coffee-buyer, freelance coordinator, radio personality, podcast scripter, scheduler, photographer, and social media manager. The upshot: Much of the actual work that this person wanted to do as a journalist was, by his own admission, “slipping through the cracks.” McKinnon-Crowley summed it up this way: “As I observed in the newsroom, if you have to return cheese trays from banquets and create fundraising emails, the split priorities lead to gaps in what the organization is able to do.” So, what should be done? McKinnon-Crowley recommends that funders give recurring money without restrictions, fund positions on a longer-term basis (5 to 10 years minimum), help pay for administrative overhead, require less paperwork burden in reporting back, and stop dictating coverage decisions. For nonprofit newsrooms, she says it’s time to start having more conversations about these issues — about what counts as unacceptable interference on the part of funders as well as what the risks are of asking journalists to do too much for too little compensation. In a service-oriented occupation like journalism, working within a “doing good” ethos of a nonprofit only accentuates the likelihood that reporters will treat their jobs like callings, get exploited in the process, and end up burned out and disillusioned (see more on that theme in the roundup below). RELATED ARTICLEA new book looks at how AI is rewiring the newsroom, for better and worseSeth C. LewisAugust 6, 2026“Human versus AI news anchors: A survey study on audience satisfaction and the emotional connection.” By Yuan Ji, in Journalism. China has been one of the world’s leading laboratories for AI news anchors. The experiment began in earnest in 2018, when the Xinhua News Agency introduced a virtual news presenter capable of delivering news around the clock. The pitch was simple: AI could provide a tireless, endlessly replicable alternative to a human anchor. Nearly a decade into that experiment, however, audiences don’t seem ready to trade in the humans. That’s the finding that stands out from a new study of 343 Chinese news consumers by researcher Yuan Ji. The study examined how audiences perceive AI anchors, including their engagement, emotional connection, and satisfaction compared with human anchors. The numbers tell a fairly clear story. Only 4.96% of respondents said they found AI anchors very engaging. Another 25.07% said they were somewhat engaging. So nearly three-quarters of respondents did not describe AI anchors as engaging in either of those ways. The satisfaction gap is even more pronounced. Just 5.25% said they were more satisfied with AI anchors than with human anchors. Another 24.78% said they were equally satisfied. That means roughly seven in 10 respondents did not report being equally or more satisfied with AI anchors. For news organizations, the finding raises an important question: What happens when technology solves a problem that audiences don’t necessarily think needs solving? AI anchors offer obvious efficiencies. They can work continuously, be reproduced across broadcasts and locations, and potentially reduce the costs associated with producing and presenting routine news. But those advantages matter less if audiences don’t find the result engaging or satisfying. That’s an important consideration for journalists as AI moves deeper into news production. The technology is getting better at mimicking the mechanics of journalism. But journalism is more than mechanics. As Yuan Ji found, audiences also respond to the people delivering the news — and to the sense of connection, credibility, and human presence those people provide. The finding doesn’t mean AI won’t change journalism. It does suggest that news organizations should think beyond what AI can do and consider what audiences actually value. Efficiency may be one reason to use an AI anchor, but efficiency alone doesn’t guarantee engagement or satisfaction. For now, the numbers offer some good news for human journalists in television. AI may be ready for the news desk, but audiences, at least for now, still seem to want a person sitting behind it. RELATED ARTICLEIn Canada, a government program to support local news tries to determine who’s most deservingSarah ScireMay 8, 2020“Government-funded watchdog journalism? Analyzing Canadian media workers’ self-perceptions of independence under the local journalism initiative.” By Chris Arsenault, in Journalism Practice. Government funding might seem like an obvious threat to journalistic independence. But Canadian journalists who receive public money say it hasn’t interfered with their work. Instead, many still point to advertisers as the bigger threat. This new study explores the journalists working under Canada’s Local Journalism Initiative, a federal program that has provided more than $128 million since 2019 to support hundreds of reporting positions at news organizations across the country. Researcher Chris Arsenault interviewed 22 journalists whose positions are supported by the program. What they said complicates the familiar concern in journalism, that accepting government money inevitably makes it harder for reporters to hold power to account. The journalists certainly recognized the optics. Many worried that government funding could make audiences question their independence or create the appearance of a conflict. But none said the funding had actually changed what they could report. None could point to a story they had avoided or softened because of the government support. And none could identify a source who had treated them differently because their salary was publicly funded. When journalists described actual threats to their independence, they were more likely to talk about advertisers. Several reporters recalled situations in which advertisers had made it more difficult to scrutinize local businesses, organizations or other powerful figures. For these journalists, commercial pressure wasn’t an abstract concern about appearances — it was something they had experienced in their newsrooms. That distinction is worth considering in an industry where the traditional business model has collapsed in many local communities. Journalists may understandably worry about accepting money from the government. But if the alternative is a newsroom with fewer reporters, fewer resources, and greater dependence on advertisers, public funding may sometimes give journalists more room to do independent reporting, not less. The journalists weren’t convinced the funding program could fix the larger financial problems facing local news, however. Many saw it as temporary help rather than a long-term solution. The findings suggest journalists may need to think differently about where threats to independence actually come from — whether from a dependence on government or advertising or some other source. Public funding may not eliminate the challenges facing local journalism, but it seems positioned to give reporters the resources and freedom to do work that commercial pressures have sometimes made harder. “‘This is how journalism has always been done’: White neutrality, newsroom norms, and an AI intervention in source diversification.” By Gavin Adamson, Asmaa Malik, Shari Okeke, and Jisele Bailey-Hay, in Journalism. Adding AI to the newsroom does not necessarily help journalists find better sources in the moment. In a new study of Canadian journalists, the technology was more useful as a mirror, helping reporters look back at their coverage and see whose voices they routinely include — and whose they don’t. Researchers interviewed 12 journalists at a mid-sized Canadian daily and demonstrated an AI tool designed to track the types of sources appearing in news stories. The tool categorizes sources into groups such as politicians, authorities, experts, organizations, and people speaking from personal experience. The journalists generally supported more inclusive sourcing. They saw it as important to accurate, fair and accountable journalism. But they also described why it can be difficult to put that ideal into practice. Time pressure, unsurprisingly, was a major obstacle. Reporters working on deadline often turn to sources they know they can reach quickly, including government officials, police, academic experts, and other institutional voices. Finding people outside those established networks takes time, particularly in newsrooms that have fewer reporters and less time for relationship-building. The result can be a heavy reliance on white and official sources, with the same voices and institutions appearing repeatedly in the news even when journalists recognize that their coverage would benefit from a broader range of perspectives. In this study, the AI tool was found to do little to change that during the reporting process. The journalists did not envision using it to tell them whom to call for a story or to help them find a source before deadline. Instead, they saw value in using it afterward, reviewing individual stories or larger collections of coverage to identify patterns in their sourcing. That makes the technology less of a reporting assistant and more of a feedback mechanism. It could help a reporter or editor notice, for example, how often official sources appear in their coverage or how rarely people with direct experience of an issue are quoted. That kind of reflection could matter if newsrooms use it as part of their regular editorial conversations. The technology can make patterns visible that are otherwise easy to overlook amid the daily rush of producing the news. But seeing a problem is not the same as fixing it. An AI system can identify who appeared in a story. It cannot build relationships with communities, earn the trust of unfamiliar sources, or give reporters more time to do the work. Overall, AI can help newsrooms see their sourcing habits more clearly, but it cannot, at present, create the conditions necessary to change them. If source diversity is going to become a sustained part of journalism, it will require newsroom expectations and resources to support it, not simply another piece of technology. “Stuck between democracy and a layoff: Connecting journalists’ personal disillusionment to overall normative press evaluations.” By Alexis Haskell, in Journalism Practice. Many journalists enter the profession believing they can make a difference. They expect to inform the public, explain complicated issues, give people a voice, and contribute to democracy. This new study suggests that when those expectations collide with the realities of working in journalism, journalists can become disillusioned with more than their own jobs. Alexis Haskell surveyed 695 U.S. journalists and found that disillusionment is a measurable experience among American journalists. The concept is different from burnout, the researcher argues. Burnout describes exhaustion and being overwhelmed by work. Disillusionment describes a deeper break between what journalists expected their careers to be and what they actually experienced. On average, the journalists surveyed were more disillusioned than not. Haskell measured the concept through their feelings about their work, their expectations for the profession and their sense of purpose. That disillusionment was also reflected in how journalists viewed journalism as a whole. Those who were more disillusioned were more likely to give the press lower marks for five of six democratic roles examined by the study. They were less positive about journalism’s ability to inform, analyze, provide a forum for public discussion, foster social empathy, and mobilize audiences. The strongest relationships were found in analysis and the public forum. More disillusioned journalists were particularly likely to believe the press was failing to help people understand complicated issues or provide space for public conversation. There was one exception: Disillusionment was not related to journalists’ evaluations of investigative journalism. Haskell suggests that investigative work may occupy a different place in journalism’s professional culture. It is highly prestigious, frequently celebrated through major awards and often associated with individual achievement. The other roles are more directly tied to journalism’s service to audiences and communities. That difference gets at what makes disillusionment important. Journalists who are disillusioned aren’t necessarily saying they can no longer do good journalism. They may instead be questioning whether journalism, as a profession, is accomplishing what they believed it was supposed to accomplish. The finding connects the personal experience of working in journalism with a broader assessment of the field. When journalists encounter low wages, layoffs, shrinking staffs, and other pressures, the consequences may extend beyond their own careers. They may begin to lose faith not just in the job, but in journalism’s ability to fulfill the public purpose that drew them to it in the first place. A previous version of this piece stated that 550 nonprofit newsrooms operate in the U.S. This is inaccurate and it is difficult to estimate the number of nonprofit newsrooms in the country.

Her main finding is blunt: “The emphasis on funding, on money, and on organizational concerns has become the top priority for individuals working for nonprofit news entities.” And, as journalists “busy themselves” with these administrative chores and organizational imperatives — to keep grant money coming in, to keep funders happy, etc. — it not only comes at the expense of the journalism product but also extracts a heavy toll of unpaid labor from the news workers involved.

This exploitation, she says, is perpetuated by the nature of nonprofit reliance, as foundations often “take decision-making power away from journalists and the institution of journalism.” A clear example of this, she says, is the grant-making process, which can require an undue level of administrative burden and can force journalists to put the priorities and interests of funders ahead of those of the community.

The result, she contends, is a pernicious cycle:

Rather than allowing space for journalists to center the needs of their community, the voices and opinions of the funders are prioritized into perpetuity as nonprofits continually need external funding. This reproduces social inequality, as journalists are incentivized to favor those who can distribute wealth, mirroring similar global trends where the news contributes to making the “information rich get information richer.” Part of the challenge is that, unlike the wall that typically exists between editorial and advertising at for-profit news organizations, there are few clear lines of separation. Funders tend to sit on boards overseeing the news outlets. They shape application forms and set renewal cycles. Journalists interviewed described the “mental formulas they are constantly calculating to keep producing the news.” While such concerns have always been present to some degree — and for-profit news managers, no doubt, are often plenty stressed about their own funding arrangements — McKinnon-Crowley suggests these problems are particularly tough for nonprofit newsrooms given how small and precarious they tend to be, and given how quickly funding provided through one grant cycle can disappear entirely in the next. Even more, the researcher found a distressing level of unpaid work that seemed to be the rule, not the exception, in small-outlet nonprofit journalism. In one example, there was a journalist who officially held titles as executive director and managing editor, though he was not necessarily compensated for such higher-level work. Moreover, that was only the start of his duties required to keep the organization humming. McKinnon-Crowley writes: From what I observed, here is a list of some of his unofficial job duties: fundraiser, party planner, grant writer, mentor, teacher, board member, publisher, figurehead, reporter, editor, tech support, building maintainer, sounding board, community-liaison, coffee-buyer, freelance coordinator, radio personality, podcast scripter, scheduler, photographer, and social media manager. The upshot: Much of the actual work that this person wanted to do as a journalist was, by his own admission, “slipping through the cracks.” McKinnon-Crowley summed it up this way: “As I observed in the newsroom, if you have to return cheese trays from banquets and create fundraising emails, the split priorities lead to gaps in what the organization is able to do.” So, what should be done? McKinnon-Crowley recommends that funders give recurring money without restrictions, fund positions on a longer-term basis (5 to 10 years minimum), help pay for administrative overhead, require less paperwork burden in reporting back, and stop dictating coverage decisions. For nonprofit newsrooms, she says it’s time to start having more conversations about these issues — about what counts as unacceptable interference on the part of funders as well as what the risks are of asking journalists to do too much for too little compensation. In a service-oriented occupation like journalism, working within a “doing good” ethos of a nonprofit only accentuates the likelihood that reporters will treat their jobs like callings, get exploited in the process, and end up burned out and disillusioned (see more on that theme in the roundup below). LewisAugust 6, 2026“Human versus AI news anchors: A survey study on audience satisfaction and the emotional connection.” By Yuan Ji, in Journalism. China has been one of the world’s leading laboratories for AI news anchors. The experiment began in earnest in 2018, when the Xinhua News Agency introduced a virtual news presenter capable of delivering news around the clock. The pitch was simple: AI could provide a tireless, endlessly replicable alternative to a human anchor. Nearly a decade into that experiment, however, audiences don’t seem ready to trade in the humans. That’s the finding that stands out from a new study of 343 Chinese news consumers by researcher Yuan Ji. The study examined how audiences perceive AI anchors, including their engagement, emotional connection, and satisfaction compared with human anchors. The numbers tell a fairly clear story. Only 4.96% of respondents said they found AI anchors very engaging. Another 25.07% said they were somewhat engaging. So nearly three-quarters of respondents did not describe AI anchors as engaging in either of those ways. The satisfaction gap is even more pronounced. Just 5.25% said they were more satisfied with AI anchors than with human anchors. Another 24.78% said they were equally satisfied. That means roughly seven in 10 respondents did not report being equally or more satisfied with AI anchors. For news organizations, the finding raises an important question: What happens when technology solves a problem that audiences don’t necessarily think needs solving? AI anchors offer obvious efficiencies. They can work continuously, be reproduced across broadcasts and locations, and potentially reduce the costs associated with producing and presenting routine news. But those advantages matter less if audiences don’t find the result engaging or satisfying. That’s an important consideration for journalists as AI moves deeper into news production. The technology is getting better at mimicking the mechanics of journalism. But journalism is more than mechanics. As Yuan Ji found, audiences also respond to the people delivering the news — and to the sense of connection, credibility, and human presence those people provide. The finding doesn’t mean AI won’t change journalism. It does suggest that news organizations should think beyond what AI can do and consider what audiences actually value. Efficiency may be one reason to use an AI anchor, but efficiency alone doesn’t guarantee engagement or satisfaction. For now, the numbers offer some good news for human journalists in television. AI may be ready for the news desk, but audiences, at least for now, still seem to want a person sitting behind it. RELATED ARTICLEIn Canada, a government program to support local news tries to determine who’s most deservingSarah ScireMay 8, 2020“Government-funded watchdog journalism? Analyzing Canadian media workers’ self-perceptions of independence under the local journalism initiative.” By Chris Arsenault, in Journalism Practice. Government funding might seem like an obvious threat to journalistic independence. But Canadian journalists who receive public money say it hasn’t interfered with their work. Instead, many still point to advertisers as the bigger threat. This new study explores the journalists working under Canada’s Local Journalism Initiative, a federal program that has provided more than $128 million since 2019 to support hundreds of reporting positions at news organizations across the country. Researcher Chris Arsenault interviewed 22 journalists whose positions are supported by the program. What they said complicates the familiar concern in journalism, that accepting government money inevitably makes it harder for reporters to hold power to account. The journalists certainly recognized the optics. Many worried that government funding could make audiences question their independence or create the appearance of a conflict. But none said the funding had actually changed what they could report. None could point to a story they had avoided or softened because of the government support. And none could identify a source who had treated them differently because their salary was publicly funded. When journalists described actual threats to their independence, they were more likely to talk about advertisers. Several reporters recalled situations in which advertisers had made it more difficult to scrutinize local businesses, organizations or other powerful figures. For these journalists, commercial pressure wasn’t an abstract concern about appearances — it was something they had experienced in their newsrooms. That distinction is worth considering in an industry where the traditional business model has collapsed in many local communities. Journalists may understandably worry about accepting money from the government. But if the alternative is a newsroom with fewer reporters, fewer resources, and greater dependence on advertisers, public funding may sometimes give journalists more room to do independent reporting, not less. The journalists weren’t convinced the funding program could fix the larger financial problems facing local news, however. Many saw it as temporary help rather than a long-term solution. The findings suggest journalists may need to think differently about where threats to independence actually come from — whether from a dependence on government or advertising or some other source. Public funding may not eliminate the challenges facing local journalism, but it seems positioned to give reporters the resources and freedom to do work that commercial pressures have sometimes made harder. “‘This is how journalism has always been done’: White neutrality, newsroom norms, and an AI intervention in source diversification.” By Gavin Adamson, Asmaa Malik, Shari Okeke, and Jisele Bailey-Hay, in Journalism. Adding AI to the newsroom does not necessarily help journalists find better sources in the moment. In a new study of Canadian journalists, the technology was more useful as a mirror, helping reporters look back at their coverage and see whose voices they routinely include — and whose they don’t. Researchers interviewed 12 journalists at a mid-sized Canadian daily and demonstrated an AI tool designed to track the types of sources appearing in news stories. The tool categorizes sources into groups such as politicians, authorities, experts, organizations, and people speaking from personal experience. The journalists generally supported more inclusive sourcing. They saw it as important to accurate, fair and accountable journalism. But they also described why it can be difficult to put that ideal into practice. Time pressure, unsurprisingly, was a major obstacle. Reporters working on deadline often turn to sources they know they can reach quickly, including government officials, police, academic experts, and other institutional voices. Finding people outside those established networks takes time, particularly in newsrooms that have fewer reporters and less time for relationship-building. The result can be a heavy reliance on white and official sources, with the same voices and institutions appearing repeatedly in the news even when journalists recognize that their coverage would benefit from a broader range of perspectives. In this study, the AI tool was found to do little to change that during the reporting process. The journalists did not envision using it to tell them whom to call for a story or to help them find a source before deadline. Instead, they saw value in using it afterward, reviewing individual stories or larger collections of coverage to identify patterns in their sourcing. That makes the technology less of a reporting assistant and more of a feedback mechanism. It could help a reporter or editor notice, for example, how often official sources appear in their coverage or how rarely people with direct experience of an issue are quoted. That kind of reflection could matter if newsrooms use it as part of their regular editorial conversations. The technology can make patterns visible that are otherwise easy to overlook amid the daily rush of producing the news. But seeing a problem is not the same as fixing it. An AI system can identify who appeared in a story. It cannot build relationships with communities, earn the trust of unfamiliar sources, or give reporters more time to do the work. Overall, AI can help newsrooms see their sourcing habits more clearly, but it cannot, at present, create the conditions necessary to change them. If source diversity is going to become a sustained part of journalism, it will require newsroom expectations and resources to support it, not simply another piece of technology. “Stuck between democracy and a layoff: Connecting journalists’ personal disillusionment to overall normative press evaluations.” By Alexis Haskell, in Journalism Practice. Many journalists enter the profession believing they can make a difference. They expect to inform the public, explain complicated issues, give people a voice, and contribute to democracy. This new study suggests that when those expectations collide with the realities of working in journalism, journalists can become disillusioned with more than their own jobs. Alexis Haskell surveyed 695 U.S. journalists and found that disillusionment is a measurable experience among American journalists. The concept is different from burnout, the researcher argues. Burnout describes exhaustion and being overwhelmed by work. Disillusionment describes a deeper break between what journalists expected their careers to be and what they actually experienced. On average, the journalists surveyed were more disillusioned than not. Haskell measured the concept through their feelings about their work, their expectations for the profession and their sense of purpose. That disillusionment was also reflected in how journalists viewed journalism as a whole. Those who were more disillusioned were more likely to give the press lower marks for five of six democratic roles examined by the study. They were less positive about journalism’s ability to inform, analyze, provide a forum for public discussion, foster social empathy, and mobilize audiences. The strongest relationships were found in analysis and the public forum. More disillusioned journalists were particularly likely to believe the press was failing to help people understand complicated issues or provide space for public conversation. There was one exception: Disillusionment was not related to journalists’ evaluations of investigative journalism. Haskell suggests that investigative work may occupy a different place in journalism’s professional culture. It is highly prestigious, frequently celebrated through major awards and often associated with individual achievement. The other roles are more directly tied to journalism’s service to audiences and communities. That difference gets at what makes disillusionment important. Journalists who are disillusioned aren’t necessarily saying they can no longer do good journalism. They may instead be questioning whether journalism, as a profession, is accomplishing what they believed it was supposed to accomplish. The finding connects the personal experience of working in journalism with a broader assessment of the field. When journalists encounter low wages, layoffs, shrinking staffs, and other pressures, the consequences may extend beyond their own careers. They may begin to lose faith not just in the job, but in journalism’s ability to fulfill the public purpose that drew them to it in the first place. RELATED ARTICLEA new book looks at how AI is rewiring the newsroom, for better and worseSeth C. LewisAugust 6, 2026“Human versus AI news anchors: A survey study on audience satisfaction and the emotional connection.” By Yuan Ji, in Journalism. China has been one of the world’s leading laboratories for AI news anchors. The experiment began in earnest in 2018, when the Xinhua News Agency introduced a virtual news presenter capable of delivering news around the clock. The pitch was simple: AI could provide a tireless, endlessly replicable alternative to a human anchor.

Nearly a decade into that experiment, however, audiences don’t seem ready to trade in the humans.

That’s the finding that stands out from a new study of 343 Chinese news consumers by researcher Yuan Ji. The study examined how audiences perceive AI anchors, including their engagement, emotional connection, and satisfaction compared with human anchors.

The numbers tell a fairly clear story. Only 4.96% of respondents said they found AI anchors very engaging. Another 25.07% said they were somewhat engaging. So nearly three-quarters of respondents did not describe AI anchors as engaging in either of those ways.

The satisfaction gap is even more pronounced. Just 5.25% said they were more satisfied with AI anchors than with human anchors. Another 24.78% said they were equally satisfied.

That means roughly seven in 10 respondents did not report being equally or more satisfied with AI anchors.

For news organizations, the finding raises an important question: What happens when technology solves a problem that audiences don’t necessarily think needs solving?

AI anchors offer obvious efficiencies. They can work continuously, be reproduced across broadcasts and locations, and potentially reduce the costs associated with producing and presenting routine news. But those advantages matter less if audiences don’t find the result engaging or satisfying.

That’s an important consideration for journalists as AI moves deeper into news production. The technology is getting better at mimicking the mechanics of journalism. But journalism is more than mechanics. As Yuan Ji found, audiences also respond to the people delivering the news — and to the sense of connection, credibility, and human presence those people provide.

The finding doesn’t mean AI won’t change journalism. It does suggest that news organizations should think beyond what AI can do and consider what audiences actually value. Efficiency may be one reason to use an AI anchor, but efficiency alone doesn’t guarantee engagement or satisfaction.

For now, the numbers offer some good news for human journalists in television. AI may be ready for the news desk, but audiences, at least for now, still seem to want a person sitting behind it.

Adding AI to the newsroom does not necessarily help journalists find better sources in the moment. In a new study of Canadian journalists, the technology was more useful as a mirror, helping reporters look back at their coverage and see whose voices they routinely include — and whose they don’t.

Finding people outside those established networks takes time, particularly in newsrooms that have fewer reporters and less time for relationship-building.

The result can be a heavy reliance on white and official sources, with the same voices and institutions appearing repeatedly in the news even when journalists recognize that their coverage would benefit from a broader range of perspectives.

In this study, the AI tool was found to do little to change that during the reporting process. The journalists did not envision using it to tell them whom to call for a story or to help them find a source before deadline. That kind of reflection could matter if newsrooms use it as part of their regular editorial conversations. The technology can make patterns visible that are otherwise easy to overlook amid the daily rush of producing the news.

But seeing a problem is not the same as fixing it. An AI system can identify who appeared in a story. It cannot build relationships with communities, earn the trust of unfamiliar sources, or give reporters more time to do the work.

Overall, AI can help newsrooms see their sourcing habits more clearly, but it cannot, at present, create the conditions necessary to change them. #122. YouTube CTR, Instagram Reels Structure, and Industry News

Here’s a recap of the most important insights, trends, and updates you need to know about today! Catch up in minutes and go into the rest of the week prepared.

🗞️ Industry news from LinkedIn, Meta, YouTube, and more

Publishing YouTube videos that get buried despite having solid content? This packaging process will help:

Use AI tools to accelerate the brainstorm at least 10 titles for your video, choosing between two title strategies depending on your goal. The SEO route targets search intent with how-to and tutorial-style titles for long-term discoverability. The curiosity route uses psychological triggers to drive clicks and virality. Both work; pick the one that matches your video's purpose.

With the packaging complete, use YouTube's built-in A/B title testing feature. Upload your video with your best title, then add a second option. YouTube will split-test both and show you which drives more watch time. A single title swap on one of Sean Cannell's videos produced a 6% improvement in performance.

This tip was shared by Sean Cannell at Social Media Marketing World 2026.

Before you post your next Reel, ask: Is there one word that would make your people feel it? “Pink Floyd” instead of “rock.” “Relocating to Nashville” instead of “moving.”

Shannon McKinstrie has watched this swap outperform the generic version again and again. Most people skip it because once a Reel is edited, the hook feels finished.

That one-word check is the first of six steps in our free guide, Unpolished Reels.

Short-form video rewards connection over production value right now, yet many businesses still create reels as if the opposite were true. Instagram growth strategist Shannon McKinstrie, host of the Good Content Podcast, shares what's working with Reels for business and the small tweaks that turn scrollers into loyal followers.

Why Unpolished Content Is Winning Right Now Discover why polished production can put distance between you and your viewers and the simple formula for choosing topics you'll stay excited to post about. Think your niche is too boring? Think again.

The Callout That Stops the Scroll Learn how to make your ideal viewer feel seen in the first second, where to find the words your audience uses to describe themselves, and the on-screen element that answers the question every viewer is silently asking.

How to Write Hooks That Feel Personal Find out why the magazine-style hooks you learned years ago are falling flat and how a tiny shift in wording can move you from faceless expert to trusted friend. Plus, get an easy way to open a story.

Editing Moves That Keep People Watching Discover the free editing features Shannon relies on to hold attention past the first few seconds and why an everyday prop might be your easiest path to more comments.

A Smarter Way to Use Trial Reels Learn how Shannon uses trial reels to test ideas with non-followers without hurting her main feed and the metric you should watch more closely than any other.

Marketing can be a lonely job. The best ideas rarely happen alone — they start with someone else's perspective, in a hallway chat or over coffee between sessions. Most of us are stuck refreshing feeds and guessing what's working, without anyone in the room to bounce it off.

Social Media Marketing World puts you in a room full of marketers working through the same problems you are. The connections made here keep going long after the event ends.

LinkedIn Adds Post Proofreader for Premium Members: LinkedIn is introducing Post Proofreader, a Premium feature designed to help members refine posts before publishing. Users can ask the tool to correct writing errors, shorten a draft, or improve its clarity, with proposed changes displayed inline for review rather than automatically applied. The feature gives users control over accepting or rejecting AI-assisted edits, although it currently works only with English drafts and does not include features such as version history or manual editing while suggestions are being reviewed. LinkedIn

LinkedIn Tests Separate Network and For You Feeds: LinkedIn is experimenting with a redesigned feed that separates content from existing connections and follows from broader recommended content. The Network tab centers on people users have deliberately chosen to connect with, while For You is intended to help users discover perspectives from practitioners across and beyond their networks. The test gives LinkedIn users a more explicit way to choose between keeping up with professional relationships and discovering new information. LinkedIn

LinkedIn Expands Verification for Members and Businesses: LinkedIn is broadening its verification system with new ways for professionals to establish credibility and companies to protect their brands. The platform is testing peer verification of employment and education history while giving verified Page admins stronger controls over false employee associations. LinkedIn is also extending its verification signals beyond its own platform through new integrations with Truecaller and PeerSpot, as its verified member base surpasses 115 million. LinkedIn

Google Adds Conversational AI and One-Click Experiences to Demand Gen: Google’s September Demand Gen update introduces new tools designed to shorten the path from discovery to conversion across YouTube, Gmail, and Maps. #123. So Begins ChatGPT’s Endless Ad Iterations; YouTube Affiliates With AliExpress

Headline: So Begins ChatGPT’s Endless Ad Iterations; YouTube Affiliates With AliExpress

One way to frame the evolution of ChatGPT ad units is on a sliding scale from transparency to obscurity.

Initially, ChatGPT ads were in clearly delineated pillboxes with darkened backgrounds. But then ads lost the heavy shading, as well as the blatant “Insert Brand” and “Sponsored” copy.

Now, the ads don’t even have the structured box (h/t to Marketplace Pulse founder Joe Kaziukėnas for flagging the latest version). The ad appears as text, more in line with normal ChatGPT responses.

But if anything’s to be learned from forerunners like Google Search and Microsoft Bing, it’s that constantly changing ad units aren’t moving toward any ideal or stable type. The amorphousness is the point.

Google and Bing never stop swapping out new colors or ways to disclose that the placement is an ad or the boldness or fuzziness of the fonts. Really, there’s no limit on ways to recombine the ad unit to look new and fresh.

Most likely, the rate of turnover in ad iterations represents how long it takes a common denominator of users to unconsciously phase the ad units out. It’s a roller coaster more seasoned ad platforms are well acquainted with.

Chinese online retail giant AliExpress (owned by Alibaba) is expanding an affiliate marketing partnership with YouTube beyond South Korea. The deal between the two companies will now cover the United States, United Kingdom, Germany and Brazil.

The integration means YouTube creators can apply insights to AliExpress’ product catalogue to find items their audience might be interested in buying, per the release. And any products the creators feature in YouTube videos will be linked to an AliExpress checkout.

The release does not mention whether AliExpress merchants or sellers have the ability to strike deals with YouTube creators directly through the program. So they probably don’t have that ability. Affiliate programs are impersonal as a matter of course.

The partnership makes sense for YouTube, which wants to cultivate live shopping and purchases via YouTube. But live shopping is paddling upstream in the US, where it doesn’t have the same cultural cache as it does in China.

Relatedly, last week, Alibaba ended Amazon’s four-year streak atop Ad Age’s annual advertiser tracking report. And it wasn’t even close. The top three went Alibaba ($30.2 billion), Amazon ($23.5 billion) and then Temu parent company PDD Holdings ($16.3 billion).

That’s another reason for YouTube to ride the wave of Alibaba marketing budgets.

In a delightfully ironic twist, developers want you to use artificial intelligence to make your hardware and software less intelligent.

Two solutions, dumbtv and cleanyourtv, promise vibe-coded solutions for getting rid of undesirable CTV elements like sponsored ads, tracking features and TV operating system bloatware, TechCrunch reports.

Many DIY types are already using Claude to recode their Smart TVs to remove advertising (with mixed results). Think of it as removing all the connectivity elements that make a smart TV, well, “smart.”

The dumb TV products also take aim at automatic content recognition (ACR), a key data collection method underpinning CTV advertising.

Smart TV ACR systems are always-on mechanisms that identify what content is playing on the TV and if/when people are in the room. That data is packaged to advertisers and is also used by smart TV providers to determine which ads to serve to viewers and when.

Removing those data connections could “have the potential to disrupt the smart TV ad industry,” TechCrunch writes.

So it’s official: Ad blocking is coming for the big screen in the living room.
