#124. ChatGPT is adding real cartoonists’ signatures to fake New Yorker cartoons

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

OpenAI’s chatbot isn’t just imitating the magazine’s style. It’s also falsely attributing AI-generated images to real artists.

At the pearly gates, Dolly Parton, in a sparkling gown, stands arm in arm with Tim Curry, dressed as Dr. Frank-N-Furter. “I knew I chose the right plus one,” Parton says to God, who is standing at heaven’s reception desk.

That’s the premise of a cartoon that went viral on Twitter in the days after the legendary entertainers’ deaths in late August. One tweet of the cartoon received 25,000 likes, while other versions of the image circulated on Facebook, Instagram, and Bluesky.

In the bottom right corner of the cartoon is the pen name “BLOPER,” the signature of New Yorker cartoonist Brendan Loper. But Loper didn’t draw the cartoon, or sign it. It was generated by ChatGPT and first posted to Facebook by a Dolly Parton fan. In the comments section of her post, she wrote she had simply asked ChatGPT to make “a New Yorker-style cartoon.”

“I had people writing to me about this cartoon, asking if it was mine,” Loper told me. First came a text from his twin brother, whose friend had seen the AI-generated image. Emails and DMs on social media from strangers followed. “It was very surreal,” he said.

A cartoon generated by ChatGPT and signed with Brendan Loper’s signature that was posted to Twitter on August 26, 2026.

This wasn’t the first time ChatGPT had reproduced Loper’s signature. In May, a stranger reached out over Instagram to warn Loper that his pen name had appeared in an image output by the chatbot. Over the summer, Loper found additional examples in a Reddit forum about ChatGPT, where users had been posting similar New Yorker-style cartoons they had generated.

Loper already knew his work was “out there, getting harvested for all of this [AI] training,” he said. But an image generator faking his signature felt more personal. “I’m not a territorial person, but my name is my name. It felt very much like a violation of my personhood.”

RELATED ARTICLE“I don’t want to outsource my brain”: How political cartoonists are bringing AI into their workAndrew DeckJune 2, 2025These days, cartoon signatures are more than a byline. In an era where cartoons are regularly stripped from their original context and circulated on blogs and social media without proper licensing, they can also act as a watermark that ties an illustration to its original creator.

“The signature for me is the certificate of authenticity. I only put it on work that I’m putting on the internet that I feel needs to be recognized as from my hand,” Loper told me. “If I put my name on it, it’s official, it’s mine. It really is a brand. It’s the mark that I made.”

Loper isn’t the only New Yorker cartoonist whose signature has been reproduced by ChatGPT. In the same online forums are dozens of images with those of other prominent contributors, including Harry Bliss, Emily Flake, Joe Dator, Pat Byrnes, Peter Vey, and Jason Adam Katzenstein. In my own tests, ChatGPT output cartoons with signatures of some of the magazine’s most established cartoonists, past and present, including George Booth, Liza Donnelly, Ellis Rosen, and Saul Steinberg. In all, I documented more than 15 New Yorker cartoonists whose signatures have been used by OpenAI’s image generator without permission or compensation.

“We believe the future of creativity is one that is fundamentally human, and our focus is on building tools that empower human creativity and creators,” said a spokesperson for OpenAI in a statement. “We very much appreciate the community flagging bugs and unintended behavior by our models, so we can address them.”

After I notified OpenAI of the issue, ChatGPT began to output a new message when I asked it to generate New Yorker-style cartoons: “This prompt may violate our guardrails concerning similarity to third-party content.” Still, as of the publication of this story, it continues to sign some of the generic cartoons it generates with the names of real New Yorker cartoonists.

In my tests, ChatGPT regularly generated cartoons with the hallmarks of the 101-year-old magazine’s house style: a black-and-white, single-panel illustration with a sparse background, clean linework, and a sardonic caption — or at least, an approximation of one. Some of ChatGPT’s punch lines don’t make sense. Not every image came with a signature, and some included pen names that were gibberish. But the signatures that did appear were regularly those of real contributors to the magazine, including older cartoonists, like Warren Miller, who published in the 1960s. “I can see the DNA of my work in there, but it still doesn’t look like something I drew,” said Emily Flake, who’s been a New Yorker contributor since 2008. Several ChatGPT-generated cartoons posted online are signed with her pen name, “e. flake.” “It’s kind of like seeing a distant cousin.” The character stances and shading contained echoes of Flake’s visual identity, but she said overall they looked more like amalgamations of several different cartoonists’ illustration styles. Each signature, though, was undeniably hers. “It’s like somebody attributed a quote to me that I didn’t say.” Left: A cartoon generated by ChatGPT and signed with Emily Flake’s signature that was posted to a Reddit forum in June. Right: A real Emily Flake cartoon published in The New Yorker on August 20, 2026 and licensed via The Cartoon Bank.

In my tests, ChatGPT regularly generated cartoons with the hallmarks of the 101-year-old magazine’s house style: a black-and-white, single-panel illustration with a sparse background, clean linework, and a sardonic caption — or at least, an approximation of one. Some of ChatGPT’s punch lines don’t make sense.

Not every image came with a signature, and some included pen names that were gibberish. But the signatures that did appear were regularly those of real contributors to the magazine, including older cartoonists, like Warren Miller, who published in the 1960s.

“I can see the DNA of my work in there, but it still doesn’t look like something I drew,” said Emily Flake, who’s been a New Yorker contributor since 2008. Several ChatGPT-generated cartoons posted online are signed with her pen name, “e. flake.” “It’s kind of like seeing a distant cousin.”

The character stances and shading contained echoes of Flake’s visual identity, but she said overall they looked more like amalgamations of several different cartoonists’ illustration styles. Each signature, though, was undeniably hers. “It’s like somebody attributed a quote to me that I didn’t say.”

Top: A cartoon generated by ChatGPT and signed with Emily Flake’s signature that was posted to a Reddit forum in June. Bottom: A real Emily Flake cartoon published in The New Yorker on August 20, 2026 and licensed via The Cartoon Bank.

In 2024, Condé Nast, The New Yorker’s parent company, signed a multi-year licensing deal with OpenAI allowing it to use much of the publisher’s content in its products. The terms of the deal aren’t public, but a spokesperson for The New Yorker told me Condé Nast has never granted an LLM developer permission to train models on its cartoons. Some ChatGPT creations reproduced The New Yorker’s logo alongside cartoons; that is also not allowed in any LLM deals, the spokesperson said.

RELATED ARTICLEHundreds of thousands of videos from news publishers like The New York Times and Vox were used to train AI modelsAndrew DeckOctober 30, 2025OpenAI declined to answer my questions about how its models might have ingested signatures from The New Yorker’s archives during the training process.

Even if Condé Nast did want to license cartoons to OpenAI, The New Yorker’s standard cartoonist contract leaves little room for it. The magazine’s two cartoon editors work with a roster of freelancers who submit their work on spec and only get paid if a cartoon is selected for publication. I reviewed several templatized contracts for New Yorker contributing cartoonists, none of which permit licensing for AI training purposes. While The New Yorker has the right to publish commissioned cartoons first, it is not a “work for hire” arrangement and the cartoonist retains ownership of their copyright.

So how did OpenAI’s models learn those signatures? It’s possible they were scraped from the internet. Court documents released last month in the ongoing New York Times v. OpenAI lawsuit reveal the extent to which OpenAI knowingly circumvented publishers’ paywalls while developing ChatGPT. Unredacted Microsoft memos described ChatGPT as a “product that destroys its supply chain” and the data scraped to train its underlying LLMs as “the largest theft of labor in human history.”

In another memo, Jack Clark, then the policy director of OpenAI, wrote, “[O]ur work on AI and Creativity is going to increasingly lead to us creating systems that substitute for the labor of the people that define the ‘culture’ of society.” (Clark went on to co-found Anthropic.)

RELATED ARTICLE“An astonishing theft of unprecedented proportions”: Court records show what Microsoft and OpenAI actually thought about AI trainingSarah ScireSeptember 18, 2026Many of the cartoonists I spoke to for this story echoed Clark’s sentiment.

“It’s an uncanny simulacrum of an impression of a joke,” said Jason Adam Katzenstein, who has been publishing cartoons in The New Yorker since 2014. “But it’s not the point for it to actually be funny or good. The point is that it’s trying to deal a death blow to labor. It’s trying to render individual cartoonists obsolete because we cost money and take time.”

Katzenstein was part of the class action lawsuit filed against Anthropic in 2024 by members of the Authors Guild, the largest professional organization for published writers in the United States. Katzenstein’s cartoons had been used in an anthology published by Harper Collins, which was pirated and used by Anthropic to train its Claude models.

Last year, a judge ruled that training Claude on the authors’ work was fair use, but that Anthropic’s decision to download and maintain copies of the pirated books was a form of mass copyright infringement. In July, a federal court approved a settlement in the case, granting a $1.5 billion payout to authors and publishers — the largest in the history of U.S. copyright law.

Katzenstein considers the reproduction of his signature by ChatGPT to be more than just a violation of intellectual property; to him, it’s closer to false impersonation. “[ChatGPT] is attaching my name to work that I do not endorse or like. It’s slop, and unlike the other slop that I’ve encountered, this is slop that’s pretending to be me.”

Several cartoonists I spoke to also differentiated ChatGPT’s ability to mimic their illustration style from the reproduction of their signature.

“I’ve had people hack my credit card,” said Joe Dator, a New Yorker contributor for the past 20 years. “That feels like less of a violation than this. When they hacked my credit card, they didn’t dress up like me.”

Top: A cartoon generated by ChatGPT and signed with Pat Byrnes’ signature. Bottom: A real cartoon by Pat Byrnes from The New Yorker Collection licensed via The Cartoon Bank.

U.S. intellectual property case law has yet to catch up with the rise of AI image generators, but the courts are also likely to treat these issues as distinct. Any copyright infringement claim, for example, would most likely hinge on ChatGPT’s reproduction of each cartoonist’s specific drawing style.

“[The signature] is an indication of authenticity, but attribution is a very small part of the fair use inquiry,” said James Grimmelmann, a professor of digital and information law at Cornell Law School. The chief legal challenge in a copyright suit, he said, is that ChatGPT isn’t usually reproducing any specific cartoon in these examples; rather, it’s mimicking a more general style.

Other cartoonists have filed copyright lawsuits against companies building AI image generators. One class-action led by the illustrator Sarah Anderson against Stability AI, Deviant Art, and Midjourney has been winding its way through the courts since 2023, but there is no reference to signatures in that filing.

RELATED ARTICLEWhat it takes to sue OpenAI as a journalism nonprofitAndrew DeckJune 25, 2025Alternatively, Grimmelmann says New Yorker cartoonists could have grounds for a “right of publicity” case, a body of state-based law that protects individuals from the unauthorized use of their name or identity. For that, there would need to be proof that the AI-generated cartoons were used for a commercial purpose, not just as a joke or gag.

While I found no evidence that these AI-generated cartoons are being bought or sold, there are signs that image generators are already displacing the work of professional cartoonists.

Last year, The Baltimore Sun fired Kevin Kallaugher, a Pulitzer finalist who had published editorial cartoons in the paper for more than 30 years. And earlier this year, the Sun began regularly publishing AI-generated cartoons in its opinions section. A quick check with OpenAI’s watermark identification tool shows the illustrations were created with OpenAI’s products.

“[We] condemn the use of AI for its theft from artists, its misuse of our planet’s resources, and its threat to original, creative thought,” Marc Murphy, the president of The Association of American Editorial Cartoonists, wrote in an open letter published last month. “The Sun is not alone among American newspapers taking this degrading way out.”

The New Yorker hasn’t taken any such turn toward publishing AI-generated cartoons, though none of the contributors I spoke to said they could support themselves solely on their commissions from the magazine. A New Yorker cartoon is a calling card, and work for the publication opens doors to commercial work, book illustrations, and other gigs that together make up a livelihood. It is this work that is most threatened by AI, they said.

In 1998, Pat Byrnes published his first cartoon in The New Yorker under the pen name “P.Byrnes.” He went on to build a decades-long career with that name. Since he first began drawing cartoons as a teenager, he has always signed it with a period at the end.

“It was like signing a letter,” he said. “Here’s my statement — my gift to you to accept or reject.”

Across the more than a dozen ChatGPT cartoons I found signed with Byrnes’ name, every one ended with a period.

Google removed the Indexing API approval form and steps from its docs. Default quotas are listed, but the pages don't say how to request more.

Google removed the Indexing API approval form from its documentation on Oct. 16, along with the instructions telling developers to ask for approval.

In September, I reported that job board operators had waited months for responses to their approval requests. Google’s changelog says it updated the quota page “to reflect the current quota limits and process” and to “remove an outdated form.” It doesn’t say whether the approval requirement itself has changed.

Before the Oct. 16 update, the quota page said the API “provides initial default quota for testing, and it requires additional approval for usage and resource provisioning.” A section titled “Request quota and approval” linked to the form and said “the quota may increase or decrease based on the document quality.” Both are gone.

The quickstart is no longer listing “Request approval and quota” as an initial set-up action. The usage page dropped three identical notes stating the API has a default quota “for testing,” in addition to instructions on how to request approval and quota. While both are dated Oct. 16 (the same), the changelog only mentions the quota page.

Google had clarified the testing language in September 2024, when its changelog said the aim was “to better explain that the default quota is for initial setup and testing.”

The quota page still lists the default limits. Each project gets 200 publish requests per day, counting both updates and removals. Per minute, a project gets 180 metadata requests and 380 requests across all endpoints. The daily limit resets at midnight Pacific Time.

The API is still limited to pages with JobPosting or BroadcastEvent embedded in a VideoObject. The usage page still says Google’s spam policies apply to submissions and tells developers not to get around submission limits, “such as by using multiple accounts.”

Google’s job posting guide, which was last updated Sept. 8, still recommends the Indexing API over sitemaps for job posting URLs and a sitemap for full-site coverage. The quickstart itself did away with the paragraph comparing the two.

Job board owners in my September report stated they had waited months without receiving an update regarding the status of their approval requests, and Google’s documents gave no timelines for reviewing such requests.

In addition, I noticed that the newly-updated Indexing API documentation no longer provides information on how to submit your application to be allowed to utilize the API; nor does it provide information as to what will happen to applications that have been previously submitted to be reviewed, or if a project that never received approval can now utilize its default quota for live job postings or livestreams.

You can check your project’s current quota in the Google API Console, where the quota page still directs you. Keep an eye on that page and the changelog for any new way to request a higher quota.

#126. Why Unpolished Reels Win: An Instagram Growth Strategy for Business

Wondering how to create Instagram Reels that actually build a loyal following without expensive equipment or hours of editing? Want to know the specific hook formulas, editing techniques, and testing strategies that turn simple, off-the-cuff videos into high-performing content?

In this article, you'll discover a complete framework for creating authentic, unpolished Instagram Reels that drive engagement, attract followers, and convert viewers into customers.

The biggest misconception about Instagram Reels is that they require professional cameras, elaborate editing, and a polished final product. Shannon McKinstrie has found the opposite is true. On a phone, people want to feel like they're talking with a friend.

Polished content creates a distance between the creator and the viewer, similar to the gap audiences feel when watching traditional television advertising.

Audiences are now craving authenticity, behind-the-scenes moments, and lived-in experiences that feel off-the-cuff. In fact, some of Shannon’s most successful content is just a six-second video with text on top. As long as the text resonates, it works.

The practical takeaway: stop waiting for perfect. Post content, collect data, and learn from it. Testing beats planning every time.

This shift traces back to a growing trust deficit. Audiences got burned by creators and brands whose marketing looked perfect but didn't deliver. That experience made people skeptical of anything that feels too produced. Even major brands have caught on. Chipotle, for example, now runs commercials made entirely from creator-shot vertical video rather than traditional ad production.

The starting point for any Instagram Reels strategy isn't a content calendar or a trending audio clip. It's finding the overlap between what the creator already knows and what genuinely excites them.

Shannon describes this as “expertise plus excitement.” Audiences can feel whether someone cares about what they're posting. Content created without genuine enthusiasm consistently underperforms. Shannon herself won't post something if she's not excited to hit the publish button, because in the past, forcing content just to stay consistent always flopped.

This doesn't mean every creator needs a single narrow niche. The days of having one tiny niche and sticking to it are over. Instagram's interest-based algorithm allows creators to branch out. A reel of Shannon's daughter putting sprinkles on a cake took off and still attracted her ideal audience of moms and similar demographics.

For creators who feel stuck, Shannon offers a useful thought exercise. Walking into a room full of strangers, what's the one topic you would most want someone to ask about? That answer often points toward the right content direction.

Not everyone needs to do talk-to-camera Reels. Shannon has clients for whom 90% of their content is simple carousel posts made directly on Instagram, and they're thriving. Others lean heavily on talk-to-camera videos. The key is choosing the format that's easiest to create, because the easier the process, the more consistently the creator will actually press post.

B-roll with text overlays, photo dumps, and Instagram Stories are all viable alternatives.

Pro Tip: When feeling stuck about what to post, think about a journey or something new you're learning. Gary Vee has recently encouraged creators to just post something random, a journey they're on, because people love to root for other humans and follow along in the moment.

Join thousands of small-business marketers at Social Media Marketing World — three days of AI, social media, and marketing strategy taught by world-class experts. April 1–3, 2027 in Anaheim.

Every session is pitch-free and built around tactics you can use yourself, no big team required. Your All-Access ticket includes an extra day of workshops, full access to AI Business World, and recordings of everything.

The Nitro Bar, a local coffee shop in Rhode Island, is a case study in enthusiasm-driven content. The shop grew from a single coffee cart into multiple locations, largely because of social media.

Every week, the team films a “most popular drink of the weekend” reveal, where an employee looks up the numbers on camera. They also put employees on the spot with emotion-based drink challenges and sprinkle in the founder's story at least once a week.

The content feels lived-in and in the moment, even though there's real strategy behind it. Someone who has never visited the shop feels like they already know the staff, the vibe, and what to order.

The single most effective tactic for driving engagement on Instagram right now is calling out the viewer's identity within the first few seconds. Why? People consume so much content daily that the fastest way to make someone stop scrolling is to make them feel seen and heard.

Identity-based hooks work by embedding specific identity markers into the first few seconds of a reel: location (Raleigh moms, North Carolina), generation (Gen X, millennial), life stage (accidental entrepreneur, new creator, 2027 brides), or personality type (type B, shy creator).

Shannon found that when she identified herself only as an “Instagram coach,” people tuned out. Adding that she's also a mom of two and type B, not organized, made audiences say, “Oh, she gets me.”

The language that hooks an audience comes from knowing what they call themselves, not just what the creator calls them. Shannon pulls this language from her own current and past clients. For creators just starting out, she recommends reviewing competitors' testimonials to identify the exact phrases people use to describe their problems and goals.

Another tool Shannon recommends is TikTok's creator search insights. At the top of TikTok's search, typing “creator search insights” reveals the topics people are actively searching for. Scrolling through to find one within a relevant niche reveals what the algorithm currently wants to push. Combining that data with what the creator's audience actually needs is, as Shannon puts it, “lightning in a bottle.”

For example, instead of a generic post about a beautiful wedding venue, the hook would read: “2027 brides getting married in D.C., did you know there's a venue 30 minutes outside the city that feels like you're in Europe?”

The accompanying video would be a five-second clip of the view. That's it. The bride sees herself in the hook, the visual matches her taste, and the result is a follow and a booked appointment.

The approach works across industries. A real estate agent targeting relocators could say, “If you're relocating to [city]” rather than a generic “homes for sale.”

Two words define what makes a hook work on Instagram: specificity and perspective.

Specificity means replacing generic language with precise, resonant details. Shannon shares an example of a reel in which a man posted a video of an old truck with Pink Floyd playing. It blew up not because the concept was random, but because it was specific. He named a particular brand of truck and said “Pink Floyd,” not just “rock and roll.” People who like that brand of truck and Pink Floyd stopped, viewed, and commented.

One of Shannon's clients gained 30,000 followers from a single reel after tweaking the hook from targeting “homeowners” to read “patiently waiting for the women who just bought a home.” That single shift from a generic label to a specific life stage made all the difference.

The other half of the equation is perspective. The shift that's working is moving from “how to” hooks to “how I” hooks. This takes content from an expert lecturing to a personal friend sharing.

Shannon cites a nutritionist client who went viral three times with the same hook structure: “the smoothie that helped my client lose 10 pounds.” That hook works because it's not “a smoothie to help you lose weight,” which anyone could find on Google or ChatGPT. It's a specific result tied to a real person's experience.

The AI Business Society filters the noise for you, with expert-led training you can put to work the same day — plus a community of marketers sharing what's actually working.

Travel agents can use the same shift. Instead of “here's a trip idea,” the hook becomes “here's where I would send you on a three-day trip with a thousand dollars.” The content may cover the same information, but the framing through personal perspective makes it feel trustworthy and specific.

Pro Tip: Shannon recommends looking at every hook right before posting and asking: Is there one tiny thing that can make the viewer feel it more? Adding an additional single word that resonates can transform a post's performance.

Shannon treats hooks for story-driven content like the opening of a movie: don't give anything away yet. The test is simple. Ask, “How would I start this at a dinner party?” That framing naturally creates a hook that feels intimate and insider-ish, like something only the creator's inner circle knows.

Timeline-based openings tap into this structure well. Starting with “one hour ago,” “ten years ago,” “yesterday,” or “I recently” immediately grounds the viewer in a moment and adds a layer of story to even straightforward educational content.

Pro Tip: Shannon records her verbal hook about five times before using it. The first few attempts tend to sound preachy. By the fifth take, the delivery sounds conversational and natural.

Shannon's standard format for talk-to-camera Reels follows a specific layered structure. The main hook text is anchored at the top of the screen. Underneath, a sub-hook (the “why do they care” credential) appears using the typewriter effect in Instagram's free editing tools, with a typing sound effect kept under two seconds.

At the two-and-a-half to three-second mark, a pop-up overlay appears on screen. This could be a screenshot of a DM, a picture of follower count growth, or a screenshot showing results from a student who went viral. These overlays serve a dual purpose: they add social proof and give the viewer a new visual element to process, thereby extending watch time.

For a reel about optimizing an Instagram bio in 2026, the main on-screen hook text reads “how to optimize your bio on Instagram in 2026.” The sub-hook underneath, using the typewriter effect, reads “from someone who's written one hundred bios.”

Then the verbal hook, the first thing the creator says out loud, is “if your bio looks like this, you're living in 2020.” Each layer adds a different dimension: the main hook states the topic, the sub-hook establishes credibility, and the verbal hook creates urgency and curiosity.

Shannon gets constant questions about her mugs, her glasses, and her shirts. Even a cat in the background or a microphone clipped to a spatula can spark engagement. Creators who teach content that might feel intimidating find that viewers often comment on the prop rather than the lesson, which still counts as engagement and signals the algorithm.

For creators who don't use physical props, having a Canva presentation visible on a laptop in the background gives viewers something else to focus on while the hook lands.

Shannon calls this broader principle “taste and identity.” When a viewer sees visual elements that match their personal aesthetic, whether that's a cozy living room, a European-looking wedding venue, or a shelf full of books, they feel an instant sense of belonging. The visual signals do the work before the creator says a word.

One underused technique for building that taste-and-identity connection is the cutout feature in Instagram edits. Creators download themed elements from Canva (a book icon, a candle, and a coffee cup), use Instagram's cutout tool to remove the background, and then place these elements around the video.

For a reel about books to read this fall, surrounding the speaker with book and candle cutouts immediately signals to book lovers that this content is for them.

The first step Shannon takes when editing is using the “cut silences” feature. After loading a video (hers are typically around ten minutes of raw footage), she taps the clip in the timeline, scrolls to the bottom, and taps “cut silences.” This removes all dead air automatically. From there, she manually adjusts each clip, cutting anything unnecessary.

For content that gets cut from the spoken portion but still adds value, Shannon types it out and adds it as a pop-up text overlay. These additional tidbits act as bonus content that keeps viewers watching for the next golden nugget.

Shannon also recommends having someone else review the edit. Her husband serves as her editing buddy and is “ruthless” about calling out moments where the content loses momentum.

Pro Tip: Extra points that don't make it into the reel can go into the caption instead.

Trial reels are shown exclusively to non-followers, making them an ideal testing ground for content outside a creator's usual niche.

Shannon edits her reel and posts it as a trial around noon. Then, at three o'clock, she posts the same reel separately to her main feed because her audience is most active in the three-to-six PM window. The order matters. Trials want original content that hasn't been posted to the feed yet. Posting to the feed first, then to the trials, results in poor performance on the trial version.

She rarely pushes a trial reel to her feed after the fact, having done so only twice. Most of the time, she lets trial reels live in their own separate algorithm while the same content performs independently on her main feed.

The real power of trial reels lies in their diagnostic value. Retention graphs reveal exactly where viewers drop off, and retention is the single most important metric for Instagram Reels right now. If a reel's retention graph drops like a rock in the first few seconds, the hook needs to be reworked. Instagram's goal is to keep users on the app, so content that maintains high retention gets pushed to more viewers.

Pro Tip: For carousels, adding a CTA such as “don't miss slide 7” in the caption drives swipe-through behavior. Placing the most valuable insight on a later slide gives viewers a reason to keep swiping, which boosts the carousel's retention signal.

Shannon McKinstrie, an Instagram growth strategist, helps business owners build a loyal following that converts. Learn more about their Reels Lab, a month-to-month membership program. Follow them on Instagram and LinkedIn.

#127. How Australian Home Lender Lendi Measures The Invisible Work Of AI

Most brands and businesses are trying to figure out how to improve their metrics when it comes to AI – and also what those metrics even are.

Problem is, measuring how chatbots shape brand discovery is mostly still a mystery.

But “you can’t improve what you can’t measure,” said Michael McCash, GM of growth at Australian home loan and property sales company Lendi Group.

McCash joined Lendi two years ago with a plan to sharpen the company’s more than $10 million in annual paid media, which has meant developing an in-house model for multi-touch attribution and bringing in Mutinex as its new marketing mix modeling (MMM) vendor. Lendi is also a pilot brand customer of Mutinex’s new AI measurement solution called AI Visibility.

Incorporating MMM has helped iron out wrinkles Lendi didn’t even know where there. For example, McCash said, the brand had been a major buyer of streaming TV and data-driven video on demand. Makes sense. For years, the industry has been betting on and investing in streaming as a major channel for growth.

But when Lendi dug in, what it found through its MMM reports is that old-school, free-to-air television had been “underweighted” and was actually a very efficient channel.

“We [started] diverting money from elsewhere in less efficient channels,” McCash said. “[And TV] just swallowed it up and kept increasing ROI.”

Media buyers often favor the channels they use themselves, he said, and many are young and consume a lot of streaming. Meanwhile, marketers trust the data they can easily see, meaning clicks, impressions, search term rates and other readily available metrics.

Which leads us to AI, the shiniest new marketing channel there is.

“With more people moving towards the Claudes and Geminis and ChatGPTs of the world, [the] initial discovery phase has become somewhat hidden again,” McCash said, like it was when Google and online search were new.

With little visibility into how AI platforms respond to prompts or surface brands, he said, many marketers are turning to information they find on forums like Reddit and X to try and piece together how people use LLMs and whether their brands show up. The platforms have made it “invisible or quite a hard task” to see how certain keywords or types of searches surface products, he added.

The Mutinex AI Visibility tool, like other AEO or GEO analytics offerings, generates insights by mass prompting LLMs with pertinent searches, like “find home loans in Western Australia,” for example, and then analyzes the results. Because there’s no reliable analytics dashboard for tracking those types of searches, the only option is to run thousands of prompts and observe the AI output.

Lendi also works with another vendor called Tracksuit that measures brand metrics and tracks how AI treats a brand compared to its competitive set. On top of that, Lendi partners with Askable for customer and mass market surveys. These tools combined help the company keep a finger on the pulse of its performance in new AI search and discovery markets.

But visibility is only part of the equation. Lendi is also testing whether advertising in AI chatbots is worth the investment.

According to McCash, the AI chatbots that include ads, such as ChatGPT and Google’s Gemini, haven’t been major ROI contributors, at least not yet.

“We’ve dipped our toes in the water,” McCash said of AI chatbot advertising. So far, though, Lendi’s MMM shows middling performance. The CPMs and customer acquisition rates are too high to justify much investment.

But what Lendi does see is a new type of customer, one who shows up to the Google search box or a Lendi-owned site having already done considerable homework on the brand. These potential home loan buyers are more knowledgeable and further down the funnel, because they’ve already done a bunch of research by prompting LLMs.

And so, for now, Lendi’s AI investment is focused less on buying chatbot ads and more on measurement and understanding how chatbots impact discovery.

McCash said he expects that the AI platforms themselves will provide more tools and help as they grow their own ad businesses, including providing data, insights and dashboards with anonymized information on the types of questions people ask and how brands show up.

Those insights are important, he said, because AI chatbots are now “the first port of call” for millions of people looking for a home or a loan. That type of data is critical for helping marketers understand how research through LLMs during the early stages can change the mindset of the customers who eventually reach them.

“All of that pre-work is being done early and in-platform now,” McCash said of AI chatbot users researching home loans. “And I think [getting access to] that knowledge is the next frontier” for marketers.

Advertising supply chain intelligence company DecryptAds uncovered more than 2,100 AI-generated recipe sites that are monetized with programmatic ads and feature fabricated author profiles.

Minerva wants to turn fragmented customer data into something marketers can use, with AI agents doing the work behind the scenes.

VideoAmp is competing in the measurement space by sharpening its focus on TV audience data, ad performance and, of course, AI. The company is also making strategic hires and promoting from within.

The Prebid Summit in New York City on Tuesday exceeded the event’s reputation for liveliness.

The ad industry has become a community of people who say things like “This is going to sound relatable” and follow it up with a sentence that may as well be Martian to 99% of America.

LG home screen inventory is now available through agentic buying, opening up a premium TV placement to faster, more automated campaign setup.

#128. How a plan to turn the Spokane Spokesman-Review into “The People’s Paper” ended in a newsroom revolt

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Newsroom staffers say that concerns about Rob Curley’s leadership festered until his August suspension — weeks before the paper was set to transfer to his nonprofit.

This report was produced in a collaboration between InvestigateWest and RANGE. When the Spokesman-Review announced plans to transfer Spokane’s 143-year-old, family-owned newspaper to a nonprofit founded by executive editor Rob Curley, it took over the front page. “The People’s Paper,” read the April 16, 2025, headline, saying ownership would transfer “to you, the community.” Key to the plan was Curley, the folksy self-proclaimed “journalism nerd” who burst into Spokane a decade ago, declaring a love for Gonzaga University basketball rivaled only by his love for Disney. The transition to Comma Community Journalism Lab was cast in media industry publications not only as a way to save Spokane’s daily newspaper, but as part of a growing movement to resurrect dying papers by making them less dependent on ads and corporate ownership and more on philanthropy and community partnerships. As proof of concept, the paper had already added several so-called “community-funded” journalists to its staff. But in the Spokesman-Review newsroom this summer, that hopeful vision ran into persistent concerns about Curley’s leadership. More than a dozen current and former employees, along with contemporaneous records reviewed by InvestigateWest and RANGE, reveal how the newsroom had raised concerns about Curley’s management for years, culminating in his suspension from the paper on Aug. 7 and a vote of no confidence from the union, the Spokane Editorial Society. He is currently on leave as the paper conducts an internal investigation. Employees said stories that might have angered powerful community figures or potential donors were killed or curtailed, and that they felt he retaliated against workers he viewed as disloyal. Staffers questioned his financial oversight of Comma, which hired his own son at a salary topping most reporters’ and recruited out-of-town executives to serve as top editors before Comma had met its fundraising goal. Current and former Spokesman-Review employees also described workplace complaints involving Curley and one of those editors, including allegations of inappropriate lewd and sexual comments around employees, including teenage interns. Curley declined to comment for this article. In a brief phone interview, Curley’s attorney, Patrick Kirby, who specializes in employment and wrongful termination cases, said, “It’s all inaccurate,” in reference to a list of claims InvestigateWest and RANGE provided to Curley prior to publication. Kirby hung up the call when a reporter pressed him on which claims specifically he believed were inaccurate. The top of Page 1 of The Spokesman-Review, April 16, 2025. Tensions in the newsroom came to a head in the first week of August, as the paper rallied to cover the most destructive wildfires in Spokane’s history and the imminent ownership transfer approached at the end of the month. Some staffers were alarmed at the prospect of working for an organization Curley founded, with even fewer checks on his authority. “The terror had been building through advertising, circulation, and this newsroom each day, getting closer to the day of knowing we would have to work for Rob without the filter of human resources and the publisher,” said one employee, speaking anonymously for fear of retribution. Reporters had grown increasingly frustrated with Comma editors meddling with stories, and Curley tried to fire a reporter who pushed back, employees say. But instead, when other Spokesman-Review editors backed the reporter, publisher William “Stacey” Cowles suspended Curley, citing “several personnel complaints” against him. It wasn’t until after Curley’s suspension that reporters were told news that called the Comma plan into question. In a meeting days after Curley had been kicked out of the building, Spokesman-Review management shared that despite public claims by Curley that several reporters were paid for by community donors — a source of optimism for the Comma plan — none of the paper’s reporting positions were currently community-funded. There were “audible gasps,” according to several reporters in the room. The paper had been promoting its community-funded reporters online, removing paywalls for stories written by those journalists. One reporter remembered how at fundraising events, Curley would point to a journalist’s face on a big screen and tell donors that their money paid for journalists’ salaries. Even the reporters took pride in sharing the claim with readers. “I’ve been lying on his behalf without even knowing it,” one reporter said. Cowles, the publisher, said he had no comment on the claims about Curley until the conclusion of the internal investigation. He said the paper is targeting Oct. 30 to close the transaction with Comma. Bill Simer, Comma Community Journalism Lab board chair, did not comment for this article. Saving local journalism Before joining the Spokesman-Review in 2016, Curley had been praised in some journalism circles as a leader in transitioning struggling newspapers away from print and into the digital world. In naming Curley as the Spokesman-Review’s new top editor, Cowles said Curley had “a proven record of delivering news that matters” and that his “innovative work” at previous newspapers helped them win top journalism awards “including a Pulitzer Prize,” the announcement said. But reporters at his previous gigs viewed him differently: as a mercurial leader who hyped expensive, ineffective initiatives, sacrificing journalism ethics to keep up cozy relationships with powerful community institutions and politicians. The Orange County Register in Southern California was criticized for favorable coverage of Disney under Curley, who served as the paper’s top editor between 2014 and 2016 and proudly said he wore a Mickey Mouse garment every day. He also faced backlash when he revised an article two months after it had been published at the request of a politician, despite police reports and other records that didn’t support the change. Curley changed the story over the objections of the reporter and did not note the changes for the public with a correction or editor’s note — a decision journalism ethicists called an “unethical overreach.” Journalists from the Las Vegas Sun in Nevada had their own problems with him. After he left the Sun in 2012, they noticed that Curley kept getting credit for the paper’s Pulitzer Prize in 2009 — credit that Cowles repeated in the 2016 hiring announcement. Sun employees clarified to the Inlander, a Spokane alt-weekly, that Curley, in fact, had nothing to do with the series that won the Pulitzer. Curley said he’d never told anyone he won a Pulitzer, blaming a series of misunderstandings for it showing up time and time again in his biography. Curley stuck around Spokane, undaunted by the controversies from his past. And with layoffs and buyouts shrinking the newsroom in a struggling industry, Curley two years ago began testing the Comma pitch among staff by signaling that it would save their jobs. Reporters said he told them privately that they’d receive big raises once the transfer happened. If Comma didn’t move forward, he said the Cowles family would likely lay off staff or maybe sell the locally owned paper to one of the hedge fund–owned companies known for downsizing newsrooms, one current employee recalled. Reporters felt Curley had compromised editorial independence at the Spokesman as well. Staffers took issue with Curley altering an article in 2025 about a bond proposal from Spokane Public Schools. In the article, reporters wrote a passage explaining how the proposal could raise property taxes. The story had been cleared by the typical story editors, but late the night before the story was published, Curley had a copy editor change that passage “to be more in line with what the school district wanted us to be saying,” said Emry Dinman, one of the article’s two reporters. “My editors were all as outraged as I was.” Staffers knew Comma was trying to partner with the school district as part of the ownership transition, though Dinman said he didn’t want to speculate on the intentions behind the late-night edit. Current and former staffers also said Curley didn’t like articles that were critical of Gonzaga, a private university downtown most known for its basketball team that Curley frequently celebrated in his columns. Rebecca Hansen-White, a former reporter at the Spokesman-Review from 2018 to 2020, said that during the COVID-19 pandemic she wrote a story about Gonzaga’s plans for an isolation facility, which included some light criticism from a local politician for the private university using government money to do so. But the story was never published. When Hansen-White asked what happened, she recalls an editor told her something to the effect of “that may have been one Rob didn’t want to run,” though she was never able to confirm if Curley spiked it himself. “That was very frustrating. I worked hard on this and I’m going out to the community and I’m getting in these tough conversations with sources,” she said. “And then I come back to the newsroom and find that my work has been changed or removed without an explanation.” Comma eventually set up shop on the Gonzaga campus in 2024. The two editors who Curley hired for Comma in fall 2025 did little to ease reporter concerns about outside interference. Donna Wares and Ron Sylvester had both worked with Curley at the Orange County Register, and when Curley brought them into the Spokesman-Review newsroom, an email sent to the staff described their roles until the transfer as “consultants” — Sylvester for “newsroom metrics and trust initiatives,” and Wares for “enterprise story assignment, editing and Northwest Passages author recruitment.” Northwest Passages is the nonprofit’s book club and event series. That distinction was crucial for Spokesman-Review staffers, who considered it a breach of journalistic integrity to have non-staffers weigh in on editorial decisions, even if it came from people who would one day be their editors. “We were told through the union that Comma editors would not be able to touch our stories until the transition happened,” said Emily White, a former reporter who left the Spokesman at the end of August. But that’s not what happened. “They were tampering with our stories with no permission,” White said. The union filed a grievance with the company, said Thomas Clouse, union president and longtime reporter. “Our understanding was that the publisher dealt with it,” he said. A newsroom altercation As Comma took longer than initially expected to reach its $2 million fundraising goal, the transition kept being delayed. The presence of Comma staff in the newsroom, meanwhile, grew louder. Comma had also hired one of Curley’s sons. Johnathan Curley made a salary of $62,400, according to a 2025 court document, topping the pay of almost every Spokesman-Review reporter. His title at Comma is “technical director,” and he handles video and audio equipment for Comma events. Previously, the 24-year-old worked as a part-time audio-visual technician for Cirque du Soleil in Las Vegas. Johnathan Curley did not respond to requests for comment. Staffers questioned how much Sylvester and Wares were getting paid to be Comma editors before the transition, and they were concerned that Wares spent half her time in California, flying back and forth on Comma’s dime. Sylvester lingered in the newsroom, with staff increasingly unclear of his role. Employees described Sylvester as a disorganized and unproductive editor who often shopped online for magician supplies while in the office. He was tasked with managing the summer internship program, they said, but his involvement was so marginal that other staff had to pick up his slack. “If you ask what his job entailed, I wouldn’t be able to give you an answer,” one staffer said. Sylvester did not respond to requests for comment. In early August, with the planned transition to Comma just weeks away, the newsroom scrambled to cover wildfires that had caught national attention. The staff worked day and night, eventually breaking the news that one of the blazes was set by an arsonist. Courts reporter Alexandra Duggan, as it turned out, had been one of the first people to see the alleged arsonist near the flames. The Review Building, which houses the Spokesman-Review office, in downtown Spokane, Washington on September 30, 2026. (Wilson Criscione/InvestigateWest)

The story had been cleared by the typical story editors, but late the night before the story was published, Curley had a copy editor change that passage “to be more in line with what the school district wanted us to be saying,” said Emry Dinman, one of the article’s two reporters. “My editors were all as outraged as I was.” Staffers knew Comma was trying to partner with the school district as part of the ownership transition, though Dinman said he didn’t want to speculate on the intentions behind the late-night edit. Current and former staffers also said Curley didn’t like articles that were critical of Gonzaga, a private university downtown most known for its basketball team that Curley frequently celebrated in his columns. Rebecca Hansen-White, a former reporter at the Spokesman-Review from 2018 to 2020, said that during the COVID-19 pandemic she wrote a story about Gonzaga’s plans for an isolation facility, which included some light criticism from a local politician for the private university using government money to do so. But the story was never published. When Hansen-White asked what happened, she recalls an editor told her something to the effect of “that may have been one Rob didn’t want to run,” though she was never able to confirm if Curley spiked it himself. “That was very frustrating. I worked hard on this and I’m going out to the community and I’m getting in these tough conversations with sources,” she said. “And then I come back to the newsroom and find that my work has been changed or removed without an explanation.” Comma eventually set up shop on the Gonzaga campus in 2024. The two editors who Curley hired for Comma in fall 2025 did little to ease reporter concerns about outside interference. Donna Wares and Ron Sylvester had both worked with Curley at the Orange County Register, and when Curley brought them into the Spokesman-Review newsroom, an email sent to the staff described their roles until the transfer as “consultants” — Sylvester for “newsroom metrics and trust initiatives,” and Wares for “enterprise story assignment, editing and Northwest Passages author recruitment.” Northwest Passages is the nonprofit’s book club and event series. That distinction was crucial for Spokesman-Review staffers, who considered it a breach of journalistic integrity to have non-staffers weigh in on editorial decisions, even if it came from people who would one day be their editors. “We were told through the union that Comma editors would not be able to touch our stories until the transition happened,” said Emily White, a former reporter who left the Spokesman at the end of August. But that’s not what happened. “They were tampering with our stories with no permission,” White said. The union filed a grievance with the company, said Thomas Clouse, union president and longtime reporter. “Our understanding was that the publisher dealt with it,” he said. A newsroom altercation As Comma took longer than initially expected to reach its $2 million fundraising goal, the transition kept being delayed. The presence of Comma staff in the newsroom, meanwhile, grew louder. Comma had also hired one of Curley’s sons. Johnathan Curley made a salary of $62,400, according to a 2025 court document, topping the pay of almost every Spokesman-Review reporter. His title at Comma is “technical director,” and he handles video and audio equipment for Comma events. Previously, the 24-year-old worked as a part-time audio-visual technician for Cirque du Soleil in Las Vegas. Johnathan Curley did not respond to requests for comment. Staffers questioned how much Sylvester and Wares were getting paid to be Comma editors before the transition, and they were concerned that Wares spent half her time in California, flying back and forth on Comma’s dime. Sylvester lingered in the newsroom, with staff increasingly unclear of his role. Employees described Sylvester as a disorganized and unproductive editor who often shopped online for magician supplies while in the office. He was tasked with managing the summer internship program, they said, but his involvement was so marginal that other staff had to pick up his slack. “If you ask what his job entailed, I wouldn’t be able to give you an answer,” one staffer said. Sylvester did not respond to requests for comment. In early August, with the planned transition to Comma just weeks away, the newsroom scrambled to cover wildfires that had caught national attention. The staff worked day and night, eventually breaking the news that one of the blazes was set by an arsonist. Courts reporter Alexandra Duggan, as it turned out, had been one of the first people to see the alleged arsonist near the flames.

Tensions in the newsroom came to a head in the first week of August, as the paper rallied to cover the most destructive wildfires in Spokane’s history and the imminent ownership transfer approached at the end of the month.

Some staffers were alarmed at the prospect of working for an organization Curley founded, with even fewer checks on his authority.

“The terror had been building through advertising, circulation, and this newsroom each day, getting closer to the day of knowing we would have to work for Rob without the filter of human resources and the publisher,” said one employee, speaking anonymously for fear of retribution.

Reporters had grown increasingly frustrated with Comma editors meddling with stories, and Curley tried to fire a reporter who pushed back, employees say. But instead, when other Spokesman-Review editors backed the reporter, publisher William “Stacey” Cowles suspended Curley, citing “several personnel complaints” against him.

It wasn’t until after Curley’s suspension that reporters were told news that called the Comma plan into question. In a meeting days after Curley had been kicked out of the building, Spokesman-Review management shared that despite public claims by Curley that several reporters were paid for by community donors — a source of optimism for the Comma plan — none of the paper’s reporting positions were currently community-funded.

There were “audible gasps,” according to several reporters in the room. The paper had been promoting its community-funded reporters online, removing paywalls for stories written by those journalists. One reporter remembered how at fundraising events, Curley would point to a journalist’s face on a big screen and tell donors that their money paid for journalists’ salaries. Even the reporters took pride in sharing the claim with readers.

“I’ve been lying on his behalf without even knowing it,” one reporter said.

Cowles, the publisher, said he had no comment on the claims about Curley until the conclusion of the internal investigation. He said the paper is targeting Oct. 30 to close the transaction with Comma. Bill Simer, Comma Community Journalism Lab board chair, did not comment for this article.

Before joining the Spokesman-Review in 2016, Curley had been praised in some journalism circles as a leader in transitioning struggling newspapers away from print and into the digital world. In naming Curley as the Spokesman-Review’s new top editor, Cowles said Curley had “a proven record of delivering news that matters” and that his “innovative work” at previous newspapers helped them win top journalism awards “including a Pulitzer Prize,” the announcement said.

But reporters at his previous gigs viewed him differently: as a mercurial leader who hyped expensive, ineffective initiatives, sacrificing journalism ethics to keep up cozy relationships with powerful community institutions and politicians. The Orange County Register in Southern California was criticized for favorable coverage of Disney under Curley, who served as the paper’s top editor between 2014 and 2016 and proudly said he wore a Mickey Mouse garment every day. He also faced backlash when he revised an article two months after it had been published at the request of a politician, despite police reports and other records that didn’t support the change. Curley changed the story over the objections of the reporter and did not note the changes for the public with a correction or editor’s note — a decision journalism ethicists called an “unethical overreach.”

Journalists from the Las Vegas Sun in Nevada had their own problems with him. After he left the Sun in 2012, they noticed that Curley kept getting credit for the paper’s Pulitzer Prize in 2009 — credit that Cowles repeated in the 2016 hiring announcement. Sun employees clarified to the Inlander, a Spokane alt-weekly, that Curley, in fact, had nothing to do with the series that won the Pulitzer. Curley said he’d never told anyone he won a Pulitzer, blaming a series of misunderstandings for it showing up time and time again in his biography.

Curley stuck around Spokane, undaunted by the controversies from his past. And with layoffs and buyouts shrinking the newsroom in a struggling industry, Curley two years ago began testing the Comma pitch among staff by signaling that it would save their jobs. Reporters said he told them privately that they’d receive big raises once the transfer happened. If Comma didn’t move forward, he said the Cowles family would likely lay off staff or maybe sell the locally owned paper to one of the hedge fund–owned companies known for downsizing newsrooms, one current employee recalled.

Reporters felt Curley had compromised editorial independence at the Spokesman as well.

Staffers took issue with Curley altering an article in 2025 about a bond proposal from Spokane Public Schools. In the article, reporters wrote a passage explaining how the proposal could raise property taxes. The story had been cleared by the typical story editors, but late the night before the story was published, Curley had a copy editor change that passage “to be more in line with what the school district wanted us to be saying,” said Emry Dinman, one of the article’s two reporters. “My editors were all as outraged as I was.”

Staffers knew Comma was trying to partner with the school district as part of the ownership transition, though Dinman said he didn’t want to speculate on the intentions behind the late-night edit.

Current and former staffers also said Curley didn’t like articles that were critical of Gonzaga, a private university downtown most known for its basketball team that Curley frequently celebrated in his columns.

Rebecca Hansen-White, a former reporter at the Spokesman-Review from 2018 to 2020, said that during the COVID-19 pandemic she wrote a story about Gonzaga’s plans for an isolation facility, which included some light criticism from a local politician for the private university using government money to do so. But the story was never published. When Hansen-White asked what happened, she recalls an editor told her something to the effect of “that may have been one Rob didn’t want to run,” though she was never able to confirm if Curley spiked it himself.

“That was very frustrating. I worked hard on this and I’m going out to the community and I’m getting in these tough conversations with sources,” she said. “And then I come back to the newsroom and find that my work has been changed or removed without an explanation.”

Comma eventually set up shop on the Gonzaga campus in 2024.

The two editors who Curley hired for Comma in fall 2025 did little to ease reporter concerns about outside interference. Donna Wares and Ron Sylvester had both worked with Curley at the Orange County Register, and when Curley brought them into the Spokesman-Review newsroom, an email sent to the staff described their roles until the transfer as “consultants” — Sylvester for “newsroom metrics and trust initiatives,” and Wares for “enterprise story assignment, editing and Northwest Passages author recruitment.” Northwest Passages is the nonprofit’s book club and event series.

That distinction was crucial for Spokesman-Review staffers, who considered it a breach of journalistic integrity to have non-staffers weigh in on editorial decisions, even if it came from people who would one day be their editors.

“We were told through the union that Comma editors would not be able to touch our stories until the transition happened,” said Emily White, a former reporter who left the Spokesman at the end of August.

“They were tampering with our stories with no permission,” White said.

The union filed a grievance with the company, said Thomas Clouse, union president and longtime reporter. “Our understanding was that the publisher dealt with it,” he said.

As Comma took longer than initially expected to reach its $2 million fundraising goal, the transition kept being delayed. The presence of Comma staff in the newsroom, meanwhile, grew louder.

Comma had also hired one of Curley’s sons. Johnathan Curley made a salary of $62,400, according to a 2025 court document, topping the pay of almost every Spokesman-Review reporter. His title at Comma is “technical director,” and he handles video and audio equipment for Comma events. Previously, the 24-year-old worked as a part-time audio-visual technician for Cirque du Soleil in Las Vegas. Johnathan Curley did not respond to requests for comment.

Staffers questioned how much Sylvester and Wares were getting paid to be Comma editors before the transition, and they were concerned that Wares spent half her time in California, flying back and forth on Comma’s dime.

Sylvester lingered in the newsroom, with staff increasingly unclear of his role. Employees described Sylvester as a disorganized and unproductive editor who often shopped online for magician supplies while in the office. He was tasked with managing the summer internship program, they said, but his involvement was so marginal that other staff had to pick up his slack.

“If you ask what his job entailed, I wouldn’t be able to give you an answer,” one staffer said. Sylvester did not respond to requests for comment.

In early August, with the planned transition to Comma just weeks away, the newsroom scrambled to cover wildfires that had caught national attention. The staff worked day and night, eventually breaking the news that one of the blazes was set by an arsonist. Courts reporter Alexandra Duggan, as it turned out, had been one of the first people to see the alleged arsonist near the flames.

The Review Building, which houses the Spokesman-Review office, in downtown Spokane, Washington on September 30, 2026. (Wilson Criscione/InvestigateWest)

On Aug. 4, Sylvester told reporters they should change how they attribute documents in stories. Instead of citing “court documents,” he said they should cite “sworn affidavits.” Despite having no clear editorial role in the Spokesman-Review newsroom, Sylvester went into Duggan’s story that night and made a change reflecting his preference — except in that instance, the record was not in fact an affidavit. It introduced an error into the paper.

Clouse, the union president, said he called a meeting with management to try to understand why Comma editors were meddling with stories again. “That never got resolved,” he said.

Two days later, Duggan, who’d worked 13 straight days, was finishing up another story about the accused arsonist. Sylvester approached her and said, in a low voice, “you’re doing it again,” several employees who witnessed or learned of the altercation told InvestigateWest and RANGE. He’d been referring to her story saying “court documents.”

Duggan walked away. But Sylvester followed, and the two shouted back and forth at each other until other editors stepped in to cool things down.

“I wanted to make sure that our stories were truthful and honest and that they were not being edited without us knowing and without any communication,” Duggan said. “And I just wanted to keep the integrity of the paper.”

Curley sided with Sylvester, telling Spokesman-Review managing editor Lindsey Treffry that night to fire Duggan.

The next morning, during a series of meetings with Cowles, Treffry and other editors shared complaints they had about Curley. Cowles decided to put Curley on administrative leave, revoking his keycard access to the paper’s offices.

A few hours later, however, Curley got in the newsroom again by asking an unsuspecting intern for their keycard. He walked around asking where he could find Treffry, who, according to several staffers there that day, was hiding from Curley in the photo room with other editors. Duggan joined them, and it was there that Duggan learned Treffry saved her job. As they hid, Duggan texted White, who was not in the newsroom at the time. White shared the texts with InvestigateWest and RANGE that described how an HR employee escorted Curley out of the building.

“They chased Rob out of the newsroom,” Duggan texted. “I can’t see because I’m hiding.”

“I’m hysterical,” Duggan wrote, crumpled into a ball and crying.

Duggan said she’d “ride or die for this paper.” She said Curley’s attempt to fire her “felt like a slap in the face — it felt like betrayal.”

In an interview for this story, she said she’ll be grateful for the rest of her life that Treffry had her back.

“She did save my job. And she protected the rest of us from something similar,” Duggan said.

Former reporter Rachel Alexander, who worked at the Spokesman-Review from October 2014 to July 2018, recalled a pattern of “cronyism and ethics violations.”

In a letter she sent to investigators after Curley’s suspension, Alexander described a departure of women on staff and in leadership roles during Curley’s first year; editors who left meetings with him looking “shaken, exhausted and at times afraid”; and how Curley didn’t keep promises to sponsor a former staff member’s work visa if he left the union.

“Despite the meaningful journalism I was able to do and the presence of many talented colleagues who I greatly admire, I could not in good conscience continue working for a man who was willing to lie to a friend and jeopardize his ability to remain in the country,” Alexander wrote. “I made the decision to leave the Spokesman in 2018 primarily because of Mr. Curley’s behavior.”

Before leaving, Alexander noticed that she was “nearly the only woman left on the desk,” according to her letter.

She also told investigators that Curley seemed to primarily “take issue with or pick fights” with women in the newsroom. Instead of talking through concerns, he made “petty” decisions, like blocking reporters on Twitter, she wrote.

In recent years, the paper has hosted high school interns as part of Curley’s effort to make Comma into a training ground for young journalists. But the behavior of Curley and Sylvester made some employees question whether they should be responsible for mentoring young journalists.

One letter shared with internal investigators described how, during a 2024 barbecue for Spokesman-Review interns at Curley’s house, two teenage interns saw sexually explicit images of women on Curley’s iPad as he scrolled through his camera roll. Curley had been giving the high school girls a tour of his home and showing off his guitar collection. He was looking for song lyrics on his iPad when the inappropriate pictures flashed on his screen, according to employees who had heard of the incident from the interns.

Several staff members also brought concerns to HR about inappropriate comments Sylvester made around interns who were in high school and college. In a conversation with another employee about the evolution of photography — and while sitting near an 18-year-old intern — Sylvester joked that if someone wanted to send a “dick pic” back in the day, they had to wait for it to develop, but today it can be done in an instant.

On a different occasion, Sylvester told another employee to wait a few seconds before downloading porn, according to several employees. It was loud enough for other employees to hear the unprompted comment, including nearby interns.

“It was very shocking to hear someone … who was supposed to be a mentor figure say that,” a staffer who witnessed the exchange said. “It’s just not appropriate for the workplace.”

Current and former staff members also described a work environment where people perceived as being against Curley or who reported issues to HR were retaliated against. They felt Curley had favorites — including Sylvester and Wares — who would not face consequences for their actions.

After an employee reported Sylvester to HR for his comment about dick pics, a letter to investigators said Curley appeared to retaliate against those he believed had made the report. Curley excluded one of the employees from important meetings and avoided another employee and gave them “distasteful looks.”

Curley needed to make sure staff was “loyal” to him, employees said. One employee, who requested anonymity for fear of retaliation, said Curley and his allies tried to get them to divulge whether certain Spokesman-Review employees were loyal or not. Staffers said Curley also dangled future “executive” positions to two young women in exchange for their loyalty.

At least one former editorial assistant filed an HR complaint against Curley. After studying creative writing at Eastern Washington University, Brooke Lauerman, now 26, was hired in December 2024 to answer newsroom calls and emails and assist with other editorial tasks. She said Curley often treated editorial assistants “like houseplants.”

“He would pretend we weren’t there. He’d have conversations leaning over our desk,” she said.

One day about a year into the job, after most employees had left for the day, Curley told Lauerman he needed to talk to her, and brought her to an empty conference room and told her to shut the door. She thought she might be getting fired. Instead, for roughly an hour, Curley “begged” her to become his personal assistant, she recalled, saying that he needed help managing his life. He told Lauerman she was “special,” that she could be an “executive lady and make a lot of money,” and that he would be her mentor.

He said he once had an assistant “like Jessica Rabbit, I could send her into a group of guys and they’d all say yes to her, and I want that again,” according to the complaint Lauerman filed.

Lauerman felt like she was being manipulated, and she didn’t understand why Curley was flattering her so much to push her into a job that had never been discussed before.

She made a report with HR, at the direction of her supervisor. Lauerman remembers the HR employee saying they’d “add it to my list” of complaints about Curley, and Lauerman requested that the complaint be kept quiet until she left the paper months later. She followed up with a letter detailing the experience in writing.

Lauerman said Curley avoided her in the months that followed. In March 2026, as her last day of work at the Spokesman approached, he asked her out to lunch, which Lauerman declined.

Shortly after Curley’s suspension was announced, the union held a vote of “no confidence” in Curley. Nearly 90% of the union’s 25 members participated, and all voted in favor of the measure, other than two who abstained.

“He was threatening the jobs of [union] members, and we would strongly object if he were to come back to this newsroom,” Clouse said.

Reporters said that since Curley’s suspension, they’ve been able to focus on journalism. The newsroom “has really felt more like home than it has for a long time,” Duggan said.

Mathew Callaghan, a Comma reporter who contributes to the Spokesman-Review, echoed similar sentiments. He called the newsroom’s editors, reporters and those on the copy desk “some of the best, most hardworking people” he knows, but expressed some concerns over Curley.

“The idea of Comma is a great idea, but I don’t trust Rob Curley to execute that idea,” he said. “I don’t think that he has the best interest of the journalists that he’s supposed to uplift. … I don’t trust him and I question his ethics.”

The publisher has told newsroom employees he will not release results of the investigation. The union believes it’s important for the community to know what the investigation found, Clouse said.

An October 1, 2026 Instagram video from the Comma Community Journalism Lab account recaps a September 23 Northwest Passages event in which Spokesman-Review executive editor Rob Curley, right, interviewed former Disney Imagineer Joe Rohde, left. (Instagram)

It’s unclear what role Curley will continue to play at the Spokesman-Review or at Comma. The result of the pending investigation could decide his fate at the Spokesman-Review. But he may still remain the executive director of Comma, where employees may work for him again anyway. George Brunt, a Comma board member and in-house legal counsel, said that the board will honor the results of the investigation if it finds something indicating it is inappropriate for Curley to be in the newsroom, “with the caveat that the methodology was sound and not biased.” Brunt added that from what he’s seen so far, “I don’t think it was done in good faith.”

Last week, Curley was set to host a Comma event featuring Joe Rohde, a former Disney Imagineer. When the event started, Wares was hosting instead, but shortly into the conversation, Wares invited Curley up to the stage to conduct the interview.

“I’d like to invite the biggest Disney fan that I know, the person who is actually the chief Imagineer of Comma, to join me on stage. Please welcome Rob Curley,” she said.

The audience inside the packed theater cheered, with about a dozen people sitting near the front giving him a standing ovation, including at least one Comma employee.

Curley rushed onto the stage, with Elton John’s “I’m Still Standing” booming through the Gonzaga auditorium.
