Webinar: The Link Building Graveyard: What to Bury & What Still Wins

A rank tracker logged Google pages missing their usual sites, some ChatGPT links lost tracking tags, and Google and Bing changed AI search links and data.

Welcome to the Pulse: This week, we’re looking at how much you can rely on your rankings and ChatGPT referral numbers, how Google and Bing display links and citations in AI search, and what Google is hiring for in Discover.

Here’s what matters for you and your work.

From Sept. 13 to Oct. 9, 8.0% of the Google results pages that rank-tracking company Nozzle could check against each keyword’s history were missing most of the keyword’s usual sites, which then came back on a later check, according to the company’s analysis. Nozzle collected those 17.8 million pages through automated searches.

That compares with 0.17% from Aug. 20 to Sept. 9. The share peaked at about a quarter of pages from Sept. 27 to 29 and has run at about 5% to 11% a day since Oct. 1. Nozzle describes these pages as “poisoned” and attributes the pattern to Google’s response to AI scraping. The report also doesn’t include a statement from Google. For keywords where a customer’s own site would typically rank, that site didn’t appear in the top 10 on 58.6% of affected pages, compared with 2.7% in the baseline.

Before adding a one-day drop from late September or October to a client report, compare the keyword with the sites that usually ranked on page 1 before mid-September (the baseline Nozzle uses). If Search Console shows a similar drop in impressions and clicks for the same query and page, the decline is more likely to be real.

Read our full coverage: Analysis: Google Is Poisoning Search Results For Rank Trackers

ChatGPT-attributed sessions in Google Analytics 4 fell sharply this month. Analysts link the drop to inline links in ChatGPT’s answers that stopped carrying the utm_source=chatgpt.com tag after GPT-6 rolled out.

Graphite CEO Ethan Smith wrote on LinkedIn that there was an approximate 45% drop in ChatGPT sessions on sites tracked by Graphite with meaningful AI Assistant Channel traffic in GA4, and that the untagged visit data could appear under the “Direct” label. Adobe’s Cedric Huesler added that OpenAI confirmed a known bug to him on October 14, and that they had started deploying a fix for this issue on October 15. At around 9 a.m. PT on October 15, according to Huesler, tagged ChatGPT clicks returned to roughly 95-100% of the same hour from the previous week across thousands of websites that he has been tracking. In contrast, SEO consultant Glenn Gabe replied that he hadn’t seen the change yet; and although OpenAI’s release notes were updated on October 15, they did not reference the above-mentioned bug or solution.

Huesler places the affected window between Oct. 8 and 15. He and Smith recommend noting it in your reports so no one mistakes the dip for lost traffic. Since most ChatGPT clicks still arrive without a referrer, Huesler suggests tracking them by their UTM tag.

Read our full coverage: ChatGPT Traffic Drop Appears To Be A Tracking Problem

Google is changing how links appear in AI Mode and AI Overviews, including updates that show inline links higher in responses more often.

Google also plans to test a section at the top of some responses that links to official pages for specific tasks. It’s starting to roll out its carousels for timely articles, which highlight a user’s Preferred Sources, to more locations and languages, though the post doesn’t name them. This week, Google also started testing creator and publisher names on AI Mode video results that link to Search profiles.

In Search Console, each link in an AI Overview is given the same position as that of the overall AI overview. Therefore, moving an inline link higher doesn’t by itself change its reported position. Users who have designated you as a preferred source can see your site highlighted in more carousels as they expand. Your website has to be included in Search generative AI features in Search Console for you to even qualify as a preferred source, as documented on Google’s documentation website.

Read our full coverage: Google Puts Inline Links Higher In More AI Search Responses

Microsoft added a beta feature called Topics Portfolio to the AI Performance report in Bing Webmaster Tools.

It groups the queries your site is cited for in AI answers into broader topics, with approximate figures for each topic’s total citations across all sites, the number of sites cited, and the number of queries. It also lists opportunity queries, where other sites appear and yours doesn’t, with citation volumes shown as ranges. The view only appears if Bing has enough data for your site.

The opportunity query list from Bing is a way for content teams to identify potential gaps in coverage of topics on their sites. However, this can also contain competitor brand terms which may be irrelevant to your website. Microsoft says to treat Topics Portfolio’s metrics as directional rather than absolute, which makes them better for comparing different topics but less useful if you need to track an exact count.

Read our full coverage: Bing Webmaster Tools Sorts AI Search Queries Into Topics

Open Google job listings describe teams that generate and recommend AI content for Discover.

A Staff ML Engineer listing says the Discover Feed Recommendation team “leads by recommending AI-generated content (AIGC) to fulfill user interests.” It also describes agentic flows that generate content for what the listing calls proactive surfaces, naming Discover and Notifications. A director-level design listing describes turning Discover into a “proactive, hyper-personalized concierge experience,” working with teams at YouTube, Shopping, Chrome, and Android.

Neither Discover listing gives a timeline or says how much of the feed AI content would fill. Search Console’s generative AI report for Discover is where your data shows Discover’s AI features linking to your site, with impressions as the only metric its help page describes.

Read our full coverage: Google Is Hiring To Generate AI Content For Discover and Google Discover To Undergo Dramatic Changes

Rank-tracker and ChatGPT referral numbers changed this week. The changes were based on how the numbers were gathered. Nozzle found that some of the Google pages it tracked had most of their usual sites missing. Some ChatGPT visits also lost the tracking tag that let analytics know where visitors came from. Each platform has limitations when it comes to reporting. An example is that an inline link moves up in an AI Overview but does not move from the overview’s single location in Search Console. And Bing provides its opportunity numbers as ranges. And finally Discover’s AI report only counts impressions (as per their help page), and Google has job openings to hire people who create AI content for the Discover feed. Therefore cross checking all numbers reported in a client’s report means using Search Console alongside the rank trackers and Direct alongside the ChatGPT lines.

Using forms to inform and guide AI's actions

Everyone's focused on writing better prompts. But the real unlock might be something you've used a hundred times and never thought of as an AI tool: a form.

You can get AI to gather information: scan a page, review a call, read through feedback. But what comes back is a summary you still have to read, interpret, and act on yourself. AI did the research, then handed you more work.

A form flips that. Instead of asking AI what it found, you give it a set of fields to fill. Every label is an instruction. Every dropdown eliminates guesswork. What comes back isn't a paragraph to interpret, it's structured data, clean enough to act on without you in the middle.

Here's the real magic: a form submission is a trigger. Every automation tool watches for “new form response.” The moment the form is filled, the next step fires on its own. Competitor intel posts to your team channel. Call notes become assigned tasks. Prospect research creates the CRM record and drafts the outreach.

That's the difference between AI that reports to you and AI that sets things in motion. Pick something you handle by hand every week. Build the form. Then set up what happens next.

#131. How Amazon Ads Plans To Make Programmatic Simple Without Taking Control From Marketers

Amazon Ads VP Kelly MacLean on how AI helps marketers connect the dots across the customer journey, with lower costs and better delivery in early tests.

Programmatic was supposed to make buying ads easier. For plenty of marketers, though, it made things more complicated. Amazon Ads thinks AI can finally close that gap.

On this episode of “Inside the Stack,” AdExchanger Editor-in-Chief Allison Schiff speaks with Kelly MacLean, VP of science, engineering and product at Amazon Ads, about the announcements that came out of Amazon unBoxed in September.

MacLean unpacks Amazon’s new AI-powered ad platform, which combines its ad console and DSP so advertisers can launch a programmatic campaign in as few as four clicks. She also explains what the marketer’s job looks like when AI handles the mechanics.

“The advertiser is owning the why and the what,” she says, “and then AI can help drive the how.”

Amazon Ads wants advertisers of every size to be able to use its DSP, not just those who already know programmatic. MacLean calls it “programmatic for everyone.”

That is a nice sentiment, but the proof is in the performance.

In beta tests, advertisers using Amazon Ads Agent to scale AI-driven campaigns saw 18% lower CPMs, 16% lower CPAs and a 65% improvement in delivery. “Those aren’t theoretical projections,” MacLean says. “Those are real live campaigns, budgets and measurable outcomes.”

MacLean gives credit to Amazon’s authenticated graph, which connects 90% of US households and allows AI to optimize against real purchase signals instead of proxies.

Access to real purchase data matters, MacLean says, because the consumer journey is never linear. A streaming TV impression might spark consideration, a display ad might reinforce it and an audio spot might close the sale. But a human managing four or five separate campaigns can’t necessarily make those connections.

Amazon’s edge comes from being able to see the whole journey, she says. “We want to make it easier for marketers to connect the dots wherever that’s happening,” MacLean says.

Also in this episode: How advertisers can move from simple campaigns to advanced settings as their trust in AI grows, why creative becomes a differentiator when execution is automated and why measurement is what MacLean calls the “validation layer” for AI-driven advertising.

Advertising supply chain intelligence company DecryptAds uncovered more than 2,100 AI-generated recipe sites that are monetized with programmatic ads and feature fabricated author profiles.

Minerva wants to turn fragmented customer data into something marketers can use, with AI agents doing the work behind the scenes.

VideoAmp is competing in the measurement space by sharpening its focus on TV audience data, ad performance and, of course, AI. The company is also making strategic hires and promoting from within.

The Prebid Summit in New York City on Tuesday exceeded the event’s reputation for liveliness.

The ad industry has become a community of people who say things like “This is going to sound relatable” and follow it up with a sentence that may as well be Martian to 99% of America.

The country’s most prestigious journalism school has initiated “a critical evaluation” of the Master of Arts program and is pausing admissions to it.

The Columbia Journalism School will pause admissions for its Master of Arts program, dean Jelani Cobb announced on Thursday. The country’s most prestigious journalism school also announced a new online, part-time degree.

In a note to alumni of the M.A. program, Cobb wrote that the administration has “initiat[ed] a critical evaluation” of the M.A. curriculum. “To give this review the focus it deserves, we are temporarily pausing admissions for the upcoming admissions cycle.”

The school’s admissions page has been updated with a similar message.

Columbia will continue to offer its Master of Science programs in Journalism and Data Journalism. Current M.A. students are not affected by the pause. The estimated cost of attendance for the nine-month M.A. for the 2026-2027 year is roughly $120,000. The M.S. costs around $130,000 and the year-long M.S. in Data Journalism costs about $180,000. According to Columbia, around 80% of students receive some sort of financial aid.

The M.A. program is a newer degree — created in 2005 — and was designed for working journalists with three or more years of professional experience “to go deeper into a specialized subject.” The M.S. degree, described as “the foundational program of the Journalism School,” is for students with “zero to three years” of experience.

The school also announced it will, for the first time in its history, offer an online degree. The new online Master of Science in Journalism program will be part-time with students earning a degree over two years.

“This new program brings an Ivy League J-School education directly to students across the United States,” reads one post from the Columbia Journalism School on X. “With guidance from CJS’s faculty of working journalists, you can develop your reporting skills while continuing to live and work in your community.”

Roughly half of enrolled M.A. candidates at Columbia Journalism School are international students, Aditya Soni and Edmund Lee reported for Reuters. Uncertainty in immigration policies and visa challenges under the Trump administration caused “a sharp drop” in international applications to Columbia, according to Reuters, and contributed to the program’s pause.

I am writing to share an update about the Master of Arts program at Columbia Journalism School.

As part of our ongoing commitment to keeping our graduate education timely and innovative, the administration is initiating a critical evaluation of the M.A. curriculum. To give this review the focus it deserves, we are temporarily pausing admissions for the upcoming admissions cycle.

We want to reassure you directly: this evaluation phase reflects our commitment to continuous excellence. It does not alter the standing, prestige, or lasting value of your CJS M.A. degree.

The M.A. degree is grounded in deep domain expertise, rigorous analytical reporting, and subject-matter authority—qualities media organizations and independent journalists need now more than ever. The groundbreaking work produced by our alumni network across global newsrooms continues to define the high standards of this program and reinforce the strength of your credential.

Periodic curricular review is a standard practice at Columbia to ensure our specialized tracks advance alongside the media landscape. Current M.A. students are completing their nine-month curriculum without interruption, receiving the full scope of concentration coursework, thesis advisement, and faculty mentorship.

We remain immensely proud of your achievements and the impact of your reporting worldwide. If you have questions, please contact Dr. George Miller, associate dean for academic affairs.

Sincerely, Jelani Cobb Dean & Henry R. Luce Professor of Journalism

New terms let Meta crawl sites tied to business users and use the content to train its products, widening rights ad buyers had already granted.

Meta’s updated Commercial Terms, which take effect Oct. 30, give the company permission to crawl websites associated with businesses that use its products and to use that content to train those products. The terms apply to any business use of Meta’s products, from running ads to managing a Facebook Page.

Nieman Lab reported this development on Oct. 15. A total of three law professionals have viewed the terms for this media outlet and believe that language in these terms could support an argument by Meta that it is permitted to scrape websites of news sites and use the scraped content to train its AI products.

On Oct. 16, Meta spokesperson Andy Stone responded on X to a post summarizing that report and called the summary false. He wrote that the update is meant to make sure Meta can pull accurate information about products for sale on third-party websites when it makes ad and content recommendations on its platforms, and that it’s “not about scraping news sites.”

Meta’s ad terms already let it crawl advertisers’ websites for uses that include training. The October version reaches businesses that don’t buy ads.

The new crawling paragraph in the Commercial Terms lets Meta, or anyone acting for it, use web scrapers, bots and other automated tools to crawl and collect content from domains and pages associated with a business’s products or services. It also covers URLs made available through the business’s use of Meta’s products or through users’ use of them.

The clause also lets Meta “create test credentials” to reach those pages. Meta may use the content to develop, improve, research and train its products, among other listed uses.

Meta’s own list of ways businesses can utilize Meta services includes advertising, marketing messages, listing your products on Meta platforms along with Meta-created tools including Ads Manager and Meta Business Suite. The very same crawl permission is included in the revised Self-Serve Ad Terms, effective Oct. 30.

A continued usage of Meta’s service for business purposes will be interpreted by Meta to mean that you have agreed to the new terms. The terms say that if you disagree with these new terms, you may cease utilizing Meta’s products for business purposes.

Media and intellectual property attorney Matt Topic, representing The Intercept in their copyright case versus OpenAI, stated to Nieman Lab that while there are no assurances if a court will ultimately enforce this provision, publishers should assume it will.

The current Commercial Terms, dated March 6, 2024, have no crawling clause. Meta’s ad terms do.

The current Self-Serve Ad Terms, dated Aug. 22, 2025, say that placing an ad order gives Meta the right to crawl content on the advertiser’s domains, webpages or URLs. The listed uses include developing advertising and other business products, maintaining integrity, and “research and training.”

Meta’s Ad Creative Generative AI Terms (May 6, 2024) permit Meta to crawl URLs provided by advertisers, for use with their ads, as part of using Meta’s generative AI ad tools. Also the Product Catalog Terms allow Meta to periodically update product catalogs from catalog URLs.

In addition, Meta has announced in its Business Help Center notice that the Product Catalog Terms will be moved into the Commercial Terms, and the Ad Creative Generative AI Terms will move into the Self-Serve Ad Terms to “reduce overlap.” The announcement did not reference crawling or training.

Further, unlike the ad terms, which referenced the placement of an advertisement purchase, the new terms tie the granting of permission to any business use, covering URLs related to a business’s products or that were otherwise made available through users’ usage of Meta’s products. Prior ad agreements allowed Meta to access the advertiser’s domain or advertiser-supplied URLs.

Also, Meta’s Seller Agreement, last updated May 26, 2026, already permits Meta to utilize automated software, including creating test credentials, to obtain information from URLs that sellers provide. The agreement says this helps Meta better assist the seller with optimizing their listings.

Meta’s spokesperson told Nieman Lab the new terms won’t change how the company crawls publishers and that “content owners can still manage how their content is accessed by using robots.txt.” Stone made both points in his post as well. Neither the updated Commercial Terms nor the updated Self-Serve Ad Terms mention robots.txt.

The legal experts told the outlet the new language gives Meta an opening to argue that its commercial terms supersede other blocking instructions. Cornell law professor James Grimmelmann said test credentials could technically let Meta sign up as a fake user to get past registration walls. Meta declined to answer whether test credentials would bypass paywalls or other paid content.

Meta’s crawler documentation says Meta-ExternalAgent crawls for uses such as training foundation AI models or improving products by indexing content directly. Meta-WebIndexer improves Meta AI search results, and Meta says allowing it helps the company cite and link to your content in Meta AI responses.

According to the documentation, Meta-ExternalFetcher may bypass robots.txt when fetching pages at a user’s request. FacebookExternalHit, which creates link previews, may also bypass it while performing security or integrity checks.

Meta’s Oct. 30 crawling and training grant comes with regular business uses of Meta’s products; thus, it includes brands and clients who have a Facebook Page or are in the Business Suite but do not buy ads.

The Robots.txt file is what Meta points to as the method to control its crawling. The Crawler Documentation listed above references Meta-AI training crawlers (Meta-ExternalAgent) and Meta AI Search Crawlers (Meta-WebIndexer); therefore, you may block the Meta-ExternalAgent crawler while allowing the Meta-WebIndexer crawler. Additionally, the new terms do not indicate if a business’s robots.txt settings restrict what it agrees to share by accepting these terms.

Meta’s new Commercial Terms are set to go into action on Oct. 30, giving website operators who use Meta for business two weeks in order to make their decision concerning whether or not they will continue to utilize Meta’s products for business. In addition, during this time, operators should review how their robots.txt files treat each Meta crawler.

The European Publishers Council (EPC) is also writing to the European Commission regarding Meta’s new terms. EPC is specifically concerned that Meta may be allowed by its terms to claim permission to use an article when a user shares a link to that story via social media.

#134. How to Create Pro-Quality AI Videos With Gemini Omni

Want to create professional-looking video content without filming yourself or hiring a production crew? Wondering how to use AI-generated video hooks to stop the scroll and boost engagement on social media?

In this article, you'll discover how to use Google's Gemini Omni to create an AI avatar, produce scroll-stopping video hooks, edit existing footage, and assemble longer videos from 10-second clips.

Google's Gemini Omni, officially called OmniFlash, is the successor to Veo3, Google's first AI video generator. Omni is built on Google's world models, which were trained on YouTube's massive video library. That training gives it an understanding of movement, environments, people, and speech inflections that sets it apart from other AI video tools.

Omni is available in several places, making AI video creation accessible at different levels.

The simplest way to access it is via the Gemini app, available on both desktop and mobile. Inside the Gemini chat interface, tapping the plus button reveals a “Video” option that runs Omni behind the scenes.

For more advanced features, particularly video editing and modification, Google Labs offers a fuller set of tools. Omni is also available through third-party aggregator platforms such as Open Art and Higgs Field, which bundle multiple AI models into a single interface.

Eve Whitaker recommends that beginners start with the Gemini app and a $20/month subscription to explore what Omni can do. The ultra tier runs about $200/month and includes access to all of Google's tools, but most users won't need that right away. Credits are consumed per generation, with higher resolution and longer clips using more. Starting at the lowest tier and buying additional credits as needed keeps costs manageable.

One limitation to be aware of is that the Gemini app imposes generation limits. Early users could generate roughly five or six videos before being throttled, though the limit resets within an hour or two. Google Labs and aggregator platforms offer more generous allowances.

Pro Tip: For anyone serious about AI video production, Eve suggests pairing a direct Google Labs subscription with a third-party aggregator. The aggregator provides access to multiple AI models from a single dashboard, while Google Labs unlocks Omni's full editing capabilities. The Gemini app alone doesn't support video editing or modification.

A clone, like those created by HeyGen, accepts a long script and generates a talking-head video in one pass. An avatar is different. Eve calls it an “AI twin”: a digital representation of a real person that can be placed into any scene, environment, or scenario through text prompts. The key constraint is that Omni generates 10-second clips of the avatar, which then need to be edited together for longer content.

Each avatar is tied to the user's account. Unlike Sora, where creators could share their avatars for others to use in their own videos, Omni restricts avatar access to the account that created it. No one else can call up or use another person's avatar. Clients who want their own avatars need to create them on their own accounts. And, while there's no option to maintain multiple avatars simultaneously, your avatar can be deleted and recreated at will.

The process takes about five minutes. Open the Gemini app on a phone, tap the plus button, and scroll down to “avatar.” The app walks through a Face ID-style capture sequence: look left, look right, look up, look down. It then displays nonsensical sentences to read aloud so it can capture your voice. The deliberately strange text is designed to capture natural speech patterns without the speaker overthinking delivery.

Once the avatar is created and named, it syncs across platforms. This means that a user who builds their avatar on their phone can also call it up in Google Labs on their desktop by typing the @ sign followed by the avatar's name.

The recording environment makes a significant difference in avatar quality, and the AI won't flag problems during capture. If the lighting is poor, the camera has a smudge, or the background is noisy, Omni will simply fill in the gaps with generated content, which may not look or sound like the real person.

Lighting: Natural light works best. Stand in front of a window or to the side of one. Filming with a window behind creates a silhouette that degrades the capture. Eve recorded hers in her living room with natural light and reports excellent results.

Audio: Minimize background noise. The AI needs a clean voice capture to reproduce speech accurately. If it can't hear something clearly, it will fabricate it.

Clothing: Whatever is worn during the recording becomes the avatar's default outfit. A red shirt and necklace worn during setup will appear in every generation unless the prompt specifies something different. Eve suggests choosing an outfit that works across multiple scenarios, since prompting a change is easy, but the default will recur.

Hats and glasses: Avoid wearing them during setup. The AI has no data on what's underneath a hat, so removing one via a prompt produces unpredictable results. The better approach is to record without a hat, then upload a photo of the desired hat as a reference image and prompt the avatar to wear it.

Voice tone: Speak naturally. If the recording is animated or exaggerated, the avatar will default to that energy level in every generation, making it harder to prompt calmer or more conversational deliveries later. Recording in a natural speaking voice preserves flexibility, since animation can always be added through prompts.

Background: The recording background matters less than it might seem. When the avatar is prompted into a specific environment, such as “put me on a beach in Mexico,” Omni knocks out the original background entirely and replaces it with the prompted scene. A clean, well-lit recording is still important for accurately capturing the face and voice, but the physical backdrop doesn't need to be polished.

Effective AI video prompting follows what Eve Whitaker calls the four-element prompting formula: subject, action, environment, and camera. Omni responds well to natural language, meaning the days of formatting prompts in JSON or coded syntax are over.

Subject: Who or what appears in the video. When using an avatar, this means calling it in with the @ sign and the avatar's name.

Action: Describes what the subject is doing: dancing, walking, talking to the camera, parachuting onto a lawn.

Environment: Sets the scene: a street, a beach in Mexico, a kitchen countertop, a park full of dogs.

Camera: Tells Omni where the camera sits relative to the subject and how it moves.

A prompt using all four elements might read:

Eve advises starting simple and iterating. If the first generation places the subject too far from the camera, the next prompt adds “she's standing close to the camera” or “she walks up to the camera.” Each generation reveals how Omni handles different types of instructions.

Omni also supports iterative refinement within a single concept. After generating a clip, the next prompt can specify:

Omni will reproduce the scene with only that one element adjusted. This makes it possible to test variations without re-prompting the entire concept from scratch.

Including a script in the prompt is important. Without one, Omni will generate its own dialog, which sometimes produces interesting accidents but more often produces unusable audio.

The most common prompting mistake is giving Omni more than 10 seconds of dialog. Rather than cutting the speaker off mid-sentence, the AI compresses all the dialog into the time frame, producing rushed, garbled speech toward the end.

Eve's workflow for scripting starts with an LLM. She tells ChatGPT, Claude, or another tool something like:

She describes what she wants, often using voice input with rough, unpolished language, then asks the LLM to suggest clarifying questions. After refining the idea collaboratively, she asks the LLM to turn the final concept into a prompt formatted for Omni.

The AI Business Society filters the noise for you, with expert-led training you can put to work the same day — plus a community of marketers sharing what's actually working.

Camera placement shapes how the viewer feels about the subject.

An extreme wide shot establishes the full environment and context. A medium shot is conversational. A close-up creates intimacy and is ideal for delivering a message directly. An extreme close-up generates discomfort or tension, which can be used deliberately to grab attention.

A “hero shot,” where the camera is positioned below the subject looking upward, makes the subject appear larger than life. A camera positioned above the subject does the opposite, making them appear smaller.

Eve's practical advice for learning camera language is to start watching television and movies, paying attention to what the camera does during emotionally resonant moments. When a scene triggers an emotion, noticing whether the camera is tight on a face, pulling back to reveal a setting, or shifting angles builds an instinct that transfers directly to prompting. Once those patterns are noticed, they become impossible to unsee.

The primary use case Eve recommends for Gemini Omni is creating attention-grabbing hooks for short-form video across TikTok, Instagram, YouTube Shorts, and other platforms.

The concept is straightforward: film a standard talking-head or direct-to-camera video the traditional way, then use Omni to generate a visually striking 2-3-second hook to open the video.

Examples of hooks Eve has created include her avatar getting Nickelodeon slime dumped on its head, getting cake shoved in its face while wearing an evening gown, standing in a park with tennis balls raining from the sky, riding a buffalo in front of a house listing, parachuting onto a lawn next to a for-sale sign, and walking across a kitchen countertop as a six-inch avatar saying, “The only thing small about this kitchen is me.”

The speed of creation is part of the appeal. Eve created the buffalo-riding hook while waiting in line for Coffee: she opened the Gemini app on her phone, called in her avatar, prompted it to ride a buffalo in front of a house listing using a Zillow photo as a reference image, and had the finished clip by the time she picked up her order. That mobile-first workflow makes it possible to produce polished hooks anywhere, without a desktop or editing software.

Eve uses an LLM to generate AI video hook concepts rather than brainstorming them alone.

The process starts by describing the topic and asking for creative visual hooks. The initial suggestions from any LLM tend to be predictable, which is where Eve's “Captain Obvious” technique comes in. The “Captain Obvious” technique is a method for steering an LLM away from its default, predictable suggestions toward more creative and distinctive ideas. The term comes from television production, where producers would pitch story ideas, and the team would flag the obvious ones.

When an LLM suggests a predictable visual, such as a person sitting at a computer with too many tabs open to represent “AI overwhelm,” Eve tells it:

This redirect consistently produces more creative and distinctive concepts.

When pairing an AI-generated hook with a traditionally filmed talking video, visual continuity matters. If the avatar appears in a different outfit than the talking video, the transition feels jarring. Eve's solution is to take a screenshot from the video and upload it as a reference image, then tell Omni to dress the avatar in the same outfit.

The hook clips and talking video are then edited together in CapCut, Instagram's Edits app, or a similar tool.

Pro Tip: Eve has tested as many as seven different hooks for the same talking video using Instagram's trial reels feature, then put promotion behind whichever hook performed best.

Gemini Omni can modify existing video using natural language prompts, making edits that once required a professional editor accessible to anyone. These capabilities, available through Google Labs and aggregator platforms, go well beyond generation. Real footage, whether shot on a phone or generated by AI, can be uploaded and transformed with a text description of the desired change.

The modifications include changing environments in real footage. For example, a summer park scene showing feet walking along a path and a camera panning up to leafy trees can be converted to winter with a single prompt. Omni keeps the shoes, the pants, and the movement identical while stripping leaves from trees and adding snow. The result looks realistic.

Motion graphics can also be added to real video by describing them in a prompt. A cooking video can show animated text slates labeling ingredients as they appear on screen, and the result looks like a motion graphics artist produced it.

Other editing capabilities include changing a subject's outfit, removing objects from a scene, converting a person into a cartoon version of themselves, and changing the background entirely. For example, a talking-head video recorded at a desk can be re-homed on a beach, in a news studio with on-screen text, or any other environment.

Pro Tip: Video uploaded for editing must be cropped to 10 seconds or less. Omni provides a built-in cropping tool, so longer footage can be trimmed to the relevant segment before applying modifications.

The 10-second generation limit doesn't prevent the creation of longer AI video content. It requires pre-production planning and a third-party editor.

For a 90-second video, the approach is to generate nine 10-second clips and edit them together. The key is planning what the last frame of each clip looks like and how it transitions into the first frame of the next clip. Eve suggests using an LLM for this planning, giving it the full concept and specifying constraints:

The LLM will suggest transitional strategies and help plan each segment. For example, Eve recently created an avatar as Gilligan on an island, saying he'd been stranded for 62 years. The LLM suggested inserting a montage of island life between clips, produced across two additional 10-second generations.

Alternatively, Google Labs offers a feature that lets the next prompt build on the clip just generated, which, in theory, helps with continuity. In practice, Eve finds the results inconsistent and prefers to generate clips independently, then edit them together in CapCut.

Pro Tip: Eve suggests using 720p resolution for social media content to conserve credits. Reserve 1080p for content that will be displayed on large screens at conferences or on television. Videos can also be upscaled after generation using third-party tools, so starting at 720p and upscaling later is a cost-effective workflow. Omni supports both vertical (9:16) and horizontal (16:9) aspect ratios, specified in the prompt.

#135. You Know Your Ideal Customer. But Can Your Media Plan Actually Reach Them?

Marketers today describe their ideal customers in extraordinary detail, with rich personas that go beyond basic demographics to include attitudes, motivations, values, preferences and even future intentions.

But a media buyer still has to turn that persona into a handful of targetable attributes. And, ironically, the more specific the picture of an ideal customer becomes, the harder it gets to find that exact person in the media ecosystem.

Segmentation research is a major investment. Having spent the money to find out who your customer is, your buy should match the audiences you’re looking for.

Consider a persona we’ll call “The Experimenter,” someone who is novelty-led, receptive to new products and open to switching brands. This definition may be incredibly useful to a marketer, but there’s no “Experimenter” button in a DSP.

Instead, the persona gets retranslated at every handoff: from consumer insights to marketing, from the media brief to the agency and finally into each buying platform. “Novelty-led and open to switching” becomes “busy professional parents who want convenience,” then “parents ages 30 to 45 with household incomes above $75,000.” By the end, the actual buy might be reduced to “adults 25 to 54.”

Each team is doing its best to translate the persona with the tools it has. Even so, the attitudes and motivations that made the persona strategically valuable are the first things to disappear.

Media teams understand this challenge and optimize campaigns to the nearest match, but brand and insights teams may be less aware. The persona goes into the brief while reporting comes back as demographic reach, CPMs and performance metrics. These two audience definitions may never even get compared.

The brand team thinks the campaign is reaching the persona it developed, while the media team knows they’re only buying the closest available approximation.

The media ecosystem is extraordinarily good at collecting signals about what people do: purchases, searches, site visits, content consumption, location and countless other observable behaviors. But those signals don’t always explain the why.

Someone researching sustainable packaging might be a true sustainability-minded shopper – or they might be researching the topic for work. A loyal brand customer will look identical online to someone actively open to switching allegiances – right up until one of them actually switches.

The missing context is already in the marketer’s hands via research. Consumer insights teams have spent decades asking people directly about their attitudes, preferences, motivations and intentions. This declared data is exactly what gives marketing personas their richness. The challenge is carrying that all the way through to the media buys.

In most cases, survey data is used for analysis but not media activation. Consumer insights and media typically operate with different teams and budgets, and research samples don’t get connected to addressable IDs.

That’s changing with consented research panels and privacy-safe identity matching. Consumers who declare relevant characteristics can become the foundation of an addressable audience. Their records can be matched to pseudonymous identifiers, modeled to find lookalikes and activated as segments in DSPs, social platforms and across CTV environments.

Media buyers no longer have to guess whether someone researching sustainable packaging is actually open to switching brands. They can activate audiences built from consumers who have definitively declared these characteristics.

The best way to learn what a consumer wants is to ask them, not to infer it from another signal.

Targeting based on declared data still faces the classic trade-off between precision and scale, of course. But a research-defined audience provides a better starting point: people who self-declare their attitudes or intentions. And modeling can expand outward when a campaign needs more reach.

Declared data also complements behavioral and transactional signals. A marketer can combine people who say they’re open to switching brands with signals showing they’re currently shopping the relevant category.

Behavioral signals determine the right timing, but declared data identifies the right people.

This dynamic also makes campaign optimization more meaningful. Algorithms learn from the audience they’re given, so beginning with more accurate data creates a better feedback loop between the ideal customer profile, reach and campaign performance.

None of this means marketers need to commission a segmentation study before every media buy. Many declared data audiences already exist. Dynata, for example, maintains more than 3,000 targeting segments built from more than 10,000 profile variables, and its syndicated audiences are already available through LiveRamp. Custom audiences using existing variables can typically be created in three to five days.

Consider an electric vehicle brand trying to find buyers for a luxury EV. Household income shows who can afford to buy one, but declared data, including readily available syndicated audience data, can help distinguish between people who would never consider an EV and those who are persuadable, already interested or simply need a different message.

Marketers are constantly searching for more signals, more data and more sophisticated modeling. But they may be overlooking some of the richest customer intelligence they already have.

Here’s a simple gut check: Look at the persona your organization says it wants to reach. Then look at the audience definitions you buy across media platforms.

How much of the desired persona survives?

The exciting part is the simplicity behind this approach. Instead of chasing ever-more-complex ways of inferring what consumers want, the biggest gains will come from acting on what they’ve already told you.

Advertising supply chain intelligence company DecryptAds uncovered more than 2,100 AI-generated recipe sites that are monetized with programmatic ads and feature fabricated author profiles.

Most brands and businesses are trying to figure out how to improve their metrics when it comes to AI – and also what those metrics even are.

Minerva wants to turn fragmented customer data into something marketers can use, with AI agents doing the work behind the scenes.

VideoAmp is competing in the measurement space by sharpening its focus on TV audience data, ad performance and, of course, AI. The company is also making strategic hires and promoting from within.

The ad industry has become a community of people who say things like “This is going to sound relatable” and follow it up with a sentence that may as well be Martian to 99% of America.

RELATED ARTICLECalifornia legislature passes a major local news funding bill: “If you hire more people, you get more money”Hanaa' TameezAugust 31, 2026At the end of August, the state of California passed a bill to give news organizations tax credits based on the number of journalists they employ. It’s the largest local news bill in the United States — expected to generate as much as $40 million for the state’s newsrooms each year — and on Wednesday, California Gov. Gavin Newsom signed it into law.

Assembly Bill 2222, known as the Community Newsroom Employment and Workforce Sustainability Act, gives newsrooms tax credits of $20,000 each for up to five journalists on staff, and $15,000 for every journalist after, as well as $7,500 credits for journalists working part-time and $15,000 new hire credits.

The nonprofit Rebuild Local News sponsored the bill. “If you hire more people, you get more money,” Matt Pearce, Rebuild Local News’s director of policy, told Nieman Lab in August. “If you lay people off, you get less money. If you don’t employ anyone, you don’t get anything.”

Newsom told reporters that he sees some downsides of the bill, including the fact that it will benefit hedge fund– and billionaire-owned newsrooms. (The guidelines about the types of newsrooms that qualify are here; the program is “designed to be broadly inclusive.”) From the L.A. Times:

While speaking with reporters on Wednesday, Newsom acknowledged some of the concerns that have been raised about those who will receive benefits from the bill’s funds, specifically hedge funds and billionaire owners and outlets that he accused of spreading propaganda.

“It does subsidize those that don’t need to be subsidized,” he said. “We have hedge funds in this space. We have billionaires in this space. We have people that are profiteering in this space by gutting the newsrooms and extracting value out of the space that also are the beneficiaries.”

Newsom said he chose not to veto the bill because he believes its benefits outweigh the liabilities. He added that he hopes the Legislature and next governor can work to narrow down who benefits most from the legislation.

“We should not be subsidizing hedge funds,” he said. “We should be focused on where the need is the greatest, in my humble opinion, and I do think when you have no cap, the limitlessness of this…to some of the most well-heeled organizations, where now they simply could pull from this bill the benefits that they didn’t even ask for or need, is self-evident.”

The law goes into effect January 1, 2027, and newsrooms should see credits beginning in 2028.

Want to know which of your YouTube videos are still working for you weeks or months after publishing? This free metric will help:

Install the no-cost version of VidIQ and add its Google Chrome plugin. Once installed, it activates a feature called VidIQ Vision, which overlays performance data directly on YouTube pages.

Look for the VPH (views per hour) number that appears next to your videos and any competitor's videos. This tells you how many views a video is currently earning every hour, regardless of when it was published.

Use VPH to identify your evergreen winners. A video posted months ago that still pulls 2 to 3 views per hour is a compounding asset. A video posted last week with 0 VPH has already stopped working.

Learn from competitors by visiting their channels with VidIQ Vision active. You can see which of their videos are still earning views, revealing what topics and formats have long-term staying power in your niche.

Pro Tip: Creators report that 50% or more of their monthly views come from content made weeks, months, or even years ago. VPH helps you see exactly which older videos are still driving that traffic so you can double down on what works.

Sean Cannell tracks VPH on his Think Media Podcast videos and shared specific examples: a video posted four months ago still earns 3 views per hour, a three-year-old video still earns 2 views per hour, and a six-month-old video still earns 2 views per hour. Those small numbers compound around the clock. YouTube is the only major platform where content continues generating views for years, and VPH is how you measure whether yours is doing that.

The NYT uses the prime real estate on its homepage to show off its free-to-air content. If it’s good enough for The NYT, it’s good enough for you.

The world’s most successful subscription publisher – The New York Times – regularly gives some of the most valuable real estate on its homepage to free articles, and, crucially, makes sure readers know they’re free.

It’s a smart strategy, particularly for paywalled publishers. Here’s why.

Not every article needs to drive an immediate subscription. Nor is it going to. Making selected articles free-to-air helps publishers maximise reach around important, highly competitive stories.

It also gives subscription publishers a better chance of competing in Search against non-paywalled competitors. If engagement metrics are Google’s most important ranking factor (they almost certainly are), then the enhanced bounce rate and suppressed time on page associated with paywalling makes reaching a new audience more challenging.

A having your cake and eating it too situation.

And the problem with being a subscription brand is that, over time, you become known for having a paywall. As the cesspit of the internet evolves and the value exchange continues to erode, people will have to get used to paying for news.

But that creates a problem: even when you make an article free, readers might assume it’s paywalled.

Users won’t automatically know that an article is free. You have to tell them. Label your content. It will improve engagement and subsequent reach.

Live blogs are a great example. Many subscription publishers make them free because they’re exceptionally competitive in Search and act as an entry point for new audiences.

But how often do those publishers explicitly label them as free? It’s an obvious, relatively inexpensive experiment.

So, don’t think of free content as lost revenue, think of it as an introduction to a cold, cool or slightly warm audience. A future opportunity.

It depends where you are in the ecosystem and subscription model maturity matrix. Which I just made up, but it sounds brilliant.

If you’re a free-to-air brand dipping their toes in the premium market, you don’t need to worry about this yet. Although having the ‘free to access’ block on your homepage is still sensible.

If you’re a legacy premium publisher, you should consider

There are very few brands that get away with hard paywalls. You’re unlikely to be in that bucket, so really think about how free content can be part of a deliberate audience acquisition strategy.

And if you’re already making content free, make sure people know about it.

#139. AI Startup Minerva Built An Agentic CDP, But Don’t Call It That

Jackson Engles, CEO of Minerva, is a realist. He knows that the data his AI startup is built on probably won’t be a competitive edge for more than a couple of years.

“Yes, sure, we have data that can help create better outcomes,” Engles told AdExchanger. “But is it a long-term, durable moat? Probably not.”

It’s an unusual thing to hear from the co-founder of a startup that recently raised $20 million to build AI agents for marketers powered by an identity graph of 270 million consumers.

So, if data isn’t the advantage, what is?

The answer, according to Engles, is to stay narrow. A specialized product built for marketing that starts with a curated set of data is more useful for brands than a general-purpose AI tool.

“What we’re trying to do, on some level, is to constrain the problem space,” he said. “Marketers shouldn’t just be using Claude and bringing in random data; they should be starting from a really opinionated view of the data that’s relevant to them.”

None of Minerva’s founders – Engles, Daniel Saedi and Mathew Joseph – have a formal marketing background. They met at Berkeley and started their careers in finance: Engles in banking at Lazard, Saedi in asset management at Bridgewater and Joseph as a quantitative researcher and data scientist at Citadel.

At Bridgewater and Citadel, Saedi and Joseph worked with web browsing and consumer spending data – known as “alternative data” in finance but standard issue in ad tech – to inform investment decisions.

Joseph helped build Citadel’s alt-data infrastructure, standardizing messy data sets and pulling out signals that the firm could trade on. They saw how valuable consumer data could be and how hard it is to make sense of it.

The three eventually left finance to start a company that would address that challenge. Getting into marketing wasn’t the original plan, Engles said, but it didn’t take long for it to become “the natural path.”

Minerva spent the first year and a half on the data itself, figuring out when people are in the market to buy and how life events impact their spending behavior. Then came the question of how brands could use these connections to drive commercial outcomes. The product grew out of that.

“The goal,” Engles said, “is to help [brands] get more out of their first-party data, better understand their customers and scale their marketing function with AI.”

Cool, cool. But plenty of startups make that pitch. Minerva says its approach is different, because it doesn’t solely rely on a brand’s own data.

The trouble is that first-party data only goes so far. Brands can’t see what customers do beyond their own channels, and even that data is hard to connect, because it sits in different systems.

Minerva says it addresses both problems. A brand plugs its CRM, data warehouse and other sources into Minerva, where an agent it built using OpenAI called the “agentic data engineer” maps it all out.

Then Minerva’s agents unify the data into a single view of each customer and supplement it with information from what Engles refers to as its “B2B2C identity graph,” which includes work email, personal email, phone number, address and online identifiers.

Ramp, a fin tech company and one of Minerva’s clients, used that link between work and personal identities to extend a direct mail campaign beyond work addresses, which boosted its marketing-qualified lead rate by around 80% in the first three months.

And for Wander, a luxury short-term rental company, Minerva built profiles of the brand’s best customers, used them to train its models and then sent lookalikes to Meta. ROAS was 3.4 times higher than with Meta’s broad targeting, according to Engles.

Minerva is also working on a second agent, an “agentic data scientist,” that would build predictive models from plain-language requests, like “Which customers are most likely to churn?” or “Who should I target with this offer?”

Like most AI marketing vendors, Minerva says its goal is to take the busywork off a marketer’s plate.

“Marketers should be spending way more time on the very human parts of their job,” Engles said. “They should be focused on telling the story of their brand, not the operational and optimization work that AI will get really good at over time.”

Behind that pitch is a bet on where marketing software is headed, which is a world in which marketers talk to agents rather than log into dashboards. Consider it the post-CDP era.

Customer data platforms promised a single view of the customer, but left many marketers with just another system to manage. Minerva reimagined the idea as an “agentic CDP,” a middle layer that uses agents to join a brand’s data with Minerva’s so they can onboard quickly.

But Minerva doesn’t market the CDP aspect at all, Engles said, because marketers care about the end, not the means.

“Customers want the outcome of a CDP; they want their data to be more queryable by less technical users,” he said. “They want a single end-to-end marketing platform with its own data, not just a single capability.”

#140. Two 23-year-olds used AI to create a daily audio briefing. It’s now the top news app in Argentina.

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

“We want society to trust [media] again, and to give them a platform built around current consumption formats that reduces friction between society and verified information.”

As an engineering student, Valentín Virasoro worked part-time at a car dealership in Cordoba, Argentina. His boss at the dealership had a habit: Every day, he’d send an audio update covering the major stories in the automotive industry.

Virasoro left the job in February to pursue a career in tech. But the idea of informative audio briefs stuck with him. Sometimes, he said, he’d get another employee to forward him his ex-boss’ voice notes. By August, Virasoro and his friend and co-founder Iván Schahovskoy Hoferek created Lisa AI, an app that uses artificial intelligence to generate personalized audio news updates.

Within days of its August launch, Lisa became one of the most-downloaded news apps in the country. As of September 30, it is the No. 1 app in the News and Magazines & Newspapers categories in the Apple App Store in Argentina. It’s also one of the top 100 most downloaded apps in the country, Virasoro said. About 70% of users who have downloaded the app actively interact with it. Audio briefs have a 90% completion rate, with about 80% of users returning to the app the next day. Virasoro declined to share the total number of downloads. Journalists have told Virasoro and Schahovskoy that they’ve been using the app to keep up with news on their beats, they said.

Virasoro and Schahovskoy are both 23. Lisa — whose name is inspired by the first Apple computer — is a response to the changing news consumption habits of young people around the world, Virasoro said.

“Younger generations like [ours] are so used to consuming personalized content through an algorithm that knows my interests perfectly and is constantly recommending content,” Virasoro said. “What Iván and I saw was: There is a journalist reporting on a topic that I am super interested in, but I don’t have a tool that directly shows me the content I care about in the formats we consume, like podcasts, threads, a language model like ChatGPT or Gemini, or a scrollable feed.”

Here’s how it works: Users download the app and indicate what topics they’re interested in, and their level of interest in each topic. Lisa then continuously scans dozens of Argentinian news outlets for recent stories about those topics. The result is a 10-minute “newscast” that summarizes articles about the user’s favorite topics and attributes the facts to the corresponding news outlets or journalists. Lisa only cites free news sites and cannot access paywalled content. It can produce up to two audio briefs per day, and each one includes a chat feature that provides links to the stories cited, so users can read the original journalism themselves. Lisa’s voice is calm, and sounds AI-generated. The voice has an authentic Argentinian accent, which Virasoro and Schahovskoy developed using voice-cloning technology.

The app is free to use. There is no subscription fee or advertising on the platform. It’s available worldwide in app stores, but only uses Argentinian news sources. Lisa is run by a volunteer team of five engineers and developers, and two advisors. Virasoro said they received some funding from angel investors, which he and Schahovskoy put toward the product development. They do not take a salary.

Intellectual property law in Argentina allows for news content to be used and redistributed within reason as long as the original sources are clearly cited, but doesn’t give the public free rein to republish news articles word for word. Excerpts of up to 1,000 words may be used for educational, informational, or scientific purposes, the law says. Similar to copyright law in other countries, Argentina’s law gives the Lisa team the ability to summarize and reference news outlets’ reporting, Schahovskoy said, and it’s why Lisa generates summaries with attributions rather than republishing articles from news outlets.

According to the Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism, 46% of Argentine adults reported that they avoided news in 2026. Trust in news fell to 26% in 2026, down 6% from the year before. While traditional media in Argentina struggles to stay afloat amid a decline in advertising revenue, nearly one in ten people reported getting news from a chatbot. Young Argentinians are increasingly turning to creators, independent journalists, and YouTube for their news. Worldwide, about half (52%) of young adults reported that they get their news from chatbots, video platforms, and social media. Podcasts continue to be popular, with 11% of adults reporting that they have used the medium to get news.

Virasoro and Schahovskoy saw the shift in news consumers’ attention to new platforms as “a societal problem” due to the lack of editorial curation of social platforms, often surfacing fake news. Even with Lisa’s early success, Virasoro and Schahovskoy don’t have plans to monetize the app anytime soon. They said they want to keep iterating for now, but are open to helping news outlets monetize for themselves within the app down the line. So far, three news outlets have reached out asking for their websites to be included in Lisa’s reading list. They don’t see the app as a competitor to news outlets, but rather a new way to help the news industry find new audiences.

“Traditional media is losing power — even though they do super professional and deeply dedicated work to ensure the information they make available to the public is fact-checked and verified,” Schahovskoy said. “We value it immensely, and we want society to trust [media] again, and to give them a platform built around current consumption formats that reduces friction between society and verified information.”

#141. Meta Wants to Run More of Your Marketing — But Should They?

​Want to know which parts of your Facebook and Instagram ad campaigns Meta AI can handle better than you can? Wondering how to use Meta's newest algorithm changes and AI tools to lower your ad costs and improve lead quality?

​In this article, you'll discover how Meta's latest updates to ad placements, creative AI, the pixel, and business agents are reshaping what marketers need to control and what they should hand over to the algorithm.

Meta is rolling out changes that remove advertisers' ability to exclude individual placements at the ad set level. This includes the ability to target only mobile users, desktop users, iPhone users, or Android users. The change has started appearing in Ads Manager for some accounts and is expected to become universal.

​This isn't a surprise for experienced advertisers. Meta has been nudging people toward Advantage+ Placements for years, displaying pop-up warnings whenever someone tried to deselect placements manually. Advantage+ Placements lets Meta's algorithm decide which ads appear on which placements and when, using its own data to optimize delivery.

​The typical spend distribution under Advantage+ tells the story: around 60% of ad spend (sometimes higher) goes to Instagram, a large share goes to Facebook, and a very small percentage goes to the Audience Network, which places ads on third-party websites. Threads, WhatsApp, and Messenger also receive ads automatically when the ad format is compatible.

​Tara Zirker has tested this extensively across client accounts. Choosing Advantage+ Placements consistently produces better results and higher-quality leads than manual selection. Removing placements manually, even the ones that seem like wasted spend, tends to make ads more expensive and reduce overall lead and sales quality. Meta's detection systems have improved to the point where the algorithm simply won't place an ad in a spot where it won't render properly, whether the font is too small or the format wouldn't translate.

Account-level controls remain available even as ad-set-level options disappear. At the account level, advertisers can still tell Meta to exclude Audience Network or other placements entirely.

​The businesses most likely to retain granular control are those in Meta's categorized industries. Enterprise healthcare accounts, financial services, and credit-related businesses often have compliance requirements dictating where ads can and cannot appear. Meta is keeping placement options open for these categorized accounts. Health and wellness is one example of a category that will continue to have access to more placement controls.

​For everyone else in the general, uncategorized bucket, the recommendation is straightforward: leave Advantage+ Placements on and let Meta's algorithm handle distribution.

Everything Meta is doing right now traces back to a larger trajectory. The company started with Advantage+, which was the entry point for AI-managed ad decisions. The destination is an algorithm called GEM, a generative model where advertisers input an image and a budget, and the AI generates all creative, iterates on its own, and optimizes delivery without human intervention.

​The current era sits between those two points. Meta's newest algorithm, Andromeda, rolled out globally in October and is now active in every ad account. Andromeda works like an organic algorithm layered into the paid system. It favors high-quality content, directs the highest-quality traffic to accounts running the highest-quality creative, and rewards ads that generate positive engagement.

​This means pay-to-play now has tiers and gates. Spending money alone no longer guarantees access to the best audience segments. The quality of creative determines what tier of traffic an account can reach and what costs it pays.

​The practical takeaway is straightforward: the more creative diversity an advertiser provides to the algorithm, the more effective the advertising becomes. Meta is demanding creative diversity across accounts because it needs massive amounts of data to build toward GEM. Advertisers who provide varied creative formats, angles, and styles give the algorithm more to work with, which in turn unlocks better performance at lower costs.

The AI creative features inside Ads Manager are advancing faster than most advertisers realize.

Join thousands of small-business marketers at Social Media Marketing World — three days of AI, social media, and marketing strategy taught by world-class experts. April 1–3, 2027 in Anaheim.

Every session is pitch-free and built around tactics you can use yourself, no big team required. Your All-Access ticket includes an extra day of workshops, full access to AI Business World, and recordings of everything.

​A beta feature observed on a client account demonstrated what's coming: Meta's AI generated two complete video ads with AI avatars using only static images that were already on the account. No script was provided. The AI pulled from the account's data to address the client's pain points, walk through benefits, handle objection overcoming, and present the intro offer. The avatars also performed a virtual walkthrough of the physical facility, constructed entirely from the uploaded images. The output was visually convincing with no detectable glitches.

​Advertisers do need to review and approve AI-generated creative before it runs. The approval interfaces vary across accounts as Meta tests different approaches, but the review step exists.

​Tara recommends turning on all AI creative options. The quality has reached a point where these tools consistently produce strong results, and the Andromeda algorithm rewards accounts that use them.

Meta's pixel has undergone a quiet transformation. The code hasn't changed, but the pixel is now AI-enhanced, making it, as Tara puts it, “ten times smarter.”

​Previously, e-commerce advertisers had to manually pass rich product data to the pixel, including detailed product descriptions and SEO-level descriptors, to help Meta match products with the right audiences. The AI-enhanced pixel reads that information directly from the website. It scans product offerings, website content, and SEO data, then delivers that data back to Meta in a usable format for audience matching.

​The action item for advertisers is straightforward: clean up pixel errors. Most accounts have configuration issues, whether it's missing access levels, broken event tracking, or incomplete setup. The cleaner the pixel installation, the more the AI features can do with the data it collects. Every time an advertiser logs in, Ads Manager surfaces these errors. Fixing them is now more consequential than ever.

Product catalogs are becoming a core input across all sales campaigns, not just catalog-specific ad formats. Meta's AI can now automatically generate and optimize shopping ad formats in real time, personalizing them for each consumer based on the data Meta holds about their preferences and behavior.

​When someone clicks on a product, Meta AI surfaces potential questions the consumer might have. For a lotion, it might prompt “Is it good for sensitive skin?” or “What are the reviews saying?” and provide answers within Meta rather than sending the user to an external website. This keeps the shopping experience on-platform and reduces friction.

​Advertisers with large catalogs also have new control over which products get featured. A department store running a shoe sale can tell Meta to focus only on shoes rather than displaying the entire catalog. These catalog controls give advertisers greater precision, while the AI handles delivery optimization.

The AI Business Society filters the noise for you, with expert-led training you can put to work the same day — plus a community of marketers sharing what's actually working.

​Deeper Shopify integration is also on the way, which should further streamline the e-commerce experience within Meta's ecosystem.

Meta has also changed how personalization works on the consumer side. Previously, users could opt in to personalization separately for their organic feed and their ad feed. Now the choice is streamlined: personalization is either on for both organic and ads, or off entirely. Opting out means the algorithm delivers random content.

​This is a strategic move for advertisers. Most consumers who initially opted out of ad personalization eventually realized they were still getting irrelevant ads. By bundling the choice, Meta is likely to increase the percentage of users who accept personalized ads, which improves targeting quality for every advertiser on the platform.

​Getting started is simple. Logging in with existing Facebook or Instagram credentials grants access. From there, asking Meta AI to connect to a Business Manager account is a one-click enable. The tool then has access to account data and can provide analysis and recommendations.

For an advertiser who is a couple of weeks into a campaign and past the learning phase, the starting prompts are conversational. Asking “What's working, what's not working, and what can I do better?” returns specific recommendations based on actual account data, including spend figures, impression counts, and performance breakdowns.

​For organic content analysis, asking Meta AI to evaluate Instagram Reels from the past 30 days returns a ranked list of top performers, along with an analysis of why each one worked. The tool can also be set to deliver recurring reports, such as a weekly Monday briefing covering key advertising and organic metrics.

​Meta AI has a mode selector similar to other AI platforms. Switching from the default “instant” mode to “thinking” mode allocates more processing power and produces deeper analysis.

The differentiator is Meta-specific data. Connecting an ad account to Claude or ChatGPT via an MCP connector is possible and useful, but Meta AI pulls proprietary platform data that isn't available through those external connections.

​Tara tested this by uploading a competitor analysis folder to Meta AI for a large client account. The tool identified the competitor's longest-running ad, analyzed its messaging, and offered to create five differentiated ad angles. That kind of competitive insight, grounded in Meta's own ad library data, gives the tool a unique perspective.

​The caveat applies here as it does with any AI platform: recommendations must be filtered through context. Some suggestions may have already been tested, and compliance requirements in sensitive industries may rule out certain approaches. If a recommendation hasn't been tried and doesn't conflict with known constraints, testing it is worthwhile. Tara has been surprised multiple times by results from ideas that initially seemed either too basic or too complex.

Meta is launching Meta Business Agent, an AI-powered assistant that operates across WhatsApp, Messenger, and Instagram DMs. The agent can answer customer questions about a business, make product recommendations from the catalog, book appointments, qualify incoming leads, and close sales on the e-commerce side. Businesses retain control over when a human team member steps in.

​The operational capabilities extend beyond customer-facing interactions. The agent can summarize customer conversations, provide insights on messaging patterns, and deliver daily briefings on communication activity.

​Tara's team has started experimenting with these agents specifically on lead gen ads, which are the on-platform ads where users don't have to leave Meta to submit their contact details. The agents are qualifying leads and helping people select the correct product. Early results are promising, though still limited in data.

The core advantage is speed. Many businesses struggle to respond to DMs in a timely manner, and staffing someone to answer them in a way that actually converts is expensive and inconsistent. AI agents handle both problems by providing instant, 24/7 responses that draw on the business's account data, previous chat conversations, and established tone.

​Businesses that sell anything with complexity benefit most. When potential customers have multiple questions before purchasing, whether about product details, logistics, pricing, or suitability, an AI agent that can answer immediately and accurately reduces friction at the most critical point in the buying process. It qualifies serious buyers faster and disqualifies tire-kickers, which is exactly what a sales process should do.

​Businesses that don't implement AI agents, whether through Meta or another provider, face a growing disadvantage. Consumer expectations are shifting toward instant answers. The companies that meet that expectation will convert at higher rates; those that don't will lose prospects to competitors who do.

​For businesses that want to enhance their sales pages specifically, tools like VideoAsk allow embedding a small corner video from a founder or team member that routes to different pre-recorded video answers based on the visitor's question. Combined with AI chat agents, this creates a layered support experience that covers both visual and text-based communication.

Tara Zirker is the founder of Successful Ads Club and the Successful Ads Accelerator, a done-with-you program that helps marketers launch and scale their ads rapidly. She’s also the co-founder of The Studio Grow Agency. Follow her on Instagram.
