Why would a site that ranked fine suddenly fail Google’s quality bar after moving domains? Here’s what I found and what I can’t yet prove.

There have been a number of reports recently of sites struggling to be properly indexed following a site migration.

I have consulted with a few sites on this issue and have developed a theory.

Please know that this theory is not something I can prove at this point. I am writing this blog post to generate discussion.

I believe that not only does a site migration trigger a new review of site quality from Google, but also that Google’s standards for site quality have become much stricter.

Let me share a case I recently investigated.

I was hired to do a site quality review for a site that blogs on a hobby topic. The site had previously performed well and was starting to see a slow decline over the last year or so. Just before I started my review, the site owner reached out to tell me that they had just started migrating to a new domain.

From what I can see, they did everything correctly. They submitted the change of address in Google Search Console, carefully mapped redirects, updated internal links, ensured Google could crawl the new site, and generated a sitemap for the new domain.

In the Page Indexing Report, 98% of their URLs were reported as not indexed.

Even worse, inspecting any page, including those 33 pages that Google said were indexed showed the same thing. The page was indeed not indexed. Google had classified it as “crawled – currently not indexed.”

There wasn’t a problem with Google finding the new page. Rather, they had crawled it and chosen not to index it.

We ran a live test in GSC on several of these pages. In each case the report told us the page was available to be indexing, but only if certain conditions were met.

That link points to this page in which Google tells us the page might not get indexed if it is subject to a manual action or a duplicate of another page. Neither of these was the case. We wondered if the site migration caused duplication issues. But Google clearly recognized the canonical as this new site, and the old page was properly redirecting to it.

However, Google lists a third possible reason for not indexing a valid page: The page quality must be high enough to warrant indexing.

In my review for this site, I noted that while the site was well written and thorough, there was very little original value on any page compared to what already exists on other sites on the web.

They were all commodity content – content that is essentially the same across other sites on the internet.

Google recently updated its documentation on creating helpful content to include new information on the “main content” of your webpage. The main content is the part of the page that helps fulfil the searcher’s need. In it, they emphasized the importance of:

That point on originality is what I think matters most here. Google describes it as “The extent to which the content offers unique, original information or perspectives that aren’t already available on other websites.”

This is the obvious question! Why was the quality acceptable on the old domain and suddenly deemed low quality after the migration?

I think that if Google applied these quality standards across the board to every site on the internet, the vast majority of websites would suffer catastrophic loss. Who knows, it is possible we will see this with a future core update.

My theory is that when the site I reviewed migrated to a new domain, this triggered a more strict quality assessment. Given that none of the pages offered information that truly was original and offered more than what is already available on other websites, Google’s systems decided not to index it.

If you cannot get indexed following a site migration, first you should thoroughly review for technical reasons. Ensure you have properly redirected old pages to new. Make sure you record the change of address in Google Search Console. Use the Live Test in GSC to verify that Google can see the content on these pages. It is a good idea to connect with an SEO who can thoroughly investigate technical issues.

It’s also worth knowing that site migrations can take time for Google to process. It is possible you just need to wait longer. In the case I mentioned above, however, it has been four months now, and only the homepage is indexed. There is definitely something wrong.

If it is indeed an issue with site quality, then I would suggest producing a small handful of truly original and insightful articles. For many sites, this requires a whole new business direction. It’s no longer good enough to write about things the world already knows. You need to find things you can create that bring something new to the internet that people will find of value.

What I don’t know, however, is whether Google will consider the value of these individual pages or whether your overall site quality score, diminished because of unoriginal content, will hinder indexing of these pages as well.

Another option to consider is to start completely over on a new domain with brand new content. I realize this is not the answer you are looking for. However, if my theory is right, then there is no technical SEO fix for many of these sites that are struggling to get their new domain indexed.

I’d go through each of the previously top-performing pages on your site and use this prompt in your LLM of choice:

#143. MMM Is Getting Smarter. It Still Can’t Do The Whole Job Alone

Every media dollar eventually has to answer the same uncomfortable question: Did it create new revenue or simply take credit for revenue that was coming anyway?

A channel with exceptional reported ROI may simply be capturing existing demand. Another may appear less efficient while creating customers who otherwise would never have entered the market. That distinction matters more than which platform receives credit for the final conversion.

A new generation of off-the-shelf automated Marketing Mix Modeling (MMM)* platforms has made it faster and easier to answer that question.

But that accessibility introduces a new risk: mistaking a polished answer for a definitive one.

In a head-to-head comparison of several MMM approaches, we found that the same business data could produce meaningfully different conclusions. Data preparation and model specifications changed the estimated contribution of individual channels. When signals conflicted, a model could identify a pattern without explaining why it existed.

A model can also evaluate only the variables it is given. If growth drivers such as pricing, competitor dynamics, distribution, seasonality, customer experience or organic demand sit outside the data set, it may overattribute performance to the media variables it can see.

MMM’s next challenge, therefore, is developing a more rigorous way to challenge, validate and apply its conclusions.

The traditional criticism of MMM was its speed and rigidity. Custom models could take months to build and be revisited only once a year at most.

Today’s platforms can ingest data more efficiently, refresh models regularly and incorporate industry benchmarks. Their scenario-planning and visualization capabilities have also made MMM more useful in executive budget conversations. A diminishing-returns scenario is far more actionable to a CMO than a table of statistical coefficients.

Some platforms are also combining methodologies. Geo holdouts and conversion-lift experiments can calibrate or challenge modeled estimates rather than living in separate reports.

That combination moves marketers beyond relationships observed in historical data toward conclusions tested against something closer to causation. But a holdout is only as credible as its design, execution and interpretation.

An MMM can fit historical data well and still lead to the wrong business decision. Statistical fit indicates how well a model explains the past. It does not establish that the model has correctly identified causation or that reallocating future investment based on its findings will generate growth.

This becomes difficult when variables move together. Television may run alongside paid search, social alongside promotions and strong fourth-quarter sales alongside holiday demand. Earned attention may also increase branded demand across several channels simultaneously.

The model must separate these effects using incomplete data and limited real-world variation. Its assumptions matter: How quickly does an advertising effect decay? How long does a channel take to produce an outcome? How much should benchmarks influence the estimate? What belongs in the business baseline rather than marketing’s incremental contribution?

These settings can materially change which channels appear effective and where the model recommends investing the next dollar.

In one off-the-shelf model we evaluated, the platform estimated that 10 paid-media channels drove approximately 75% of new-customer volume. That immediately raised questions because it was significantly higher than anything we had observed in the business. To date, I have seen models identify 1%-18% incrementality from paid media.

We then gave the same underlying data to a data scientist for an independent custom build. That model estimated the combined incremental contribution of those channels at less than 1%.

The point is not that the custom model was automatically correct. A result below 1% deserves as much scrutiny as a result of 75%. But a gap of that magnitude makes either conclusion impossible to treat as decision-ready without further investigation.

That investigation revealed that the client’s media variables had limited ability to explain changes in the outcome that the models were attempting to predict.

When client data provides a weak or ambiguous signal, a Bayesian MMM may remain heavily influenced by its prior assumptions from other brands or benchmarks. These priors can stabilize a model when data is sparse, but they can also shape the answer more heavily than marketers realize.

Marketers need to understand when a conclusion is driven primarily by their own business data. Otherwise, a company could make major allocation decisions based on an industrywide expectation that does not reflect its individual business.

Data-hygiene issues and small specification changes could also materially alter which channels appeared to work. When model runs disagreed, the software could produce both answers without explaining which was more credible.

The risk is that a platform can return a statistically plausible allocation of contribution even when the evidence separating one channel’s impact from another is weak.

That risk grows when an analysis is limited mainly to paid media. If owned, earned, operational and market-level drivers are absent, marketers may debate how to divide contribution among the variables included in the model while overlooking the variables that actually explain the business.

This is where experienced practitioners remain essential: testing specifications, diagnosing conflicts, incorporating business knowledge and challenging recommendations.

Off-the-shelf MMM platforms can be effective, and not every company needs a fully custom model. The strongest approach often combines the speed and structure of a platform with the flexibility to adapt the model to the business. That takes people who understand how the business works and can question the model’s assumptions, inputs and results.

Platforms can accelerate data ingestion, model development and scenario planning. Custom analysis can test alternative specifications and investigate implausible results. Business teams can add context about pricing, distribution and operational changes. Controlled experiments can then test whether modeled relationships produce genuinely incremental behavior.

The objective is not to select the model that produces the most favorable answer—or even the strongest statistical fit. It is to determine which conclusions remain credible when the data, assumptions, business reality and resulting recommendations are all challenged.

MMM is becoming faster, more accessible and more sophisticated. That is real progress. But the smartest model is still not a substitute for knowing when its answer should not be trusted.

*We have moved away from Media Mix Modeling, as most models include all marketing variables (promotions, pricing, etc).

#144. Federal appeals court upholds Thomson Reuters’ landmark AI copyright win

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

On Tuesday, a U.S. federal appeals court ruled in favor of Thomson Reuters, upholding the company’s landmark win in a copyright infringement case against the now-defunct legal AI startup Ross Intelligence. The ruling marks the first federal appeals case to reject a fair use argument for using publisher content, without permission or compensation, to train a commercial AI product.

“The undisputed evidence reflects that Thomson Reuters’s materials possess a creative spark, and ROSS aspired to be a direct competitor by using them for a highly similar purpose,” wrote Judge Tamika Montgomery-Reeves, who sits on the 3rd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in Philadelphia, in her decision.

Notably, Montgomery-Reeves points out that the case does not concern a large-language model (LLM) or other generative AI tool. Ross’s competing AI search engine didn’t generate original text, but instead retrieved existing passages from judicial opinions. She argues that this may limit its impact on other AI copyright litigation.

RELATED ARTICLETrump administration says a New York Times win in OpenAI lawsuit would “threaten national security” and hurt small newsroomsAndrew DeckSeptember 2, 2026“Under ROSS’s framing, this case appears to concern the future of AI legal technology. But appearances can be deceiving,” she writes. “In truth, this is no more than an ordinary copyright case.”

Thomson Reuters filed its lawsuit back in 2020, long before the release of ChatGPT and other generative AI chatbots as we know them. The first known AI copyright lawsuit in the U.S., the case echoes many more recent lawsuits between news publishers and AI companies like OpenAI and Anthropic. Thomson Reuters argued that Ross had copied thousands of “headnotes,” short summaries of the legal issues in a given case, that were published on its legal research platform Westlaw. These headnotes were then used to train Ross’s own competing AI-powered legal search engine.

In a February 2025 ruling, judge Stephanos Bibas sided with Thomson Reuters in the case. He rejected the argument that using copyrighted work to train the commercial AI model was legally permissible, as Ross had argued in court. One of the main factors in a fair use case is whether the infringing work impacts the market value of the original.

“Even taking all facts in favor of Ross, it meant to compete with Westlaw by developing a market substitute,” wrote Bibas in his original ruling. “And it does not matter whether Thomson Reuters has used the data to train its own legal search tools; the effect on a potential market for AI training data is enough.”

Legal experts have been keeping a close eye on Ross’s appeal with the 3rd U.S Circuit Court of Appeal. As the first AI copyright case to reach a federal appeals court, there was potential for it to set far-reaching legal precedent on fair use — precedent that could be taken advantage of by news publishers arguing in similar AI copyright cases.

RELATED ARTICLEWhat it takes to sue OpenAI as a journalism nonprofitAndrew DeckJune 25, 2025Ultimately, Montgomery-Reeves’ ruling emphasizes that an AI tool that reproduces a copyrighted work’s text in order to compete directly with that work in the market, will likely not hold up to a fair use test. But she leaves room for generative AI tools to be considered more transformative than Ross’s AI search engine.

In the lawsuit Bartz vs. Anthropic, filed by members of the Authors Guild, a judge ruled that Anthropic’s use of published books to train its Claude LLMs was, in fact, fair use. It was only Anthropic’s decision to pirate books and store copies of them that lost them in that case. That ruling in June 2025 resulted in the largest settlement in U.S. copyright law history, granting a $1.5 billion payout to authors and publishers.

“Unlike the AI models in Bartz…ROSS’s AI platform cannot generate original expression, and the evidence here supports the opposite conclusion about transformativeness,” wrote Montgomery-Reeves, implying that her ruling does not contradict the ruling in that case.

In other words, if Ross had built a product that could output summaries of Westlaw’s headnotes with its own “original expression,” this fair use ruling could have looked very different.

#145. Creating AI Image Libraries, Showing Up in AI Results, and Industry News

Friday is almost here! Before you unplug, here's one last round of insights and updates. Whether you read them now or save them for later, you won't want to miss these.

🗞️ Industry news from Gemini, Meta, and more

If you've ever sat down to create an AI video or social post for a product and realized you only have one decent photo to work with, you're not stuck. That single image can become the seed for an entire shot library — no reshoot required.

Feed your image into an AI image tool with the right approach, and it becomes a reference point the model can build new, consistent shots from. Close-ups, alternate angles, different settings, all visually tied back to that original photo.

The bigger strategic gain is what happens to the images that don't make the final cut.

In a normal creative process, rejected drafts just get deleted. But when everything you generate traces back to the same source image, those “extras” aren't waste — they share the same lighting, color palette, and visual style as the shots you did use. A close-up you skip today might be exactly the B-roll you need for next month's Instagram story.

Treated this way, one product photo stops being a single-use asset. It becomes a growing library that delivers value long after the original project wraps.

Webinar: The Link Building Graveyard: What to Bury & What Still Wins

Approved forums and social platforms can send content and interaction signals through a separate pipeline. Here's who can apply and how it compares to crawling.

For most websites, crawling is still how you get into Google Search. Googlebot finds a URL and retrieves the page; then, independently, Google’s systems determine if they want to add this page to their index.

On Oct. 8, Google added Search Central documentation describing how approved forums and social platforms can submit user-generated content directly to Google.

The UGC Fresh Data Program allows approved platforms to submit content and interaction signals through a “dedicated data ingestion pipeline” that accepts data submission from those platforms. Google states that the pipeline is separate from both traditional crawlers and the Indexing API. According to Google, participation in the UGC Fresh Data Program does not ensure your content will be included in Google Search.

Google has partnered with individual social platforms before, including Twitter in 2009 and Reddit in 2024. This time the criteria are posted and there’s an application form, so you can check most of Google’s requirements against a platform’s own pages before applying. The form asks how many monthly active users the platform has and when it launched.

The Search Central documentation changelog links to the page under the entry for Oct. 8: “Added documentation on the UGC Fresh Data Program.” Google wrote that the page is meant to explain the program’s purpose and help applicants “understand the eligibility criteria and how to participate.”

The program page opens with this description:

The UGC Fresh Data Program is an initiative designed to help platforms display fresh, high quality, and authentic user-generated content (UGC) across various features on Search.

Google says sending content through the pipeline “helps ensure that fresh content is processed and quickly updated in Search.” The page gives no time frame for “quickly.” It also says the program “doesn’t guarantee that content will appear in Search.”

The page limits the program to “trending UGC content.” It describes the pipeline as “independent of the Google Indexing API and traditional organic crawling for general web content.”

Oct. 8 is when the page went up. Neither the page nor the changelog entry says when the pipeline started operating.

Google lists six criteria, using the labels below.

Submitting an application “doesn’t guarantee participation,” according to the page, and Google will share developer documents “once accepted into the program.”

The form has seven required fields: company name, service domain, 10 sample URLs with UGC, monthly active users, launch date, a Search Console owner’s email and a contact email. It calls a submission “merely an expression of interest” and says Google “has no obligation to incorporate your content in our features.”

The form goes further than the page on where content could show up, saying submitted content “is eligible to serve on Google Search and other surfaces, especially for time-sensitive or fresh content.” It adds, “we never guarantee serving as that is determined entirely by ranking algorithms.”

Any site can ask Google to crawl its pages, according to Google’s recrawl documentation. Owners and full users of a Search Console property can request crawls of individual URLs in the URL Inspection tool, within a quota, and sitemaps cover larger sets of URLs. Google says crawling “can take anywhere from a few days to a few weeks,” and that a request “does not guarantee that inclusion in search results will happen instantly or even at all.”

The Indexing API is narrower. It covers pages with JobPosting, or BroadcastEvent embedded in a VideoObject, and lets their owners tell Google when a page is added, updated or removed. This “allows Google to schedule pages for a fresh crawl.” There is a “default 200 quota” available for API onboarding and submission testing; however, the API “requires additional approval for usage and resource provisioning.” In a September post I noted several job boards had gone months without a reply to their approval requests.

Recrawls, sitemaps, the Indexing API provide the URL for crawling. Platforms submit what Google calls “content and interaction signals” through the UGC program, but this does not replace public URLs. The criteria still require that the content be accessible via Googlebot.

The Indexing API has a default quota for onboarding and testing, with additional approval required for further usage. The UGC program requires Google to approve applicants. Neither guarantees that submitted content will appear in Search. Of the three options being compared here, recrawl requests and sitemaps do not include a request for approval. The program’s “within minutes” wording covers sending, not indexing.

On Dec. 7, 2009, Google launched real-time search results that showed “live updates from people on popular sites like Twitter and FriendFeed.” The post named Facebook, MySpace, FriendFeed, Jaiku and Identi.ca as new partners, along with Twitter, which Google said it had announced “a few weeks ago.”

In July 2011, Google said “that agreement expired on July 2,” as Datamation reported at the time. In May 2015, Google said it was bringing Tweets to Search on mobile, and it added desktop that August.

In February 2024, Google stated that it “now has access” to Reddit’s Data API. According to Google, this Data API delivers “real-time, structured, unique content.” Google noted that accessing the Data API would provide “enhanced signals that will help us better understand Reddit content and display, train on, and otherwise use it.” Furthermore, Google states that this partnership does not affect its use of publicly accessible (crawl-able) content from the Internet for indexing, training or displaying such content in Google products.

Those partnerships mentioned above are the ones Google announced with named entities. However, those earlier posts did not provide sufficient technical information so as to allow comparison with the new pipeline. While the 2024 description notes “access to Reddit’s Data API,” the Oct. 8 posting describes approved platforms providing data through a Google ingestion pipeline. There was no reference to the Reddit partnership in the program page or the form.

As noted previously, one of the uses listed in the 2024 post is training. However, neither the program posting nor the posted application form referenced “training.”

There is a clear distinction between what has been published about the new program and the earlier partnerships. Google has made available to the general public both the eligibility criteria for participation in the new program and an online application. As previously discussed, Google provided identification of individual social platform partners through prior announcements.

Google’s support for the markup the program names predates it by almost three years. In November 2023, Google added discussion forum and profile page structured data, which I covered at the time. Google said the markup works with features “designed to show first-person perspectives from social media platforms, forums, and other communities,” and that using it “does not guarantee appearance.”

In June 2024, the changelog confirmed that SocialMediaPosting markup is also supported, “to more accurately reflect how the data ingestion for these features work.” In March 2026, Google added forum and Q&A properties “for providing more clarity on comment thread structure to Google ingestion systems.” The update included labels for AI-generated and bot content, which I covered in March.

Google’s current discussion forum markup page lists five interaction types it supports in interactionStatistic: likes or upvotes, dislikes or downvotes, views, comments, and reshares. The program page names the same markup, with interactionStatistic, as its example of what applicants should have on their pages.

Neither the forum documentation nor the program page says how Google uses those counts in ranking.

Google documents point to a separate intake for trending posts from forums and social platforms, apart from the crawling it uses for general web content. Approved platforms send the posts and their interaction signals themselves, while recrawl requests, sitemaps and the Indexing API all hand Google a URL to crawl.

Any platform that includes only feed items; requires login credentials for post views; or has user generated posts that cannot be linked back to a public profile does not qualify under the current specifications regardless of the size of their platform. The ten example URLs provided are intended to represent the format the platform plans to send to Google.

Whether or not the platform chooses to apply, the technical SEO can focus on the markup. Valid on-page structured data is one of the requirements, and in 2023 Google provided Search Console reporting and Rich Results Test support for both forum and profile markup. Those reports show errors, warnings, and valid items related to marked-up forum and profile pages.

If a site’s primary source of content is not user-generated content, then it fails the first qualification. However, these types of sites may still be competing against User Generated Content (Forum/Social) on the same searches, but Google did not name any participants. If you find your searches yielding more forum results, currently, there is no way within either the program page or form to determine whether the program is responsible for those increased results.

As of Oct. 15, none of the program page, form, or changelog entry (Oct. 8) names a participating platform. None of these items establish a numerical value for “a significant user base” despite this being one of the values requested via the Form to be reported as Monthly Active Users.

The program page references “various features on Search,” while the form says “Google Search and other surfaces.” They don’t identify a feature. The 72-hour counter window isn’t explained either.

The three listed documents also do not indicate how Google utilizes the interaction signals/engagement counts provided by participants; nor do they specify if participants will receive any reporting.

Applications are open through the form linked from the program page. Google says it will get back to applicants “within 6-8 weeks with a response on the status of your application.” Selected platforms then get “detailed technical integration documentation and onboarding instructions,” with no stated schedule for that step.

Google’s Search Central changelog records the Oct. 8 addition. It’s a place to watch for future changes to the documentation.

#147. Meta’s New TOS Dubbed A Total POS; Another Nail In Search Traffic’s Coffin

Media companies and legal professionals see Meta’s new commercial terms as a data grab at the expense of site owners and a way to avoid paying AI licensing fees.

Meta’s current terms of service stipulate that business accounts on Facebook and Instagram consent to having their social media content scraped to train Meta’s AI models. But starting on October 30, Meta is extending its scraping privileges to all websites linked on its platforms, Niemen Lab reports.

There is no way for businesses to opt out, other than to stop advertising with Meta altogether.

Meta says the update consolidates a maze of policies in one place and doesn’t change any rules. Some legal experts warn otherwise. They argue that “the new language creates an opening for Meta to argue its commercial terms supersede other blocking instructions,” like robots.txt files, according to Niemen Lab.

Danielle Coffey, president & CEO of the News/Media Alliance, calls the new terms “an appalling, bad-faith policy, and a clear abuse of the company’s market power” in a statement posted to social media.

It’s a “remarkable provision to bury in [the] terms of service,” Matt Topic, a media and intellectual property attorney at Loevy & Loevy, tells Niemen Lab.

Topic adds it “would give Meta access to material that would likely cost many millions of dollars in a licensing market.”

British news publisher The Independent’s social-commerce revenue narrowly surpassed SEO-based commerce revenue for the first time last month, its CEO Christian Broughton said at Digiday’s recent Media Strategies event in London.

The Independent doesn’t disclose its revenue mix, so it’s hard to say for certain whether it’s seen impressive growth in social commerce.

Rather, it could be the case that SEO-driven commerce (or, in layman’s terms, affiliate marketing) has been usurped by social commerce because of a precipitous, AI-driven drop-off in search traffic.

According to Broughton, the old business model in which publishers could buy and earn abundant traffic from search engines and social networks and monetize that traffic with ads is “dead.”

Ouch. No wonder social commerce has taken the baton.

Broughton cited four areas of investment that are expected to account for more than half of The Independent’s revenue this year: AI (because you have to fight fire with fire, we guess), creator-led studio work, ecommerce and memberships.

Ecommerce sellers must answer a tough question: “Do they embrace outside agents in hopes of a sales boost, or do they resist them?”

The Wall Street Journal notes that there are countervailing forces behind the question.

There’s the obvious traffic incentive for integrating with agents. But then there’s all the hassle AI agents bring: automated purchases to authenticate, inevitable returns and customer service issues, credit-card chargebacks.

Amazon blocks third-party AI agents because it has the leverage to do so and it knows the vast value of its data. But other big-name companies like Walmart and Target cut licensing deals with OpenAI, Anthropic, et al.

And it’s not just retailers that have to decide which incentives will win out.

Real estate brokerages and listings marketplaces like Zillow and Compass are clashing over how sellers can list and market their properties and how much transparency to give users.

The Journal, in a separate story this week, weighs the potential antitrust challenges of Compass, which became America’s largest brokerage this year, paying sellers to delist their properties from other platforms.

There’s another angle to the sudden lack of transparency in listings markets, though: Companies are preserving their data exclusivity – and thus their value to LLMs.

But again, there’s a tension between preserving your data value and licensing it for quick cash. Zillow, for instance, signed a deal with Google to license data for Gemini AI.

#148. How publishers are rethinking audience engagement: Five takeaways from the Future of Media Technology Conference

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

“It would be a mistake to try to replicate the creator economy.”

Earlier this month, just across from the Tate Modern in central London, journalists and media managers gathered for this year’s Future of Media Technology Conference, a one-day event hosted by Press Gazette. Speakers included journalists, technologists, and media professionals like The Economist’s Andrew Palmer, Politico UK’s Katie Palisoul, The Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism’s Mitali Mukherjee, The Logic’s David Skok, and News UK’s Tom Jackson. Here are five takeaways from the event.

RELATED ARTICLESearch traffic has declined so much that some publishers are considering opting out of Google entirelyNeel DhaneshaJuly 22, 2026RELATED ARTICLE“Affiliation, not just access”: Newsrooms try to move beyond membership to a focus on “belonging”Sarah EbnerMay 12, 2026In the age of declining traffic, publishers are grappling with how to engage and retain audiences. There’s a shift away from volume toward relationship-building, with publishers exploring new ways to measure engagement beyond pure clicks.

App downloads, frequency of visits, and newsletter signups were identified as important indicators by The Guardian’s chief support officer, Liz Wynn. “You build motivation, support, effective comprehension of our mission, our purpose, why we exist, why we should keep coming back,” she said. “[It’s a] very important emotional driver, but it’s not enough on its own. We have to focus also on the habit and the value of driving people day to day.”

To build those habits, publishers are focusing on community-building, with some even employing AI tools to achieve that goal. Predictive models, such as using AI to recommend users their next read, were cited as a common example of how AI can help drive user engagement. Anna Sbuttoni, deputy head of digital at The Times and The Sunday Times, said her team is now using AI to help with another aspect of audience engagement: comment moderation.

“[Content moderation] is still overseen by humans, but it’s just brought that work way down, and it’s freed up that team to now do much more interesting and innovative community-focused work than they were doing when they were just spending hours and hours on this moderation job,” she said.

RELATED ARTICLENews creators get more attention in countries where traditional media strugglesHanaa' TameezOctober 28, 2025Another challenge for news media is increased competition from independent journalists and news creators. This phenomenon has been well-documented in research by the Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism (RISJ) and was a running thread of discussion across various panels, where legacy media organizations discussed how to adopt creator-led practices while preserving institutional trust, editorial authority and sustainable revenues.

The Economist is a prime example of this. The magazine has moved away from its legacy of journalistic anonymity toward putting its journalists’ faces, names, and personalities at the forefront of its value proposition. Its executive editor, Andrew Palmer, said one of the reasons the publication has begun to showcase its journalists is a desire to highlight the humans behind the journalism as AI advances.

Like many newsrooms, The Economist is fostering in-house talent to put in front of the camera as a way to respond to growing audience interest in creators. The team at The Times and The Sunday Times is also thinking about its talent strategy as the next step in audience engagement. Putting journalists in front of the camera is one strategy it is beginning to employ to reach people who might not otherwise engage with the papers.

“How can we make people consider getting a Times subscription? A big part of that has been just a complete change in how we approach our social video formats, and that’s really putting our journalists at the front and center of that. Getting people to know the real journalists,” explained Sbuttoni.

Earlier this year, The Guardian announced the formation of Guardian Studios — a new creative hub for video-first, personality-led journalism. Leah Green, who leads the initiative, said the team is looking to create a new slate of YouTube shows built around on-screen talent. Green agreed that legacy media has a lot to learn from creators. But news media has one thing that individual creators don’t: brand recognition.

“There can be a [certain] panic and [an] overcorrection from legacy brands. There’s so much to learn from the creator economy: personality and how to create fandom,” said Green. “But brand is one thing that an individual creator can never have. It would be a mistake to try to replicate the creator economy.”

Jasmine Dawson, senior vice president of BBC Studios, said one of the main things legacy publishers can learn from creators is a deep understanding of their audience. Creators, unlike broadcasters and publishers, “live and breathe” in their audience’s world: They understand them and know what they want.

“Obsessing about your audience means not only knowing where they are, but what they want to talk about, what they want to hear from you, what they want to see from you,” she said.

“There’s a real tension that exists in terms of what’s happening in partnerships and their relationship with audiences,” said RISJ’s director, Mitali Mukherjee. “We don’t have a clear sign of what exactly will happen.”

RELATED ARTICLEProtein grams and retirement plans: Service journalism enters its next eraSarah EbnerSeptember 15, 2026This uncertainty is one of the main reasons publishers are investing in strengthening direct relationships with their audiences. At the same time, they are examining their relationships with AI companies and their presence in AI search. They want to remain visible across search and AI services while protecting the value of original journalism.

The world of AI search was described as the “Wild West,” with the rules of the game still unclear. No one knows exactly what gets to the top of AI search results, for example, making it difficult to build an optimization strategy around a technology with so many unknowns.

Tom Jackson, chief technology officer at News UK, underlined the need for news publishers to adapt their content to AI-driven search and discovery, while warning that the field is changing too quickly to make major strategic decisions based on today’s patterns.

“One thing I’m finding quite interesting, given my background, is that they’re saying richer metadata may become increasingly important,” said Jackson. “It’s going to be interesting to reopen that tagging and metadata box in this new, agentic AI–focused world.”

Despite the uncertainty, publishers still want to experiment with how they can maintain a presence on these platforms. Carly Steven, director of SEO and editorial e-commerce at the Daily Mail, said that, while the publisher’s default position is to protect its IP and focus on creating original content, it has also started experimenting in the AI search space.

“We are starting to test a nuanced approach to that…to be more visible on these platforms,” said Steven. “We know our readers are looking for information on these platforms and are starting to look for brands they trust.”

“We are building some foundational elements to be able to show the value of our paid-for content, which is our policy journalism,” she said.

The question of monetization extended beyond audiences to conversations around AI, particularly the tension between the short- and long-term economics of allowing AI platforms to use publishers’ content.

In the short term, publishers have an incentive to participate in AI platforms — even if the compensation or referral traffic is small — because their content can be relatively fungible. But if every publisher accepts that weaker value exchange, does it undermine the economics of journalism in the long term?

Steven from the Daily Mail said that the question of fungibility has never been particularly relevant to the organization, as it strives to create content that is exclusive, original, and not replaceable.

“We are really focused on the absolute conviction that our business is valuable, and that that value needs to be paid for,” she said. “We are experimenting, adapting to the landscape as it changes, as new technologies emerge and they become established standards, but fundamentally believe that [our content] has value.”

Jackson from News UK framed licensing and deal-making as a core monetization path when it comes to AI, with a strategy that combines partnerships with legal action. This has led the company to strike a deal with Meta while also entering licensing conversations with other AI companies.

“Ideally we want to have relationships with all of these people and get fair value back. But if they come in and steal that content, we will sue them,” said Jackson. “It’s not just the monetary value of that deal, which is material. It’s also the ability to then have that close relationship with these organizations.”

In the midst of such a future-oriented conference, one old piece of technology stood out as a winner across the panels: newsletters. They were framed as direct, differentiated products that deepen reader relationships and reduce reliance on platform algorithms. Many of the news organizations showcased at the conference have invested in newsletters, which remain a strong way to engage directly with audiences and counter declining referral traffic.

For The Logic, a Canadian newsroom focused on tech and business, newsletters have been a core part of the organization since the beginning. David Skok, The Logic’s CEO and editor-in-chief, said the publication hasn’t seen a drop-off in open rates, while advertiser performance has continued to grow. He attributes their success to treating the newsletter as a premium, central product of the newsroom. The Logic considers its daily newsletter briefing, which is written specifically by its journalists, the front page of the newspaper.

“The way we treat newsletters is really more as their own product,” said Skok. “We were a bit ahead of the curve in that we had this direct relation with our readers, because we just decided very early on that we weren’t going to build our business on the top of some of these algorithms.”

Politico Playbook also demonstrates the enduring appeal of newsletters, having spawned numerous global iterations since its launch in 2007. Palisoul from Politico attributed its success to an “obsession with audience”: The team knows exactly who its readers are and what they want from the product.

“The Playbook is written with an exact audience in mind: a prime minister, a cabinet minister…But authors think of that person as a person. They don’t think of that person as an MP,” explained Palisoul. “It’s fun. It’s cheeky. It’s got good humor. Great puns. It tells them where they can go for a drink. It’s really focused on the daily life of that individual.”

#149. How to Think Like a Filmmaker: AI Video With Seedance

Wondering how to create AI-generated video that looks cinematic instead of cheap? Want a repeatable workflow for turning a simple concept into polished AI video content using tools like Seedance?

​In this article, you'll discover a step-by-step process for producing professional-quality AI video, from developing a concept and building key visuals to generating clips with Seedance and assembling them into a finished piece.

The biggest misconception about AI video is that it's easy. Typing a prompt into a video model produces output, but its quality depends entirely on the creator's ability to communicate with the tool. Ross Symons points out that most people who dismiss AI video as “sloppy” are seeing the result of vague prompts, not the limits of the technology.

​The first thing to understand is the difference between how large language models and diffusion models process instructions. An LLM like ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini understands conversational intent. A diffusion model, the underlying technology that powers most AI image and video generators, including Midjourney and Seedance, does not.

Diffusion models extract visual keywords from a prompt and ignore conversational filler. Telling Midjourney to “create me an image of a cat walking on the beach with a cowboy hat on” works, but the model isn't parsing that sentence the way a chatbot would. It's scanning for visual keywords: cat, beach, cowboy hat.

​The prompting strategies that work well in a chat window don't transfer directly to image and video generation. Each model has its own prompt structure, and learning that structure is what separates polished output from generic results.

Ross notes that certain tools excel at certain jobs. Midjourney, for example, remains the preferred tool among creatives for art direction, ideation, and creative exploration. ChatGPT's image generation has the advantage of a reasoning layer that interprets intent, but many professionals still prefer the aesthetic output of a dedicated image model.

​For those who don't know how to write structured prompts for a tool like Midjourney, there's a practical shortcut. Instead of learning the syntax, tell ChatGPT what the desired image should look like and ask it to write the prompt in Midjourney's format. ChatGPT will convert conversational descriptions into the structured, keyword-based format that diffusion models respond to, producing significantly better results.

​Pro Tip: Image generation is the foundation for AI video. Mastering how to create and refine still images first leads to a much higher success rate when moving into video, because the same principles of prompting, composition, and visual direction apply.

A concept is the idea behind what the video is trying to communicate. It doesn't need to be elaborate or deeply artistic. It can be as simple as “I want to show my product in an unexpected environment” or “I want to explain this technique with a visual metaphor.” The point is to have an intention before touching a tool.

​Ross illustrates this with a project he originally created as a stop-motion animation years ago. The concept: a Red Bull can sits on a table. A piece of paper slides in, folds itself into an origami bull, runs into the can, opens it, drinks the liquid, sprouts wings, and flies away. The whole piece is a play on “Red Bull gives you wings.”

That concept translated across mediums. He recreated it recently using Seedance, feeding the sequence into the AI video model with a couple of image references, and the concept held up because the idea was strong regardless of the production tool.

​Ross recommends using an LLM to further develop a concept. Even a basic idea can be expanded by asking ChatGPT to help extrapolate the narrative, suggest visual sequences, or propose variations. The goal is to have a clear sense of the story before moving into visual development.

Once the concept exists, the next step is developing the key visuals that will anchor the video. Ross breaks this into three components: the subject (or hero), the environment, and a secondary character or element.

Every session is pitch-free and built around tactics you can use yourself, no big team required. Your All-Access ticket includes an extra day of workshops, full access to AI Business World, and recordings of everything.

​The Subject or Hero: This is the story's focal point. It could be a product, a person, or any object that drives the narrative. For a fragrance ad Ross created, the hero was the bottle itself. He generated a mock product image using Midjourney, establishing the bottle's look before doing anything else. Creating mock products with ChatGPT, Midjourney, or Gemini is a valid starting point when professional product photography isn't available.

​The Environment: This is the setting where the story takes place. Ross built a jungle environment in Midjourney for the fragrance ad. The environment can be created in any image-generation tool or sourced from reference images on Pinterest, Shutterstock, or a personal photo library.

What matters is articulating specific visual qualities. Rather than telling the model to make something “cool,” Ross recommends describing what's appealing about a reference: the time of day, how light falls on surfaces, the color temperature, and the depth of field. The more specific the direction, the better the output.

​A Secondary Character or Element: This is whatever else appears in the scene to support the narrative. In the fragrance example, Ross added a black panther walking into the shot and eventually staring at the camera, then jumping toward it. This secondary element created tension and movement in what would otherwise be a static product shot.

​Pro Tip: When using a personal photo as the character, isolate the subject against a plain background. Don't use a photo with busy surroundings or other people in it. Provide multiple photos taken from different angles, all showing the subject wearing the same clothing. This gives the model clear data to work with when placing the character in new environments, poses, and scenarios.

Camera perspective is one of the fastest ways to elevate AI-generated visuals beyond the flat, centered composition most models produce. A few basic cinematography principles make an enormous difference. A low-angle shot makes a character look powerful and dominant. A high-angle shot can make a character appear submissive or vulnerable. A close-up creates intensity. A wide, zoomed-out shot with empty space around the subject suggests isolation or vulnerability.

​The practical tip for those without a film background: use ChatGPT to analyze a film still. Upload the image and ask the model to explain what's creating a specific emotional effect. Is it the camera angle? Dramatic lighting? Soft bokeh? The contrast? ChatGPT will break it down using proper cinematography terminology, which can then be fed directly into image and video prompts.

​Ross tested this approach by asking ChatGPT to generate “six of Guy Ritchie's most used shots” in a single image. The result included close-ups, high-angle shots, and several techniques Ross hadn't encountered before, each one usable as a reference for future prompts.

The AI Business Society filters the noise for you, with expert-led training you can put to work the same day — plus a community of marketers sharing what's actually working.

Creators can reference specific directors or films without needing to know technical vocabulary. Saying “make this character look like Aladdin in this scene” or “show me a Guy Ritchie-style shot of this character in this environment” produces results that look distinct from the generic, centered output most people get.

A keyframe in the context of AI video is an image used as a reference point for the model. A storyboard is a sequence of 6 to 12 keyframes that map out the major moments of a video, establishing the angle, lighting, and composition for each beat.

​The storyboard serves the creator more than the model. It provides structure, prevents overloading a single clip with too many actions, and establishes a clear sequence of events before any video generation begins. Ross emphasizes that the storyboard doesn't need to be professional. It's a planning tool, and rough images work fine as long as they communicate what each moment should look and feel like.

​There are two primary approaches to using keyframes with AI video models.

​Start Frame Plus End Frame Plus Prompt: This method provides the model with an image for where the video should begin, an image for where it should end, and a text prompt describing what happens between them. For example, the start frame is an empty surface. The end frame shows a Red Bull can centered in the shot. The prompt reads: “Red Bull can slides in from the right at a slow pace and stops directly in the center.” The combination of visual anchors and text instruction gives the model clear constraints.

​Start Frame Plus Prompt Only: This method uses only a starting image and lets the prompt guide the action without a fixed endpoint. It offers more creative latitude. For a 10-second clip, the start frame might be an empty surface, and the prompt might read: “Red Bull can slides in from the left, paper jet flies in from the top, lands next to the can, unfolds into a flat piece of paper.” The model fills in the motion and timing.

​Pro Tip: To build a longer video, chain clips together by extracting the final frame from the previous clip and using it as the start frame for the next one. This creates visual continuity across a multi-clip sequence without having to regenerate consistent elements from scratch.

The most frequent error Ross sees is people cramming too many actions into a short clip. A 5-second clip can only accommodate one or two actions. Writing a long paragraph describing a can sliding in, paper flying, a bull forming, and an explosion all within five seconds overwhelms the model. The result is distorted limbs, warped perspectives, and visual artifacts. The fix is matching the complexity of the prompt to the duration of the clip.

​Ross also distinguishes between using images as keyframes versus using them as references. Keyframes require exact replication at specific points in the video, which often results in awkward transitions and unnatural camera movements as the model forces itself between two rigid endpoints. References give the model a sense of the desired look and feel without demanding pixel-level accuracy, and they tend to produce smoother, more natural results. Ross recommends using references over keyframes in most cases.

Seedance, developed by ByteDance (the company behind TikTok), stands out for its adherence to prompts and reference image accuracy. Ross describes it as near flawless in both areas, a significant leap from the video models of even two years ago.

​Seedance isn't a stand-alone app. It's a model accessed through aggregator platforms. Ross recommends Luma AI (lumalabs.ai) as a preferred platform, along with Flora, Figma Weave, Artlist, Imagine Art, Open Art, and Krea. These platforms provide access to Seedance alongside other video models such as Kling 3.0, Veo 3, and others, all connected via an API.

​Google's Veo 3 (available through Gemini) offers free video generations and was considered state-of-the-art before Seedance and Kling 3.0 arrived. Ross notes that while Veo is useful, skills learned on one model don't automatically transfer to another. Each video model has its own prompt structure. Practicing with Veo builds general familiarity with AI video, but producing the best results on Seedance requires learning how Seedance specifically responds to prompts, timing instructions, and reference images.

Seedance supports time-segmented prompting, which allows creators to specify what happens during specific intervals within a single clip.

For a 15-second clip, the prompt can be structured as: “Between 0 and 4 seconds, this happens. Between 4 and 8 seconds, this happens. Between 8 and 12 seconds, this happens.” The model adheres to these timing instructions, making it possible to choreograph multi-beat sequences within a single generation rather than chaining multiple short clips.

​Seedance offers a duration selector ranging from 5 to 30 seconds per clip. Ross advises beginners to start with shorter, lower-resolution clips to learn the workflow. Creating a 30-second, high-resolution clip without experience often results in wasted money and unsatisfying results.

A 30-second Seedance clip at 720p resolution costs approximately $14. Bumping the resolution to 1080p roughly doubles the cost to $28–$32. These prices are significantly higher than earlier AI video models, where 5-second clips cost less than $0.20, but the quality gap is equally significant.

​A cost-effective alternative is to generate at a lower resolution and upscale afterward. Ross generated a 480p clip for about $6, then upscaled it twice using built-in platform tools to reach near-4K quality for an additional $3. The total cost of $9 produced a quality comparable to that of a native high-resolution render at roughly a third of the price. The two leading upscaler tools are Topaz Labs and Magnific, both of which are integrated into most aggregator platforms.

Ross Symons is the co-founder and Chief Creative Officer of Zen Robot, a studio that helps marketers and creators produce AI-powered visuals and video. He's also the head educator at Zen Robot Academy. Find Ross on LinkedIn.

#150. ChatGPT Traffic Drop Appears To Be A Tracking Problem via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

In this webinar, learn to rewrite spec-sheet product copy into the words shoppers use, and make product pages readable to AI.

Invalid traffic on AI Max search doubled to 5.28%. Get the channel-by-channel retail benchmarks before Black Friday.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Webinar: The Link Building Graveyard: What to Bury & What Still Wins

ChatGPT-attributed traffic fell sharply in several analytics datasets this month, and analysts tie the drop to ChatGPT links that open without tracking tags.

The number of ChatGPT-attributed sessions in Google Analytics 4 fell by 22% to 57%, for sites tracked by Graphite with meaningful traffic in the AI Assistant channel, starting Oct. 9, stated Graphite CEO Ethan Smith in his LinkedIn post. Smith estimates this represents an approximate 45% fall from the previous baseline. LLM Pulse reported that, relative to the same days in the last two weeks, sessions from ChatGPT on the sites LLM Pulse has been monitoring were approximately 46% less during Oct. 9–11. Total traffic on those sites remained relatively constant over the same period.

Smith says that ChatGPT started opening links in the answer text without the utm_source=chatgpt.com tag or a referrer, therefore visits from these links can appear as Direct in GA4. There are other analyses suggesting the same change in tracking. However, there is not enough data yet to determine whether there was also some loss of visitation.

Cedric Huesler, a senior director of product management at Adobe, compared Oct. 9–13 with the week before on about 500 pages where ChatGPT drove at least 5% of visits. He reported on LinkedIn that ChatGPT visits to those pages fell by about 31,000 a day while Direct visits rose by about 26,000 a day. Search traffic fell 7%, in line with search elsewhere.

Direct rose on two of every three pages that lost ChatGPT traffic, compared with about half the week before. Huesler says the new Direct visitors also behave like ChatGPT visitors. On mobile, the share of Direct visitors who saw the consent banner, his sign of a first visit, went from 36% to 44%, moving toward the 55% he sees among ChatGPT visitors. He calls the findings early, based on four days of sampled data.

Huesler says that after the GPT-6 rollout, ChatGPT began opening links in a new tab with a browser setting that withholds the referrer, and leaving off the utm_source tag that ChatGPT’s citations carried when its search launched in 2024.

Smith noted that inline links in answer text lost the tag, while links in the Sources panel and shopping links retained it. He also shared that 95% of mobile ChatGPT visits to Graphite’s sites relied on the tag alone, making app traffic the most exposed.

Profound ties the change to a new answer format. Among the ChatGPT answers with citations that it collected, the share with at least one tagged source link fell from about 98% on Oct. 8 to 66% by Oct. 14. Over the same days, Intelligent UI, ChatGPT’s format for charts, comparisons and small tools, went from 2% of all the answers Profound collected to about 35%. Links reached by opening a product or information panel still carried tags.

When I covered the GPT-6 rollout on Oct. 7, OpenAI’s announcement didn’t say how sources would appear in those formats. GPT-6 began rolling out to paid plans that day and to Free and Go users on Oct. 8, and LLM Pulse saw no drop on Oct. 7.

Tomek Rudzki at Peec AI ran the same 1 million prompts from October 2 through October 7 and then again from October 9 through October 13. He observed that ChatGPT put a direct URL for a webpage into 42% of the responses compared with a rate of about 8-10% previously; that 54% of these URLs point to home pages, he reports. He says there are also no tags or referrers associated with the links. The figures represent links displayed by ChatGPT but do not represent actual user click-throughs.

The authors of LLM Pulse stated that the team did not observe an increase in site traffic for Direct. They said that Direct is much larger than ChatGPT and as such even an increase in a relatively small number of sessions would be difficult to detect. Additionally they stated that the aggregated data made it impossible to distinguish traffic that was lost from traffic that was no longer labeled as coming from ChatGPT.

Smith called the change a bug on OpenAI’s side and wrote that he expects OpenAI to fix it “very soon.” Huesler now says OpenAI confirmed to him on Oct. 14 that it was a bug. In a follow-up post, he wrote that a fix began rolling out early on Oct. 15 and that by 9 a.m. PT, tagged ChatGPT clicks were back to roughly 95% to 100% of the same hour a week earlier, across thousands of domains he tracks. He added that most ChatGPT clicks still arrive without a referrer, so he recommends counting the UTM tag instead. SEO consultant Glenn Gabe replied that he wasn’t seeing the change yet on paid or free accounts. Profound says it hasn’t seen official word on a fix, and OpenAI’s ChatGPT release notes for Oct. 1 through Oct. 15 don’t mention link tracking.

Graphite, LLM Pulse, Profound and Peec AI sell SEO or AI search services and tools, and Huesler works at Adobe. The LLM Pulse and Profound posts don’t give sample sizes.

A 50% or so decline in GA4 referrals from ChatGPT in just one week may be an indicator that you are experiencing changes to how your tracking data is being reported more than a real change in visitor interest. Both Smith and Huesler suggest you annotate the October 8 date in your reporting prior to anyone interpreting it as a loss of traffic, and Huesler now puts the window at Oct. 8–15.

In addition, until further notice, review your ChatGPT and Direct traffic side-by-side for each page ChatGPT referred visitors to, and your homepage, where Rudzki has indicated more than half of the direct links he saw point.

At the time of the introduction of Google Analytics’ AI Assistant channel in May, I stated that if users accessed content via an AI assistant but did not have a referrer, their session would also report as part of the Direct channel. The ChatGPT tag provided a way to capture this additional traffic (especially on mobile). According to Smith, if you set your own UTM parameters within a click from ChatGPT Ads they should be unaffected.

The open question now is how quickly the tags return for every account, since OpenAI hasn’t mentioned the fix in its release notes. Profound notes that restoring them could help with future reports, though it wouldn’t bring back attribution that’s already been lost. Gemini took a different direction two weeks ago, adding UTM parameters to its links, as Roger Montti covered.

#153. How YouTube’s Algorithm Can Find Your Customers for Free

Want to stop paying for distribution and let YouTube's AI find the right audience for your business? Wondering how to create content that turns casual viewers into loyal customers without spending a dollar on ads?

​In this article, you'll discover how to build a YouTube content strategy that lets the algorithm find and deliver your ideal customers without paid ads.

Most businesses approach YouTube as a content repository, uploading videos without a coherent strategy. When they do develop a strategy, they tend to make a foundational error: targeting customers instead of viewers.

​Derral Eves explains that YouTube's AI-based algorithm isn't designed to serve customers. Since 2013, when YouTube shifted from a view-based algorithm to an AI-driven one, the platform has been engineered to do one thing: identify viewers who want specific content and keep them on the platform longer. The algorithm matches content to the right audiences without the creator spending anything on distribution.

​That goal creates an opportunity most marketers miss. Instead of crafting content aimed at someone ready to buy, the approach is to create content that brings genuine value to someone who doesn't yet know the brand. YouTube then acts as a free, organic distribution engine, recommending that content to similar viewers based on their watch history and topical interests.

​One of Derral's students ran an e-commerce business selling used office furniture sourced from office foreclosures. His entire traffic strategy was YouTube-based, with no email list and no paid advertising. Rather than filming product listings, he created content designed for viewers: review videos, comparison breakdowns, and videos detailing what to look for when buying specific types of furniture.

​Derral coached him to expand further, suggesting formats like S-tier to F-tier ranking videos that would appeal to gamers searching for affordable gaming chairs. The student also used live streams to engage viewers directly and answer questions.

​The strategy succeeded because YouTube surfaced his videos in both YouTube search and Google search results, creating dual visibility. Approximately 75–80% of his views came from YouTube recommendations alone. Viewers who arrived through search would watch three or four videos, prompting YouTube to recommend his content with increasing frequency. He expanded from one warehouse to two.

​When he eventually layered in traditional marketing tools such as email drip sequences alongside YouTube, his sales surpassed $20 million, all with zero ad spend on distribution. He also created his own annual May sales event featuring live streams that outperformed his Black Friday numbers.

To stop thinking about the end customer and start thinking about who would naturally find value in a piece of content, Derral recommends focusing on psychographics over demographics.

​Demographics inform how to present content. A video for Gen Alpha looks different from one aimed at boomers, even if the core information is the same. Psychographics, however, reveal what motivates a viewer based on their values, needs, fears, and life circumstances, and that motivation is what drives viewing behavior.

​Derral uses Abraham Maslow's hierarchy of needs as a lens for understanding viewer motivation. The emotional connection a viewer has to content is driven by where they sit on that hierarchy, and understanding those needs shapes everything from topic selection to how a video opens.

​For example, an immunologist wanted to use YouTube to attract more patients to her practice. Several of her videos had gained traction, with one approaching a million views. Derral's approach was to examine who was actually watching. The audience skewed 45 to 65-plus.

​That demographic insight pointed toward psychographic understanding: these viewers were likely experiencing health wake-up calls, noticing declining energy, dealing with blood pressure issues, or processing the loss of someone close to them.
