​That psychographic profile led to a specific content strategy. A video on ten foods to naturally lower blood pressure reached 1.7 million views. The follow-up, a video on five mistakes people make when checking their blood pressure, accumulated 865,000 views in less than two weeks.

​YouTube recognized the topical connection and recommended the second video to viewers who had watched the first.

​The business impact followed naturally. As viewers watched multiple videos, they came to trust the doctor. They discovered she sold supplements like B12 and offered virtual visits. Derral frames this as YouTube operating as the top of a funnel: each video brings viewers closer through the know, like, and trust progression until they're ready to explore what the creator offers, without ever being pitched directly.

​To find outliers, Derral suggests searching YouTube for the type of content you’re planning and identifying videos that fit that pattern. Those URLs can be saved to a spreadsheet or a YouTube playlist for later analysis.

​The most valuable data often comes from comments. Comments reveal how viewers derived value from a video and where they felt it fell short. The gaps viewers identify become opportunities for differentiated content. Derral also recommends reviewing commenter profiles to see who is engaging. Profile details and commenting patterns reveal whether the audience skews younger, older, or spans a specific demographic, which helps validate psychographic assumptions.

​AI tools like Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini can accelerate this analysis. Creators can feed these tools batches of video URLs and ask what the comments have in common, what viewers found valuable, and what questions went unanswered.

​Pro Tip: A common mistake is the belief that content should appeal to everyone. Derral challenges this assumption. There is always a core audience that will be more receptive, and identifying that core audience is what allows the algorithm to function effectively. The more precisely a creator understands who finds their content valuable, the more effectively YouTube can match that content to similar viewers.

Once the target viewer is defined, the next challenge is earning the click. Derral identifies curiosity as the primary driver.

​The title and thumbnail need to create a curiosity gap specific to the viewer's situation. For the immunologist, a title like “Top 10 Foods to Bring Down Your Blood Pressure Naturally” works because it addresses an active need and creates curiosity about whether the viewer is already eating those foods.

​After the click, the decision window is narrow. Viewers watch about 5 to 10 seconds of a long-form video before deciding whether to stay or leave. On mobile, that window contracts further. On shorts, the threshold is measured in milliseconds. The opening seconds must reinforce the curiosity that earned the click, confirming immediately that the viewer is in the right place and that the promised value is coming.

​Pro Tip: Derral warns against a mistake common among marketers: applying ad copy techniques to organic video. Marketers who attend conferences and learn about selling, credibility stacking, and promotional frameworks often bring those instincts to YouTube. The result is an opening that feels like a pitch, and viewers click away. You have to switch from “sell” to “help.” If a viewer can get full value from the video alone, without being sent to a landing page or offer, that builds the foundation for everything that follows.

The real value of YouTube isn't a single view. It's sustained viewership across multiple videos, the point at which a casual viewer becomes an engaged follower.

​Derral explains that delivering value early in a video produces a compounding effect. When viewers receive substantive value in the first minutes, they become more patient and stay through the entire video. That extended watch time signals to YouTube that the content is worth recommending, which brings additional viewers and creates more opportunities for the know, like, and trust cycle to deepen. Viewers who find genuine value also share content organically, often identifying four or five people who would benefit, thereby amplifying it beyond what the algorithm alone would.

The AI Business Society filters the noise for you, with expert-led training you can put to work the same day — plus a community of marketers sharing what's actually working.

​He monitored his comments closely, noticed viewers expressing that they were struggling to get their lives together, and created content that addressed those needs directly. His most popular video, “When You Just Ain't Got It Together,” has 8.5 million views. The next two address loneliness and how to be a proper man. Some videos have 18,000 comments.

​The content resonates because it meets a real need: a predominantly younger male audience seeking candid guidance and validation they aren't finding elsewhere. The value proposition is authenticity, delivered without concern for production polish or strategic positioning.

​The business result followed the same pattern. His Wrangler School, a week-long cowboy experience, sold out, with a three-and-a-half-year waitlist. Every sale came from viewers who had consumed enough content to feel a sense of trust and familiarity with the creator. Derral says that when the know-like-trust cycle is executed well, creators don't need to sell directly. They present an offer, and the audience responds.

​Pro Tip: A critical mistake is withholding value behind a gate. If every video ends with a redirect to a landing page for the remaining information, viewers lose trust. Occasional calls to action are appropriate, but consistently reserving the best content for a paid offer undermines the relationship that YouTube is uniquely positioned to build.

Your voice is what separates channels that grow from channels that plateau.

​For creators who default to a promotional persona on camera, adopting an elevator pitch or a polished marketing delivery that reads as inauthentic to viewers, the adjustment is more straightforward than most creators expect.

​Derral recommends imagining the camera as a friend at dinner, someone genuinely interested in the topic who doesn't need to be sold. That conversational register is what performs on YouTube. Podcasts succeed for the same reason: they function as conversations, not presentations.

​The solution was environmental. The creator setup a Zoom call with students visible on a screen behind him and recorded himself presenting to them. He needed the nonverbal cues, the eye contact, and the energy of an audience to access his authentic delivery.

​The first video produced under this arrangement earned 1.5 million views. Over time, he internalized the approach and no longer needed the live audience, but the initial setup was what allowed his natural voice to emerge.

​Pat Flynn's Deep Pocket Monsters channel demonstrates another dimension of voice.

​Pat entered the Pokémon niche not as an expert but as someone genuinely curious about collecting. It took him about a year to find his voice on the new channel, but once he did, the combination of authentic curiosity, storytelling, and humor drove billions of views.

​Pat produces videos that run over an hour with high retention, and the audience response reflects the depth of connection. His in-person events now draw 9,500 attendees.

​Derral notes that Pat had to unlearn what worked on his business-focused channels. The audience, tone, and format that worked for one audience didn't translate to another.

​Derral adds that authenticity is becoming even more important as AI reshapes content creation. Audiences still seek human connection, and creators who build genuine communities around their authentic voice will maintain a lasting competitive advantage. The channels that sustain growth are those where the creator's identity is distinctive and unmistakable.

YouTube content strategy starts with understanding what the target audience is already watching. Derral recommends compiling a list of successful videos in a niche and analyzing their commonalities: the formats they use, how they capture attention, and how they sustain it.

​The editing style itself carries information. Fast cuts and rapid pacing typically indicate a younger audience, while a more measured delivery with deeper content focus suggests millennials, Gen X, or boomers.

​Derral calls the structural element that keeps viewers engaged throughout a video a “mechanism,” a content format or device that creates a natural progression, giving viewers a reason to keep watching from beginning to end.

​The easiest mechanism for creators just starting out is the listicle, such as: five biggest mistakes, ten top foods, five things most people don't know. Listicles create a natural progression in which viewers move from item to item, and retention stays high as long as each segment delivers value and the pacing remains consistent. An uneven listicle, where one point runs for 10 minutes and the next for 2 minutes, causes a drop-off.

​For creators who want to go beyond listicles, storytelling is the most powerful mechanism. Derral recommends the ABC storyline structure.

​The A storyline is what the video is about, and it should match the title. The B storyline is the why: why should someone care, why is this video being made? The C storyline is a common thread that ties together the A and B storylines, creating continuity and emotional investment.

​Other mechanisms include time-bound challenges, where a creator attempts to accomplish something within a set period, and collection or completion challenges, like Pat Flynn's quest to collect every card in a Pokémon set.

​Pro Tip: Device type shapes content length decisions. YouTube analytics reveal whether viewers are watching on TV or mobile. TV viewers are in a lean-back experience, less likely to skip, and often watching with someone else. Those viewers can handle hour-long content. Mobile viewers tend to watch during breaks or while multitasking, making shorter formats more appropriate for that device.

​Short-form video serves a specific strategic role. Shorts are effective for discovery and for developing the skill of capturing attention quickly. On YouTube, shorts can be linked to long-form videos on the same channel, making them a direct traffic source. Derral describes the typical viewer progression: a compelling short generates curiosity, prompting the viewer to seek out the full podcast or long-form video and engage more deeply with the creator.

Derral operates on a four-step cycle: plan, execute, analyze, and adjust. YouTube provides more granular, real time analytics than any other social platform, and creators who ignore that data are, in Derral's words, repeating the same approach and expecting different results.

​The analysis starts with retention data. If viewers drop off in the first ten seconds, the problem is one of two things: the title and thumbnail attracted the wrong audience, or the opening didn't reinforce the curiosity that earned the click. If the drop-off happens at minute three, the video is taking too long to deliver value, or it's missing a re-engagement tease, something that signals bigger value is still coming.

​Each video becomes an experiment. When a creator tests a new opening approach, and retention improves from 50% drop-off to 30% in the first ten seconds, the adjustment worked. The next step is to identify the next drop-off point and address it. Over time, this iterative process builds an intuitive understanding of what the audience responds to, and that understanding compounds.

​The creators who succeed on YouTube aren't the ones who guess right on the first try. They're the ones who treat every upload as data, learn from it, and apply those lessons to the next video.

Derral Eves is a video marketing strategist who helps businesses and creators grow on YouTube at Channel Jump Start. Check out his latest book, The YouTube Formula 2.0. Follow him on YouTube and LinkedIn.

#154. NPR, the quintessential audio news brand, adapts to a video-first future

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

NPR’s new chief content officer Nadine Zylstra on how the public media company acquired Machine Gods — which she thinks can be “the Car Talk of AI.”

After just eight weeks on the job, NPR’s new chief content officer Nadine Zylstra had big news to share: NPR had landed Machine Gods, the new video-first podcast from veteran tech journalists Casey Newton and Kevin Roose.

The deal, announced earlier this month, was something of a coup for NPR. Newton and Roose had announced they were leaving their podcast Hard Fork at The New York Times to build something independent. The news that their next show was headed to NPR, another legacy outlet, was greeted with some surprise — especially because NPR has been cutting jobs and offering buyouts in its first full year without federal funding.

“I don’t think NPR has been buying, is the bottom line,” Zylstra said about the surprised reaction. “I don’t think people thought we would be open to that kind of big swing.”

“Candidly, it’s been a tough year,” she added. “It’s not a shock that everyone would be like, ‘How are those guys doing? I hope they’re okay over there.’ But we really are.”

Zylstra told me she feels she’s been “training [her] whole life” for the job. (She said something similar when she was hired.) Zylstra works from NPR’s Culver City offices. Originally from South Africa, she was previously an executive at Pinterest, YouTube, and Sesame Workshop. She does not have a journalism background.

“News as a content type is not where I feel confident,” Zylstra acknowledged. “But thank goodness for [Thomas] Evans, because he’s the editor-in-chief, and actually nobody wants my opinion on what’s the news anyway.”

Instead, Zylstra was tasked with helping NPR bloom in the next digital era. No one — especially not Nieman Lab readers — will be surprised to learn that involves video.

“We were always audio-first. But as you move into the digital world, you have to turn the lights on, right?” Zylstra said. “You can’t be in the digital world without video being part of the experience.”

Machine Gods is not NPR’s first video-first show. Wild Card and Newsmakers (and Tiny Desk Concerts, for that matter) all precede it. But acquiring the popular podcast may help NPR as it seeks to shift from “reaching people wherever they are” to nudging users toward NPR’s own platforms. NPR CEO Katherine Maher described third-party platforms as the “top of the funnel” in a recent interview and has directed funds toward overhauling NPR’s own app.

The press release calls Machine Gods a “major programming acquisition,” but Zylstra said she prefers the term “partnership.” NPR will pay Roose and Newton, who each own half of Machine Gods Media, and then sell sponsorships on the podcast and “all the various touchpoints” for the show, as Zylstra put it. (NPR declined to comment on the price and duration of the partnership. Bloomberg had previously reported the deal was approaching $5 million.) Machine Gods will get wide distribution and help with ad sales while staying independent. The twice-weekly video podcast will debut as a radio show next year — allowing the journalists to reach some of the roughly 33% of Americans who never or rarely listen to podcasts.

NPR, meanwhile, gets a built-in audience and a popular show focused on one of the biggest news stories in the world — plus a partnership that brings proven, solidly journalistic (read: relatively brand-safe) creators into the NPR fold.

Acquiring and distributing an external podcast like Machine Gods is a bit of departure for NPR, which has often chosen to elevate in-house talent or expand existing franchises. Two other launches, announced alongside the Machine Gods partnership, fall into that more familiar pattern.

During its four-year run with The New York Times, Hard Fork didn’t shy away from critical reporting, covering decision-making at tech companies as well as federal inaction on AI and other tech regulation. The news analysis from Newton and Roose, two well-connected and thoughtful journalists, was one of the strongest aspects of the show. (Other strengths, in this frequent listener’s opinion: the show is genuinely funny, and the co-hosts can productively disagree.)

I asked Zylstra how she is thinking about the news analysis element when much of NPR’s journalism is delivered with a just-the-facts straightness.

“I think our mandate is to be deeply reported and to express that in a way that represents our voice, and the guys’ journalism fits that perfectly,” she said. “It might have more of a op-ed spirit because there is more opinion in there than some of our news magazines — but that’s not where we are delivering headlines. We’re putting it in the context of a conversation between two friends in the same way that Car Talk would have. I feel like there’s space for both styles.”

In the original announcement, Newton said keeping Machine Gods free and widely accessible was a deciding factor in choosing NPR. “What sold us on NPR is its public-service mission,” Newton said. “We get to bring sharp, independent reporting on AI to millions of people for free, right where they already listen.”

Zylstra thinks NPR’s distribution could be a competitive advantage in future deals, too, as she tries to land more “big-swing” partnerships. New episodes of Machine Gods will appear on the NPR app, yes, but also YouTube, Apple Podcasts, and more. In January, the series will expand into an hour-long radio program distributed across NPR member stations.

Part of the power of public media, Zylstra said, is that its mandate is to distribute its journalism to as many people as possible.

“We don’t have the same [need to say], ‘We need to put it behind a paywall to drive subscription in order to blah blah blah blah,'” she said.

Member stations can choose when (and if) they’ll air Machine Gods. “I’m hoping they do it after [All Things Considered] in a kind of late-night vibe,” Zylstra mused.

Here's a habit worth carrying into any new AI tool you try: before you do anything else, test what happens when you type an @ symbol or a / (slash) in the prompt box. Most tools tuck a whole menu of features behind one of these two characters, and there's rarely a pop-up telling you they exist.

In ChatGPT, typing @ opens a menu where you can attach files, trigger a web search, pull up Deep Research, or call in a connected plugin or skill. Typing / instead opens something closer to quick settings: you can branch your current chat into a new one, switch models mid-conversation, add the chat to a project, or jump straight to personalization.

Neither command is ChatGPT-exclusive, and the specific menu varies tool to tool. Claude, Gemini, and most modern AI assistants have their own version of this shortcut system, and it's usually one of the fastest ways to discover a feature you didn't know existed.

Next time you're in a new tool, or one you use daily, try typing @ or / before assuming you've seen everything it can do. You might find a feature that's been there the whole time.

#156. A lack of professional AI guidelines leads to feelings of “AI shame,” a new study finds

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Are you a journalist who has used AI for work in some capacity but been nervous to tell anyone about it? Worried about how your bosses might see you, or that your work might be discredited?

A new study, titled “Guidance over guidelines? Unpacking the uses and concerns of generative AI in communication science” and published in Information, Communication and Society, uncovers how communication scholars are using generative artificial intelligence in their academic work.

Researchers from the National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University in Taiwan, the University of Amsterdam, and Utrecht University surveyed more than 1,100 communication scholars from 77 countries about their use of AI, their concerns about AI in the workplace, and the kind of guidance they seek about AI use in their work. They also held four focus group discussions.

This is the first systematic, field-wide, international empirical investigation of generative AI practices in communication research. We surveyed 1,138 scholars across 77 countries + did 4 focus groups. Small thread with 5 key findings

— Hannes Cools (@hannescools.bsky.social) September 28, 2026 at 6:50 AM

The study reveals a disconnect between researchers’ beliefs about AI and their use of it. Nearly 70% of survey respondents already used generative AI in at least one research-related task, but respondents also mostly considered AI use to be inappropriate for most research-related tasks. While just over half of respondents said that using AI for writing texts (55%) and generating code (50.4%) were appropriate use cases, the study’s authors note that survey participants did not reach a consensus on appropriate or ethical uses of AI in their work.

The lack of institutional guidance on how best to use AI in research means researchers must develop their own ethical standards. This creates a stigma around AI use, according to the study’s authors. Refraining from AI use may put researchers at a disadvantage and slow down their work, but using AI could also be a disadvantage if journals reject research that discloses AI use. “Researchers may recognize an ethical obligation to disclose genAI assistance while fearing that doing so will lead others to perceive their work as less authentic or credible,” the study’s authors write. “This tension has been described as a transparency paradox.”

All of this results in feelings of “AI shame,” the authors say.

“While such hesitation is understandable given that reporting genAI use might reduce the chances of publication, it ultimately hampers open discussion about how these tools can be used ethically and responsibly in research,” the study says. “Transparency is therefore essential, as effective and meaningful guidelines can only be developed when we understand when and how genAI is being used.”

The study’s authors recommend that the communication research community — including individuals, institutions, and journals — create a “disclosure-positive” culture in its field by requiring researchers to disclose the stages of their work at which they used generative AI.

“Simply forbidding the use of genAI — or pretending that it is not being used — is neither sustainable nor constructive,” the authors write. “Instead, acknowledging its presence and defining transparent boundaries for its use will help align ethical standards with actual scholarly practices, fostering honesty, accountability, and trust within the research community.”

#157. How to Get AI to Recommend Your Business

Want to know how to create content that AI tools cite and recommend? Wondering how to optimize your website so AI systems treat your business as a trusted source?

​In this article, you'll discover how to create content that gets recommended by AI tools like ChatGPT, Claude, and Perplexity, including how to structure your website, repurpose your newsletter, and optimize for AI citations that drive traffic and trust.

Most content creators and business owners are still producing content exclusively for human consumption. They write blog posts with story arcs, hooks, and dramatic tension. They structure YouTube videos with a beginning, middle, and end. They craft Instagram posts designed to stop the scroll.

​Liron Segev explains that this approach overlooks a fundamental shift underway. Machines are reading content too, and they don't consume it the way humans do. AI doesn't start at the top and read all the way down to the bottom. It doesn't get excited about the setup or look for the payoff.

​Each approach to content production is necessary and serves a different audience with different needs. Content for humans still follows the rules marketers have always known. Content for AI follows a different set of rules entirely.

The shift toward AI-driven content mirrors what happened when the internet replaced the Yellow Pages. Liron draws a direct parallel: businesses that once named themselves “AAA Locksmith” to land first in the phone book had to adapt when consumers moved to Google. Some adapted and thrived. Others clung to the old model and disappeared.

​That same split is happening now. Roughly 68% of Google search queries no longer result in a click to a website. Consumers are increasingly having private conversations with AI tools instead of opening 29 browser tabs to research a vacation, compare prices, or evaluate service providers.

​AI has become what Liron calls the “trusted friend” and “trusted advisor.” When someone asks their AI to plan a three-day road trip, the AI already knows their food preferences, their kids' ages, and their budget. The recommendations it returns are the starting point, and for many users, they're also the endpoint. Businesses that don't appear in those recommendations face a real problem.

AI doesn't just take a question and find a direct answer. It uses what Liron calls “fan-out queries,” a process where AI automatically generates and executes dozens of related searches beyond the original question. Someone researching a competitor might receive market analysis, pricing data, and analytics they never requested, all because AI inferred the broader intent behind the question.

​This means your content that answers a narrow question while also connecting to related topics has a better chance of being surfaced.

​The process of getting your business surfaced starts with your newsletter and website.

​Most newsletters die after hitting the inbox. Liron's approach turns that dead content into an AI asset.

​Once the initial newsletter issue has been sent and performance has been proven, publish the exact same newsletter on your business website so AI can find, crawl, and index it. Then, Liron recommends creating a second version of that newsletter specifically structured for AI consumption, with different headings, keywords, and formatting.

​The two versions address two different audiences simultaneously, both living within the same domain.

Join thousands of small-business marketers at Social Media Marketing World — three days of AI, social media, and marketing strategy taught by world-class experts. April 1–3, 2027 in Anaheim.

Every session is pitch-free and built around tactics you can use yourself, no big team required. Your All-Access ticket includes an extra day of workshops, full access to AI Business World, and recordings of everything.

A consulting company was losing to established competitors because the firm couldn't outspend them on ads, and, as Liron points out, ads are renting attention. The second the spending stops, the attention disappears.

​Within three weeks, the consulting firm owned 72% of its category in AI recommendations. It outstripped competitors who had been publishing content for years and had much larger online followings. The difference wasn't volume or history. It was understanding who the new audience was and how to reach them.

AI prioritizes content that offers something it can't generate itself. When it searches for an answer, AI has billions of pages to choose from and uses a filtering process to decide which content to surface.

The first filter is originality. AI recognizes its own output. If a business published content that AI could have generated itself, there's no additional value to cite.

​Liron offers a simple test for your content: if someone can swap your company name in an article for a competitor's name and the content still makes sense, AI has no reason to favor it. That content is generic. It adds nothing that the AI doesn't already have.

​What AI wants is content it can't produce on its own. That means personal stories, proprietary data, specific results, and firsthand experience.

​A financial advisor who writes “10 Tips for Retirement Planning” is competing with millions of identical articles. A financial advisor who writes about what happened when a specific client restructured their portfolio during a market downturn is providing something unique.

Liron stresses that AI can help create content, but the output needs personal enrichment. A generic prompt asking AI to write “seven things to do in Anaheim” produces generic content AI will never cite. Content built using AI as a drafting tool but enriched with personal stories, specific data points, and firsthand experience gives AI something it can't generate on its own.

​Liron gives the example of a conference organizer writing about what attendees should do before an event.

The AI Business Society filters the noise for you, with expert-led training you can put to work the same day — plus a community of marketers sharing what's actually working.

​A generic list of local attractions is forgettable. But content that references specific experiences from past events, mentions how many people attended a particular dinner, or describes a specific restaurant discovery from the previous year becomes unique. AI's predictive algorithms recognize personal details as a source of added value.

AI doesn't read an article from top to bottom. It uses a process Liron calls “chunking”: the extraction of a specific, self-contained piece of content from a larger article that directly answers a user's question. That chunk is pulled out and returned to the user, often with a citation linking to the source.

​This changes how content should be structured.

​Each section of your content needs to stand on its own, making sense without the paragraphs that come before or after it. If AI can extract a two- or three-sentence answer that's accurate, unique, and useful, it will use that chunk and attribute it to the source.

When AI repeatedly pulls from the same business's content, that business builds compounding authority. Users who see the same name appearing across multiple AI responses start to trust that brand, the same way they'd trust a friend who keeps recommending the same restaurant.

​To become that trusted source, traditional marketing principles still apply. Understanding the audience's psychographics, what keeps them up at night, what confuses them, and what they need to make a decision, drives the entire content strategy for AI.

​Liron recommends mining existing business data for content topics. Support tickets reveal the problems customers actually face. Sales calls surface recurring questions. The rule from every college lecture hall applies: if one person asks a question, dozens of others had the same question but didn't raise their hand.

​The key is mapping the full customer journey, not just the bottom-of-funnel purchase decision.

​A real estate agent specializing in first-time home buyers in Phoenix, Arizona, shouldn't only write about buying homes. Liron explains that potential buyers start much higher up the funnel. They're asking whether Phoenix is safe, what the school systems are like, what the HOA rules are, and what the property taxes are like.

​The agent who answers all those questions across separate pieces of content builds AI-driven authority at every stage of the journey.

Beyond content strategy, there's a technical layer that determines whether AI can even access a business's content. Liron outlines several checkpoints.

Apply a Q&A Format to Content: Liron recommends formatting your content with clear questions and direct answers. The answer should appear within the first 100 words. Each answer should be written with the target audience in mind, so when AI chunks it out, the extracted piece speaks directly to the person who asked.

​Check the Robots.txt File: Legacy settings on your website may be blocking AI crawlers without you knowing. Liron has worked with several businesses that couldn't get traction in AI recommendations, and the problem turned out to be a robots.txt file that disallowed AI access entirely.

​Review Cloudflare Settings: Cloudflare includes an AI blocker feature. Liron notes it should be off by default, but some users have found it turned on without their action. Checking this setting takes minutes and could remove a significant barrier.

​Minimize JavaScript Rendering Issues: Pages that render based on user interactions, scroll-triggered content, or dynamically loaded elements can be difficult for AI to parse. Static, straightforward HTML content is easier for AI to crawl and understand.

​Maintain Active Sitemaps: An XML sitemap is standard for machine readability, but Liron recommends also maintaining an HTML sitemap. Having both formats gives AI two entry points to discover content.

​Your pages don't need to be linked from the main navigation menu to have value. As long as the sitemap references them, AI can still crawl and index them. For WordPress users, this means content can live on a page rather than a blog post, unlinked from the main menu but still fully discoverable through the sitemap. Liron notes that several clients have published their entire newsletter archive this way, keeping the content crawlable and indexable without cluttering the site's navigation.

​Use Structured Data and Schema Markup: FAQ schemas, list schemas, and other structured data formats help AI understand content organization. All existing SEO best practices still apply. Liron emphasizes that SEO isn't dead. It simply has a different feel when the audience includes machines as well as humans.

Liron Segev is an AI strategist who helps business owners create content that gets recommended by AI. His company, Answer Content Engine, offers a free AI audit tool to assess your business’ position in AI recommendations. Follow him on YouTube, X, and LinkedIn.

#158. OpenAI doubles support for Lenfest’s AI and local news fellowships

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

With an additional $10 million in program funding, the Lenfest Institute will consider new applicants in local TV news and statewide public service journalism.

OpenAI announced on Monday that it’s doubling its support for the Lenfest Institute’s AI Collaborative and Fellowship Program. Since the program launched in October 2024, it has placed AI fellows in 11 local newsrooms across the U.S., mainly in metro newspapers like The Philadelphia Inquirer, The Baltimore Banner, and The Minnesota Star Tribune.

As the program moves forward, Lenfest plans to keep the same approach of embedding full-time engineering staff in local newsrooms for two years. In this next grant cycle, though, the program is expanding its reach beyond metro newspapers to consider fellowships for local TV news and statewide public service journalism.

“The key success factor seems to be that the fellows are hired locally, report locally, and are viewed as part of their local team, because they are,” Jim Friedlich, executive director and CEO of the Lenfest Institute, told me. “They’re not Lenfest employees, and they’re certainly not Microsoft or OpenAI employees. They’re free to work in any technology that they deem appropriate, and in every case, they were the first full-time AI employee at each news organization.”

RELATED ARTICLEThe Centre Daily Times unionizes after backlash to McClatchy’s AI toolAndrew DeckJune 10, 2026The first cohort was funded with $10 million from OpenAI and Microsoft. Each company contributed $2.5 million in cash and $2.5 million in credits that could be used for enterprise licenses, cloud storage, and tokens for generative AI products.

Microsoft began distributing its grant funds six months after OpenAI and hasn’t decided yet whether it will renew its commitment once that cycle ends in 2027. OpenAI, meanwhile, is expanding its support, contributing $10 million to the program on its own: $5 million in cash and $5 million in credits.

“Funding supports people and implementation; credits allow for experimentation and make our technology accessible,” said Tom Rubin, the chief of intellectual property and content at OpenAI. “The goal is to create lasting capability for news organizations: deeper research, stronger reporting, richer user experiences, improved workflows, and more sustainable businesses.”

When the fellowship launched in 2024, OpenAI had just closed a funding round that valued it at $157 billion. Earlier this month, The New York Times reported that the company is considering a new funding round that could value the company at $1.5 trillion ahead of its IPO.

Alongside that growth, the company is expanding its role as a funder of journalism initiatives and institutions. In July, OpenAI renewed its funding of the Product & AI Studio, a program run through The American Journalism Project (AJP) to help nonprofit local newsrooms experiment with AI. The $5 million in cash and $3 million in credits will support the more than 50 news organizations in AJP’s portfolio. They’re encouraged to build tools and infrastructure that can be used by other newsrooms.

RELATED ARTICLEThe San Francisco Standard gets $150K to build an AI-powered news appAndrew DeckFebruary 18, 2026This month, OpenAI also announced it is donating subscriptions for more than 400 enterprise-level ChatGPT accounts to students and faculty at the Medill School of Journalism at Northwestern University and the Craig Newmark Graduate School of Journalism at the City University of New York. In the announcement, OpenAI hinted at further donations to journalism schools down the line.

The Lenfest Institute fellowship is unique in that it brings full-time staffers with technical expertise into news organizations and assigns them newsroom leaders, or “executive sponsors,” to manage their work and ensure they aren’t isolated.

“You get a full-time person to follow the thread and be creative and attack problems as they come in,” said Tristan Loper, the head of national programs at Lenfest. “It’s not a part-time, or consulting, or project-based role. You live and breathe the problem…I think that leads to a lot of organic problem solving and cross-team collaboration.”

Sapna Satagopan, Newswell director of product and innovation, at Lenfest’s AI summit in Philadelphia in August. Photo courtesy of the Lenfest Institute.

At The Philadelphia Inquirer, AI engineer Kevin Hoffman has custom-built several tools during his two-year fellowship. Dewey, an AI chatbot that helps reporters dig through the newspaper’s digitized archives, has access to hundreds of thousands of articles dating back to the 1970s. The tool has been used by investigative reporters to do historical research, political reporters to verify whether public figures have flipped on policy positions, and, most recently, by crime reporters digging into an Olney neighborhood home linked to several missing persons.

While The Inquirer also experiments with models that aren’t owned by OpenAI, the fellowship credits have been important for prototyping and deploying custom-built tools, said Matt Boggie, the chief technology and product officer at The Inquirer.

“Every token costs something. Even if you’re just trying to get started and don’t know where you’re going and you’re asking open-ended questions, that’s burning money,” he said. Though Dewey was up and running quickly, The Inquirer has continued to expand its use cases, most recently by processing more than 270,000 images in its photo archive. “They’re only about five cents each, but that adds up. I would much rather do that under these credits than on my own dime.”

RELATED ARTICLEReaders turned to these local newspapers for real-time safety updates and weekend readsSophie CulpepperJuly 30, 2026As part of the fellowship, participating newsrooms join collaborative Slacks, travel to fellowship summits with training from OpenAI and Microsoft, and receive support to attend journalism conferences. After The Inquirer presented Dewey to the rest of its cohort, a fellow from The Baltimore Banner said they had been working on similar problems with archives in their own newsroom.

“Their fellow sat down with Kevin, walked through the code, and made some adjustments to their particular setup,” said Boggie. The Banner has since launched its own version of the tool.

A fellow from Chicago Public Media, which owns WBEZ Chicago and the Chicago Sun-Times, also customized a version of Dewey to interact with radio transcripts. Dewey is open-source, and the underlying code is available on GitHub to newsrooms outside the program as well.

Moving into the second iteration of the fellowship, Lenfest wants to emphasize the collaborative parts of the program further, prioritizing reusable AI tools that can be easily copied and customized for other news organizations.

As part of that push, Lenfest has brought on Sonali Verma, who leads INMA’s Newsroom Innovation Initiative and previously worked on Sophi, an AI-powered paywall product first built in-house at Canada’s Globe and Mail. This week, Lenfest is launching a new newsletter called Context Window, written by Verma, that will share what fellows have learned and link to specific tools and GitHub resources. It’s “all with an eye toward how this can be adopted” by other newsrooms, Loper said.

Chase Davis, formerly at The Minnesota Star Tribune’s AI Lab, where he oversaw the Lenfest fellowship, has also come on board as the program’s technical lead. Among other responsibilities, he’ll help newsrooms productize any AI-powered tools they develop.

Lenfest is encouraging all 11 of the current participating newsrooms to reapply for the next grant cycle, but Friedlich said half, at most, will be reaccepted, leaving room for more news organizations to join.

RELATED ARTICLEThe Local aims to reinvent TV news in four states, and beyondCorey HutchinsMay 5, 2025With this next cohort, Friedlich says he’s interested in exploring how AI can support the business of local TV news. He also sees promise in using AI to support regional public service journalism, such as accountability reporting on state legislatures.

OpenAI’s renewal comes as the U.S. local news industry continues to contract, in part because of traffic declines related to AI search. This month McClatchy laid off more than 90 unionized workers across 70 publications. USA Today Co. also made major cuts, referencing AI search–related traffic declines. Against this backdrop, many local newspapers are turning to AI to assist with story drafting, while AI agent–led news publications with little to no human editorial oversight continue to pop up across the country.

Lenfest says it will not invest in newsrooms that plan to use AI primarily to displace human reporting and writing.

“We believe really strongly that there should be a human in the lead, not just a human in the loop — [someone who] is leading the use of AI and its personalization and its adaptations, rather than double-checking the work when it’s about to go out,” said Friedlich. “That may sound old-fashioned, but we think it’s really important.”

This story has been updated to correct Chase Davis’s role at The Minnesota Star Tribune.

Annalisa Quinn’s story published Tuesday in The Boston Globe Magazine — “A Western Mass. lesbian bar required KN-95 masks. When it changed the rules, all hell broke loose” — is, in this reporter’s opinion, a perfect piece.

That’s in part because it is written in such a neutral register, containing paragraphs like:

Three housemates in their mid-20s opened it together, hoping to fill the void left by two local queer bars that had shuttered. One of the trio, Asa Rosario, a drag performer who uses it/its pronouns, envisioned a venue where it and its friends could perform.

But by the time of Last Ditch’s monthly community meeting on September 11, only one of the original founders, Matellian, is still involved. The two others stepped back from the daily operation months before, Matellian says, citing various pressures and health issues. One had enrolled in clown school.

Moreover, the Zoom attendees speculate that the mediator’s licensed status makes her a mandated reporter — an agent of the state, akin to police. One person going by “Moss” asks if the mediator could have them hospitalized against their will, adding that her presence is “wildly unsafe.”

Nonetheless, the Globe would rather be in this position than not. “Great article!” one commenter wrote. “It reads almost like a visit to another planet, which it kind of is.” Conveniently, that other planet is in driving distance of Globe headquarters.

#160. When disaster strikes, newsrooms scramble. A new website aims to help tame the chaos.

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Emergency Mode for News has checklists and other tools to help journalists respond to disasters before, during, and after they happen.

On the day Hurricane Helene hit Western North Carolina in September 2024, Laura Lee was thousands of miles away on vacation in Peru.

“I feel guilty about not being on the ground with everybody when it actually went down, but it kind of was a blessing in disguise,” Lee, who was the news director of Asheville-based Blue Ridge Public Radio (BPR) at the time, said. “I was in a place that had stable internet, so I could make calls and run point on some things that I don’t know I would have been able to do otherwise.”

Lee had created an emergency plan for the station long before the storm hit, but it was primarily geared around mass shootings. Helene, however, was an all-encompassing disaster: alongside more than 230 deaths and billions of dollars’ worth of physical damage, it knocked out water, power, and cellular services, in some places for weeks. When Lee made it back to Asheville with a car full of supplies she’d picked up in Charlotte, she had to put together a plan on the fly: The station would move to 12-hour coverage, rather than its usual cadence of two live shifts a day, and they’d air every single one of the county’s twice-daily updates, followed by a recap and debrief by the station’s reporters.

But first, she had to take care of some of the station’s most basic needs.

“One of my first tasks was just cleaning out the toilets and setting up a camp toilet, because we didn’t have running water,” Lee, who’s now the editorial director of the nonprofit news organization NC Local, told me. “When we think about emergency planning, sometimes we think just about the news and how we’re going to get the information out, which is obviously a huge part of it. But there’s also just this basic hierarchy of needs: People have to have a place to go to the bathroom. They have to have water. They have to have food. I didn’t worry if my reporters were fed on a daily basis prior to [Hurricane Helene].”

For the most part, Lee and her colleagues had to figure out how to respond to and cover the storm on their own. But a new service, built out of the lessons Lee and other editors around the country learned from covering disasters themselves, aims to change that. It’s called Emergency Mode for News.

RELATED ARTICLEInside Grist’s new toolkit for navigating disastersNeel DhaneshaJuly 15, 2025“Having the time or the funding to create emergency plans for your newsroom is a luxury,” said Jessica Morrison, co-director of OpenNews, one of the three organizations — along with NC Local and Newspack — behind the initiative, which was started using a three-year, $1.2 million grant from Press Forward. That’s why Emergency Mode’s website has pre-made checklists for various kinds of extreme weather disasters, like hurricanes, wildfires, or extreme heat, written by journalists who have experience covering those types of disasters. The website also links to Grist’s disaster toolkit and has a module to help create an “action pack” with resources that change depending on whether the journalists coming to the site are preparing for a threat ahead of time, in the midst of an emergency, or recovering from a disaster.

“This isn’t about teaching you how to cover breaking news or emergencies or disasters,” Morrison said. “We know that journalists know how to do that. It’s about shoring up your operations.”

When Hurricane Helene knocked out cell service in Western North Carolina, Lee and her colleagues heard from audience members who couldn’t load the BPR website because cell service was too spotty. So they worked with Newspack and NC Local to create a text-only, low-data version of the website, which could be loaded quickly even when cell signal was scarce. (As Josh wrote in October of that year, NPR enabled a similar feature for its local stations as Hurricane Milton bore down on Florida.) Newspack used its experience with Helene to create a WordPress-based “lite-site” plugin that newsrooms could easily incorporate into their own websites, and is in the process of developing a second plugin to quickly enable liveblogging so journalists can post updates to developing stories as they come in.

Open News is also distributing $30,000 in microgrants to help newsrooms pay for things like specialized training, and hosting workshops to bring together journalists from across multiple newsrooms to share knowledge and create a sort of Emergency Mode community. “There’s a lot of knowledge in the field already, and we’re hoping to bring it together,” Morrison said. “A lot of what we have found in this first year was that what people actually wanted to do was just talk to each other about their experiences.”

RELATED ARTICLEWith Hurricane Milton looming, NPR stations got a lower-bandwidth way to reach residentsJoshua BentonOctober 10, 2024In the aftermath of Hurricane Helene, Lee received emails from editors around the country offering help and support, including one from an editor in Lahaina, Hawaii, which had dealt with devastating wildfires in 2023, who wrote to say that “even if it feels like this is endless, it’s not,” she told me. Another editor helped set up a network of freelancers who helped triage Lee’s inbox, which was filling up with press requests from national outlets, updates from her newsroom, and messages from BPR’s audience.

“There’s so much that you can draw from what other people have experienced,” Lee said. “There’s no reason to have people reinventing the wheel every single time and feeling isolated while doing so.”

Emergency Mode also offers a variety of mental health resources, which Lee learned firsthand are essential during and after a disaster. “Our Slack just turned into a channel of horrors,” Lee told me. She instituted a practice of checking in with her reporters about what they’d do to help their mental health each day. “In those scenarios your brain is cooked,” Lee said. “You’ve been riding adrenaline, and you’re sleeping two or three hours a night, and you’re just adapting as best as you can.”

Disasters can take many forms, but for now Emergency Mode is focused on extreme weather and climate disasters. It’s on its second year of the Press Forward grant; the first year was spent building the resources that went on the site, including reaching out to contributors to write the checklists, and the second year, which is ongoing, will be focused on getting feedback from newsrooms and adjusting the site accordingly. (Morrison told me that one of the early points of feedback from newsrooms was that they needed the information to be broken up into smaller chunks than currently exist.) Those conversations will help shape what Emergency Mode becomes in its third year, and if it might exist beyond that.

“What is emergency preparedness for?” Morrison asked. “It’s to reduce the number of decisions that you need to make during a disaster. Journalism is hard. People are experiencing burnout, and to add to that, you’re a person living through an emergency or a disaster that you’re also covering. Is there something that we could do to make emergency preparedness a shared infrastructure effort for newsrooms? That’s the main project.”

#161. David Ellison will get control of CNN after all (and don’t pretend an “independent editorial board” will mean otherwise)

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

In exchange for dropping their lawsuit against Paramount’s acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, state AGs have negotiated “independent” oversight of CNN. You shouldn’t expect much oversight.

Eighteen months ago, David Ellison was mostly known as an ATM for Hollywood producers seeking to pencil out budgets for quarter-zip dadcore flicks like Jack Ryan: Shadow Recruit, Jack Reacher: Never Go Back, and Transformers: Rise of the Beasts. But now, thanks to a timely reallocation of his father’s money, he’s set to be one of the biggest news media moguls in American history. Having already taken control of CBS News — with little to show for it audience-wise but plenty ideologically — he now seems clear to add CNN to his roster of outlets.

His acquisition, through Paramount, of Warner Bros. Discovery has been held up by a lawsuit filed by blue-state attorneys general over antitrust questions. One reported goal of the AGs was to have Ellison sell CNN in order to close the deal, though California’s Rob Bonta labeled that speculation. But this morning, those AGs appear to have thrown in the towel. Here are Benjamin Mullin, David McCabe, Shawn Hubler, and Laurel Rosenhall at The New York Times:

Paramount reached an agreement on Monday to resolve an antitrust lawsuit delaying its $111 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, according to four people familiar with the negotiations, eliminating the last significant barrier to the creation of an entertainment and media colossus.

A group of states, led by California’s attorney general, Rob Bonta, a Democrat, sued Paramount in July, arguing that an acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery would concentrate too much power over cable TV and blockbuster films under one company.

After weeks of on-again-off-again negotiations, Paramount and the states agreed to a number of concessions to complete the deal, according to the people, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss details not yet made public. The entertainment giant has agreed to establish a board of journalists to ensure the editorial independence of CNN and CBS News and committed to distributing 30 movies in theaters every year. The company also pledged to spend an additional $1.5 billion on film production over the next five years.

So while another major national news outlet will be under the control of a major Donald Trump ally…at least there’ll be “a board of journalists to ensure [its] editorial independence”! (That this is all happening while the president Ellison supports bans all CNN reporters from the White House adds a tragicomic character to it all.)

If this particular move sounds familiar, it’s because it’s been a part of past news company acquisitions where concerns about antitrust or editorial control end up being downshifted into similar (and mostly toothless) “boards.” Their effectiveness has been, to be generous, extremely limited. Here are two of the most prominent examples — both involving Rupert Murdoch, and neither offering much reason for “independence” optimism.

When Murdoch wanted to purchase The Times of London and The Sunday Times in 1981, he faced skepticism from both newspapers’ editors. In order to avoid an inquiry by the British antitrust authority, he agreed to empower a set of “Independent National Directors” who would have to sign off on the firing or hiring of a top editor, and who would also resolve any major disputes between Murdoch and editors.

How did it work? Here’s how the legendary editor Harold Evans put it in his 1983 book Good Times, Bad Times:

[Murdoch had] guaranteed that the editors would have control of the political policy of their newspapers; that they would have freedom within fixed annual budgets; that the editors would not be subject to instruction from either the proprietor or management on the selection and balance of news and opinion; that instructions to journalists would be given only by their editor; and that any future sale of the titles would require the agreement of a majority of the independent national directors. In my year as editor of The Times, Murdoch broke all these guarantees. He put his point of view very simply to the home editor of The Times, Fred Emery, when he summoned him from holiday on 4 March to his office shortly before asking for my resignation: ‘I give instructions to my editors all round the world, why shouldn’t I in London?’ He was reminded of the undertakings to the Secretary of State [for Trade, John Biffen]. ‘They’re not worth the paper they’re written on,’ Murdoch replied.

Murdoch is right. The guarantees are not worth the paper they are written on — unless the proprietor shares the spirit of them. If he does, they are merely ornamental; if he does not, they are unworkable. There is no point in trying to make them stronger. Internal freedom cannot be acquired by external rules, and at Times Newspapers and The Observer the State has gone as far as it ought in attempting to lay down rules for the conduct of a private enterprise. The true role for the State must be to administer the anti-trust laws honestly and effectively. Once an acquisition has been agreed, it is too late for petty bureaucracy. There is justification for firmness here, since there is a universal recognition that monopoly power represents a danger, in the words of the Fair Trading Act, to ‘the accurate reporting of news and the free expression of opinion’…

Editorial guarantees are a paltry defence and they may be delusive as well. At Times Newspapers their invention enabled an air of respectability to be given to an unnecessary and hazardous extension of monopoly power, and they suggest that The Times’s tradition has been maintained when behind the fake ivy it can so easily be plundered. The theory of the constitution is that the independent national directors would not permit this to happen. As one of the architects of the constitution, I believed this too. I found in reality that the national directors are incapable of monitoring the daily turmoil of a newspaper. This has nothing to do with their theoretical powers, and increasing or entrenching them would make no difference.

The Tory MP Woodrow Wyatt would later write about how he’d “had all the rules bent for” Murdoch in order to get his Times acquisition approved: “Through Margaret I got it arranged that the deal didn’t go to the Monopolies Commission which almost certainly would have blocked it.”

Evans lasted only a year under Murdoch’s ownership. A longer run was had by the conservative editor Andrew Neil, who edited The Sunday Times from 1983 to 1994. Giving parliamentary testimony in 2007, Neil said that the “independence” offered by these outside board members was not about real authority — it was about smoothing the path of an important news outlet into regime-friendly hands:

First of all, let us just remind ourselves. It was a conceit invented by John Biffen and the Thatcher Government to allow Mr. Murdoch to take over these papers in the first place, and it was put in place for that reason. It was not really put in place to protect the independence of the editors.

Then you look at the kind of people who became these trustees, and I do not know who they are today, but in my time they were really just a bunch of establishment worthies and Murdoch policemen and they had no real role. There was one exception which was Alistair Burnet who really did know and helped me on one occasion. When I rather foolishly, although the story was entirely accurate, published the story, “Queen dismayed by uncaring Thatcher,” which meant I had managed to pick a fight with both the Prime Minister and the Monarch in one day, the trustees then came into action. The trustees wanted my resignation and they petitioned Murdoch to get rid of me, and it was Alistair Burnett that dug his heels in and said, “Excuse me, the story’s true and it is not our job to get the resignation of the Editor, it is our job to protect the Editor,” so that was my only experience of them.

Even if they had a more worthwhile role to play, as I say, in reality, in practice, no matter how good the trustees are or how supportive, if you and the proprietor have fallen out of love, your position is untenable over time.

(That Sunday Times story may be familiar to fans of “The Crown.”)

Neil — arguably the most prominent conservative British journalist of the past half-century, and thus no fellow traveler of the left-wing Guardian — contrasted its control by the Scott Trust with the kabuki theater of an “independent board”:

The Scott Trust is a perfectly legitimate way of running a newspaper and, as you can see from the success of The Guardian and its on-line success globally, it works. That works. It is entirely different from the strong proprietor who controls the shares and the business of that company appointing a couple of trustees as a fig-leaf. 2007: Murdoch acquires The Wall Street Journal In 2007, Murdoch made an unsolicited offer to the Bancroft family to acquire Dow Jones and its flagship newspaper, The Wall Street Journal. Several family members were concerned about what Murdoch ownership might do to the newspaper’s quality, and as part of the eventual sale, Murdoch agreed to the appointment of a “Dow Jones Special Committee” that would — much like its London predecessor — have final say over the hiring and firing of top editors, as well as changes that could be construed as forcing an editor out. (Things like “material reduction in compensation, relocation of principal place of employment, material change in duties or responsibilities…changes to the authority, reporting relationship and consultation rights,” and such.) With that guarantee in place, enough hesitant Bancrofts were convinced to sell — though not everyone was on board. “Although I’m convinced that News Corp. offer is very generous in financial terms,” Dow Jones director Dieter von Holtzbrinck wrote in his resignation letter, “I’m very worried that Dow Jones unique journalistic values will long-term strongly suffer after the proposed sale…I do not believe that the Special Committee can finally prevent Mr. Murdoch from doing what he wants to do, from acting his way.” Barely four months after the transaction closed, he was proved right. Murdoch managed a nifty end run around the “special committee” and ousted the newsroom’s top editor, Marcus Brauchli. Murdoch didn’t fire Brauchli. Instead, he layered over him, naming former Times of London editor Robert Thomson as publisher — but giving him direct oversight of the newsroom rather than the position’s usual business-side responsibilities. Brauchli, frozen out of major decisions in the newsroom he allegedly led, sent a note to staff saying he had “come to believe the new owners should have a managing editor of their choosing.” Brauchli was well compensated with a nice “consulting” gig for Dow Jones. Because Brauchli had resigned rather than be fired, the approval of the “special committee” was not required. Murdoch informed its members as a fait accompli, telling one “I have no doubt that the New York Times will make trouble with it for a day or two, but I’m not too bothered by it.” The committee later issued a statement in which members “expressed the view that learning of the Brauchli matter after the fact failed to meet the letter and the spirit of the agreement.” But alas, the committee “decided there was no practical way to ‘unresign’ Brauchli and start the process over.” Sarah Ellison1, in her book on the Murdoch takeover of the Journal, described the special committee as “an artificial set of rules he would inevitably circumvent,” which seems dead on. Right now, we don’t know much about what a CNN (or CBS News) “independent editorial board” will look like. Bloomberg reports that it “will be composed only of journalists, with no executives or shareholders allowed to join” and that “the board will be required to have political balance.” The deal does not appear to have any sort of hard enforcement mechanism built in for any violations of the “the letter and the spirit” of the editorial independence agreement. (By contrast, it does include a $30 million penalty for each film Paramount promises to release to theaters but doesn’t.) But let’s be blunt. No matter how well-intentioned the members of these committees may be, if David Ellison wants to get around them, he will. It’s an artificial set of rules that a billionaire owner will inevitably circumvent. These “independent” boards are PR gestures, not vehicles for editorial protection. As Andrew Neil said, they are tools to get a controversial deal across the finish line. And at that, they seem to have succeeded once again. Photo of Paramount Studios by Romain Malaunay. Sarah Ellison, the longtime Wall Street Journal, Washington Post, and Vanity Fair reporter, is no relation to David Ellison. Neither is Minnesota attorney general Keith Ellison, who was among the final holdouts for this Paramount settlement. Lots of Ellisons everywhere. [↩]

#162. “An astonishing theft of unprecedented proportions”: Court records show what Microsoft and OpenAI actually thought about AI training

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Would you call large language models training on an internet’s worth of content “an astonishing theft of unprecedented proportions”? Or perhaps you prefer the “largest theft of labor in human history”?

Take your pick because those two options — and many more — appear in a newly unredacted court filing in the ongoing New York Times v. OpenAI/Microsoft case. The motion was filed by a group of news publishers led by The New York Times. The most inflammatory language was not written by the Times’ lawyers, however, but by OpenAI’s and Microsoft’s own executives.

“Millions of people around the world will soon consider large models ‘hoovering up’ all their work to be an astonishing theft of unprecedented proportions,” wrote Brent Hecht, Microsoft’s director of applied science, in the unearthed documents. “Almost no one intended for content they created to be used in this fashion, nor are they compensated for its use,” he wrote

In an emailed statement, a Microsoft spokesperson said Hecht’s comments “reflect one employee’s individual perspective, are not a legal analysis, and do not represent the company’s views.”

AI companies have publicly argued that their training falls under the legal doctrine of fair use. Publishers, however, have long warned that the AI companies’ plan to take content without compensation will severely undermine the news industry whose work trains those models. It appears at least some within the AI industry agree with the assessment.

Internal Microsoft communications identified the “real risk” that generative AI could “significantly disrupt the employment of the very people who generated the data on which the foundation model was trained.” A separate policy document put it like this: “LLMs are a product that destroys its supply chain.”

The current approach has created a “doom loop,” according to another internal Microsoft document.

“Our AI content strategy has started a ‘doom loop’ that will hurt the performance of our models and the entire web at the same time,” the document reads. “It is highly unusual that an end-product threatens the economic foundations of its essential suppliers, but that is the situation we have created for our LLM business with respect to its ‘content supply chain.’”

Elsewhere, Nick Turley, OpenAI’s head of ChatGPT, acknowledged that publishers face an “existential threat” from OpenAI’s products. The AI tools “are largely substitutive, period” and “will get more and more substitutive as they get better.”

OpenAI president and co-founder Greg Brockman told his colleagues: “[W]e are excellent at news btw. every time i do any generative stuff on NYT it seems to predict the next sentence pretty well.” Brockman also wrote that OpenAI’s model “seems to be particularly good at predicting text of news articles like whenever i have it complete in the middle of a sentence in a NYT article, it seems to complete the sentence on point.”

The filing also shows that OpenAI employees went out of their way to evade news paywalls to scrape websites. (When told about “a hack to get around nytimes paywall,” Brockman responded “ah nice.”)

Previously, these statements were heavily redacted or under seal. Some portions remain sealed.

“Easy to see why the AI companies had so many redactions,” wrote Digital Content Next CEO Jason Kint, who first shared the unredacted documents on X. “Their own people wrote the lede for NYT.”
